{{flu}}

The '''2009 swine flu pandemic''', caused by the [[influenza A virus subtype H1N1|H1N1/swine flu/influenza virus]] and declared by the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) from June 2009 to August 2010, was the third recent flu [[pandemic]] involving the H1N1 virus (the first being the 1918–1920 [[Spanish flu]] pandemic and the second being the [[1977 Russian flu]]).<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |date=April 1999 |title=Influenza Pandemic Plan. The Role of WHO and Guidelines for National and Regional Planning |url=https://www.who.int/csr/resources/publications/influenza/whocdscsredc991.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203084733/https://www.who.int/csr/resources/publications/influenza/whocdscsredc991.pdf |archive-date=3 December 2020 |publisher=World Health Organization |pages=38, 41}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{cite journal |vauthors=Michaelis M, Doerr HW, Cinatl J |date=August 2009 |title=Novel swine-origin influenza A virus in humans: another pandemic knocking at the door |journal=Medical Microbiology and Immunology |volume=198 |issue=3 |pages=175–83 |doi=10.1007/s00430-009-0118-5 |pmid=19543913 |s2cid=20496301 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The first identified human case was in [[La Gloria, Veracruz|La Gloria]], Mexico, a rural town in Veracruz.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="NYT6-23" /> The virus appeared to be a new strain of H1N1 that resulted from a previous triple [[reassortment]] of bird, swine, and human flu viruses which further combined with a Eurasian pig flu virus,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Trifonov V, Khiabanian H, Rabadan R |s2cid=205105276 |title=Geographic dependence, surveillance, and origins of the 2009 influenza A (H1N1) virus |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=361 |issue=2 |pages=115–19 |date=July 2009 |pmid=19474418 |doi=10.1056/NEJMp0904572 |doi-access=free}}</ref> leading to the term "[[swine flu]]".<ref>{{Cite news |vauthors=Hellerman C |url=http://www.cnn.com/2009/HEALTH/06/11/swine.flu.who/ |title=Swine flu 'not stoppable,' World Health Organization says |publisher=CNN |date=11 June 2009 |access-date=3 April 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307163916/http://www.cnn.com/2009/HEALTH/06/11/swine.flu.who/ |archive-date=7 March 2010}}</ref>

Unlike most strains of influenza, the pandemic H1N1/09 virus did not disproportionately infect adults older than 60&nbsp;years; this was an unusual and characteristic feature of the H1N1 pandemic.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Bautista E, Chotpitayasunondh T, Gao Z, Harper SA, Shaw M, Uyeki TM, Zaki SR, Hayden FG, Hui DS, Kettner JD, Kumar A, Lim M, Shindo N, Penn C, Nicholson KG |display-authors=6 |title=Clinical aspects of pandemic 2009 influenza A (H1N1) virus infection |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=362 |issue=18 |pages=1708–19 |date=May 2010 |pmid=20445182 |doi=10.1056/NEJMra1000449 |hdl=2381/15212 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Even in the case of previously healthy people, a small percentage develop [[pneumonia]] or [[acute respiratory distress syndrome]] (ARDS). This manifests itself as increased breathing difficulty and typically occurs three to six days after the initial onset of flu symptoms.<ref name="WHObriefingnoteOct16">{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_clinical_features_20091016/en/ |title=Clinical features of severe cases of pandemic influenza |date=16 October 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=25 October 2009 |location=Geneva, [[Switzerland|CH]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091025105555/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_clinical_features_20091016/en/ |archive-date=25 October 2009}}</ref><ref name="RongGongLinNov21">{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-me-flu-guidelines21-2009nov21,0,2717012.story |title=When to take a sick child to the ER |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |vauthors=Lin II RG |date=21 November 2009 |access-date=4 January 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091125135818/http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-me-flu-guidelines21-2009nov21%2C0%2C2717012.story |archive-date=25 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The pneumonia caused by the flu can be either direct [[viral pneumonia]] or a secondary [[bacterial pneumonia]]. A November 2009 ''[[New England Journal of Medicine]]'' article recommended that flu patients whose [[chest X-ray]] indicates pneumonia receive both [[antiviral]]s and [[antibiotic]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Jain S, Kamimoto L, Bramley AM, Schmitz AM, Benoit SR, Louie J, Sugerman DE, Druckenmiller JK, Ritger KA, Chugh R, Jasuja S, Deutscher M, Chen S, Walker JD, Duchin JS, Lett S, Soliva S, Wells EV, Swerdlow D, Uyeki TM, Fiore AE, Olsen SJ, Fry AM, Bridges CB, Finelli L |display-authors=6 |title=Hospitalized patients with 2009 H1N1 influenza in the United States, April–June 2009 |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=361 |issue=20 |pages=1935–44 |date=November 2009 |pmid=19815859 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa0906695}} This study involved a total of 272 patients, which represents approximately 25% of US hospitalized patients with lab-confirmed H1N1 whose cases were reported to the US [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) from 1{{nbsp}}May to 9{{nbsp}}June 2009. The study found that "the only variable that was significantly associated with a positive outcome was the receipt of antiviral drugs within two days after the onset of illness" [Outcomes section, 2nd paragraph] and also that "only 73% of patients with radiographic evidence of pneumonia received antiviral drugs, whereas 97% received antibiotics." [Discussion section, 8th paragraph]. It is recommended that such patients receive both.</ref> In particular, it is a warning sign if a child seems to be getting better and then relapses with high fever, as this relapse may be bacterial pneumonia.<ref name="DeniseGradySept3" />

Some studies estimated that the real number of cases including asymptomatic and mild cases could be 700 million to 1.4 billion people—or 11% to 21% of the global population of 6.8 billion at the time.<ref name="cases">{{cite web |date=8 August 2011 |title=Study puts global 2009 H1N1 infection rate at 11% to 21% |url=http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2011/08/study-puts-global-2009-h1n1-infection-rate-11-21 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125151837/https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2011/08/study-puts-global-2009-h1n1-infection-rate-11-21 |archive-date=25 November 2020 |access-date=25 January 2020 |publisher=Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy |vauthors=Roos R}}</ref> The lower value of 700 million is more than the 500 million people estimated to have been infected by the Spanish flu pandemic.<ref name="age-specific cumulative incidence">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kelly H, Peck HA, Laurie KL, Wu P, Nishiura H, Cowling BJ |date=5 August 2011 |title=The age-specific cumulative incidence of infection with pandemic influenza H1N1 2009 was similar in various countries prior to vaccination |journal=PLOS One |volume=6 |issue=8 |article-number=e21828 |bibcode=2011PLoSO...621828K |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0021828 |pmc=3151238 |pmid=21850217 |doi-access=free}}</ref> However, the Spanish flu infected approximately a third of the world population at the time, a much higher proportion.<ref name="brutal">{{cite web |date=2 April 2020 |title=The 1918 Flu Pandemic Was Brutal, Killing More Than 50 Million People Worldwide |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/04/02/826358104/the-1918-flu-pandemic-was-brutal-killing-as-many-as-100-million-people-worldwide |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119213925/https://www.npr.org/2020/04/02/826358104/the-1918-flu-pandemic-was-brutal-killing-as-many-as-100-million-people-worldwide |archive-date=19 January 2021 |access-date=24 July 2020 |publisher=NPR |vauthors=Hagemann H}}</ref>

The number of lab-confirmed deaths reported to the WHO is 18,449<ref name="WHO100" /> and is widely considered a gross underestimate.<ref>{{Cite web |publisher=World Health Organization |title=Summary of WHO Technical Consultation: H1N1pdm Mortality Estimates, 25-26 October 2011 |url=https://www.who.int/influenza/publications/surveillance_monitoring/H1N1pdmMortalityEstimates_WHOconsultation.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211102220723/https://www.who.int/influenza/publications/surveillance_monitoring/H1N1pdmMortalityEstimates_WHOconsultation.pdf |archive-date=2 November 2021 |access-date=1 November 2021}}</ref> The WHO collaborated with the US [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) and the Netherlands Institute for Health Services Research (NIVEL) to produce two independent estimates of the influenza deaths that occurred during the global pandemic using two distinct methodologies. The 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic is estimated to have actually caused about 284,000 (range from 150,000 to 575,000) excess deaths by the WHO-USCDC study and 148,000–249,000 excess respiratory deaths by the WHO-NIVEL study.<ref name=CDCDeathtolls>{{cite web |date=25 June 2012 |title=First Global Estimates of 2009 H1N1 Pandemic Mortality Released by CDC-Led Collaboration |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/spotlights/pandemic-global-estimates.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200303012120/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/spotlights/pandemic-global-estimates.htm |archive-date=3 March 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020 |website=[[cdc.gov]] |ref=CDCDeathtollsNov2019}}</ref><ref name="mortality estimate worldwide">{{cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Simonsen L, Spreeuwenberg P, Lustig R, Taylor RJ, Fleming DM, Kroneman M, Van Kerkhove MD, Mounts AW, Paget WJ |date=November 2013 |title=Global mortality estimates for the 2009 Influenza Pandemic from the GLaMOR project: a modeling study |journal=PLOS Medicine |volume=10 |issue=11 |article-number=e1001558 |doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1001558 |pmc=3841239 |pmid=24302890 |doi-access=free}}</ref> A study done in September 2010 showed that the risk of serious illness resulting from the 2009 H1N1 flu was no higher than that of the yearly [[Flu season|seasonal flu]].<ref>{{cite web |title=H1N1 Swine Flu No Worse Than Seasonal Flu |url=https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/news/20100907/h1n1-swine-flu-no-worse-than-seasonal-flu |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201017085947/https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/news/20100907/h1n1-swine-flu-no-worse-than-seasonal-flu |archive-date=17 October 2020 |access-date=13 March 2020 |website=WebMD |vauthors=DeNoon DJ}}</ref> For comparison, the WHO estimates that 250,000 to 500,000 people die of seasonal flu annually.<ref name="death toll estimate">{{cite web |date=27 June 2012 |title=CDC estimate of global H1N1 pandemic deaths: 284,000 |url=http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2012/06/cdc-estimate-global-h1n1-pandemic-deaths-284000 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919203235/https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2012/06/cdc-estimate-global-h1n1-pandemic-deaths-284000 |archive-date=19 September 2020 |access-date=23 March 2020 |website=CIDRAP |vauthors=Roos R}}</ref> However, the H1N1 influenza epidemic in 2009 resulted in a large increase in the number of new cases of [[narcolepsy]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Narcolepsy Fact Sheet |url=https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/narcolepsy |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160727232102/http://www.ninds.nih.gov/disorders/narcolepsy/detail_narcolepsy.htm |archive-date=27 July 2016 |access-date=23 September 2020 |website=Liaison National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke}}</ref>

==Name==

{{further|Pandemic H1N1/09 virus#Nomenclature}}

The [[World Health Organization]] uses the term "(H1N1) 2009 pandemic" when referring to the event, and officially adopted the name "A(H1N1)pdm09" for the virus in 2010, after the conclusion of the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/influenza/gisrs_laboratory/terminology_ah1n1pdm09/en/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120505042135/http://www.who.int/influenza/gisrs_laboratory/terminology_ah1n1pdm09/en/ |archive-date=5 May 2012 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=31 March 2020 |title=Standardization of terminology of the pandemic A(H1N1)2009 virus}}</ref>

Controversy arose early on regarding the wide assortment of terms used by journalists, academics,
and officials. Labels like "H1N1 flu", "Swine flu", "Mexican flu", and variations thereof were typical. Criticism centered on how these names may confuse or mislead the public. It was argued that the names were [[Jargon|overly technical]] (e.g. "H1N1"), incorrectly implying that the disease is caused by contact with [[pigs]] or pig products, or provoking stigmatization against certain communities (e.g. "Mexican"). Some academics of the time asserted there is nothing wrong with such names,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=de Lamballerie X, Gould EA |title=With reference to Mexican flu |journal=Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses |volume=3 |issue=5 |page=203 |date=September 2009 |pmid=21462392 |pmc=4941550 |doi=10.1111/j.1750-2659.2009.00097.x}}</ref> while research published years later (in 2013) concluded that Mexican Americans and Latino Americans had indeed been stigmatized due to the frequent use of the term "Mexican flu" in the news media.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=McCauley M, Minsky S, Viswanath K |title=The H1N1 pandemic: media frames, stigmatization and coping |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=13 |article-number=1116 |date=December 2013 |pmid=24299568 |pmc=3907032 |doi=10.1186/1471-2458-13-1116 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Official entities adopted terms with varying consistency over the course of the pandemic. The [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] used names like "novel influenza A (H1N1)" or "2009 H1N1 flu".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance/cruiseships.htm |title=Interim Novel Influenza A (H1N1) Guidance for Cruise Ships |date=5 August 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=30 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091001112752/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance/cruiseships.htm |archive-date=1 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Netherlands National Institute for Public Health and the Environment]] used the term "Pig Flu" early on. Officials in Taiwan suggested use of the names "H1N1 flu" or "new flu".<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.chinapost.com.tw/health/infectious-diseases/2009/04/29/206057/p2/Renamed-swine.htm |title=Renamed swine flu certain to hit Taiwan |date=28 April 2009 |work=The China Post |location=Taiwan (ROC) |access-date=26 September 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163957/http://www.chinapost.com.tw/health/infectious-diseases/2009/04/29/206057/p2/Renamed-swine.htm |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> The [[World Organisation for Animal Health]], an [[Intergovernmental organization|IGO]] based in Europe, proposed the name "North American influenza".<ref name="NYT 2009-04-28">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/29/world/asia/29swine.html |title=The naming of swine flu, a curious matter |vauthors=Bradsher K |date=28 April 2009 |work=The New York Times |access-date=29 April 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110204092042/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/29/world/asia/29swine.html |archive-date=4 February 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref> The [[European Commission]] adopted the term "novel flu virus". Officials in Israel and South Korea briefly considered adoption of the name "Mexican virus" due to concern about the use of the word "swine".<ref name="mexflu">{{Cite news |url=http://www.morungexpress.com/analysis/27870.html |title=Swine Flu: A pandemic |vauthors=Kikon CS |work=The Morung Express |access-date=28 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714120650/http://www.morungexpress.com/analysis/27870.html |archive-date=14 July 2011}}</ref> In Israel, objections stemmed from sensitivity to [[Religious restrictions on the consumption of pork|religious restrictions on eating pork]] in the Jewish and Muslim populations,<ref>{{cite news |title=What's in a name? Governments debate 'swine flu' versus 'Mexican' flu |vauthors=Pilkington E |date=28 April 2009 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/apr/28/mexican-swine-flu-pork-name |access-date=10 December 2016 |archive-date=1 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090501104953/http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2009/apr/28/mexican-swine-flu-pork-name |url-status=live}}</ref> in South Korea, concerns were influenced by the importance of [[pork]] and [[domestic pig]]s.

As terminology changed to deal with these and other such issues, further criticism was made that the situation was unnecessarily confusing. For example, the news department at the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' produced an article with the humorous title "Swine Flu Names Evolving Faster Than Swine Flu Itself".<ref>{{cite news |title=Swine Flu Names Evolving Faster Than Swine Flu Itself |vauthors=Enserink M |date=8 May 2009 |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/swine-flu-names-evolving-faster-swine-flu-itself |publisher=[[Science (magazine)|Science]] |access-date=30 June 2022 |archive-date=25 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220425153811/https://www.science.org/content/article/swine-flu-names-evolving-faster-swine-flu-itself |url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==

Analysis of the genetic divergence of the virus in samples from different cases indicated that the virus jumped to humans in 2008, probably after June, and not later than the end of November,<ref name=NsFirstJumped>{{cite journal |vauthors=MacKenzie D |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg20227073.500-swine-flu-can-science-save-us-from-the-second-wave.html |title=Swine flu: Can science save us from the second wave? |journal=[[New Scientist]] |date=9 May 2009 |issue=2707 |pages=4–5 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090509093515/http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg20227073.500-swine-flu-can-science-save-us-from-the-second-wave.html |archive-date=9 May 2009 |doi=10.1016/S0262-4079(09)61215-X |url-access=subscription}} [http://hxnxflu.blogspot.com/2009/05/can-science-save-us-from-second-wave.html Alt URL] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200425092922/http://hxnxflu.blogspot.com/2009/05/can-science-save-us-from-second-wave.html |date=25 April 2020 }}</ref> likely around September 2008.<ref name="Nature" /><ref name="circles globe" /> The research also indicated the virus had been latent in pigs for several months prior to the outbreak, suggesting a need to increase agricultural surveillance to prevent future outbreaks.<ref name=OxfordU>{{cite journal |vauthors=Smith GJ, Vijaykrishna D, Bahl J, Lycett SJ, Worobey M, Pybus OG, Ma SK, Cheung CL, Raghwani J, Bhatt S, Peiris JS, Guan Y, Rambaut A |display-authors=6 |title=Origins and evolutionary genomics of the 2009 swine-origin H1N1 influenza A epidemic |journal=Nature |volume=459 |issue=7250 |pages=1122–25 |date=June 2009 |pmid=19516283 |doi=10.1038/nature08182 |bibcode=2009Natur.459.1122S |doi-access=free |hdl=10722/59392 |hdl-access=free}}
*{{lay source |template=cite web |date=11 June 2009 |title=Swine flu origins revealed |url=http://www.ox.ac.uk/media/news_stories/2009/090611_1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130425212949/http://www.ox.ac.uk/media/news_stories/2009/090611_1.html |archive-date=25 April 2013 |publisher=University of Oxford}}</ref> In 2009, U.S. agricultural officials speculated, although emphasizing that there was no way to prove their hypothesis, that "contrary to the popular assumption that the new swine flu pandemic arose on [[intensive animal farming|factory farms]] in Mexico, [the virus] most likely emerged in pigs in Asia, but then traveled to North America in a human."<ref name="NYT6-23">{{Cite news |vauthors=McNeil Jr DG |title=In New Theory, Swine Flu Started in Asia, Not Mexico |work=The New York Times |date=23 June 2009 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/24/health/24flu.html |access-date=1 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090807164633/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/24/health/24flu.html |archive-date=7 August 2009}}</ref> However, a subsequent report<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Mena I, Nelson MI, Quezada-Monroy F, Dutta J, Cortes-Fernández R, Lara-Puente JH, Castro-Peralta F, Cunha LF, Trovão NS, Lozano-Dubernard B, Rambaut A, van Bakel H, García-Sastre A |display-authors=6 |title=Origins of the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic in swine in Mexico |journal=eLife |volume=5 |article-number=e16777 |date=June 2016 |pmid=27350259 |pmc=4957980 |doi=10.7554/eLife.16777 |doi-access=free}}</ref> by researchers at the [[Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai|Mount Sinai School of Medicine]] in 2016 found that the 2009 H1N1 virus likely originated from pigs in a very small region of central Mexico.<ref name="swine flu originated in Mexico">{{cite web |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/06/160627160935.htm |title=2009 swine flu pandemic originated in Mexico, researchers discover |publisher=Science Daily |date=27 June 2016 |access-date=18 March 2020 |archive-date=14 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200314073206/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/06/160627160935.htm |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:2009 Mexican military giving out swine flu masks.jpg|thumb|right|Mexican soldiers distributing protective masks to citizens]]
Initially called an "outbreak", widespread H1N1 infection was first recognized in the state of [[Veracruz]], Mexico, with evidence that the virus had been present for months before it was officially called an "epidemic".<ref name="NYT6-23"/> The Mexican government closed most of Mexico City's public and private facilities in an attempt to contain the spread of the virus; however, it continued to spread globally, and clinics in some areas were overwhelmed by infected people. The new virus was first isolated in late April by American and Canadian laboratories from samples taken from people with flu in Mexico, Southern California, and Texas. Soon the earliest known human case was traced to a case from 9{{nbsp}}March 2009 in a 5-year-old boy in La Gloria, Mexico, a rural town in Veracruz.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |vauthors=Lacey M |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/29/world/americas/29mexico.html |title=From Édgar, 5, Coughs Heard Round the World |date=28 April 2009 |work=The New York Times |access-date=21 February 2020 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=2 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202014813/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/29/world/americas/29mexico.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NYT6-23"/> In late April, the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) declared its first ever [[public health emergency of international concern]] (PHEIC),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090425/en/ |title=WHO – Swine influenza |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506113902/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090425/en/ |archive-date=6 May 2014}}</ref> and in June, the WHO and the U.S. CDC stopped counting cases and declared the outbreak a [[pandemic]].<ref name="MargaretChanJune11">{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_pandemic_phase6_20090611/en/index.html |title=World now at the start of 2009 influenza pandemic |vauthors=Chan M |date=11 June 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=25 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091022123810/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_pandemic_phase6_20090611/en/index.html |archive-date=22 October 2009}}</ref>
 
The H1N1 flu virus cannot be contracted by eating pork products;<ref name="fluandyou"/><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nation-and-world/la-na-pigs-flu5-2009dec05,0,6902061.story |title=Don't call it 'swine flu,' farmers implore |vauthors=Huffstutter PJ |date=5 December 2009 |access-date=5 December 2009 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207163910/http://www.latimes.com/news/nation-and-world/la-na-pigs-flu5-2009dec05,0,6902061.story |archive-date=7 December 2009}}</ref> similar to other influenza viruses, it is typically contracted by person-to-person transmission through respiratory droplets.<ref name=CDCOct16AntiviralRecommendations>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/recommendations.htm |title=Updated Interim Recommendations for the Use of Antiviral Medications in the Treatment and Prevention of Influenza for the 2009–2010 Season |date=8 September 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=17 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090917030300/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/recommendations.htm |archive-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Symptoms usually last 4–6 days.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1673658-overview |title=H1N1 Influenza (Swine Flu) |vauthors=Bronze MS |date=13 November 2009 |work=eMedicine |publisher=Medscape |access-date=10 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091227210136/http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1673658-overview |archive-date=27 December 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Antivirals]] ([[oseltamivir]] or [[zanamivir]]) were recommended for those with more severe symptoms or those in an at-risk group.<ref name=CDCOct16AntiviralRecommendations/>

|vauthors=Mckay B |title=The Flu Season That Fizzled |date=2 March 2010 |access-date=14 April 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150117223520/http://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703429304575095743102260012 |archive-date=17 January 2015}}</ref> and by May 2010, the number of cases was in steep decline.<ref name="WHOMay14update">{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/csr/don/2010_05_14/en/index.html |title=Pandemic (H1N1) 2009 |date=14 May 2010 |work=Disease Outbreak News |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=14 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100518163428/http://www.who.int/csr/don/2010_05_14/en/index.html |archive-date=18 May ==Signs and symptoms==

{{main|Influenza#Signs and symptoms}}

The symptoms of H1N1 flu are similar to those of other [[influenza]]s, and may include fever, cough (typically a "dry cough"), headache, dizziness, sneezing, [[Myalgia|muscle]] or [[Arthralgia|joint]] pain, [[Acute pharyngitis|sore throat]], [[Rigor (medicine)|chills]], [[fatigue (medical)|fatigue]], and [[Rhinorrhea|runny nose]]. [[Diarrhea]], vomiting, and [[neurology|neurological]] problems have also been reported in some cases.<ref name="CDC090724">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/media/transcripts/2009/t090724.htm |title=CDC Briefing on Investigation of Human Cases of H1N1 Flu |date=24 July 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=28 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090829202445/http://www.cdc.gov/media/transcripts/2009/t090724.htm |archive-date=29 August 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="CDCgeninfo">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance_homecare.htm |title=Interim Guidance for 2009 H1N1 Flu (Swine Flu): Taking Care of a Sick Person in Your Home |date=5 August 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=1 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103194946/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance_homecare.htm |archive-date=3 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> People at higher risk of serious complications include people over 65, children younger than 5, children with [[Neurodevelopmental disorder|neurodevelopmental conditions]], pregnant women (especially during the third trimester),<ref name="WHObriefingnoteOct16"/><ref name="AndrePicardNov1">{{Cite news |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/health/h1n1-swine-flu/updated-reader-questions-on-h1n1-answered/article1329448/ |title=Reader questions on H1N1 answered |vauthors=Picard A |date=1 November |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091104040801/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/health/h1n1-swine-flu/updated-reader-questions-on-h1n1-answered/article1329448/ |archive-date=4 November infected with HIV).<ref name="NYT5-27">{{Cite news |vauthors=Hartocollis A |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/28/health/policy/28flu.html |title='Underlying conditions' may add to flu worries |archive-date=25 April 2013 |url-status=live}}</ref> More than 70% of hospitalizations in the U.S. have been people with such underlying conditions, according to the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB124502116646013713 |title=Flu Pandemic Spurs Queries About Vaccine |vauthors=Whalen J |date=15 June 2009 |newspaper=The Wall In September 2009, the CDC reported that the H1N1 flu "seems to be taking a heavier toll among chronically ill children than the seasonal flu usually does".<ref name=DeniseGradySept3>{{Cite news
