===Severe cases===

The [[World Health Organization]] reports that the clinical picture in severe cases is strikingly different from the disease pattern seen during epidemics of seasonal influenza. While people with certain underlying medical conditions are known to be at increased risk, many severe cases occur in previously healthy people. In severe cases, patients generally begin to deteriorate around three to five days after symptom onset. Deterioration is rapid, with many patients progressing to respiratory failure within 24 hours, requiring immediate admission to an [[intensive care unit]]. Upon admission, most patients need immediate respiratory support with [[mechanical ventilation]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_clinical_features_20091016/en/index.html |title=Clinical features of severe cases of pandemic influenza |date=16 October 2009 |work=Pandemic (H1N1) 2009 briefing note 13 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=17 January 2010 |location=Geneva, Switzerland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100119214956/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_clinical_features_20091016/en/index.html |archive-date=19 January 2010}}</ref>

===Complications===

Most complications have occurred among previously unhealthy individuals, with [[obesity]] and [[respiratory disease]] as the strongest risk factors. [[Pulmonary]] complications are common. Primary influenza [[pneumonia]] occurs most commonly in adults and may progress rapidly to acute lung injury requiring [[mechanical ventilation]]. Secondary [[bacterial pneumonia|bacterial infection]] is more common in children. ''[[Staphylococcus aureus]]'', including methicillin-resistant strains, is an important cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia with a high mortality rate; ''[[Streptococcus pneumoniae]]'' is the second most important cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia for children and primary for adults. [[Neuromuscular]] and [[cardiac]] complications are unusual but may occur.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rothberg MB, Haessler SD |title=Complications of seasonal and pandemic influenza |journal=Critical Care Medicine |volume=38 |issue=4 Suppl |pages=e91–97 |date=April 2010 |pmid=19935413 |doi=10.1097/CCM.0b013e3181c92eeb |s2cid=43882788 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

A United Kingdom investigation of risk factors for hospitalisation and poor outcome with pandemic A/H1N1 influenza looked at 631 patients from 55 hospitals admitted with confirmed infection from May through September 2009. 13% were admitted to a high dependency or intensive care unit and 5% died; 36% were aged <16 years and 5% were aged ≥65 years. Non-white and pregnant patients were over-represented. 45% of patients had at least one underlying condition, mainly [[asthma]], and 13% received antiviral drugs before admission. Of 349 with documented chest x-rays on admission, 29% had evidence of [[pneumonia]], but bacterial co-infection was uncommon. Multivariate analyses showed that physician-recorded obesity on admission and pulmonary conditions other than asthma or [[chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] (COPD) were associated with a severe outcome, as were radiologically confirmed pneumonia and a raised [[C-reactive protein]] (CRP) level (≥{{Nowrap|100 mg/L)}}. 59% of all in-hospital deaths occurred in previously healthy people.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nguyen-Van-Tam JS, Openshaw PJ, Hashim A, Gadd EM, Lim WS, Semple MG, Read RC, Taylor BL, Brett SJ, McMenamin J, Enstone JE, Armstrong C, Nicholson KG |display-authors=6 |title=Risk factors for hospitalisation and poor outcome with pandemic A/H1N1 influenza: United Kingdom first wave (May–September 2009) |journal=Thorax |volume=65 |issue=7 |pages=645–51 |date=July 2010 |pmid=20627925 |pmc=2921287 |doi=10.1136/thx.2010.135210}}</ref>

[[Fulminant]] (sudden-onset) [[myocarditis]] has been linked to infection with H1N1, with at least four cases of myocarditis confirmed in patients also infected with A/H1N1. Three out of the four cases of H1N1-associated myocarditis were classified as fulminant, and one of the patients died.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Bratincsák A, El-Said HG, Bradley JS, Shayan K, Grossfeld PD, Cannavino CR |title=Fulminant myocarditis associated with pandemic H1N1 influenza A virus in children |journal=Journal of the American College of Cardiology |volume=55 |issue=9 |pages=928–29 |date=March 2010 |pmid=20153131 |doi=10.1016/j.jacc.2010.01.004 |doi-access=free}} (primary source)
*{{lay source |template=cite web |url=http://www.modernmedicine.com/modernmedicine/Modern+Medicine+Now/Myocarditis-Linked-to-Pandemic-H1N1-Flu-in-Childre/ArticleNewsFeed/Article/detail/656746?contextCategoryId=40137 |title=Myocarditis Linked to Pandemic H1N1 Flu in Children |website=Modern Medicine |date=2010-02-11}}</ref>
Also, there appears to be a link between severe A/H1N1 influenza infection and [[pulmonary embolism]]. In one report, five out of 14 patients admitted to the intensive care unit with severe A/H1N1 infection were found to have pulmonary emboli.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/10/091014111549.htm |title=Those With Severe H1N1 at Risk For Pulmonary Emboli, Researchers Find |publisher=ScienceDaily |date=18 October 2009 |access-date=3 April 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307163910/http://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/10/091014111549.htm |archive-date=7 March 2010}}</ref>

An article published in ''[[JAMA (journal)|JAMA]]'' in September 2010<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Belongia EA, Irving SA, Waring SC, Coleman LA, Meece JK, Vandermause M, Lindstrom S, Kempf D, Shay DK |display-authors=6 |title=Clinical characteristics and 30-day outcomes for influenza A 2009 (H1N1), 2008–2009 (H1N1), and 2007–2008 (H3N2) infections |journal=JAMA |volume=304 |issue=10 |pages=1091–98 |date=September 2010 |pmid=20823435 |doi=10.1001/jama.2010.1277 |doi-access=free}}</ref> challenged previous reports and stated that children infected in the 2009 flu pandemic were no more likely to be hospitalised with complications or get pneumonia than those who catch seasonal strains. Researchers found that about 1.5% of children with the H1N1 swine flu strain were hospitalised within 30 days, compared with 3.7% of those sick with a seasonal strain of H1N1 and 3.1% with an H3N2 virus.<ref name="bloomberg.com"/>

==Diagnosis==

Confirmed diagnosis of pandemic H1N1 flu requires testing of a [[Nasopharyngeal swab|nasopharyngeal]], nasal, or [[oropharyngeal]] tissue swab from the patient.<ref name="specimen">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/specimencollection.htm |title=Interim Guidance on Specimen Collection, Processing, and Testing for Patients with Suspected Novel Influenza A (H1N1) Virus Infection |date=13 May 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=23 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126020551/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/specimencollection.htm |archive-date=26 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Real-time polymerase chain reaction|Real-time]] [[RT-PCR]] is the recommended test as others are unable to differentiate between pandemic H1N1 and regular [[seasonal flu]].<ref name="specimen"/> However, most people with flu symptoms do not need a test for pandemic H1N1 flu specifically, because the test results usually do not affect the recommended course of treatment.<ref name="diagpub">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/diagnostic_testing_public_qa.htm |title=Influenza Diagnostic Testing During the 2009–2010 Flu Season |date=29 September 2009 |work=H1N1 Flu |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=23 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126004503/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/diagnostic_testing_public_qa.htm |archive-date=26 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The U.S. CDC recommend testing only for people who are hospitalized with suspected flu, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems.<ref name="diagpub"/> For the mere diagnosis of influenza and not pandemic H1N1 flu specifically, more widely available tests include [[rapid influenza diagnostic test]]s (RIDT), which yield results in about 30 minutes, and [[direct fluorescent antibody|direct]] and indirect [[immunofluorescence]] assays ([[Direct fluorescent antibody|DFA]] and IFA), which take 2–4 hours.<ref name="diagnostic">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance/diagnostic_tests.htm |title=Interim Recommendations for Clinical Use of Influenza Diagnostic Tests During the 2009–10 Influenza Season |date=29 September 2009 |work=H1N1 Flu |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=23 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126022419/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/guidance/diagnostic_tests.htm |archive-date=26 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Due to the high rate of RIDT [[false negative]]s, the CDC advises that patients with illnesses compatible with novel influenza A (H1N1) virus infection but with negative RIDT results should be treated empirically based on the level of clinical suspicion, underlying medical conditions, severity of illness, and risk for complications, and if a more definitive determination of infection with influenza virus is required, testing with rRT-PCR or virus isolation should be performed.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5830a2.htm |title=Evaluation of Rapid Influenza Diagnostic Tests for Detection of Novel Influenza A (H1N1) Virus – United States, 2009 |date=7 August 2009 |work=Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=5 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091217043745/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5830a2.htm |archive-date=17 December 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The use of RIDTs has been questioned by researcher Paul Schreckenberger of the [[Loyola University Chicago|Loyola University]] Health System, who suggests that rapid tests may actually pose a dangerous [[public health]] risk.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.loyolamedicine.org/News/News_Releases/news_release_detail.cfm?var_news_release_id=973441074 |title=Could Widely Used Rapid Influenza Tests Pose A Dangerous Public Health Risk? |date=17 November 2009 |publisher=Loyola Medicine |access-date=4 December 2009 |location=Maywood, Illinois, U.S. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207163917/http://www.loyolamedicine.org/News/News_Releases/news_release_detail.cfm?var_news_release_id=973441074 |archive-date=7 December 2009}}</ref> Nikki Shindo of the WHO has expressed regret at reports of treatment being delayed by waiting for H1N1 test results and suggests, "[D]octors should not wait for the laboratory confirmation but make diagnosis based on clinical and epidemiological backgrounds and start treatment early."<ref name="NikkiShindoNov12"/>

On 22 June 2010, the CDC announced a new test called the "CDC Influenza 2009 A (H1N1)pdm Real-Time RT-PCR Panel (IVD)". It uses a molecular biology technique to detect influenza A viruses and specifically the 2009 H1N1 virus. The new test will replace the previous real-time RT-PCR diagnostic test used during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which received an emergency use authorization from the U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration]] in April 2009. Tests results are available in four hours and are 96% accurate.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.cdc.gov/media/pressrel/2010/r100622.htm |title=New CDC Test to Detect Human Infections with the 2009 H1N1 Influenza Virus Authorized for Use by FDA |location=Atlanta |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |date=22 June 2010 |access-date=25 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100826205400/http://www.cdc.gov/media/pressrel/2010/r100622.htm |archive-date=26 August 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Cause==

{{Main|Pandemic H1N1/09 virus}}

The virus was found to be a novel strain of influenza for which existing [[vaccination|vaccines]] against seasonal flu provided little protection. A study at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published in May 2009 found that children had no preexisting immunity to the new strain but that adults, particularly those older than 60, had some degree of [[immunity (medical)|immunity]]. Children showed no [[Cross-reactivity|cross-reactive]] [[antibody]] reaction to the new strain, adults aged 18 to 60 had 6–9%, and older adults 33%.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/cidrap/content/influenza/swineflu/news/may2109serum-jw.html |title=Some immunity to novel H1N1 flu found in seniors |vauthors=Schnirring L |date=21 May 2009 |publisher=Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy |access-date=26 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090923225423/http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/cidrap/content/influenza/swineflu/news/may2109serum-jw.html |archive-date=23 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="MMWR">{{cite journal |author1=Centers for Disease Control Prevention (CDC) |date=24 April 2009 |title=Swine Influenza A (H1N1) Infection in Two Children – Southern California, March–April 2009 |url=http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5815a5.htm |url-status=live |journal=Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] |volume=58 |issue=15 |pages=400–402 |pmid=19390508 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090910141510/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5815a5.htm |archive-date=10 September 2009 |access-date=25 April 2009}}</ref> While it has been thought that these findings suggest the partial immunity in older adults may be due to previous exposure to similar seasonal influenza viruses, a November 2009 study of a rural unvaccinated population in China found only a 0.3% cross-reactive antibody reaction to the H1N1 strain, suggesting that previous vaccinations for seasonal flu and not exposure may have resulted in the immunity found in the older U.S. population.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Chen H, Wang Y, Liu W, Zhang J, Dong B, Fan X, de Jong MD, Farrar J, Riley S, Smith GJ, Guan Y |display-authors=6 |title=Serologic survey of pandemic (H1N1) 2009 virus, Guangxi Province, China |journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases |volume=15 |issue=11 |pages=1849–50 |date=November 2009 |pmid=19891883 |pmc=2857250 |doi=10.3201/eid1511.090868}}</ref>

Analyses of the genetic sequences of the first isolates, promptly shared on the [[GISAID]] database according to Nature and WHO,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Butler D |title=Swine flu goes global |journal=Nature |volume=458 |issue=7242 |pages=1082–83 |date=April 2009 |pmid=19407756 |doi=10.1038/4581082a |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/Gene_sequences_20090425.pdf |title=Viral gene sequences to assist update diagnostics for swine influenza A(H1N1) |date=15 April 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization |access-date=6 September 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170807182539/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/Gene_sequences_20090425.pdf |archive-date=7 August 2017}}</ref> soon determined that the strain contains genes from five different flu viruses: North American swine influenza, North American avian influenza, human influenza, and two swine influenza viruses typically found in Asia and Europe. Further analysis has shown that several [[protein]]s of the virus are most similar to strains that cause mild symptoms in humans, leading [[virologist]] Wendy Barclay to suggest on 1{{nbsp}}May 2009, that the initial indications are that the virus was unlikely to cause severe symptoms for most people.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/8028371.stm |title=What scientists know about swine flu |publisher=BBC News |author=Emma Wilkinson |date=1 May 2009 |access-date=26 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090929231136/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/8028371.stm |archive-date=29 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The virus was less lethal than previous pandemic strains and killed about 0.01–0.03% of those infected; the [[1918 flu pandemic|1918 influenza]] was about one hundred times more lethal and had a case fatality rate of 2–3%.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Donaldson LJ, Rutter PD, Ellis BM, Greaves FE, Mytton OT, Pebody RG, Yardley IE |title=Mortality from pandemic A/H1N1 2009 influenza in England: public health surveillance study |journal=BMJ |volume=339 |article-number=b5213 |date=December 2009 |pmid=20007665 |pmc=2791802 |doi=10.1136/bmj.b5213}}</ref> By 14 November 2009, the virus had infected one in six Americans with 200,000 hospitalisations and 10,000 deaths—as many hospitalizations and fewer deaths than in an average flu season overall, but with much higher risk for those under 50. With deaths of 1,100 children and 7,500 adults 18 to 64, these figures were deemed "much higher than in a usual flu season" during the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nation-and-world/la-sci-swine-flu11-2009dec11,0,6351332.story |title=Swine flu has hit about one in six Americans, CDC says |vauthors=Maugh II TH |work=Los Angeles Times |date=11 December 2009 |access-date=13 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091213114305/http://www.latimes.com/news/nation-and-world/la-sci-swine-flu11-2009dec11%2C0%2C6351332.story |archive-date=13 December 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In June 2010, scientists from [[Hong Kong]] reported discovery of a new swine flu virus: a hybrid of the pandemic H1N1 virus and viruses previously found in pigs. It was the first report of a reassortment of the pandemic virus, which in humans had been slow to evolve. [[Nancy Cox (virologist)|Nancy Cox]], head of the influenza division at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has said, "This particular paper is extremely interesting because it demonstrates for the first time what we had worried about at the very onset of the pandemic, and that is that this particular virus, when introduced into pigs, could reassort with the resident viruses in pigs and we would have new gene constellations. And bingo, here we are." Pigs have been termed the mixing vessel of flu because they can be infected both by avian flu viruses, which rarely directly infect people, and by human viruses. When pigs become simultaneously infected with more than one virus, the viruses can swap genes, producing new variants which can pass to humans and sometimes spread amongst them.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vijaykrishna D, Poon LL, Zhu HC, Ma SK, Li OT, Cheung CL, Smith GJ, Peiris JS, Guan Y |display-authors=6 |title=Reassortment of pandemic H1N1/2009 influenza A virus in swine |journal=Science |volume=328 |issue=5985 |page=1529 |date=June 2010 |pmid=20558710 |pmc=3569847 |doi=10.1126/science.1189132 |bibcode=2010Sci...328.1529V}}</ref> "Unlike the situation with birds and humans, we have a situation with pigs and humans where there's a two-way street of exchange of viruses. With pigs it's very much a two-way street."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/h1n1-swaps-genes-with-other-pig-viruses-scientists-1.523986 |title=H1N1 swaps genes with other pig viruses: scientists |date=18 June 2010 |publisher=CTV News |agency=[[The Canadian Press]] |access-date=14 April 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727124022/http://edmonton.ctv.ca/servlet/an/local/CTVNews/20100618/swine-flu-virus-100618/20100618/?hub=EdmontonHome |archive-date=27 July 2011}}</ref>

===Transmission===

Spread of the H1N1 virus is thought to occur in the same way that seasonal flu spreads. Flu viruses are spread mainly from person to person through coughing or sneezing by people with influenza. Sometimes people may become infected by touching something—such as a surface or object—with flu viruses on it and then touching their face.<ref name="fluandyou">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/H1N1flu/qa.htm |title=2009 H1N1 Flu ("Swine Flu") and You |date=10 February 2010 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=26 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100304031110/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/qa.htm |archive-date=4 March 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The [[basic reproduction number]] (the average number of other individuals whom each infected individual will infect, in a population which has no immunity to the disease) for the 2009 novel H1N1 is estimated to be 1.75.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Balcan D, Hu H, Goncalves B, Bajardi P, Poletto C, Ramasco JJ, Paolotti D, Perra N, Tizzoni M, Van den Broeck W, Colizza V, Vespignani A |display-authors=6 |title=Seasonal transmission potential and activity peaks of the new influenza A(H1N1): a Monte Carlo likelihood analysis based on human mobility |journal=BMC Medicine |volume=7 |issue=45 |article-number=45 |date=September 2009 |pmid=19744314 |pmc=2755471 |doi=10.1186/1741-7015-7-45 |arxiv=0909.2417 |bibcode=2009BMCM....7...45B |doi-access=free}}</ref> A December 2009 study found that the transmissibility of the H1N1 influenza virus in households is lower than that seen in past pandemics. Most transmissions occur soon before or after the onset of symptoms.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cauchemez S, Donnelly CA, Reed C, Ghani AC, Fraser C, Kent CK, Finelli L, Ferguson NM |display-authors=6 |title=Household transmission of 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) virus in the United States |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=361 |issue=27 |pages=2619–27 |date=December 2009 |pmid=20042753 |pmc=3840270 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa0905498 |author-link4=Azra Ghani |author-link2=Christl Donnelly}}</ref>

The H1N1 virus has been transmitted to animals, including [[swine]], [[turkey (bird)|turkeys]], [[ferret]]s, [[Cat|household cats]], at least one dog, and a [[cheetah]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://consults.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/11/05/can-pets-get-swine-flu/000 |title=Can Pets Get Swine Flu? |vauthors=Murray L |newspaper=The New York Times |date=5 November 2009 |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091108173748/http://consults.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/11/05/can-pets-get-swine-flu/ |archive-date=8 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://well.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/11/05/the-cat-who-got-swine-flu/ |title=The Cat Who Got Swine Flu |vauthors=Parker-Pope T |newspaper=The New York Times |date=5 November 2009 |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091108150018/http://well.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/11/05/the-cat-who-got-swine-flu/ |archive-date=8 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>
{{Cite news |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/pet-dog-recovers-from-h1n1-1.832773 |title=Pet dog recovers from H1N1 |newspaper=[[CBC News]] |date=22 December 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091224082642/http://www.cbc.ca/health/story/2009/12/22/h1n1-us-dog-who.html |archive-date=24 December 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.usda.gov/documents/FINAL_RESULTS_2009_PANDEMIC_H1N1_INFLUENZA_CHT.pdf |title=2009 Pandemic H1N1 Influenza Presumptive and Confirmed Results |date=4 December 2009 |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091203233039/http://www.usda.gov/documents/FINAL_RESULTS_2009_PANDEMIC_H1N1_INFLUENZA_CHT.pdf |archive-date=3 December 2009}}</ref>

==Prevention==

{{See also|Prevention of influenza|2009 swine flu pandemic vaccine|Influenza vaccine#2009-2010 Northern Hemisphere winter season}}

Because the H1N1 vaccine was initially in short supply in the United States, the CDC recommended that initial doses should go to priority groups such as pregnant women, people who live with or care for babies under six months old, children six months to four years old and health-care workers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/PDF/rr/rr5810.pdf |title=Use of Influenza A (H1N1) 2009 Monovalent Vaccine: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), 2009 |work=[[Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report]] |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |date=28 November 2009 |access-date=2 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103202202/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/pdf/rr/rr5810.pdf |archive-date=3 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> In the United Kingdom, the NHS recommended vaccine priority go to people over six months old who were clinically at risk for seasonal flu, pregnant women and households of people with compromised immunity.<ref name="nhs-april">{{Cite news |url=http://www.nhs.uk/news/2009/04april/pages/swineflulatest.aspx |title=Swine flu latest from the NHS |date=25 September 2009 |work=NHS Choices |publisher=[[National Health Services|NHS]] |access-date=28 September 2009 |agency=NHS Knowledge Service |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091008013912/http://www.nhs.uk/News/2009/04April/Pages/swineflulatest.aspx |archive-date=8 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Although it was initially thought that two injections would be required, clinical trials showed that the new vaccine protected adults "with only one dose instead of two;" thus the limited vaccine supplies would go twice as far as had been predicted.<ref name="NYT9-12-09">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/11/health/11vaccine.html |title=One Vaccine Shot Seen as Protective for Swine Flu |vauthors=McNeil Jr DG |date=10 September 2009 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164052/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/11/health/11vaccine.html |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/briefing_20091030/en/index.html |title=Experts advise WHO on pandemic vaccine policies and strategies |date=30 October 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=2 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091102051824/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/briefing_20091030/en/index.html |archive-date=2 November 2009}}</ref> Health officials worldwide were also concerned because the virus was new and could easily mutate and become more virulent, even though most flu symptoms were mild and lasted only a few days without treatment. Officials also urged communities, businesses, and individuals to make contingency plans for possible school closures, multiple employee absences for illness, surges of patients in hospitals, and other effects of potentially widespread outbreaks.<ref name="WSJ-7-18-09">{{Cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB124787226825260533 |title=New Push in H1N1 Flu Fight Set for Start of School |vauthors=McKay B |date=18 July 2009 |newspaper=The Wall Street Journal |access-date=31 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090922053424/http://online.wsj.com/article/SB124787226825260533.html?mod=googlenews_wsj |archive-date=22 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Disaster response organizations such as Direct Relief helped by providing protective items to clinical workers to help them stay healthy throughout flu season.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.directrelief.org/2009/11/478-community-clinics-49-states-receiving-needed-h1n1-protective-supplies/ |title=478 Community Clinics in 49 States Receiving Needed H1N1 Protective Supplies |vauthors=Hutain J |date=21 November 2009 |website=Direct Relief |access-date=25 April 2019 |archive-date=25 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425140651/https://www.directrelief.org/2009/11/478-community-clinics-49-states-receiving-needed-h1n1-protective-supplies/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nbcsandiego.com/news/health/Clinics-Swamped-with-Flu-Patients.html |title=Clinics Swamped with Flu Patients |vauthors=Stickney R |website=NBC 7 San Diego |date=4 May 2009 |access-date=25 April 2019 |archive-date=25 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425140254/https://www.nbcsandiego.com/news/health/Clinics-Swamped-with-Flu-Patients.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

In February 2010, the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted for "universal" flu vaccination in the United States to include all people over six months of age. The 2010–2011 vaccine will protect against the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus and two other flu viruses.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/qa/1011_vac_selection.htm |title=Vaccine Selection for the 2010–2011 Influenza Season |publisher=[[U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=25 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101006224851/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/qa/1011_vac_selection.htm |archive-date=6 October 2010}}</ref>

===Public health response===

{{See also|2009 swine flu pandemic by country}}

On 27 April 2009, the [[European Union]] health commissioner advised Europeans to postpone nonessential travel to the United States or Mexico. This followed the discovery of the first confirmed case in Spain.<ref name="Guardian 27/4">{{Cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/apr/27/swine-flu-mexico |title=Europeans urged to avoid Mexico and US as swine flu death toll exceeds 100 |date=27 April 2009 |work=The Guardian |access-date=27 April 2009 |location=London |vauthors=Nasaw D |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430094402/http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2009/apr/27/swine-flu-mexico |archive-date=30 April 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 6{{nbsp}}May 2009, the [[Public Health Agency of Canada]] announced that their [[National Microbiology Laboratory]] (NML) had mapped the genetic code of the swine flu virus, the first time that had been done.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.iol.co.za/index.php?art_id=nw20090506191835578C369647&click_id=31&set_id=1 |title=H1N1 virus genome: 'This is a world first' |date=6 May 2009 |work=Independent |access-date=31 August 2009 |agency=Agence France-Presse |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163941/http://www.iol.co.za/index.php?art_id=nw20090506191835578C369647&click_id=31&set_id=1 |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> In the United Kingdom, the [[National Health Service]] launched a website, the National Pandemic Flu Service,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pandemicflu.direct.gov.uk/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163952/https://www.pandemicflu.direct.gov.uk/ |archive-date=7 October 2009 |title=National Pandemic Flu Service |publisher=NHS, NHS Scotland, NHS Wales, DHSSPS |access-date=4 October 2009}}</ref> allowing patients to self-assess and get an authorisation number for antiviral medication. The system was expected to reduce the burden on [[general practitioner]]s.<ref name="nhs-april"/>

U.S. officials observed that six years of concern about [[H5N1]] [[avian flu]] did much to prepare for the current H1N1 outbreak, noting that after H5N1 emerged in Asia, ultimately killing about 60% of the few hundred people infected over the years, many countries took steps to try to prevent any similar crisis from spreading further.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.pe.com/localnews/rivcounty/stories/PE_News_Local_S_swineflu08.4301c9d.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107164010/http://www.pe.com/localnews/rivcounty/stories/PE_News_Local_S_swineflu08.4301c9d.html |archive-date=7 January 2010 |title=Health officials evaluate response to swine flu |vauthors=Hines L |date=7 June 2009 |work=Riverside Press-Enterprise |access-date=17 September 2009}}</ref> The CDC and other U.S. governmental agencies<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/08/09/AR2009080902447.html |title=Preparing for Swine Flu's Return |vauthors=Stein R |date=10 August 2009 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=4 October 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164155/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/08/09/AR2009080902447.html |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> used the summer lull to take stock of the United States response to H1N1 flu and attempt to patch any gaps in the [[public health]] safety net before flu season started in early autumn.<ref name="reuters20090604">{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/domesticNews/idUSN0423008520090604?sp=true |title=As swine flu wanes, U.S. preparing for second wave |vauthors=Steenhuysen J |date=4 June 2009 |agency=Reuters |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164813/http://www.reuters.com/article/domesticNews/idUSN0423008520090604?sp=true |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> Preparations included planning a second influenza vaccination program in addition to the one for seasonal flu, and improving coordination between federal, state, and local governments and private health providers.<ref name="reuters20090604"/> On 24 October 2009, U.S. President [[Barack Obama|Obama]] declared swine flu a national emergency, giving [[Secretary of Health and Human Services]] [[Kathleen Sebelius]] authority to grant waivers to requesting hospitals from usual federal requirements.<ref name="ObamaAuthorizesSebelius">{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/10/24/AR2009102401061.html |title=President Obama declares H1N1 flu a national emergency |vauthors=Shear MD, Stein R |date=24 October 2009 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=25 October 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091107164213/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/10/24/AR2009102401061.html |archive-date=7 November 2009}}</ref>

===Vaccines===

{{Main|2009 swine flu pandemic vaccine}}
[[File:A nurse vaccinates Barack Obama against H1N1.jpg|thumb|President [[Barack Obama]] being vaccinated against H1N1 flu on 20 December 2009]]

By 19 November 2009, doses of vaccine had been administered in over 16 countries. A 2009 review by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) concluded that the 2009 H1N1 vaccine has a safety profile similar to that of the seasonal vaccine.

In 2011, a study from the US Flu Vaccine Effectiveness Network estimated the overall effectiveness of all pandemic H1N1 vaccines at 56%. A CDC study released 28 January 2013, estimated that the Pandemic H1N1 vaccine saved roughly 300 lives and prevented about a million illnesses in the US. The study concluded that had the vaccination program started two weeks earlier, close to 60% more cases could have been prevented. The study was based on an effectiveness in preventing cases, hospitalizations, and deaths of 62% for all subgroups except people over 65, for whom the effectiveness was estimated at 43%. The effectiveness was based on European and Asian studies and expert opinion. The delay in vaccine administration demonstrated the shortcomings of the world's capacity for vaccine-production, as well as problems with international distribution. Some manufacturers and wealthy countries had concerns regarding liability and regulations, as well as the logistics of transporting, storing, and administering vaccines to be donated to poorer countries.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fineberg HV |title=Pandemic preparedness and response—lessons from the H1N1 influenza of 2009 |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=370 |issue=14 |pages=1335–42 |date=April 2014 |pmid=24693893 |doi=10.1056/NEJMra1208802 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Accusations of conflict of interest===

In January 2010, [[Wolfgang Wodarg]], a German deputy who trained as a physician and chaired the health committee at the [[Council of Europe]], claimed that major firms had organized a "campaign of panic" to put pressure on the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) to declare a "false pandemic" to sell vaccines. Wodarg said the WHO's "false pandemic" flu campaign is "one of the greatest medicine scandals of the century". He said that the "false pandemic" campaign began in May 2009 in Mexico City, when a hundred or so "normal" reported influenza cases were declared to be the beginning of a threatening new pandemic, although he said there was little scientific evidence for it. Nevertheless, he argued that the WHO, "in cooperation with some big pharmaceutical companies and their scientists, re-defined pandemics," removing the statement that "an enormous amount of people have contracted the illness or died" from its existing definition and replacing it by stating simply that there has to be a virus, spreading beyond borders and to which people have no immunity.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.news.com.au/world/swine-flu/story-e6frfkyi-1225818388508 |title=Swine flu 'a false pandemic' to sell vaccines, expert says |date=13 January 2010 |publisher=[[News.com]] |access-date=13 January 2010 |vauthors=Pollard C |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100114013335/http://www.news.com.au/world/swine-flu/story-e6frfkyi-1225818388508 |archive-date=14 January 2010}}</ref>

The WHO responded by stating that they take their duty to provide independent advice seriously and guarded against interference from outside interests. Announcing a review of the WHO's actions, spokeswoman Fadela Chaib stated: "Criticism is part of an outbreak cycle. We expect and indeed welcome criticism and the chance to discuss it".<ref name="reuters 2010-01-12"/><ref>Bloomberg {{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601091&sid=ahj0H_RH8U68 |title=WHO to Clarify H1N1 Data After False Pandemic Claim (Update1) |access-date=21 August 2017 |publisher=Bloomberg News |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307164337/http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601091&sid=ahj0H_RH8U68 |archive-date=7 March 2010}}</ref> The WHO also stated on their website that "The world is going through a real pandemic. The description of it as a fake is wrong and irresponsible".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fumento |first=Michael |date=5 February 2010 |title=Why The WHO Faked A Pandemic |work=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/2010/02/05/world-health-organization-swine-flu-pandemic-opinions-contributors-michael-fumento.html |access-date=21 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100208182828/https://www.forbes.com/2010/02/05/world-health-organization-swine-flu-pandemic-opinions-contributors-michael-fumento.html |archive-date=8 February 2010}}</ref> In March 2010, the Council of Europe launched an enquiry into "the influence of the pharmaceutical companies on the global swine flu campaign", and a preliminary report was in preparation.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Flynn P |url=http://assembly.coe.int/CommitteeDocs/2010/20100329_MemorandumPandemie_E.pdf |title=The handling of the H1N1 pandemic: more transparency needed |publisher=memorandum, Social, Health and Family Affairs Committee, The [[Council of Europe]] |date=23 March 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110223021733/http://assembly.coe.int/CommitteeDocs/2010/20100329_MemorandumPandemie_E.pdf |archive-date=23 February 2011}}</ref>

On 12 April 2010, Keiji Fukuda, the WHO's top influenza expert, stated that the system leading to the declaration of a pandemic led to confusion about H1N1 circulating around the world and he expressed concern that there was a failure to communicate in regard to uncertainties about the new virus, which turned out to be not as deadly as feared. WHO Director-General Margaret Chan appointed 29 flu experts from outside the organization to conduct a review of WHO's handling of the H1N1 flu pandemic. She told them, "We want a frank, critical, transparent, credible and independent review of our performance."<ref name=letter>{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2010/letter_bmj_20100608/en/index.html |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |author=Chan M |date=8 June 2010 |title=WHO Director-General's letter to BMJ editors |access-date=30 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110130000141/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2010/letter_bmj_20100608/en/index.html |archive-date=30 January 2011}}</ref>

In June 2010, [[Fiona Godlee]], editor-in-chief of the ''[[BMJ]]'', published an editorial which criticised the WHO, saying that an investigation had disclosed that some of the experts advising WHO on the pandemic had financial ties with drug companies which were producing antivirals and vaccines.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Godlee F |title=Conflicts of interest and pandemic flu |journal=BMJ |volume=340 |article-number=c2947 |date=June 2010 |pmid=20525680 |doi=10.1136/bmj.c2947 |s2cid=323055 |url=http://www.bmj.com/content/340/bmj.c2947.full#ref-1 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101221213507/http://www.bmj.com/content/340/bmj.c2947.full |archive-date=21 December 2010 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Margaret Chan, Director-General of the WHO, replied stating, "Without question, the ''BMJ'' feature and editorial will leave many readers with the impression that WHO's decision to declare a pandemic was at least partially influenced by a desire to boost the profits of the pharmaceutical industry. The bottom line, however, is that decisions to raise the level of pandemic alert were based on clearly defined virological and epidemiological criteria. It is hard to bend these criteria, no matter what the motive".<ref name=letter/>

===Infection control===
====Travel precautions====

[[File:ChineseFluInspectors.JPG|thumb|Flu inspection on a flight arriving in China]]
[[File:Airport Thermographic Camera.jpg|thumb|Thermal imaging camera and screen, photographed in an airport terminal in Greece. Thermal imaging can detect elevated body temperature, one of the signs of swine flu.]]

On 7 May 2009, the WHO stated that containment was not feasible and that countries should focus on mitigating the effect of the virus. They did not recommend closing borders or restricting travel.<ref name="WHO Travel">{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/frequently_asked_questions/travel/en/index.html |title=Influenza A(H1N1) – Travel |date=7 May 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=17 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618104753/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/frequently_asked_questions/travel/en/index.html |archive-date=18 June 2009}}</ref> On 26 April 2009, the [[Government of the People's Republic of China|Chinese government]] announced that visitors returning from flu-affected areas who experienced flu-like symptoms within two weeks would be quarantined.<ref name="reuters">{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/europeCrisis/idUST344175 |title=Asia moves to ward off new flu virus |agency=Reuters |date=9 February 2009 |access-date=26 April 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430041910/https://www.reuters.com/article/europeCrisis/idUST344175 |archive-date=30 April 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

U.S. airlines had made no major changes as of the beginning of June 2009, but continued standing practices which include looking for passengers with symptoms of flu, [[measles]] or other infections, and relying on in-flight [[air filter]]s to ensure that aircraft were sanitised.<ref name="airlines"/> Masks were not generally provided by airlines and the CDC did not recommend that airline crews wear them.<ref name="airlines"/> Some non-U.S. airlines, mostly Asian, including [[Singapore Airlines]], [[China Eastern Airlines]], [[China Southern Airlines]], [[Cathay Pacific]] and [[Aeromexico]], took measures such as stepping up cabin cleaning, installing state-of-the-art air filters and allowing in-flight staff to wear face masks.<ref name="airlines">{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/asiaCrisis/idUSN27536654 |title=Global airlines move to reduce infection risks |vauthors=Jacobs K |date=3 June 2009 |agency=Reuters |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164721/http://www.reuters.com/article/asiaCrisis/idUSN27536654 |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref>

According to studies conducted in Australia and Japan, screening individuals for influenza symptoms at airports during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak was not an effective method of infection control.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gunaratnam PJ, Tobin S, Seale H, Marich A, McAnulty J |title=Airport arrivals screening during pandemic (H1N1) 2009 influenza in New South Wales, Australia |journal=The Medical Journal of Australia |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=290–92 |date=March 2014 |pmid=24641156 |doi=10.5694/mja13.10832 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nishiura H, Kamiya K |title=Fever screening during the influenza (H1N1-2009) pandemic at Narita International Airport, Japan |journal=BMC Infectious Diseases |volume=11 |article-number=111 |date=May 2011 |pmid=21539735 |pmc=3096599 |doi=10.1186/1471-2334-11-111 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

====Schools====

U.S. government officials were especially concerned about schools because the H1N1 flu virus appeared to disproportionately affect young and school-age people, between six months and 24 years of age.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.businesswire.com/portal/site/google/?ndmViewId=news_view&newsId=20090820006035&newsLang=en |title=New CDC H1N1 Guidance for Colleges, Universities, and Institutions of Higher Education |date=20 August 2009 |work=Business Wire |access-date=17 September 2009 |archive-date=7 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163952/http://www.businesswire.com/portal/site/google/?ndmViewId=news_view&newsId=20090820006035&newsLang=en |url-status=live}}</ref>
The H1N1 outbreak led to numerous precautionary school closures in some areas. Rather than closing schools, the CDC recommended that students and school workers with flu symptoms should stay home for either seven days total, or until 24 hours after symptoms subsided, whichever was longer.<ref name=24hours>{{Cite news |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/health/6557550.html |title=Schools revamp swine flu plans for fall |vauthors=George C |date=1 August 2009 |newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]] |access-date=31 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163939/http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/health/6557550.html |archive-date=7 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The CDC also recommended that colleges should consider suspending fall 2009 classes if the virus began to cause severe illness in a significantly larger share of students than the previous spring. They also urged schools to suspend rules, such as penalties for late papers or missed classes or requirements for a doctor's note, to enforce "self-isolation" and prevent students from venturing out while ill;<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/08/20/AR2009082003449.html |title=Colleges Warned About Fall Flu Outbreaks on Campus |vauthors=de Vise D |date=20 August 2009 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164136/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/08/20/AR2009082003449.html |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> schools were advised to set aside a room for people developing flu-like symptoms while they waited to go home and to have ill students or staff and those caring for them use face masks.<ref name="AJC8-14">{{Cite news |url=http://www.ajc.com/health/content/shared-auto/healthnews/flu-/630021.html |title=Get Smart About Swine Flu for Back-to-School |date=14 August 2009 |newspaper=[[Atlanta Journal-Constitution]] |access-date=31 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164012/http://www.ajc.com/health/content/shared-auto/healthnews/flu-/630021.html |archive-date=7 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In California, school districts and universities were on alert and worked with health officials to launch education campaigns. Many planned to stockpile medical supplies and discuss worst-case scenarios, including plans to provide lessons and meals for low-income children in case elementary and secondary schools closed.<ref name="swine-flu-goes-to-camp"/> [[University of California]] campuses stockpiled supplies, from paper masks and hand sanitizer to food and water.<ref name="swine-flu-goes-to-camp">
{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-me-camp-flu27-2009jul27,0,5762666.story |title=Swine flu goes to camp. Will it go to school next? |vauthors=Mehta S, Santa Cruz N |date=27 July 2009 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090807164438/http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-me-camp-flu27-2009jul27,0,5762666.story |archive-date=7 August 2009}}</ref> To help prepare for contingencies, [[University of Maryland School of Medicine]] professor of [[pediatrics]] James C. King Jr. suggested that every county should create an "influenza action team" to be run by the local [[health department]], parents, and school administrators.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/08/02/opinion/02king.html |title=The ABC's of H1N1 |vauthors=King Jr JC |date=1 August 2009 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164239/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/08/02/opinion/02king.html |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> By 28 October 2009, about 600 schools in the United States had been temporarily closed, affecting over 126,000 students in 19 states.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.foxnews.com/story/0,2933,570129,00.html |title=H1N1 Closes Hundreds of Schools Across the U.S. |date=28 October 2009 |publisher=Fox News |access-date=28 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091101132151/http://www.foxnews.com/story/0%2C2933%2C570129%2C00.html |archive-date=1 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Workplace====

Fearing a worst-case scenario, the U.S. [[Department of Health and Human Services]] (HHS), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the [[Department of Homeland Security]] (DHS) developed updated guidance<ref name="fluguidance"/> and a video for employers to use as they developed plans to respond to the H1N1 outbreak. The guidance suggested that employers consider and communicate their objectives, such as reducing transmission among staff, protecting people who are at increased risk of influenza-related complications from becoming infected, maintaining business operations, and minimising adverse effects on other entities in their [[supply chain]]s.<ref name="fluguidance">{{cite web |url=http://www.flu.gov/plan/workplaceplanning/guidance.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090830005155/http://www.flu.gov/plan/workplaceplanning/guidance.html |archive-date=30 August 2009 |title=Business Planning |work=Flu.gov |publisher=U.S. Department of Health & Human Services |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The CDC estimated that as much as 40% of the workforce might be unable to work at the peak of the pandemic due to the need for many healthy adults to stay home and care for an ill family member,<ref name="LATimes7-25">
{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-sci-swine-flu25-2009jul25,0,3387335.story |title=Swine flu could kill hundreds of thousands in U.S. if vaccine fails, CDC says |vauthors=Maugh II TH |date=25 July 2009 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090807165302/http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-sci-swine-flu25-2009jul25,0,3387335.story |archive-date=7 August 2009}}</ref> and advised that individuals should have steps in place should a workplace close down or a situation arise that requires [[remote work]].<ref name="Fox-7-17-09">{{Cite news |url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/swine-flu-why-you-should-still-be-worried |title=Swine Flu: Why You Should Still Be Worried |vauthors=Fiore M |date=17 July 2009 |publisher=Fox News |access-date=31 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090909132519/http://www.foxnews.com/story/0,2933,533591,00.html |archive-date=9 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> The CDC further advised that persons in the workplace should stay home sick for seven days after getting the flu, or 24 hours after symptoms end, whichever is longer.<ref name=24hours/>

In the UK, the [[Health and Safety Executive]] (HSE) also issued general guidance for employers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hse.gov.uk/news/2009/swineflu.htm |title=Swine flu – HSE News Announcement |publisher=Health and Safety Executive |date=18 June 2009 |access-date=31 August 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090827061646/http://www.hse.gov.uk/news/2009/swineflu.htm |archive-date=27 August 2009}}</ref>

====Face masks====

[[File:Swine Flu Masked Train Passengers in Mexico City.jpg|thumb|[[Mexico City Metro]]]]
[[File:Influenza-Shock2009(1).jpg|thumb|right|[[Osaka Loop Line]], Japan]]

The U.S. CDC did not recommend the use of face masks or [[respirator]]s in non-health care settings, such as schools, workplaces, or public places, with a few exceptions: people who were ill with the virus when around other people, and people who were at risk for severe illness while caring for someone with the flu.<ref name="cdcmasks">
{{Cite news |url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/chi-tc-health-flu-masks-0923sep27,0,7442578.story |title=Masks may help prevent flu, but aren't advised |vauthors=Roan S |date=27 September 2009 |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=28 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091001105331/http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/chi-tc-health-flu-masks-0923sep27%2C0%2C7442578.story |archive-date=1 October 2009}}</ref> There was some disagreement about the value of wearing face masks, as some experts feared that masks may have given people a false sense of security and should not have replaced other standard precautions.<ref name="LATimes4-30-09">
{{Cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-sci-swine-mask30-2009apr30,0,7635596.story |title=Face masks aren't a sure bet against swine flu |vauthors=Roan S, Rong-Gong II L |date=30 April 2009 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090503142056/http://www.latimes.com/features/health/la-sci-swine-mask30-2009apr30%2C0%2C7635596.story |archive-date=3 May 2009}}</ref>
Yukihiro Nishiyama, professor of virology at [[Nagoya University]]'s School of Medicine, commented that the masks are "better than nothing, but it's hard to completely block out an airborne virus since it can easily slip through the gaps".<ref name="42bp"/><ref name="fashionnetwork"/>
According to mask manufacturer [[3M]], masks will filter out [[Atmospheric particulate matter|particles]] in industrial settings, but "there are no established exposure limits for [[biological agent]]s such as swine flu virus".<ref name="LATimes4-30-09"/> However, despite the lack of evidence of effectiveness, the use of such masks is common in Asia.<ref name="42bp">{{Cite news |url=https://www.smh.com.au/world/face-masks-part-of-japan-fashion-chic-for-decades-20090504-as48.html |title=Face masks part of Japan fashion chic for decades |date=4 May 2009 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |access-date=7 July 2020 |archive-date=8 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200708085652/https://www.smh.com.au/world/face-masks-part-of-japan-fashion-chic-for-decades-20090504-as48.html |url-status=live}}</ref>
<ref name="fashionnetwork">{{Cite news |url=https://ww.fashionnetwork.com/news/Face-masks-part-of-japan-fashion-chic-for-decades,61629.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703170614/https://ww.fashionnetwork.com/news/Face-masks-part-of-japan-fashion-chic-for-decades,61629.html |archive-date=3 July 2020 |title=Face masks part of Japan fashion chic for decades |date=4 May 2009 |work=Fashion Network |publisher=FashionNetwork.com |access-date=3 July 2020 |agency=AFP}}</ref>
<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Business/wireStory?id=8870908 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091024125412/https://abcnews.go.com/Business/wireStory?id=8870908 |archive-date=24 October 2009 |title=Flu-Related Products May Lift U.S. Makers' Profits |vauthors=Wohl J |date=20 October 2009 |publisher=ABC News |location=United States |access-date=28 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> They are particularly popular in Japan, where cleanliness and hygiene are highly valued and where etiquette obligates those who are sick to wear masks to avoid spreading disease.<ref name="42bp"/><ref name="fashionnetwork"/>

====Quarantine====

During the height of the fear of a pandemic, some countries initiated or threatened to initiate [[quarantine]]s of foreign visitors suspected of having or being in contact with others who may have been infected. In May 2009, the Chinese government confined 21 U.S. students and three teachers to their hotel rooms.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.cnn.com/2009/HEALTH/05/28/us.china.swine.flu/ |title=China quarantines U.S. school group over flu concerns |publisher=CNN |date=28 May 2009 |access-date=26 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163940/http://www.cnn.com/2009/HEALTH/05/28/us.china.swine.flu/ |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> As a result, the [[US State Department]] issued a travel alert about China's anti-flu measures and warned travellers against travelling to China if ill.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://washingtontimes.com/news/2009/jun/29/kralev-us-warns-travelers-of-chinas-flu-rules/ |title=U.S. warns travelers of China's flu rules |vauthors=Kralev N |date=29 June 2009 |work=The Washington Times |access-date=26 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163928/http://washingtontimes.com/news/2009/jun/29/kralev-us-warns-travelers-of-chinas-flu-rules/ |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> In Hong Kong, an entire hotel was quarantined with 240 guests;<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2009/05/03/2003442656 |title=Tensions escalate in Hong Kong's swine-flu hotel |date=3 May 2009 |work=Taipei Times |access-date=26 September 2009 |author=DPA |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091107164145/http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2009/05/03/2003442656 |archive-date=7 November 2009}}</ref> Australia ordered a cruise ship with 2,000 passengers to stay at sea because of a swine flu threat.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/stories/2009/05/28/2583515.htm?section=justin |title=Ship passengers cruisy in swine flu quarantine |date=28 May 2009 |publisher=ABC News |location=Australia |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164303/http://www.abc.net.au/news/stories/2009/05/28/2583515.htm?section=justin |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> Egyptian Muslims who went on the annual [[pilgrimage]] to [[Mecca]] risked being quarantined upon their return.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.philstar.com/breaking-news/469538/egypt-warns-post-hajj-swine-flu-quarantine |title=Egypt warns of post-hajj swine flu quarantine |author=Anonymous |date=21 May 2009 |work=The Philippine Star |access-date=16 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140829044024/http://www.philstar.com/breaking-news/469538/egypt-warns-post-hajj-swine-flu-quarantine |archive-date=29 August 2014}}</ref> Russia and Taiwan said they would quarantine visitors with fevers who come from areas where the flu was present.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.accessmylibrary.com/article-1G1-198655440/swine-flu-cases-europe.html |archive-date=22 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822021339/https://www.cengage.com/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Japan quarantined 47 airline passengers in a hotel for a week in mid-May,<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P6fEMGHoQPE |title=Japan Swine Flu Quarantine Ends for Air Passengers |date=17 May 2009 |publisher=New Tang Dynasty Television |access-date=26 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207164750/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P6fEMGHoQPE |archive-date=7 December 2009}}</ref> then in mid-June India suggested pre-screening "outbound" passengers from countries thought to have a high rate of infection.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.internationalreporter.com/News-4898/india-wants-us-to-screen-passengers-for-swine-flu.html |title=India wants US to screen passengers for swine flu |date=16 June 2009 |work=International Reporter |access-date=28 September 2009 |author=MIL/Sify.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100923000245/http://internationalreporter.com/News-4898/india-wants-us-to-screen-passengers-for-swine-flu.html |archive-date=23 September 2010}}</ref>

====Pigs and food safety====

{{Main|2009 swine flu pandemic actions concerning pigs}}

The pandemic virus is a type of swine influenza, derived originally from a strain which lived in pigs, and this origin gave rise to the common name of "swine flu". This term is widely used by mass media, though the Paris-based [[World Organisation for Animal Health]] as well as industry groups such as the U.S. [[National Pork Board]], the [[American Meat Institute]], and the Canadian Pork Council objected to widespread media use of the name "swine flu" and suggested it should be called "North American flu" instead, while the World Health Organization switched its designation from "swine influenza" to "influenza A (H1N1)" in late April 2009.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.france24.com/en/20090501-finally-flu-name-game-resolved- |vauthors=Leela J |title=Finally, the flu name game is resolved |work=[[France 24]] |date=1 May 2009 |access-date=21 March 2020 |archive-date=21 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321080405/https://www.france24.com/en/20090501-finally-flu-name-game-resolved- |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10569528 |title=Label 'swine flu' gets up the nose of world's pig farmers |work=The New Zealand Herald |date=30 April 2009 |access-date=21 March 2020 |archive-date=15 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200415055256/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10569528 |url-status=live}}</ref> The virus has been found in U.S. hogs,<ref>{{Cite news |vauthors=Jordan D |title=Minnesota Pig Tests Positive for H1N1 |url=http://www.newson6.com/Global/story.asp?S=11341148 |publisher=KOTV |date=20 October 2009 |access-date=10 December 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207164317/http://www.newson6.com/Global/story.asp?S=11341148 |archive-date=7 December 2009}}</ref> and Canadian<ref>{{Cite news |vauthors=Evans B |title=News Conference with Minister of Health and Chief Public Health Officer |url=http://www.phac-aspc.gc.ca/alert-alerte/h1n1/conferences/nc-2009-05-02-eng.php |date=5 May 2009 |access-date=10 December 2009 |publisher=Public Health Agency of Canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091214162720/http://www.phac-aspc.gc.ca/alert-alerte/h1n1/conferences/nc-2009-05-02-eng.php |archive-date=14 December 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> as well as in hogs in Northern Ireland, Argentina, and Norway.<ref>{{cite web |title=Human swine flu in pigs |url=http://scienceblogs.com/effectmeasure/2009/10/human_swine_flu_in_pigs.php |date=20 October 2009 |access-date=10 December 2009 |work=Effect Measure |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091108035341/http://scienceblogs.com/effectmeasure/2009/10/human_swine_flu_in_pigs.php |archive-date=8 November 2009}}</ref> Leading health agencies and the [[United States Secretary of Agriculture]] have stressed that eating properly cooked pork or other food products derived from pigs will not cause flu.<ref name=CDC_pork>{{cite press release |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090430/en/index.html |title=Joint FAO/WHO/OIE Statement on influenza A(H1N1) and the safety of pork |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |date=7 May 2009 |access-date=26 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090923210159/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090430/en/index.html |archive-date=23 September 2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |vauthors=Desmon S |title=Pork industry rues swine flu |work=The Baltimore Sun |volume=172 |issue=233 |date=21 August 2009 |pages=1, 16 |url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/health/bal-md.hs.flu21aug21,0,5219798.story |access-date=1 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164004/http://www.baltimoresun.com/health/bal-md.hs.flu21aug21,0,5219798.story |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> Nevertheless, on 27 April, [[Azerbaijan]] imposed a ban on the importation of [[animal husbandry]] products from the entire Americas.<ref name="trend">{{Cite news |url=http://news-en.trend.az/society/health/1462401.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090716080338/http://news-en.trend.az/society/health/1462401.html |archive-date=16 July 2009 |publisher=[[Trend News Agency]] |title=Prevention against "swine flu" stabile in Azerbaijan: minister |date=28 April 2009 |access-date=28 April 2009}}</ref> The Indonesian government also halted the importation of pigs and initiated the examination of {{Nowrap|9 million}} pigs in Indonesia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://nasional.kompas.com/read/xml/2009/04/27/11120229/cegah.flu.babi.pemerintah.gelar.rapat.koordinasi |title=Cegah flu babi, pemerintah gelar rapat Egyptian government ordered the slaughter of all pigs in Egypt on 29 April.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/stories/2009/04/30/2556545.htm?section=justin%20Egypt%20orders%20pig%20cull ==Treatment==

{{Further|Treatment of influenza}}

A number of methods have been recommended to help ease symptoms, including adequate liquid intake and rest.<ref name=Mayo>{{cite web |url=http://www.mayoclinic.com/health/influenza/DS00081/DSECTION=treatments-and-drugs |author=Mayo Clinic Staff |publisher=[[Mayo Clinic]] |work=Diseases and Conditions |title=Influenza (flu) treatments and drugs |access-date=20 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164218/http://www.mayoclinic.com/health/influenza/DS00081/DSECTION=treatments-and-drugs |archive-date=7 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Over-the-counter drug|Over-the-counter]] pain medications such as [[paracetamol]] and [[ibuprofen]] do not kill the virus; however, they may be useful to reduce symptoms.<ref name="Medline"/> [[Aspirin]] and other salicylate products should not be used by people under 16 with any flu-type symptoms because of the risk of developing [[Reye syndrome]].<ref name="National Reyes Syndrome Foundation">{{cite web |url=http://www.reyessyndrome.org/aspirin.html |publisher=National Reye's Syndrome Foundation |title=Aspirin / Salicylates and Reyes Syndrome |access-date=14 April 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719104914/http://www.reyessyndrome.org/aspirin.html |archive-date=19 July 2011 |year=1974}}</ref>

If the fever is mild and there are no other complications, fever medication is not recommended.<ref name="Medline">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003090.htm |publisher=[[U.S. National Library of Medicine]] |encyclopedia=Medline Plus Medical Encyclopedia |title=Fever |access-date=20 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090515173838/http://www.nlm.nih.gov/medlineplus/ency/article/003090.htm |archive-date=15 May 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Most people recover without medical attention, although ones with pre-existing or underlying medical conditions are more prone to complications and may benefit from further treatments.<ref name=CDC_symptoms>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/sick.htm |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |title=What To Do If You Get Sick: 2009 H1N1 and Seasonal Flu |date=7 May 2009 |access-date=1 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103195142/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/sick.htm |archive-date=3 November 2009}}</ref>

People in at-risk groups should be treated with [[antivirals]] (oseltamivir or zanamivir) as soon as possible when they first experience flu symptoms. The at-risk groups include pregnant and [[post partum]] women, children under two years old, and people with underlying conditions such as respiratory problems.<ref name=CDCOct16AntiviralRecommendations/> People who are not in an at-risk group who have persistent or rapidly worsening symptoms should also be treated with antivirals. People who have developed [[Pneumonia#Diagnosis|pneumonia]] should be given both antivirals and antibiotics, as in many severe cases of H1N1-caused illness, bacterial infection develops.<ref name="NikkiShindoNov12">{{Cite news |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/vpc_transcript_12_november_09_nikki_shindo.pdf |title=Transcript of virtual press conference with Gregory Hartl, Spokesperson for H1N1, and Dr Nikki Shindo, Medical Officer, Global Influenza Programme, World Health Organization |date=12 November 2009 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=18 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091129180559/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/vpc_transcript_12_november_09_nikki_shindo.pdf |archive-date=29 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Antivirals are most useful if given within 48 hours of the start of symptoms and may improve outcomes in hospitalised patients.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Jain S, Kamimoto L, Bramley AM, Schmitz AM, Benoit SR, Louie J, Sugerman DE, Druckenmiller JK, Ritger KA, Chugh R, Jasuja S, Deutscher M, Chen S, Walker JD, Duchin JS, Lett S, Soliva S, Wells EV, Swerdlow D, Uyeki TM, Fiore AE, Olsen SJ, Fry AM, Bridges CB, Finelli L |display-authors=6 |title=Hospitalized patients with 2009 H1N1 influenza in the United States, April–June 2009 |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=361 |issue=20 |pages=1935–44 |date=November 2009 |pmid=19815859 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa0906695}}</ref> In those beyond 48 hours who are moderately or severely ill, antivirals may still be beneficial.<ref name=CDCOct16AntiviralRecommendations/> If [[oseltamivir]] (Tamiflu) is unavailable or cannot be used, [[zanamivir]] (Relenza) is recommended as a substitute.<ref name=CDCOct16AntiviralRecommendations/><ref name="WHOAug21antiviralrecommendations">{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_use_antivirals_20090820/en/index.html |title=Recommended use of antivirals |date=21 August 2009 |work=Global Alert and Response (GAR) |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=6 November 2009 |location=Geneva |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091104171524/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_use_antivirals_20090820/en/index.html |archive-date=4 November 2009}}</ref> [[Peramivir]] is an experimental [[antiviral drug]] approved for hospitalised patients in cases where the other available methods of treatment are ineffective or unavailable.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/emergency-use-authorization-granted-for-biocrysts-peramivir-65876107.html |title=Emergency Use Authorization Granted For BioCryst's Peramivir |date=23 October 2009 |agency=PR Newswire |access-date=30 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606053938/http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/emergency-use-authorization-granted-for-biocrysts-peramivir-65876107.html |archive-date=6 June 2011}}</ref>

To help avoid shortages of these drugs, the U.S. CDC recommended oseltamivir treatment primarily for people hospitalised with pandemic flu; people at risk of serious flu complications due to underlying medical conditions; and patients at risk of serious flu complications. The CDC warned that the indiscriminate use of antiviral medications to prevent and treat influenza could ease the way for [[drug-resistant]] strains to emerge, which would make the fight against the pandemic that much harder. In addition, a British report found that people often failed to complete a full course of the drug or took the medication when not needed.<ref name=Tami1>{{Cite news |url=http://www.washingtonexaminer.com/economy/ap/53932902.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164124/http://www.washingtonexaminer.com/economy/ap/53932902.html |archive-date=7 October 2009 |title=WHO: Healthy people who get swine flu don't need Tamiflu; drug for young, old, pregnant |vauthors=Cheng M |date=21 August 2009 |work=[[Washington Examiner]] |access-date=17 September 2009}}</ref>

===Side effects===

Both medications mentioned above for treatment, oseltamivir and zanamivir, have known side effects, including lightheadedness, chills, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and trouble breathing. Children were reported to be at increased risk of self-injury and confusion after taking oseltamivir.<ref name=Mayo/> The WHO warned against buying antiviral medications from online sources and estimated that half the drugs sold by online pharmacies without a physical address were counterfeit.<ref name=onlinedrugs>{{Cite news |url=http://www.webmd.boots.com/cold-and-flu/news/20090508/warning-against-buying-flu-drugs-online |title=Warning against buying flu drugs online |publisher=[[Boots (company)|Boots]] |author=BMJ Group |date=8 May 2009 |access-date=16 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017005011/http://www.webmd.boots.com/cold-and-flu/news/20090508/warning-against-buying-flu-drugs-online |archive-date=17 October 2013}}</ref>

===Resistance===

In December 2012, the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) reported 314 samples of the 2009 pandemic H1N1 flu tested worldwide have shown resistance to [[oseltamivir]] ([[Tamiflu]]).<ref name="Update on oseltamivir resistance to influenza H1N1 (2009) viruses">
{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/influenza/2010_12_15_weekly_web_update_oseltamivir_resistance.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110127001912/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/influenza/2010_12_15_weekly_web_update_oseltamivir_resistance.pdf |archive-date=27 January 2011 |title=Update on oseltamivir resistance to influenza H1N1 (2009) viruses |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |date=15 December 2010 |access-date=30 December 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> It is not totally unexpected as 99.6% of the seasonal H1N1 flu strains tested have developed resistance to oseltamivir.<ref>
{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly39.htm |title=2008–2009 Influenza Season Week 39 ending October 3, 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |date=9 October 2009 |access-date=20 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100306015519/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly39.htm |archive-date=6 March 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> No circulating flu has yet shown any resistance to [[zanamivir]] ([[Relenza]]), the other available anti-viral.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly32.htm |title=2008–2009 Influenza Season Week 32 ending August 15, 2009 |work=Flu Activity & Surveillance |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |date=21 August 2009 |access-date=4 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103235431/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly32.htm |archive-date=3 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Antivirals effectiveness questioned in healthy adults===

On 8 December 2009, the [[Cochrane Collaboration]], which reviews medical evidence, announced in a review published in ''[[BMJ]]'' that it had reversed its previous findings that the antiviral drugs [[oseltamivir]] (Tamiflu) and [[zanamivir]] (Relenza) can ward off [[pneumonia]] and other serious conditions linked to influenza. They reported that an analysis of 20 studies showed oseltamivir offered mild benefits for healthy adults if taken within 24 hours of onset of symptoms, but found no clear evidence it prevented lower respiratory tract infections or other [[complication (medicine)|complications]] of influenza.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601100&sid=a9acc7qIJFdU |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107164229/http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601100&sid=a9acc7qIJFdU |archive-date=7 January 2010 |title=Roche's Tamiflu Not Proven to Cut Flu Complications, Study Says |vauthors=Cortez MF |date=9 December 2009 |publisher=Bloomberg News L.P |access-date=11 December 2009}}</ref><ref name=BMJDec8>{{cite journal |vauthors=Jefferson T, Jones M, Doshi P, Del Mar C |title=Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza in healthy adults: systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=BMJ |volume=339 |article-number=b5106 |date=December 2009 |pmid=19995812 |pmc=2790574 |doi=10.1136/bmj.b5106}}</ref> Of note, their published finding related only to use in healthy adults with influenza but not in patients judged to be at high risk of complications (pregnant women, children under five and those with underlying medical conditions), and uncertainty over its role in reducing complications in healthy adults still left it as a useful drug for reducing the duration of symptoms. In general, the Cochrane Collaboration concluded "Paucity of good data".<ref name=BMJDec8/><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Godlee F |date=10 December 2009 |title=We want raw data, now |journal=BMJ |url=http://www.bmj.com/cgi/content/full/339/dec10_2/b5405 |doi=10.1136/bmj.b5405 |volume=339 |article-number=b5405 |s2cid=72788639 |access-date=14 April 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307163921/http://www.bmj.com/cgi/content/full/339/dec10_2/b5405 |archive-date=7 March 2010 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
