While it is not known precisely where or when the virus originated,<ref name=Nature>{{cite journal |vauthors=Butler D |title=How severe will the flu outbreak be? |journal=Nature |volume=459 |issue=7243 |pages=14–15 |date=May 2009 |pmid=19424121 |pmc=7095218 |doi=10.1038/459014a}}</ref><ref>{{cite video |people=Larry Pope |title=Smithfield Foods CEO on flu virus |url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/21134540 |format=flv |medium=Television production |publisher=NBC News |access-date=16 September 2009 |archive-date=29 January 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130129090138/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/21134540/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> analyses in scientific journals have suggested that the H1N1 strain responsible for the 2009 outbreak first evolved in September 2008 and circulated amongst humans for several months, before being formally recognised and identified as a novel strain of influenza.<ref name=Nature/><ref name="circles globe">{{cite journal |vauthors=Cohen J, Enserink M |title=Infectious diseases. As swine flu circles globe, scientists grapple with basic questions |journal=Science |volume=324 |issue=5927 |pages=572–73 |date=May 2009 |pmid=19407164 |doi=10.1126/science.324_572}}</ref>

===Mexico===

{{Further|2009 swine flu pandemic in Mexico}}

The virus was first reported in two U.S. children in March 2009, but health officials have reported that it apparently infected people as early as January 2009 in Mexico.<ref name="Reuters6-11">{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/middleeastCrisis/idUSN11399103 |title=New flu has been around for years in pigs – study |vauthors=Fox M |date=11 June 2009 |agency=Reuters |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164740/http://www.reuters.com/article/middleeastCrisis/idUSN11399103 |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> The outbreak was first identified in Mexico City on 18 March 2009;<ref name="NYT4-26">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/27/health/27questions.html |title=Flu Outbreak Raises a Set of Questions |vauthors=McNeil Jr DG |date=26 April 2009 |work=The New York Times |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110215221659/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/27/health/27questions.html |archive-date=15 February 2011}}</ref> immediately after the outbreak was officially announced, Mexico notified the U.S. and World Health Organization, and within days of the outbreak Mexico City was "effectively shut down".<ref name="Fox5-12">{{Cite news |url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/study-mexico-has-thousands-more-swine-flu-cases |title=Study: Mexico Has Thousands More Swine Flu Cases |date=12 May 2009 |publisher=Fox News |access-date=17 September 2009 |agency=Associated Press |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090924031546/http://www.foxnews.com/story/0,2933,519902,00.html |archive-date=24 September 2009}}</ref> Some countries cancelled flights to Mexico while others halted trade. Calls to close the border to contain the spread were rejected.<ref name="Fox5-12"/> Mexico already had hundreds of non-lethal cases before the outbreak was officially discovered, and was therefore in the midst of a "silent epidemic". As a result, Mexico was reporting only the most serious cases which showed more severe signs different from those of normal flu, possibly leading to a skewed initial estimate of the case fatality rate.<ref name="NYT4-26"/>

===United States===

{{Further|2009 swine flu pandemic in the United States}}
[[File:Barack Obama Meeting Swine Flu Outbreak 5-1.jpg|thumb|President Obama at [[United States Homeland Security Council|Homeland Security Council]] meeting in Cabinet Room to discuss the H1N1 flu on 1 May 2009]]

The new strain was first identified by the CDC in two children, neither of whom had been in contact with pigs. The first case, from [[San Diego County, California]], was confirmed from clinical specimens ([[nasopharynx|nasopharyngeal]] [[Cotton swab|swab]]) examined by the CDC on 14 April 2009. A second case, from nearby [[Imperial County, California]], was confirmed on 17 April. The patient in the first confirmed case had flu symptoms including fever and cough upon clinical examination on 30 March and the second on 28 March.<ref name="MMWR" />

The first confirmed H1N1/09 pandemic flu death, which occurred at [[Texas Children's Hospital]] in Houston, Texas, was of a toddler from Mexico City who was visiting family in [[Brownsville, Texas]], before being air-lifted to Houston for treatment.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://abc13.com/archive/6786416/ |title=Swine flu victim dies in Houston |date=29 April 2009 |publisher=KTRK-TV/DT |access-date=18 November 2009 |location=Houston, Texas |agency=Associated Press |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091107164755/http://abclocal.go.com/ktrk/story?section=news%2Fhealth&id=6786416&rss=rss-ktrk-article-6786416 |archive-date=7 November 2009}}</ref> The Infectious Diseases Society of America estimated that the total number of deaths in the U.S. was 12,469.<ref name="Estimating the Burden of 2009 Pandemic Influenza A (H1N1) in the United States (April 2009 – April 2010)">{{cite journal |vauthors=Shrestha SS, Swerdlow DL, Borse RH, Prabhu VS, Finelli L, Atkins CY, Owusu-Edusei K, Bell B, Mead PS, Biggerstaff M, Brammer L, Davidson H, Jernigan D, Jhung MA, Kamimoto LA, Merlin TL, Nowell M, Redd SC, Reed C, Schuchat A, Meltzer MI |display-authors=6 |title=Estimating the burden of 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) in the United States (April 2009 – April 2010) |journal=Clinical Infectious Diseases |volume=52 |issue=Suppl 1 |pages=S75-82 |date=January 2011 |pmid=21342903 |doi=10.1093/cid/ciq012 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Data reporting and accuracy<!-- This section is linked to by Template:2009 flu pandemic menu -->===

{{See also|GISAID|National Influenza Centers|Disease surveillance|Clinical surveillance}}

Influenza surveillance information "answers the questions of where, when, and what influenza viruses are circulating. Sharing of such information is especially crucial during an emergent pandemic as in April 2009, when the genetic sequences of the initial viruses were rapidly and openly shared via the GISAID Initiative within days of identification,<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2009/06/pandemic-reveals-strengths-new-flu-database |title=Pandemic reveals strengths of new flu database |work=CIDRAP |access-date=2017-09-06 |archive-date=6 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906092102/http://www.cidrap.umn.edu/news-perspective/2009/06/pandemic-reveals-strengths-new-flu-database |url-status=live}}</ref> playing a key role in facilitating an early response to the evolving pandemic.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Elbe S, Buckland-Merrett G |title=Data, disease and diplomacy: GISAID's innovative contribution to global health |journal=Global Challenges |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=33–46 |date=January 2017 |pmid=31565258 |pmc=6607375 |doi=10.1002/gch2.1018 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017GloCh...1...33E}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/better-flu-vaccine/ |title=Building a Better Flu Vaccine – and Giving Chickens a Rest |vauthors=Greenemeier L |work=Scientific American |access-date=2017-09-06 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906093448/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/better-flu-vaccine/ |archive-date=6 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=McCauley JW |title=Viruses: Model to accelerate epidemic responses |journal=Nature |volume=542 |issue=7642 |page=414 |date=February 2017 |pmid=28230113 |doi=10.1038/542414b |bibcode=2017Natur.542..414M |doi-access=free}}</ref> Surveillance is used to determine if influenza activity is increasing or decreasing, but cannot be used to ascertain how many people have become ill with influenza."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/fluactivity.htm |title=Flu Activity & Surveillance |date=30 November 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=2 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126143103/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/fluactivity.htm |archive-date=26 November 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> For example, as of late June, influenza surveillance information showed the U.S. had nearly 28,000 laboratory-confirmed cases including 3,065 hospitalizations and 127 deaths. But mathematical modelling showed an estimated {{Nowrap|1 million}} Americans had the 2009 pandemic flu at the time, according to [[Lyn Finelli]], a flu surveillance official with the CDC.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2009/06/25/us-swine-flu-cases-may-ha_n_221240.html |title=US Swine Flu Cases May Have Hit 1 Million |vauthors=Stobbe M |date=25 June 2009 |work=The Huffington Post |access-date=2 December 2009 |agency=Associated Press |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207163916/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2009/06/25/us-swine-flu-cases-may-ha_n_221240.html |archive-date=7 December 2009}}</ref> Estimating deaths from influenza is also a complicated process. In 2005, influenza only appeared on the death certificates of 1,812 people in the US. The average annual US death toll from flu is, however, estimated to be 36,000.<ref name="Ellenberg">{{Cite news |url=http://www.slate.com/id/2218367/ |title=Influenza Body Count |vauthors=Ellenberg J |date=4 July 2009 |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |access-date=2 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100115031919/http://www.slate.com/id/2218367/ |archive-date=15 January 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> The CDC explains:<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/disease/us_flu-related_deaths.htm |title=Questions and Answers Regarding Estimating Deaths from Influenza in the United States |date=4 September 2009 |work=Seasonal Influenza (Flu) |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=2 December 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091201101247/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/disease/us_flu-related_deaths.htm |archive-date=1 December 2009}}</ref> "[I]nfluenza is infrequently listed on death certificates of people who die from flu-related complications" and hence, "Only counting deaths where influenza was included on a death certificate would be a gross underestimation of influenza's true impact."

Influenza surveillance information on the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic is available, but almost no studies attempted to estimate the total number of deaths attributable to H1N1 flu. Two studies were carried out by the CDC; the later of them estimated that between 7,070 and 13,930 deaths were attributable to H1N1 flu from April to 14 November 2009.<ref name="WHOestimateNov">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/estimates_2009_h1n1.htm |title=CDC Estimates of 2009 H1N1 Influenza Cases, Hospitalizations and Deaths in the United States, April – December 12, 2009 |date=15 January 2010 |work=H1N1 Flu |publisher=CDC |access-date=17 January 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100119201425/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/estimates_2009_h1n1.htm |archive-date=19 January 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> During the same period, 1,642 deaths were officially confirmed as caused by H1N1 flu.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2009-2010/weekly45.htm |title=CDC week 45 |date=14 November 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=14 December 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107165447/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2009-2010/weekly45.htm |archive-date=7 January 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly34.htm |title=CDC week 34 |date=30 August 2009 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=14 December 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107165933/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly34.htm |archive-date=7 January 2010}}</ref> The WHO stated in 2010 that total mortality (including unconfirmed or unreported deaths) from H1N1 flu was "unquestionably higher" than their own confirmed death statistics.<ref name="WHOstatement">{{Cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601124&sid=akODnI6cicxw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107163907/http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601124&sid=akODnI6cicxw |archive-date=7 January 2010 |vauthors=Gale J |title=Clinical features of severe cases of pandemic influenza |date=4 December 2009 |publisher=Bloomberg News |access-date=4 December 2009}}</ref>

The initial outbreak received a week of near-constant media attention. [[Epidemiologist]]s cautioned that the number of cases reported in the early days of an outbreak can be very inaccurate and deceptive, due to several causes, among them [[selection bias]], [[media bias]] and incorrect reporting by governments. Inaccuracies could also be caused by authorities in different countries looking at differing population groups. Furthermore, countries with poor health care systems and older laboratory facilities may take longer to identify or report cases.<ref>{{Cite news |agency=Reuters |url=http://www.alertnet.org/thenews/newsdesk/IRIN/2687d9562c28b487c30aca4e889c5e93.htm |title=No A (H1N1) cases – reality or poor lab facilities? |date=8 May 2009 |access-date=9 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090511130411/http://www.alertnet.org/thenews/newsdesk/IRIN/2687d9562c28b487c30aca4e889c5e93.htm |archive-date=11 May 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> "[E]ven in developed countries the [numbers of flu deaths] are uncertain, because medical authorities don't usually verify who actually died of influenza and who died of a flu-like illness".<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Sandman P, Lanard J |year=2005 |title=Bird Flu: Communicating the Risk |journal=Perspectives in Health Magazine |volume=10 |issue=2 |url=http://www.paho.org/English/DD/PIN/Number22_article1a.htm |access-date=14 April 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110423155359/http://www.paho.org/English/DD/PIN/Number22_article1a.htm |archive-date=23 April 2011}}</ref> Joseph S. Bresee, then CDC flu division's epidemiology chief and [[Michael Osterholm]], director of the [[Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy]] pointed out that millions of people have had H1N1 flu, usually in a mild form, so the numbers of laboratory-confirmed cases were actually meaningless, and in July 2009, the WHO stopped keeping count of individual cases and focused more on major outbreaks.<ref name="WHO-Briefing-Note-3">{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_surveillance_20090710/en/index.html |title=Pandemic (H1N1) 2009 briefing note 3 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=17 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090722084146/http://www.who.int/csr/disease/swineflu/notes/h1n1_surveillance_20090710/en/index.html |archive-date=22 July 2009}}</ref>

===Follow-up===

A Wisconsin study published in the ''[[Journal of the American Medical Association]]'' in September 2010, reported that findings showed that the 2009 H1N1 flu was no more severe than the seasonal flu. "The risk of most serious complications was not elevated in adults or children", the study's authors wrote. "Children were disproportionately affected by 2009 H1N1 infection, but the perceived severity of symptoms and risk of serious outcomes were not increased." Children infected in the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic were no more likely to be hospitalized with complications or get pneumonia than those who catch seasonal strains. About 1.5% of children with the H1N1 swine flu strain were hospitalized within 30 days, compared with 3.7% of those sick with a seasonal strain of H1N1 and 3.1% with an H3N2 virus.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Randall T |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2010-09-07/swine-flu-in-children-is-no-more-severe-than-seasonal-virus-study-finds.html |title=Swine Flu Found No More Severe Than Seasonal Virus |publisher=Bloomberg News |date=7 September 2010 |access-date=24 May 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100910101552/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2010-09-07/swine-flu-in-children-is-no-more-severe-than-seasonal-virus-study-finds.html |archive-date=10 September 2010}}</ref>

CDC illness and death estimates from April 2009 to April 2010, in the US are as follows:
* between 43&nbsp;million and 89&nbsp;million cases of 2009 H1N1 occurred between April 2009 and 10 April 2010. The mid-level in this range is about 61&nbsp;million people infected with 2009 H1N1.
* between about 195,000 and 403,000 H1N1-related hospitalizations occurred between April 2009 and 10 April 2010. The mid-level in this range is about 274,000 2009 H1N1-related hospitalizations.
* between about 8,870 and 18,300 2009 H1N1-related deaths occurred between April 2009 and 10 April 2010. The mid-level in this range is about 12,470 2009 H1N1-related deaths.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/estimates_2009_h1n1.htm |title=Updated CDC Estimates of 2009 H1N1 Influenza Cases, Hospitalizations and Deaths in the United States, April 2009 – April 10, 2010 |publisher=Cdc.gov |access-date=24 May 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101209191245/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/estimates_2009_h1n1.htm |archive-date=9 December 2010}}</ref><ref name="Estimating the Burden of 2009 Pandemic Influenza A (H1N1) in the United States (April 2009 – April 2010)"/><ref name="Flu Season Continues; Severity Indicators Rise">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/news/flu-severity-rises.htm |title=Flu Season Continues; Severity Indicators Rise |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases (NCIRD) |date=17 January 2014 |access-date=24 January 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140121064156/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/news/flu-severity-rises.htm |archive-date=21 January 2014}}</ref>

It has been stated that about 36,000 die from the seasonal flu in the U.S. each year,<ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Mason M |url=http://health.nytimes.com/health/guides/disease/the-flu/overview.html |title=Flu – Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment of Flu – NY Times Health Information |access-date=24 May 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714223418/http://health.nytimes.com/health/guides/disease/the-flu/overview.html |archive-date=14 July 2011 |newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref> and this is frequently understood as an indication that the H1N1 strain was not as severe as seasonal influenza. The 36,000 estimate was presented in a 2003 study by CDC scientists and refers to a period from 1990 to 1991 through 1998–99. During those years, the number of estimated deaths ranged from 17,000 to 52,000, with an average of about 36,000. Throughout that decade, influenza A (H3N2) was the predominant virus during most of the seasons, and H3N2 influenza viruses are typically associated with higher death rates. The ''JAMA'' study also looked at seasonal influenza-associated deaths over a 23-year period, from 1976 to 1977 and 1998–99 with estimates of respiratory and circulatory influenza-associated deaths ranging from about 5,000 to about 52,000, and an average of about 25,000. CDC believes that the range of deaths over the past 31 years (~3,000 to ~49,000) is a more accurate representation of the unpredictability and variability of flu-associated deaths.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/disease/us_flu-related_deaths.htm#how-many-die |title=Seasonal Influenza (Flu) – Questions and Answers Regarding Estimating Deaths from Influenza in the United States |publisher=Cdc.gov |access-date=23 October 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111016052954/http://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/disease/us_flu-related_deaths.htm#how-many-die |archive-date=16 October 2011}}</ref> The annual toll from seasonal influenza in the US between 1979 and 2001 is estimated at 41,400 deaths on average.<ref name="Average Flu Deaths" /> Therefore, the H1N1 pandemic estimated mortality of 8,870 to 18,300 is just below the mid-range of estimates.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://flu.gov/individualfamily/about/h1n1/estimates_2009_h1n1.html#The%20Numbers |title=CDC Estimates of 2009 H1N1 Influenza Cases, Hospitalizations and Deaths in the United States, April – November 14, 2009 |publisher=Flu.gov |access-date=23 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111209165809/http://www.flu.gov/individualfamily/about/h1n1/estimates_2009_h1n1.html |archive-date=9 December 2011}}</ref>

The 2009 pandemic caused US hospitals to make significant preparations in terms of hospital surge capacities, especially within the emergency department and among vulnerable populations. In many cases, hospitals were relatively successful in making sure that those patients most severely affected by the influenza strain were able to be seen, treated, and discharged in an efficient manner. A case-study of the preparation, planning, mitigation, and response efforts during the fall of 2009 is that of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) which took several steps to increase the emergency department (ED) surge capacity response. CHOP used portions of the main lobby area as an ED waiting room; several of the region's hospital-based outpatient facilities were in use during evening and weekend hours for non-emergency cases; the ED's 24-hour short-stay unit was utilized to care for ED patients in a longer-term capacity; non-board certified physicians (in pediatric emergency medicine) and inpatient-unit medical nurses were utilized for ED patient care; hospital units normally utilized for other medical or therapeutic purposes were transformed into ED patient rooms; and rooms normally used for only one patient were expanded to at least a capacity of 2.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Scarfone RJ, Coffin S, Fieldston ES, Falkowski G, Cooney MG, Grenfell S |title=Hospital-based pandemic influenza preparedness and response: strategies to increase surge capacity |journal=Pediatric Emergency Care |volume=27 |issue=6 |pages=565–72 |date=June 2011 |pmid=21642799 |doi=10.1097/PEC.0b013e31821dc9d1 |s2cid=11222604}}</ref>

==Comparisons to other pandemics and epidemics==
Annual influenza epidemics are estimated to affect 5–15% of the global population. Although most cases are mild, these epidemics still cause severe illness in {{Nowrap|3–5 million}} people and 290,000–650,000 deaths worldwide every year.<ref name="WHO Influenza">{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal) |title=Influenza: Fact sheet |date=6 November 2018 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=25 January 2020 |archive-date=17 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191217001215/https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(seasonal) |url-status=live}}</ref> On average 41,400 people die of influenza-related illnesses each year in the United States, based on data collected between 1979 and 2001.<ref name="Average Flu Deaths">{{cite journal |vauthors=Dushoff J, Plotkin JB, Viboud C, Earn DJ, Simonsen L |title=Mortality due to influenza in the United States – an annualized regression approach using multiple-cause mortality data |journal=American Journal of Epidemiology |volume=163 |issue=2 |pages=181–87 |date=January 2006 |pmid=16319291 |doi=10.1093/aje/kwj024 |quote=The regression model attributes an annual average of 41,400 (95% confidence interval: 27,100, 55,700) deaths to influenza over the period 1979–2001. |doi-access=free}}</ref> In industrialised countries, severe illness and deaths occur mainly in the high-risk populations of infants, the elderly and [[chronic illness|chronically ill]] patients,<ref name="WHO Influenza" /> although the H1N1 flu outbreak (like the 1918 [[Spanish flu]]) differs in its tendency to affect younger, healthier people.<ref name="Swine flu affect the young">{{cite web |url=http://bulletin.aarp.org/yourhealth/diseases/articles/swine_flus_tendency_to_strike_the_young_is_causing_confusion.html |title=Swine flu's tendency to strike the young is causing confusion |date=18 September 2009 |work=Los Angeles Times |vauthors=Kaplan K |access-date=18 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090919215923/http://bulletin.aarp.org/yourhealth/diseases/articles/swine_flus_tendency_to_strike_the_young_is_causing_confusion.html |archive-date=19 September 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In addition to these annual epidemics, Influenza A virus strains caused three global pandemics during the 20th century: the Spanish flu in 1918, [[1957–1958 influenza pandemic|Asian flu]] in 1957, and [[Hong Kong flu]] in 1968–69. These virus strains had undergone [[antigenic shift|major genetic changes]] for which the population did not possess significant [[immunity (medical)|immunity]].<ref name="EID_Pandemics">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kilbourne ED |title=Influenza pandemics of the 20th century |journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=9–14 |date=January 2006 |pmid=16494710 |pmc=3291411 |doi=10.3201/eid1201.051254 |bibcode=2006EIDis..12....9K}}</ref> Recent genetic analysis has revealed that three-quarters, or six out of the eight genetic segments, of the 2009 flu pandemic strain arose from the North American swine flu strains circulating since 1998, when a new strain was first identified on a factory farm in North Carolina, and which was the first-ever reported triple-hybrid flu virus.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.hsus.org/farm/news/ournews/swine_flu_virus_origin_1998_042909.html |title=CDC Confirms Ties to Virus First Discovered in U.S. Pig Factories |vauthors=Greger M |date=26 August 2009 |publisher=The Humane Society of the United States |access-date=21 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090903111344/http://www.hsus.org/farm/news/ournews/swine_flu_virus_origin_1998_042909.html |archive-date=3 September 2009}}</ref>

The [[Spanish flu]] began with a wave of mild cases in the spring, followed by more deadly waves in the autumn, eventually killing hundreds of thousands in the United States and 50–100 million worldwide.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/health/2009-05-26-swine-flu-decrease_N.htm |title=CDC expert says flu outbreak is dying down – for now |vauthors=Sternberg S |date=26 May 2009 |work=USA Today |access-date=17 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007163933/http://www.usatoday.com/news/health/2009-05-26-swine-flu-decrease_N.htm |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref> The great majority of deaths in the 1918 flu pandemic were the result of secondary bacterial pneumonia. The influenza virus damaged the lining of the [[bronchial tube]]s and lungs of patients, allowing common bacteria from the nose and throat to infect their lungs. Subsequent pandemics have had many fewer fatalities due to the development of antibiotic medicines which can treat pneumonia.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Morens DM, Taubenberger JK, Fauci AS |title=Predominant role of bacterial pneumonia as a cause of death in pandemic influenza: implications for pandemic influenza preparedness |journal=The Journal of Infectious Diseases |volume=198 |issue=7 |pages=962–70 |date=October 2008 |pmid=18710327 |pmc=2599911 |doi=10.1086/591708}}</ref>
{{Notable flu pandemics}}

The influenza virus has caused several pandemic threats over the past century, including the pseudo-pandemic of 1947 (thought of as mild because although globally distributed, it caused relatively few deaths),<ref name="EID_Pandemics" /> the [[1976 swine flu outbreak]] and the [[Influenza A virus subtype H1N1#1977 Russian flu|1977 Russian flu]], all caused by the H1N1 subtype.<ref name="EID_Pandemics"/> The world has been at an increased level of alert since the [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome|SARS]] epidemic in Southeast Asia (caused by the [[SARS coronavirus]]).<ref>{{Cite news |date=29 April 2009 |vauthors=Brown D |title=System set up after SARS epidemic was slow to alert global authorities |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/29/AR2009042904911.html |access-date=26 September 2009 |archive-date=7 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090507163851/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/29/AR2009042904911.html |url-status=live}}</ref> The level of preparedness was further increased and sustained with the advent of the [[Influenza A virus subtype H5N1|H5N1 bird flu]] outbreaks because of H5N1's high fatality rate, although the strains currently prevalent have limited human-to-human transmission ([[anthroponotic]]) capability, or epidemicity.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Beigel JH, Farrar J, Han AM, Hayden FG, Hyer R, de Jong MD, Lochindarat S, Nguyen TK, Nguyen TH, Tran TH, Nicoll A, Touch S, Yuen KY |display-authors=6 |title=Avian influenza A (H5N1) infection in humans |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=353 |issue=13 |pages=1374–85 |date=September 2005 |pmid=16192482 |doi=10.1056/NEJMra052211 |collaboration=Writing Committee of the World Health Organization (WHO) Consultation on Human Influenza A/H5}}</ref>

People who contracted influenza before 1957 appeared to have some immunity to H1N1 flu. According to Daniel Jernigan, head of flu epidemiology for the U.S. CDC "Tests on blood serum from older people showed that they had antibodies that attacked the new virus&nbsp;... That does not mean that everyone over 52 is immune, since Americans and Mexicans older than that have died of the new flu".<ref name="Don McNeil, 20 May">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/21/health/21swineflu.html |title=U.S. Says Older People Appear Safer From New Flu Strain |work=The New York Times |vauthors=McNeil Jr DG |date=20 May 2009 |access-date=26 September 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007164253/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/21/health/21swineflu.html |archive-date=7 October 2009}}</ref>

In June 2012, a model based study found that the number of deaths related to the H1N1 influenza may have been fifteen times higher than the reported laboratory confirmed deaths, with 80% of the respiratory and cardiovascular deaths in people younger than 65 years and 51% occurring in southeast Asia and Africa. A disproportionate number of pandemic deaths might have occurred in these regions and that efforts to prevent future influenza pandemics need to effectively target these regions.<ref name="zenodo yahoo"/>

A WHO-supported 2013 study estimated that the 2009 global pandemic respiratory mortality was ~10-fold higher than the World Health Organization's laboratory-confirmed mortality count (18.631). Although the pandemic mortality estimate was similar in magnitude to that of seasonal influenza, a marked shift toward mortality among persons less than 65 years of age occurred, so that many more life-years were lost. Between 123,000 and 203,000 pandemic respiratory deaths were estimated globally for the last nine months of 2009. The majority (62–85%) were attributed to persons under 65 years of age. The burden varied greatly among countries. There was an almost 20-fold higher mortality in some countries in the Americas than in Europe. The model attributed 148,000–249,000 respiratory deaths to influenza in an average pre-pandemic season, with only 19% in persons <65 years of age.<ref name="mortality estimate worldwide"/>

The [[COVID-19 pandemic]] is not caused by an influenza virus but [[SARS-CoV-2]], a coronavirus which also primarily affects the respiratory system.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: 2025 Birthday Honours
======================================================================

{{Short description|Appointments made by King Charles III}}
{{Use British English|date=June 2025}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2025}}
The '''2025 King's Birthday and Operational Honours''' are appointments by some of the 15 [[Commonwealth realm]]s of [[Charles III|King Charles III]] to [[Orders and decorations of the Commonwealth realms|various orders and honours]] to reward and highlight good works by citizens of those countries. The [[Birthday Honours]] are awarded as part of the [[King's Official Birthday]] celebrations during the month of June. The honours list for the United Kingdom was announced on 14 June 2025.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4g64e1e5xyo |title=King's Birthday Honours: How does the UK honours system work? |date=8 June 2025 |work=[[BBC News Online]] |access-date=10 June 2025}}</ref> The 2025 Operational Honours (June) were awarded embedded with the Birthday Honours list.<ref>{{cite web |title=2025 Birthday and Operational Honours |url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/all-notices/content/104381 |publisher=London Gazette |access-date=15 June 2025}}</ref>

The King appoints members to the orders upon the advice of his ministers. However, the [[Order of the Garter]], the [[Order of the Thistle]], the [[Order of Merit]] and the [[Royal Victorian Order]] are bestowed solely by the sovereign.

In the 2025 Birthday Honours, former [[rugby league]] player [[Billy Boston]] received a knighthood for his services, becoming the first rugby league personality to have that honour. His knighthood was made public earlier than the official announcement due to concerns regarding Boston's health.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz0d5zr2g20o.amp | title=Billy Boston becomes first ever rugby league knight }}</ref> The knighthood came one week after media criticism regarding the fact that no one from the sport had ever been knighted, with analysts stating that this is an illustration of how people from working class backgrounds are overlooked in the honours lists. In the previous honours list, the BBC reported that 4% of recipients were from a working class upbringing.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgeg74j4w1ro.amp | title=Rugby league honours: Anger at no knighthoods in 130 years | date=31 May 2025 }}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy
======================================================================

{{Short description|Fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle}}
{{Redirect|Mad cow}}
{{cs1 config|name-list-style=vanc}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2024}}
