WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Chinese government response to COVID-19
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2022}}
{{COVID-19 pandemic sidebar}}
During the [[COVID-19 pandemic in mainland China]], the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP) and [[government of China]] under CCP general secretary [[Xi Jinping]]'s [[General secretaryship of Xi Jinping|administration]] pursued a [[zero-COVID]] strategy to prevent the domestic spread of [[COVID-19]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mallapaty |first1=Smriti |title=China's zero-COVID strategy: what happens next? |journal=Nature |date=27 January 2022 |volume=602 |issue=7895 |pages=15–16 |doi=10.1038/d41586-022-00191-7 |pmid=35087249 |bibcode=2022Natur.602...15M |s2cid=246360742 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-022-00191-7 |access-date=13 February 2022 |language=en|quote="China's stringent zero-COVID strategy is likely to face its toughest test yet in the next few weeks, as millions of people travel around the country for Chinese New Year, and the Winter Olympics begin in Beijing. The approach — which was introduced by the central government early in the pandemic and has involved large-scale lockdowns, mass testing and international travel bans..."|url-access=subscription }}</ref> until late 2022.<ref name=":222"/> Aspects of the response have been controversial, with the zero-COVID approach being praised<ref name="Lancet-ID-Burki-2020">{{cite journal |journal=The Lancet Infectious Diseases |first=Talha |last=Burki |volume=20 |issue=11 |pages=1240–1241 |date=8 October 2020 |doi=10.1016/S1473-3099(20)30800-8 |title=China's successful control of COVID-19|pmid=33038941 |pmc=7544475 }}</ref><ref name="Policy Design and Practice">{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=Alex Jingwei|last2=Shi|first2=Yuda|last3=Liu|first3=Hongdou|date=2020-07-02|title=Crisis governance, Chinese style: distinctive features of China's response to the Covid-19 pandemic|journal=Policy Design and Practice|volume=3|issue=3|pages=242–258|doi=10.1080/25741292.2020.1799911|s2cid=225430128|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the government's lack of transparency,<ref name=ap24fbadc58cee3a40bca2ddf7a14d2955>{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/united-nations-coronavirus-pandemic-china-only-on-ap-bats-24fbadc58cee3a40bca2ddf7a14d2955|title=China clamps down in hidden hunt for coronavirus origins|website=AP News|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|date=29 December 2020|access-date=20 June 2022|last1=Kang|first1=Dave|last2=Cheng|first2=Maria|last3=McNeil|first3=Sam|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220618002421/https://apnews.com/article/united-nations-coronavirus-pandemic-china-only-on-ap-bats-24fbadc58cee3a40bca2ddf7a14d2955|archive-date=18 June 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=pbschinas-covid-secrets>{{cite web|date=2 February 2021|title=China's COVID secrets - Transcript|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/documentary/chinas-covid-secrets/transcript/?|work=PBS|access-date=2 February 2022}}</ref> censorship,<ref name=nyt20201219>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/19/technology/china-coronavirus-censorship.html|title=No 'Negative' News: How China Censored the Coronavirus|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=20 June 2022|url-access=limited|date=19 December 2020|last1=Zhong|first1=Raymond|last2=Mozur|first2=Paul|last3=Kao|first3=Jeff|last4=Krolik|first4=Aaron|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615075513/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/19/technology/china-coronavirus-censorship.html|archive-date=15 June 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=bbc55355401>{{Cite web|title=China Covid-19: How state media and censorship took on coronavirus|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-55355401|website=[[BBC News]]|publisher=[[BBC]]|date=29 December 2020|access-date=20 June 2022|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513231506/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-55355401|archive-date=13 May 2022}}</ref> and spread of misinformation<ref name=doi10.37016mr-2020-025>{{Cite journal|last1=Molter|first1=Vanessa|last2=DiResta|first2=Renee|date=8 June 2020|title=Pandemics & propaganda: how Chinese state media creates and propagates CCP coronavirus narratives|url=https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/pandemics-propaganda-how-chinese-state-media-creates-and-propagates-ccp-coronavirus-narratives/|journal=Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review|language=en-US|volume=1|issue=3|doi=10.37016/mr-2020-025|doi-access=free|access-date=8 February 2021|archive-date=9 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109173716/https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/pandemics-propaganda-how-chinese-state-media-creates-and-propagates-ccp-coronavirus-narratives/|url-status=live}}</ref> being criticized. The government abandoned its zero-COVID policy on 7 December 2022.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Dyer |first=Owen |date=2023 |title=Covid-19: China stops counting cases as models predict a million or more deaths |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=380 |page=2 |doi=10.1136/bmj.p2 |doi-access=free |issn=1756-1833 |pmid=36596574 |s2cid=255373483 }}</ref>

After discovery of a cluster of patients with [[pneumonia]] of unknown [[Cause (medicine)|etiology]] in [[Wuhan]], Hubei Province, a public notice on the outbreak was distributed on 31 December 2019.<ref name="Science-Tian-2020"/> Three days earlier on 28 December 2019, Chinese researchers in Beijing uploaded a fully mapped sequence of COVID-19's structure to the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] [[GenBank]], but the report was never publicly accessible due to it missing technical, non-scientific information required for submission despite NIH attempts to communicate with the report author.<ref name=WSJ17Jan2024>{{Cite news|last=Strobel|first=Warren P.|date=17 January 2024|title=Chinese Lab Mapped Deadly Coronavirus Two Weeks Before Beijing Told the World, Documents Show|work=The Wall Street Journal|url=https://www.wsj.com/world/china/chinese-lab-mapped-deadly-coronavirus-two-weeks-before-beijing-told-the-world-documents-show-9bca8865|url-status=live|url-access=subscription|access-date=17 January 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117224039/https://www.wsj.com/world/china/chinese-lab-mapped-deadly-coronavirus-two-weeks-before-beijing-told-the-world-documents-show-9bca8865|archive-date=17 January 2024|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> On 8 January 2020, a new [[coronavirus]] ([[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]]) was announced by Chinese scientists as the cause of the new disease;<ref name=WSJ9Jan2020>{{Cite news|last=Khan|first=Natasha|date=9 January 2020|title=New Virus Discovered by Chinese Scientists Investigating Pneumonia Outbreak|work=The Wall Street Journal|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/new-virus-discovered-by-chinese-scientists-investigating-pneumonia-outbreak-11578485668|url-status=live|url-access=subscription|access-date=2 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202154104/https://www.wsj.com/articles/new-virus-discovered-by-chinese-scientists-investigating-pneumonia-outbreak-11578485668|archive-date=2 February 2020|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> and on 10 January a nearly identical virus to the 28 December upload was sequenced and its genome made available online.<ref name=CDC13Jan2020>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/novel-coronavirus-2019.html|title=Novel Coronavirus 2019 {{!}} CDC|date=13 January 2020|website=www.cdc.gov|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200114084712/https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/novel-coronavirus-2019.html|archive-date=14 January 2020|access-date=14 January 2020}}</ref> On 17 January 2024, ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' released a report about the former 28 December upload that officially contradicted the Chinese government's claim that knowledge of the cause of the outbreak in the early weeks of January 2020 was unknown, and that information was shared as soon as it was available.<ref name=WSJ17Jan2024 />

On 23 January 2020, the Chinese government banned travel to and from Wuhan, enforced [[COVID-19 lockdown in China|strict quarantines in affected regions]] and initiated a national response.<ref name="Science-Tian-2020"/> The [[COVID-19 pandemic in Hubei|epidemic in Hubei province]] peaked on 4 February 2020.<ref name="Science-Tian-2020">{{cite journal |title=An investigation of transmission control measures during the first 50 days of the COVID-19 epidemic in China |date=31 March 2020 |journal=Science |volume=368 |issue=6491 |pages=638–642 |doi=10.1126/science.abb6105 |first1=Huaiyu |last1=Tian|first2=Yonghong |last2=Liu |first3=Yidan |last3=Li |first4=Chieh-Hsi |last4=Wu |first5=Bin |last5=Chen |first6=Moritz U. G. |last6=Kraemer |first7=Bingying |last7=Li |first8=Jun |last8=Cai |first9=Bo |last9=Xu |first10=Qiqi |last10=Yang |first11=Ben |last11=Wang |first12=Peng |last12=Yang |first13=Yujun |last13=Cui |first14=Yimeng |last14=Song |first15=Pai |last15=Zheng |first16=Quanyi |last16=Wang |author17-link=Ottar Nordal Bjørnstad |first17=Ottar N. |last17=Bjornstad |first18=Ruifu |last18=Yang |first19=Bryan T. |last19=Grenfell |first20=Oliver G. |last20=Pybus |first21=Christopher |last21=Dye|pmid=32234804 |pmc=7164389 |bibcode=2020Sci...368..638T }}</ref> Large temporary hospitals were built in Wuhan to [[Isolation (health care)|isolate]] patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms, with the first opening on 5 February 2020.<ref name="Lancet-ID-Burki-2020"/> The epidemic was heavily concentrated within Hubei province and Wuhan. Through 22 March 2020, over 80% of the recorded cases in China were in Hubei province, with over 60% of cases nationwide occurring in Wuhan alone.<ref name="JTD-Zanin-2020">
{{cite journal |journal=Journal of Thoracic Disease |doi=10.21037/jtd-20-2363 |volume=12 |issue=8 |pages=4434–4449 |title=The public health response to the COVID-19 outbreak in mainland China: a narrative review |first1=Mark |last1=Zanin |first2=Cheng |last2=Xiao |first3=Tingting |last3=Liang |first4=Shiman |last4=Ling |first5=Fengming |last5=Zhao |first6=Zhenting |last6=Huang |first7=Fangmei |last7=Lin |first8=Xia |last8=Lin |first9=Zhanpeng |last9=Jiang |first10=Sook-San |last10=Wong |date=August 2020 |pmid=32944357|pmc=7475588 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

By the summer of 2020, China had largely brought [[2020 COVID-19 outbreak in mainland China|the outbreak]] under control, ending widespread community transmission.<ref name="Lancet-COVID-China-lessons">{{cite journal |title=COVID-19 and China: lessons and the way forward |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31637-8 |journal=The Lancet |date=25 July 2020 |volume=396 |issue=10246 |page=213|last1=Lancet |first1=The |pmid=32711779 |pmc=7377676 }}</ref> After the initial outbreak, lockdowns and other restrictive measures were eased throughout China.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021">{{cite journal |journal=Global Health Action |doi=10.1080/16549716.2021.1875601 |title=COVID-19 in Germany and China: mitigation versus elimination strategy |date=20 January 2021 |first1=Guangyu |last1= Lu |first2=Oliver |last2=Razum |first3=Albrecht |last3=Jahn |first4=Yuying |last4=Zhang |first5=Brett |last5=Sutton |first6=Devi |last6=Sridhar |first7=Koya |last7=Ariyoshi |first8=Lorenz |last8=von Seidlein |first9=Olaf |last9=Müllerc|volume=14 |issue=1 |article-number=1875601 |pmid=33472568 |pmc=7833051 |s2cid=231663818 }}</ref> The lockdown in Wuhan was lifted on 8 April 2020.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/> It is estimated that the epidemic control measures held the death toll due to COVID-19 in Wuhan to under 5,000 from January to March 2020.<ref name="BMJ-Liu-2021">{{cite journal |journal=The BMJ |doi=10.1136/bmj.n415 |title=Excess mortality in Wuhan city and other parts of China during the three months of the covid-19 outbreak: findings from nationwide mortality registries |date=24 February 2021 |first1=Jiangmei |last1=Liu |first2=Lan |last2=Zhang |first3=Yaqiong |last3=Yan |first4=Yuchang |last4=Zhou |first5=Peng |last5=Yin |first6=Jinlei |last6=Qi |first7=Lijun |last7=Wang|volume=372 |article-number=n415 |pmid=33627311 |pmc=7900645 }}</ref>

China was one of a small number of countries that pursued an elimination strategy, sustaining zero or low case numbers over the long term.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/>  Until late 2022, most cases in China were imported from abroad, and several new outbreaks were quickly controlled through intense short-term public health measures, including large-scale testing, contact tracking technology, and mandatory isolation of infected individuals.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/> In the 18 months following containment of the initial outbreak in Wuhan, two COVID-19 deaths were recorded.<ref name="BMJ-An-2021"/><ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/> In December 2022, the Chinese government ended its zero-COVID policy and mass testing following [[2022 COVID-19 protests in China|protests across the country]].<ref name=":222">{{cite news |date=7 December 2022 |title=China Eases 'Zero Covid' Restrictions in Victory for Protesters |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/07/world/asia/china-zero-covid-protests.html |url-status=live |url-access=subscription |access-date=12 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221210072410/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/07/world/asia/china-zero-covid-protests.html |archive-date=10 December 2022}}</ref>

In 2020 and 2021, China was the largest exporter of COVID-19 critical medical products.<ref name="WTO-medical-goods-2021">{{cite report |title=Trade in Medical Goods in the Context of Tackling COVID-19: Developments in the First Half of 2021 |publisher=World Trade Organization |url=https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/news21_e/covid_30jun21b_e.htm |date=14 December 2021 |access-date=25 December 2021}}</ref><ref name="WTO-medical-goods-2020">{{cite report |title=Trade in Medical Goods in the Context of Tackling COVID-19: Developments in the First Half of 2020 |publisher=World Trade Organization |url=https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/news20_e/covid_22dec20_e.htm |date=22 December 2020 |access-date=25 December 2021}}</ref> China was the world's largest exporter of [[Face masks during the COVID-19 pandemic|face masks]], increasing exports by around 600% in the first half of 2020.<ref name="WTO-medical-goods-2020"/> A number of [[COVID-19 vaccine]]s have been developed in China, which have been used in its [[COVID-19 vaccination in mainland China|vaccination programme]] and international [[vaccine diplomacy]]. Through November 2021, China was the world's largest exporter of COVID-19 vaccines, with a cumulative share of around 40% of worldwide exports (totalling around 1.5 billion doses), according to the [[World Trade Organization]].<ref name="WTO-vaccine-tracker">{{cite web |publisher=World Trade Organization |title=WTO-IMF COVID-19 Vaccine Trade Tracker |date=17 December 2021 |access-date=25 December 2021 |url=https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/covid19_e/vaccine_trade_tracker_e.htm}}</ref>

China's response to the initial [[Wuhan Coronavirus outbreak|Wuhan COVID-19 outbreak]] has been both praised and criticised. In October 2020, ''The Lancet Infectious Diseases'' reported: "While the world is struggling to control COVID-19, China has managed to control the pandemic rapidly and effectively."<ref name="Lancet-ID-Burki-2020"/> The Chinese government has been criticized for [[Censorship in China|censorship]], which observers have attributed to a culture of institutional censorship affecting the country's [[Mass media in China|press]] and [[Internet in China|Internet]]. The government censored [[whistleblower]]s, [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on journalism|journalists]], and [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on social media|social media posts]] about the outbreak. During the beginning of the pandemic, the Chinese government made efforts to clamp down on discussion and hide reporting about it, as such information was seen as unfavorable for local officials. Efforts to fund and control [[Investigations into the origin of COVID-19|research into the virus's origins]] have continued up to the present.<ref name="ChinaClampsDownAp">{{cite news|last1=Cheng|first1=Maria|last2=Kang|first2=Dake|last3=McNeil|first3=Sam|date=30 December 2020|title=China clamps down in hidden hunt for coronavirus origins|website=AP News|publisher=Associated Press|url=https://apnews.com/article/united-nations-coronavirus-pandemic-china-only-on-ap-bats-24fbadc58cee3a40bca2ddf7a14d2955|access-date=18 January 2022}}</ref>

== Initial response ==
{{See also|2020 COVID-19 outbreak in mainland China}}
Based on retrospective case analysis of Chinese government published data, the first person known to have fallen ill with COVID-19 in Wuhan first began experiencing symptoms on 1 December 2019.<ref name="Nature-Zhang-Jan2021">{{cite journal |title=Transmission dynamics and control measures of COVID-19 outbreak in China: a modelling study |date=29 January 2021 |journal=Scientific Reports |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-81985-z  |doi-access=free|first1=Xu-Sheng |last1=Zhang |first2=Emilia |last2=Vynnycky |first3=Andre |last3=Charlett |first4=Daniela |last4=De Angelis |first5=Zhengji |last5=Chen |first6=Wei |last6=Liu |volume=11|issue=1 |page=2652 |pmid=33514781 |pmc=7846591 |bibcode=2021NatSR..11.2652Z }}</ref> However, according to secret government documents reported on by the ''[[South China Morning Post]]'', index cases were traced back to 17 November.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/society/article/3074991/coronavirus-chinas-first-confirmed-covid-19-case-traced-back | title=China's first confirmed Covid-19 case traced back to November 17 | date=13 March 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/mar/13/first-covid-19-case-happened-in-november-china-government-records-show-report | title=First Covid-19 case happened in November, China government records show - report | website=[[TheGuardian.com]] | date=13 March 2020 }}</ref> In mid December 2019, Wuhan doctors noticed a pattern of unusual white spots in patients' lung scans. On 24 December, a sample was sent to a Chinese lab called Vision Medicals. On the 26th, a tech at Vision Medicals obtained a partial DNA sequence and noticed it was similar to [[SARS]]. The alarmed tech forwarded the information to his boss, but the information was not made public at the time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzbcG7CRYgQ|title=China's COVID secrets (full documentary)|work=PBS|date=2 February 2021|access-date=25 December 2021|at=11:00-15:00}}</ref> Doctors in Wuhan noticed a cluster of patients with pneumonia of unknown etiology in late December 2019. A public notice on the outbreak was released by Wuhan health authority on 31 December; the initial notice informed Wuhan residents that there was no clear evidence of human-to-human transmission of the virus, that the disease is preventable and controllable, and that people can wear masks when going out. WHO picked up news reports of the outbreak on the same day. Warnings by doctors were at first ignored by local government officials.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/30/world/asia/china-coronavirus.html|title=25 days that changed the world: how Covid-19 slipped China's grasp|first1=Chris|last1=Buckley|first2=David D.|last2=Kirkpatrick|first3=Amy|last3=Qin|first4=Javier C.|last4=Hernández|date=30 December 2020|access-date=11 January 2022|work=The New York Times}}</ref> Chinese researchers had mapped and fully sequenced COVID-19's genome by at least 28 December 2019, when Dr. Lili Ren, a virologist at the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College in Beijing uploaded its sequence to the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] [[GenBank]]. The submission was never publicly available after it failed to include technical, non-scientific information required for publication, and attempts by the NIH to contact Dr. Ren went unanswered.<ref name=WSJ17Jan2024 />

On 7 January 2020, the [[Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party|Politburo Standing Committee]] of the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP) discussed COVID-19 prevention and control.<ref>{{cite news |title=Highlights: China's Xi recounts early role in coronavirus battle |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-xi-highlights/highlights-chinas-xi-recounts-early-role-in-coronavirus-battle-idUSKBN20B1MC |access-date=18 January 2024 |work=Reuters |date=17 February 2020 }}</ref> On 8 January 2020, a new [[coronavirus]] ([[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]]) was announced by Chinese scientists as the cause of the new disease;<ref name=WSJ9Jan2020 /> and on 10 January a nearly identical virus to the 28 December upload was sequenced and its genome made available online.<ref name=CDC13Jan2020 /> On 17 January 2024, ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' released a report detailing the former 28 December submission, contradicting the Chinese government's claims that the cause of the outbreak was unknown in early January 2020 and information was shared as soon as it was made available.<ref name=WSJ17Jan2024 />

Within three weeks of the first known cases, the government built sixteen large mobile hospitals in Wuhan and sent 40,000 medical staff to the city.<ref name=":0242">{{Cite book |last=Jin |first=Keyu |title=The New China Playbook: Beyond Socialism and Capitalism |date=2023 |publisher=Viking |isbn=978-1-9848-7828-1 |location=New York |author-link=Keyu Jin}}</ref>{{Rp|page=137}}

Initially, the Chinese government was against the World Health Organization declaring a public health emergency, but eventually a public health emergency was declared on 30 January.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/11/02/world/who-china-coronavirus.html|title = In Hunt for Virus Source, W.H.O. Let China Take Charge|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 2 November 2020|last1 = Gebrekidan|first1 = Selam|last2 = Apuzzo|first2 = Matt|last3 = Qin|first3 = Amy|last4 = Hernández|first4 = Javier C.}}</ref>

=== 2020 Chinese New Year ===
The Wuhan government, which announced a number of new measures such as cancelling the [[Chinese New Year]] celebrations, in addition to measures such as checking the temperature of passengers at transport terminals first introduced on 14 January.

Beginning on 23 January 2020, [[2020 Hubei lockdowns|extensive lockdown measures]] were taken in Hubei province, and then in much of China. Travel in and out of Wuhan was halted on 23 January,<ref name="Policy Design and Practice"/> and travel restrictions were implemented throughout China.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/> A group tasked with the prevention and control of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] was established on 26 January, led by [[Premier of the People's Republic of China|Chinese Premier]] [[Li Keqiang]]. The leading group decided to extend the Spring Festival [[Golden Week (China)|holiday]] to contain the outbreak.

China Customs started requiring that all passengers entering and exiting China fill in an extra health declaration form from 26 January. The health declaration form was mentioned in China's Frontier Health and Quarantine Law, granting the customs rights to require it if needed. On 27 January, the [[General Office of the State Council]] of China, declared a nationwide extension on the New Year holiday and the postponement of the coming spring semester. The office extended the previously scheduled [[Public holidays in China|public holiday]] from 30 January, to 2 February, while it said school openings for the spring semester would be announced in the future.

=== Declaration of emergency ===
[[File:A_Screen_Display_During_Wuhan_Coronavirus_Outbreak.jpg|right|thumb|A screen display in [[Hefei]] showing "early detection, early reporting, early quarantine, early diagnosis, early treatment" during the COVID-19 pandemic]]

Hong Kong's [[Chief Executive of Hong Kong|Chief Executive]] [[Carrie Lam]] declared an emergency at a press conference on 25 January, saying [[Government of Hong Kong|the government]] would close primary and secondary schools for two more weeks on top of the previously scheduled New Year holiday, pushing the date for school reopening to 17 February. Macau closed several museums and libraries, and prolonged the New Year holiday break to 11 February for higher education institutions and 10 February for others.{{fact|date=May 2026}}

On 1 February 2020, Xinhua News reported that China's [[Supreme People's Procuratorate]] (SPP) had "asked procuratorates nationwide to fully play their role to create a favourable judicial environment in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic". This included severe punishments for those found guilty of dereliction of duty and the withholding of information for officials. Tougher charges were proscribed for commercial criminal activities such as increasing prices, profiteering along with the "production and sale of fake and shoddy protective equipment and medicines". Prosecuting actions against patients who deliberately spread the infection or refuse examination or compulsory isolation along with threats of violence against medical personnel were also urged. The statement also included urging to prosecute those found fabricating and spreading COVID-19-related information and also stressed "harshly punishing the illegal hunting of wildlife under state protection, as well as improving inspection and quarantine measures for fresh food and meat products".{{fact|date=May 2026}}

=== Cordon sanitaire ===
[[File:Wuhan_citizens_rush_to_buy_vegetables_during_Wuhan_coronavirus_outbreak.jpg|thumb|Wuhan residents buying vegetables at a market after the lockdown was announced]]

{{Main|COVID-19 lockdown in China}}
On 23 January 2020, a [[cordon sanitaire (medicine)|cordon sanitaire]] on [[Lockdown|travel in and out]] of Wuhan was imposed in an effort to stop the spread of the virus out of Wuhan. Flights, trains, public buses, the metro system, and long-distance coaches were suspended indefinitely. Large-scale gatherings and group tours were also suspended. By 24 January 2020, a total of 15 cities in Hubei, including Wuhan, were placed under similar quarantine measures.

Due to lockdown measures, Wuhan residents rushed to stockpile essential goods, food, and fuel; prices rose significantly. 5,000,000 people left Wuhan, with 9,000,000 left in the city. The city of [[Shantou]] in Guangdong declared a partial lockdown on 26 January, though this was reversed two hours later. Local authorities in Beijing and several other major cities, including [[Hangzhou]], [[Guangzhou]], Shanghai, and [[Shenzhen]], announced on the same day that these cities will not impose a lockdown similar to those in Hubei province.

By 6 February 2020, a total of four Zhejiang cities—Wenzhou, Hangzhou, Ningbo, and Taizhou—were under the "passport" system, allowing only one person per household to leave their home every two days. These restrictions apply to over 30&nbsp;million people.

=== Specialty hospitals ===
[[File:Wuhan_Huoshenshan_Hospital_under_construction_02.jpg|right|thumb|Construction site of [[Huoshenshan Hospital]] as it appeared on 24 January]]
A specialty hospital named [[Huoshenshan Hospital]] has been constructed as a countermeasure against the outbreak and to better quarantine the patients. Wuhan City government had demanded that a state-owned enterprise construct such a hospital "at the fastest speed" comparable to that of the [[2002–2004 SARS outbreak|SARS outbreak in 2003]]. Upon opening, the specialty hospital had 1,000 beds and took up 30,000 square metres. The hospital is modelled after the {{ill|Xiaotangshan Hospital|zh|小汤山医院|preserve=1}}, which was fabricated for the SARS outbreak of 2003, itself built in only seven days.

On 24 January 2020, the authority announced that they would convert an empty building in [[Huangzhou District]], Huanggang to a 1,000-bed hospital named [[Dabie Mountain Regional Medical Centre]]. Works began the next day by 500 personnel and the building began accepting patients on 28 January 2020 at 10:30&nbsp;pm. In Wuhan, authorities seized dormitories, offices and hospitals to create more beds for patients. On 25 January authorities announced plans for [[Leishenshan Hospital]], a second specialty hospital, with a capacity of 1,600 beds; operations are scheduled to start by 6 February. The hospital opened on 8 February.

By 16 February 2020, 217 teams of a total of 25,633 medical workers from across China went to Wuhan and other cities in Hubei to help open up more facilities and treat patients. A total of 14 temporary hospitals were constructed in China in total, but all were reported to have closed after the crisis was determined be under control on 10 March 2020.<ref>{{cite news|date=10 March 2020|title=Coronavirus: China says disease 'curbed' in Wuhan and Hubei|work=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-china-51813876}}</ref> On 31 March, the Chinese government announced that large-scale domestic transmission of COVID-19 had been stopped.<ref name="Policy Design and Practice" />

=== End of the first outbreak ===
The public health measures put in place from 23 January 2020 onward suppressed transmission of the virus below the critical threshold, bringing the [[basic reproduction number]] of the virus to near zero.<ref name="Science-Tian-2020"/> On 4 February 2020, around two weeks after the beginning of the lockdowns in Hubei province, case counts peaked in the province and began to decline thereafter.<ref name="Science-Tian-2020"/> The outbreak remained largely concentrated within Hubei province, with over 80% of cases nationwide through 22 March 2020 occurring there.<ref name="JTD-Zanin-2020"/>

As the epidemic receded, the focus shifted towards restarting economic activity and preventing a resurgence of the virus.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020">{{cite journal |journal=Clinical Infectious Diseases |title=One Hundred Days of Coronavirus Disease 2019 Prevention and Control in China |date=5 June 2020 |volume=72 |issue=2 |pages=332–339 |doi=10.1093/cid/ciaa725 |first1=Lei |last1=Zhou |first2=Zunyou |last2=Wu |first3=Zhongjie |last3=Li |first4=Yanping |last4=Zhang |first5=Jennifer M |last5=McGoogan |first6=Qun |last6=Li |first7=Xiaoping |last7=Dong |first8=Ruiqi |last8=Ren |first9=Luzhao |last9=Feng |first10=Xiaopeng |last10=Qi |first11=Jingjing |last11=Xi |first12=Ying |last12=Cui |first13=Wenjie |last13=Tan |first14=Guoqing |last14=Shi |first15=Guizhen |last15=Wu |first16=Wenbo |last16=Xu |first17=Xiaoqi |last17=Wang |first18=Jiaqi |last18=Ma |first19=Xuemei |last19=Su |first20=Zijian |last20=Feng |first21=George F |last21=Gao|pmid=33501949 |pmc=7314211 }}</ref> Low- and medium-risk areas of the country began to ease social distancing measures on 17 February 2020.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/> Reopening was accompanied by an increase in testing and the development of electronic "health codes" (using smartphone applications) to facilitate contact tracing.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/> Health code applications contain personalized risk information, based on recent contacts and test results.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/> Wuhan, the last major city to reopen, ended its lockdown on 8 April 2020.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/>

China reported its first imported COVID-19 case from an incoming traveler on 30 January.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/> As the number of imported cases rose and the number of domestic cases fell, China began imposing restrictions on entry into the country.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/> Inbound flights were restricted, and all incoming passengers were required to undergo quarantine.<ref name="CID-Zhou-2020"/>

The death toll in China during the first outbreak was approximately 4,600 according to official figures, and has been estimated at under 5,000 by a scientific study of excess pneumonia mortality published in [[The BMJ]].<ref name="BMJ-Liu-2021"/>

Blood samples taken by the Chinese CDC from a random sampling of 34,000 citizens in Wuhan and other parts of China one month after the virus first wave was contained showed 4.43% of sampled community members in Wuhan had antibodies. In the wider Hubei area, 0.44% of those sampled were positive for antibodies, while of 12,000 nationally representative samples taken only two recorded positive results.<ref>{{Cite web|last=中国疾控中心|title=科学认识人群新冠病毒抗体流行率——全国新冠肺炎血清流行病学调查结果问答|url=http://mp.weixin.qq.com/s?__biz=MzA3MzU2MzIwMg==&mid=2650695310&idx=1&sn=12e022a9f94c2a7d70f6b14624ba1474&chksm=8707eba3b07062b556c4dbebbb69c2d3dbb10389ae588819263088dac9f1d3135bd2ad31b8cf#rd|access-date=22 May 2021|website=Weixin Official Accounts Platform}}</ref>

=== Early censorship and police responses ===
{{See also|Censorship in China|Internet censorship in China|Human rights issues related to the COVID-19 pandemic#Censorship}}
[[File:李文亮的训诫书.png|right|thumb|Document issued by the Wuhan Police ordering [[Li Wenliang]] to stop "spreading rumours" about a possible 'SARS virus' dated 3 January]]
The early response by city authorities was criticised as prioritising a control of information that might be unfavorable for local officials over public safety, and China was also criticised for cover-ups and downplaying the initial discovery and severity of the outbreak. By the time China had informed the WHO of the new coronavirus on 31 December 2019, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that the government was still keeping "its own citizens in the dark".<ref name="TrueCost">{{Cite news|date=7 February 2020|title=The true cost of China's coronavirus cover-up: How state censorship let the outbreak spread|newspaper=National Post|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/the-true-cost-of-chinas-coronavirus-cover-up-how-state-censorship-let-the-outbreak-spread|access-date=7 March 2020|publisher=Financial Times}}</ref><ref name="FaceXi">{{cite news|last=Griffiths|first=James|title=Wuhan is the latest crisis to face China's Xi, and it's exposing major flaws in his model of control|work=CNN|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/01/23/asia/wuhan-china-coronavirus-sars-response-intl-hnk/index.html|url-status=live|access-date=10 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208194710/https://www.cnn.com/2020/01/23/asia/wuhan-china-coronavirus-sars-response-intl-hnk/index.html|archive-date=8 February 2020}}</ref> Observers have attributed this to the censorship institutional structure of the country's press and internet, exacerbated by Chinese Communist Party leader [[Xi Jinping]]'s crackdown on independent oversight such as journalism and social media that left senior officials with inaccurate information on the outbreak and "contributed to a prolonged period of inaction that allowed the virus to spread".<ref name="TrueCost" /><ref name="FaceXi" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Kristof|first1=Nicholas|date=29 January 2020|title=Coronavirus Spreads, and the World Pays for China's Dictatorship|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/29/opinion/coronavirus-china-government.html|access-date=2 March 2020|work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref name="auto5">{{cite web|title=China's slow response to coronavirus has shown the weakness of its centralised model|url=https://www.newstatesman.com/world/asia/2020/01/china-s-slow-response-coronavirus-has-shown-weakness-its-centralised-model|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128134506/https://www.newstatesman.com/world/asia/2020/01/china-s-slow-response-coronavirus-has-shown-weakness-its-centralised-model|archive-date=28 January 2020|access-date=10 February 2020|website=New Statesman|date=27 January 2020}}</ref>

A group of eight medical personnel, including [[Li Wenliang]], an ophthalmologist from Wuhan Central Hospital who in late December posted warnings on a new coronavirus strain akin to SARS, were taken into custody by Wuhan police and threatened with prosecution for "spreading rumours" for likening it to SARS.<ref>{{cite web|date=7 February 2020|title=新冠肺炎吹哨醫師 李文亮病逝 民眾激憤|url=https://www.worldjournal.com/6771702/article-新冠肺炎第一個吹哨者-李文亮醫師過世/|access-date=10 February 2020|website=世界新聞網|language=zh-TW|archive-date=6 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200206232604/https://www.worldjournal.com/6771702/article-%E6%96%B0%E5%86%A0%E8%82%BA%E7%82%8E%E7%AC%AC%E4%B8%80%E5%80%8B%E5%90%B9%E5%93%A8%E8%80%85-%E6%9D%8E%E6%96%87%E4%BA%AE%E9%86%AB%E5%B8%AB%E9%81%8E%E4%B8%96/}}</ref><ref name="auto6">{{Cite news|date=7 February 2020|title=Coronavirus kills Chinese whistleblower doctor|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-51403795|access-date=10 February 2020}}</ref>  Li Wenliang later died of the disease on 7 February, and was widely hailed as a whistleblower in China, but some of the trending hashtags on [[Sina Weibo|Weibo]] such as "Wuhan government owes Dr Li Wenliang an apology" and "We want freedom of speech" were blocked.<ref name="auto3">{{cite news|last=Zhong|first=Raymond|date=27 January 2020|title=As Virus Spreads, Anger Floods Chinese Social Media|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/27/technology/china-coronavirus-censorship-social-media.html|url-status=live|access-date=10 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128115157/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/27/technology/china-coronavirus-censorship-social-media.html|archive-date=28 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=7 February 2020|title=Li Wenliang: Coronavirus death of Wuhan doctor sparks outpouring of anger|work=[[BBC News]]|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-china-51409801|url-status=live|access-date=10 February that was permitted for coverage.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite news|title=Li Wenliang's death is a new crisis for China's rulers|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/china/2020/02/07/li-wenliangs-death-is-a-new-crisis-for-chinas-rulers|access-date=12 February 2020|issn=0013-0613}}</ref>

As part of the central government's "bifurcated approach to diffuse discontent", citizens were permitted to criticise local officials so long as they did not "question the basic legitimacy of the party".<ref>{{Cite news|title=In coronavirus pandemic, China's leaders scramble to avert a Chernobyl moment|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/in-coronavirus-outbreak-chinas-leaders-scramble-to-avert-a-chernobyl-moment/2020/01/29/bc4eb52a-4250-11ea-99c7-1dfd4241a2fe_story.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204085411/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/in-coronavirus-outbreak-chinas-leaders-scramble-to-avert-a-chernobyl-moment/2020/01/29/bc4eb52a-4250-11ea-99c7-1dfd4241a2fe_story.html|archive-date=4 February 2020|access-date=10 February 2020|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> The [[Cyberspace Administration of China|Cyberspace Administration]] (CAC) declared its intent to foster a "good online atmosphere," with CAC notices sent to video platforms encouraging them "not to push any negative story, and not to conduct non-official livestreaming on the virus".<ref name="auto">{{Cite news|date=11 February 2020|title=China's online censors tighten grip after brief coronavirus respite|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-censorship-idUSKBN2051BP|access-date=12 February 2020}}</ref> Censorship has been observed being applied on news articles and social media posts deemed to hold negative tones about COVID-19 and the governmental response, including posts mocking Xi Jinping for not visiting areas of the epidemic,<ref name="theguardianxi">{{Cite news|last=Kuo|first=Lily|date=4 February 2020|title=Taking credit, avoiding blame? Xi Jinping's absence from coronavirus frontline|work=The 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204231032/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/feb/04/blame-xi-jinping-absence-coronavirus-frontline-china-crisis|archive-date=4 February 2020|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> an article that predicted negative effects of the epidemic on the economy, and calls to remove local government officials.<ref name="auto5" /><ref name="auto3" /><ref name="auto7">{{cite news|last=Griffiths|first=James|title=China is waking up to the dangers of knee-jerk censorship in a crisis|work=CNN|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/01/31/asia/wuhan-virus-china-censorship-intl-hnk/index.html|url-status=live|access-date=2 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202033436/https://www.cnn.com/2020/01/31/asia/wuhan-virus-china-censorship-intl-hnk/index.html|archive-date=2 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite authorities' consent.<ref name="auto3" /><ref name="auto4">{{Cite news|date=11 February 2020|title=China's online censors tighten grip after brief coronavirus 2020}}</ref>

== Zero-COVID policy, January 2020 – December 2022<span class="anchor" id="Zero-COVID_policy"></span> ==
{{See also|Zero-COVID}}
China and a small number of other countries pursued an [[Zero-COVID|elimination strategy]], also known as a "zero-COVID strategy" ({{Lang-zh|t=|p=Dòngtài qīng líng|l=Dynamic Clearing|s=动态清零}}),<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-28 |title=上海封城一个月：官方坚持"动态清零"政策不变 如何解除危机 |url=https://www.bbc.com/zhongwen/simp/chinese-news-61242081 |access-date=2022-04-28 |website=BBC News 中文 |language=zh-hans}}</ref> which aimed to eliminate local transmission of the virus.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/>

The initial public health response was successful in reducing transmission to near zero within China.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/> In the 18 months after containing  the initial outbreak, China had two COVID-19 deaths.<ref name="BMJ-An-2021">{{cite journal |title=Vaccination strategy and challenges for consolidating successful containment of covid-19 with population immunity in China |doi=10.1136/bmj-2021-066125 |date=2 December 2021 |journal=The BMJ |first1=Zhijie |last1=An |first2=Fuzhen |last2=Wang |first3=An |last3=Pan |first4=Zundong |last4=Yin |first5=Lance |last5=Rodewald |first6=Zijian |last6=Feng |volume=375 |article-number=e066125 |pmid=34853010|pmc=8634348 }}</ref>

In March and April 2020, as lockdowns and other restrictions were eased, attention shifted to preventing imported cases from abroad from causing a resurgence of the virus within China.<ref name="JTD-Zanin-2020"/> International flights to China were heavily restricted, and incoming travelers were required to undergo [[PCR testing]] and quarantine.<ref name="JTD-Zanin-2020"/> Through November 2020, these quarantine measures prevented nearly 4,000 infected international travelers from entering the wider community.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021">{{cite journal |title=Comprehensive large-scale nucleic acid–testing strategies support China's sustained containment of COVID-19 |date=15 April 2021 |journal=Nature Medicine |volume=27 |pages=740–742 |doi=10.1038/s41591-021-01308-7 |pmid=33859409 |first1=Zhongjie |last1=Li |first2=Fengfeng |last2=Liu |first3=Jinzhao |last3=Cui |first4=Zhibin |last4=Peng |first5=Zhaorui |last5=Chang |first6=Shengjie |last6=Lai |first7=Qiulan |last7=Chen |first8=Liping |last8=Wang |first9=George F. |last9=Gao |first10=Zijian |last10=Feng|issue=5 |s2cid=233258711 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In June 2020, the [[China CDC]] COVID-19 Emergency Response Team described its elimination strategy.<ref name="Lancet-Li-2020-Active-case-finding">{{cite journal | title=Active case finding with case management: the key to tackling the COVID-19 pandemic |journal=The Lancet |date=4 June 2020 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31278-2 |first1=Zhongjie |last1=Li |first2=Qiulan |last2=Chen |first3=Luzhao |last3=Feng |first4=Lance |last4=Rodewald |first5=Yinyin |last5=Xia |first6=Hailiang |last6=Yu |first7=Ruochen |last7=Zhang|volume=396 |issue=10243 |pages=63–70 |pmid=32505220 |pmc=7272157 }}</ref> The measures employed to contain new outbreaks include aggressive contact tracing, isolation of infected people, quarantine of their close contacts, large-scale nucleic acid testing and domestic travel restrictions from high-risk areas.<ref name="Lancet-Li-2020-Active-case-finding"/> Contact tracing is aided by the use of "health code" smartphone applications.<ref name="Lancet-Li-2020-Active-case-finding"/>

In order to detect new outbreaks early, routine PCR testing was carried out on all patients with fever or respiratory symptoms, medical staff and workers who handle imported goods.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/> When an infected person was identified, all close contacts are required to undergo a 14-day centralized quarantine, with multiple rounds of PCR testing.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/> During outbreaks, community-wide PCR testing was carried out in order to identify infected people, including those without symptoms.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/> Community-wide screening was intended to rapidly isolate infected people from the general population, and to allow a quicker return to normal economic activity.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/> Community-wide screening was first carried out from 14 May to 1 June 2020 in Wuhan, and as of 2021 was used in subsequent outbreaks in China.<ref name="NatMed-Li-2021"/>
[[File:Aus team members with staff in dining hall Zhangjiakou Village (Snowboard) edit.jpg|thumb|The [[Australia at the Winter Paralympics|Australian team]] pictured with local staff at the [[2022 Winter Paralympics]]. All wear [[personal protective equipment]] in adherence with China's [[bio-secure bubble]] at the event.]]
China's zero-COVID policy had implications for the [[2022 Winter Olympics]] and [[2022 Winter Paralympics|Paralympics]] in Beijing. Protocols included a [[bio-secure bubble]] for international athletes separated from the Chinese public, with only local spectators at a strict capacity limit permitted to attend.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Overseas fans banned from 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2021/9/29/winter-olympics-2022-china-to-allow-fans-only-from-mainland |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=www.aljazeera.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Beijing Olympics organizers hope to have 30% capacity in venues |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Spotlight/Sports/Beijing-Winter-Olympics/Beijing-Olympics-organizers-hope-to-have-30-capacity-in-venues |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=Nikkei Asia |language=en-GB}}</ref> Beijing has maintained one of the strictest COVID controls in the world, which is why thousands of people showed defiance against Chinese authorities by protesting at universities and in major cities. Their demands included not only freedom from constant Covid tests and lockdowns, but also an end to strict censorship and tight control of the Communist Party over all aspects of life.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-28 |title=Thousands in China protest zero-COVID policy in largest demonstrations in decades |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/thousands-in-china-protest-zero-covid-policy-in-largest-demonstrations-in-decades |access-date=2023-07-29 |website=PBS NewsHour |language=en-us}}</ref>

=== Response to subsequent outbreaks ===

After the end of the initial outbreak in Hubei province, there were additional, smaller outbreaks caused by imported cases throughout 2020, which were controlled through short-term, localized intense public health measures.<ref name="GHA-Lu-2021"/>

In June and July 2020, the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Beijing]] showed a second outbreak. The first case was discovered on 11 June, after 56 days without any known local transmission.<ref name="JAMA-Wu-2020-Beijing"/> The outbreak was centered on an agricultural wholesale market. Residents of the surrounding neighborhoods and close contacts of known cases were tested, and a total of 368 people infected with the virus were discovered.<ref name="JAMA-Wu-2020-Beijing"/> The outbreak was brought to a halt by 5 July 2020, less than a month after it began.<ref name="JAMA-Wu-2020-Beijing">{{cite journal |title=Time Course of a Second Outbreak of COVID-19 in Beijing, China, June-July 2020 |date=24 August 2020 |first1=Zunyou |last1=Wu |first2=Quanyi |last2=Wang |first3=Jing |last3=Zhao |first4=Peng |last4=Yang |first5=Jennifer M. |last5=McGoogan |first6=Zijian |last6=Feng |first7=Chun |last7=Huang |doi=10.1001/jama.2020.15894 |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association|volume=324 |issue=14 |pages=1458–1459 |pmid=32852518 |pmc=7445627 }}</ref>

In October 2020, after a period of two months without any known domestically transmitted COVID-19 cases, three new cases were detected in the port city of [[Qingdao]].<ref name="NEJM-Qingdao-2020">{{cite journal |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |date=18 November 2020 |doi=10.1056/NEJMc2032361 |first1=Yuhan |last1=Xing |first2=Gary W.K. |last2=Wong |first3=Wei |last3=Ni |first4=Xiaowen |last4=Hu |first5=Quansheng |last5=Xing |title=Rapid Response to an Outbreak in Qingdao, China |volume=383 |issue=23 |page=e129 |pmid=33207089|pmc=7722691 }}</ref> Two dock workers with asymptomatic infections were subsequently identified as the probable source of the outbreak.<ref name="NEJM-Qingdao-2020"/> The population of Qingdao was screened using [[COVID-19 testing#Pooled testing|pooled PCR testing]], with total of 10.9 million people being tested within 5 days of the detection of the first cases.<ref name="NEJM-Qingdao-2020"/> This led to the identification of 9 additional cases.<ref name="NEJM-Qingdao-2020"/> Travel restrictions were imposed on the city, requiring people leaving the city to present a negative PCR test and to quarantine for one week. The outbreak was brought to an end without a lockdown.<ref name="NEJM-Qingdao-2020"/>

From July through August 2021, China experienced and contained 11 outbreaks of the [[SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant|Delta variant]], with a total of 1,390 detected cases.<ref name="CCDCW-Zhou-Oct2021"/> The largest of these outbreaks, in both geographic extent and in the number of people infected, began in [[Nanjing]].<ref name="CCDCW-Zhou-Oct2021"/> The [[index case]] of the outbreak, an airport worker, tested positive on 20 July 2021, and the outbreak was traced back to an infected passenger on a flight from Moscow that had arrived on 10 July.<ref name="CCDCW-Zhou-Oct2021"/> The outbreak spread to multiple provinces before it was contained. Through 26 August, 1,162 infections related to the Nanjing outbreak were reported.<ref name="CCDCW-Zhou-Oct2021">{{cite journal |doi=10.46234/ccdcw2021.213 |pmid=34703643 |title=Eleven COVID-19 Outbreaks with Local Transmissions Caused by the Imported SARS-CoV-2 Delta VOC — China, July–August, 2021 |journal=China CDC Weekly |date=8 October 2021 |first1=Lei |last1=Zhou |first2=Kai |last2=Nie |first3=Hongting |last3=Zhao |first4=Xiang |last4=Zhao |first5=Bixiong |last5=Ye |first6=Ji |last6=Wang |first7=Cao |last7=Chen |first8=Hong |last8=Wang |first9=Jiangli |last9=Di |first10=Jinsong |last10=Li|volume=3 |issue=41 |pages=863–868 |pmc=8521157 }}</ref>

China's later response to the pandemic has been praised by some foreign leaders and scientists. After the lockdown of Wuhan, it was reported in the journal ''Policy Design and Practice'' that "China has managed to contain this unprecedented public health crisis reasonably swiftly".<ref name="Policy Design and Practice"/>

==== 2022 outbreaks and end of zero-COVID policy ====
{{See also|2022 COVID-19 protests in China}}
In April 2022, amidst the largest outbreak in China since early 2020 driven by the [[SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant|Omicron variant]], China continued to uphold its zero-COVID policy,<ref name=":4" /> although a reduction was made to quarantine periods and self-testing kits were made more widely available.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-04-04 |title=China: How is its zero-Covid strategy changing? |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/59882774 |access-date=2022-04-19}}</ref> Notably, the city of [[COVID-19 pandemic in Shanghai|Shanghai]] was placed in a strict [[COVID-19 pandemic in Shanghai March 2022|city-wide lockdown]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-04-05 |title=Shanghai Covid lockdown extended to entire city |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-60994022 |access-date=2022-04-19}}</ref><ref name=":4" />

On 12 May 2022, the [[National Immigration Administration]] announced further rules to restrict overseas travel, putting a strict halt on "unnecessary" exits, over COVID concerns. The original verbal advice against traveling is to be upgraded to direct limitations on passport issue. Overseas study, work, and business trips are still allowed.<ref>{{cite web |title=China says it will 'strictly limit' citizens from going abroad |url=https://www.ft.com/content/b91c64e9-d67c-46e7-8923-69de55f5c38b |website=Financial Times |date=12 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |trans-title=NIA press conference: No issuing of entry/exit identification such as normal passports for non-essential and non-emergency exit rationale|script-title=zh:国家移民管理局新闻发布会：对非必要、非紧急出境事由暂不签发普通护照等出入境证件 |url=https://www.nia.gov.cn/n741435/n1194535/n1432665/index.html |website=国家移民管理局 |access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Yeh |first1=Nadya |title=China restricts overseas travel, ostensibly to keep COVID at bay |url=https://supchina.com/2022/05/12/china-restricts-overseas-travel-ostensibly-to-keep-covid-at-bay/ |website=SupChina |date=12 May 2022}}</ref>

In November 2022, despite the number of cases in China reaching the highest levels in months, the Chinese government decided to ease the COVID-19 restrictions. Under the new rules, the quarantine period for close contacts was reduce to five days in a state facility and three days at home. Besides, the policy which penalized airlines for bringing in too many cases was also scrapped. The decision was taken citing the economic situation, which faced a blow due to China's zero-COVID policy. The authorities, however, stated that their war against the pandemic remains "unchanged".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-63594255|title=China Covid: Beijing eases some curbs despite rising cases|work=BBC News |date=11 November 2022 |access-date=11 November 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/nov/11/china-covid-rules-quarantine-periods|title=China eases Covid rules but insists 'war' against pandemic will continue|date=11 November 2022|access-date=11 November 2022|website=The Guardian|first=Verna|last=Yu}}</ref> On 15 November, the lockdown policies led to the breakout of [[2022 COVID-19 protests in China|nationwide protests]].<ref name=":2b">{{Cite news |date=2022-11-26 |title=China Xinjiang: Urumqi rocked by Covid lockdown protests after deadly fire |language=en-GB |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-63766125 |access-date=2022-11-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Chien |first1=Amy Chang |last2=Che |first2=Chang |last3=Liu |first3=John |last4=Mozur |first4=Paul |date=2022-11-25 |title=In a challenge to Beijing, unrest over COVID lockdowns spreads |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2022/11/25/asia-pacific/china-covid-lockdown-unrest/ |access-date=2022-11-27 |website=[[The Japan Times]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 7 December 2022, after the protests, the Chinese government lifted many of the most stringent rules, reducing lockdowns and allowing people testing positive for COVID-19 to quarantine at home rather instead of being detained in a hospital or mass quarantine site;<ref name=":2">{{cite news |title=China Eases 'Zero Covid' Restrictions in Victory for Protesters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/07/world/asia/china-zero-covid-protests.html |access-date=12 December 2022 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221210072410/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/07/world/asia/china-zero-covid-protests.html |archive-date=10 December 2022|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Ruwitch |first1=John |title=China rolls back some of its most controversial COVID restrictions |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/12/07/1141363515/china-rolls-back-some-of-its-most-controversial-covid-restrictions |access-date=12 December 2022 |work=[[National Public Radio]] |date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221210040654/https://www.npr.org/2022/12/07/1141363515/china-rolls-back-some-of-its-most-controversial-covid-restrictions |archive-date=10 December 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kelter |first=Frederik |title=China's 'zero-COVID' U-turn leads to loss of faith in leadership |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/1/5/chinas-zero-covid-u-turn-leads-to-loss-of-faith-in-leadership |access-date=2023-01-06 |website=www.aljazeera.com |language=en}}</ref> these changes effectively led to the end of the zero-COVID policy.<ref>{{Cite news |date=16 December 2022 |title=Economists Rush to Adjust China Forecasts as Covid Zero Ends |language=en |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-12-16/china-s-covid-zero-exit-sees-analysts-rush-to-adjust-forecasts |access-date=27 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=17 December 2022 |title=Xi Jinping tied himself to zero-Covid. Now he keeps silent as it falls apart |work=[[CNN]] |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2022/12/16/china/china-zero-covid-uturn-xi-jinping-intl-hnk-mic/index.html |access-date=27 May 2023}}</ref> By the end of December, Chinese authorities effectively ended mass testing and changed their reporting criteria in a way that excludes most deaths caused by COVID-19 from being reported.<ref name=":0" />

==== Xinjiang ====
{{Further|COVID-19 pandemic in Xinjiang}}

In August 2020, an outbreak in [[Urumqi]], the capital of Xinjiang, caused officials to declare a state of "wartime" lockdown.<ref>{{Cite news |date=18 July 2020 |title=China coronavirus: 'Wartime state' declared for Urumqi in Xinjiang |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-53458412 |access-date=11 January 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gan |first=Nectar |date=20 July 2020 |title=Xinjiang capital in lockdown over spike in coronavirus cases |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/20/asia/coronavirus-xinjiang-urumqi-intl-hnk/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720091723/https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/20/asia/coronavirus-xinjiang-urumqi-intl-hnk/index.html |archive-date=20 July 2020 |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=CNN}}</ref> Transportation including trains and buses were canceled, and residents started protests.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Feng |first=Emily |date=26 August 2020 |title=China Calls It A 'Wartime Mode' COVID-19 Lockdown. And Residents Are Protesting |language=en |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2020/08/26/906206090/china-calls-it-a-wartime-mode-covid-19-lockdown-and-residents-are-protesting |access-date=11 January 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=22 January 2021 |title=In Xinjiang, Rare Protests Came Amid Lockdown |url=https://www.chinafile.com/reporting-opinion/viewpoint/xinjiang-rare-protests-came-amid-lockdown |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=ChinaFile |language=en}}</ref> Some online claims reported residents had been forced to use [[traditional Chinese medicine]], handcuffed to buildings, and told to stay indoors for weeks.<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 August 2020 |title=Xinjiang residents handcuffed to their homes in Covid lockdown |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/aug/25/xinjiang-residents-handcuffed-to-their-homes-in-covid-lockdown |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en}}</ref>

In October 2020, it was reported that China's largest outbreak in months appeared to be occurring in a Xinjiang factory linked to "forced labour and the government's controversial policies towards Uighur residents".<ref>{{Cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=29 October 2020 |title=Large Covid outbreak in China linked to Xinjiang forced labour |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/oct/29/large-covid-outbreak-in-china-linked-to-xinjiang-forced-labour |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en}}</ref> The outbreak prompted officials in northwestern China's Xinjiang region to implement a mandatory lockdown of residents in [[Ghulja]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=China's Xinjiang Region On Lockdown Amid Report Of New Cluster Of Coronavirus Cases |language=en |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/10/30/929609054/chinas-xinjiang-region-on-lockdown-amid-report-of-new-cluster-of-coronavirus-cas |access-date=11 January 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Mandatory lockdown ordered in Ghulja amid COVID surge in northern Xinjiang |url=https://www.rfa.org/english/news/uyghur/ghulja-lockdown-10132021194542.html |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=Radio Free Asia |date=13 October 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

Tight restrictions on information flowing out of Xinjiang have added to the confusion over the virus's spread in the province.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=18 February 2020 |title=Coronavirus would be "disastrous" for China's Muslim concentration camp prisoners and the world might never find out, Uighur activist warns |url=https://www.newsweek.com/coronavirus-uighur-muslim-chinese-camps-activist-1487781 |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=Newsweek |language=en}}</ref>

=== Case and death count statistics ===
As of 2020, papers from academic journals and publishers such as ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maier|first1=Benjamin|last2=Brockmann|first2=Dirk|date=15 May 2020|title=Effective containment explains subexponential growth in recent confirmed COVID-19 cases in China| url=|journal=Science|volume=368|issue=6492|pages=742–746|bibcode=2020Sci...368..742M|doi=10.1126/science.abb4557|issn=0036-8075|pmc=7164388|pmid=32269067}}</ref> ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cyranoski|first=David|date=17 March 2020|title=What China's coronavirus response can teach the rest of the world|journal=Nature|volume=579|issue=7800|pages=479–480|bibcode=2020Natur.579..479C|doi=10.1038/d41586-020-00741-x|pmid=32203360|doi-access=free|s2cid=214628991}}</ref> ''[[The Lancet]]'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Burki|first=Talha|date=1 November 2020|title=China's successful control of COVID-19|url=|journal=The Lancet Infectious Diseases|volume=20|issue=11|pages=1240–1241|doi=10.1016/S1473-3099(20)30800-8|issn=1473-3099|pmc=7544475|pmid=33038941}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lancet|first1=The|date=25 July 2020|title=COVID-19 and China: lessons and the way forward|url=|journal=The Lancet|volume=396|issue=10246|page=213|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31637-8|issn=0140-6736|pmc=7377676|pmid=32711779}}</ref> and [[Karger Publishers]]<ref name=":1"/> had regarded China's measures to domestically contain COVID-19 to be effective. A study in March 2020 published in ''Science Magazine'' concluded that the Wuhan travel ban and national emergency response may have prevented more than 700,000 COVID-19 cases outside the city.<ref>{{Cite news|date=April 2020|title=China's Controls May Have Headed Off 700,000 COVID-19 Cases: Study|work=[[U.S. News & World Report]]|url=https://www.usnews.com/news/health-news/articles/2020-04-08/chinas-controls-may-have-headed-off-700-000-covid-19-cases-study}}</ref> {{As of|2021|12|31}}, official statistics showed 102,083 cumulative confirmed cases{{efn|name=confirmed_case_def|text=The government only classifies cases as "confirmed" when the patient meets specific criteria. As of March 2022, the current requirements are a positive test and ''two'' out of three signs: COVID symptoms, CT pneumonia diagnosis, and blood count changes;<ref>{{cite web |author1=National Health Commission |trans-title=COVID-19 diagnosis and treatment guidelines, trial ninth edition|script-title=zh:新型冠状病毒肺炎诊疗方案 (试行第九版) |url=https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2022-03/15/5679257/files/49854a49c7004f4ea9e622f3f2c568d8.pdf |date=March 2022}}</ref> the remainder is termed "asymptomatic". In other words, one can be labelled "asymptomatic" despite showing cold-like symptoms.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Olcott |first1=Eleanor |last2=Yu |first2=Sun |last3=Barnes |first3=Oliver |last4=Lin |first4=Andy |title=China's Covid death data obscure true impact of Omicron, experts say |url=https://www.ft.com/content/45f4b975-443f-44b7-92b8-5d2417491015 |website=Financial Times |date=17 April 2022 |quote=This means tens of thousands of people who tested positive and had cold-like symptoms were recorded as "asymptomatic", unlike in many other countries.}}</ref> Cases which are asymptomatic are reported separately.<ref>{{cite news |title=Live news from March 29: Russia says it will ease military activities in Kyiv, EU states expel Russian diplomats |url=https://www.ft.com/content/326062fb-5581-4dfa-bcba-32316ac8bbac |access-date=7 April 2022 |work=Financial Times |date=29 March 2022 |quote=Chinese official data counts "asymptomatic" cases, when an individual tests positive for the virus, separately from "confirmed" cases, where infected individuals have their symptoms verified through medical observation.}}</ref>}} and 4,636 cumulative deaths in [[mainland China]].<ref name="NHC-31Dec2021">{{cite web |publisher=National Health Commission |url=http://www.nhc.gov.cn/xcs/yqtb/202112/23a38cc3f6574003a5212d3a4ec965fa.shtml|title=Jiézhì 12 yuè 30 rì 24 shí xīnxíng guānzhuàng bìngdú fèiyán yìqíng zuìxīn qíngkuàng|script-title=zh:截至12月30日24时新型冠状病毒肺炎疫情最新情况|trans-title=The latest situation of the new coronavirus pneumonia epidemic as of A study published in ''[[The BMJ]]'' found that 4573 additional pneumonia deaths occurred in Wuhan from January to March 2020, compared with the same period in 2019.<ref name="BMJ-Liu-2021"/> Outside of Wuhan, no measurable increase in pneumonia deaths was observed.<ref name="BMJ-Liu-2021"/> Though there were confirmed COVID-19 deaths outside of Wuhan, the authors speculated that lockdowns suppressed influenza transmission sufficiently to offset these deaths.<ref name="BMJ-Liu-2021"/>

A survey of [[seroprevalence]] conducted in April 2020 found that 4.4% of people in Wuhan had antibodies to SARS-CoV-2, indicating that they had been infected.<ref name="LancetRHWP-Li2021"/> Seroprevalence fell with distance from Wuhan, indicating that the initial outbreak had been largely contained to the city.<ref name="LancetRHWP-Li2021"/> Elsewhere in [[Hubei province]], 0.4% of people had antibodies, while outside of Hubei province, less than 0.1% of people had antibodies.<ref name="LancetRHWP-Li2021">{{cite journal |journal=The Lancet Regional Health - Western Pacific
