Influenza entered Australia for the first time in January 1919 after a strict maritime quarantine had shielded the country through 1918.<ref name="Holbrook-2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Holbrook C | title = Public Health in a Federation: Lessons from the Spanish Influenza in Australia | journal = Social History of Medicine | volume = 35 | issue = 3 | pages = 818–846 | date = August 2022 | pmid = 36046217 | pmc = 9383459 | doi = 10.1093/shm/hkac005 }}</ref> It assumed epidemic proportions first in [[Melbourne]], peaking in mid-February.<ref name="Shanks">{{Cite web |vauthors=Shanks GD |title=Australia's Experience of the 1918–19 Influenza Pandemic: Lessons Learned |url=https://www.otago.ac.nz/wellington/otago711857.pdf |website=University of Otago |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=19 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919223943/https://www.otago.ac.nz/wellington/otago711857.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The flu soon appeared in neighboring [[New South Wales]] and [[South Australia]].<ref name="Holbrook-2022" /> New South Wales experienced its first wave of infection between mid-March and late May,<ref name="Curson-2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Curson P, McCracken K | title = An Australian perspective of the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic | journal = New South Wales Public Health Bulletin | volume = 17 | issue = 7–8 | pages = 103–107 | date = 2006 | pmid = 17136138 | doi = 10.1071/NB06025 | doi-access = free }}</ref> while a second, more severe wave occurred in [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]] between April and June.<ref name="Shanks"/> Land quarantine measures hindered the spread of the disease. [[Queensland]] was not infected until late April; [[Western Australia]] avoided the disease until early June, and [[Tasmania]] remained free from it until mid-August.<ref name="Holbrook-2022"/> Out of the six states, Victoria and New South Wales experienced generally more extensive epidemics. Each experienced another significant wave of illness over the winter. The second epidemic in New South Wales was more severe than the first,<ref name="Curson-2006"/> while Victoria saw a third wave that was somewhat less extensive than its second, more akin to its first.<ref name="Shanks"/>

The disease also reached other parts of the world for the first time in 1919, such as [[Madagascar]], which saw its first cases in April; the outbreak had spread to practically all sections of the island by June.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for AUGUST 22, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 34 | pages = 1927–1968 | date = August 1919 | pmid = 19314683 | pmc = 1996930 }}</ref> In other parts, influenza recurred in the form of a true "third wave". [[British Hong Kong|Hong Kong]] experienced another outbreak in June,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ho PL, Chow KH | title = Mortality burden of the 1918–1920 influenza pandemic in Hong Kong | journal = Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses | volume = 3 | issue = 6 | pages = 261–263 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19903207 | pmc = 4941390 | doi = 10.1111/j.1750-2659.2009.00105.x }}</ref> as did South Africa during its fall and winter months in the [[Southern Hemisphere]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for MAY 30, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 22 | pages = 1171–1241 | date = May 1919 | pmid = 19314671 | pmc = 1996920 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for AUGUST 1, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 31 | pages = 1673–1742 | date = August 1919 | pmid = 19314680 | pmc = 1996928 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for AUGUST 29, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 35 | pages = 1969–2012 | date = August 1919 | pmid = 19314684 | pmc = 1996931 }}</ref> [[Dominion of New Zealand|New Zealand]] experienced some cases in May.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for AUGUST 15, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 33 | pages = 1823–1926 | date = August 1919 | pmid = 19314682 | pmc = 1996932 }}</ref>

Parts of South America experienced a resurgence of pandemic activity throughout 1919. A third wave hit Brazil between January and June.<ref name="Chandra-2020"/> Between July 1919 and February 1920, [[Chile]], which had been affected for the first time in October 1918, experienced a severe second wave, with mortality peaking in August 1919.<ref name="Chowell-2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chowell G, Simonsen L, Flores J, Miller MA, Viboud C | title = Death patterns during the 1918 influenza pandemic in Chile | journal = Emerging Infectious Diseases | volume = 20 | issue = 11 | pages = 1803–1811 | date = November 2014 | pmid = 25341056 | pmc = 4214284 | doi = 10.3201/eid2011.130632 }}</ref> [[Montevideo]] similarly experienced a second outbreak between July and September.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cristina J, Pollero R, Pellegrino A | title = The 1918 influenza pandemic in Montevideo: The southernmost capital city in the Americas | journal = Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses | volume = 13 | issue = 3 | pages = 219–225 | date = May 2019 | pmid = 30422393 | pmc = 6468140 | doi = 10.1111/irv.12619 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The third wave particularly affected Spain, [[Serbia]], [[Mexico]] and Great Britain, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths.<ref name="CollegePhysiciansPhiladelphia">{{cite web |url=https://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/influenza-1919-2019 |title=Influenza in 1919 and 100 Years Later |vauthors=Najera RF |publisher=[[College of Physicians of Philadelphia]] |date=2 January 2019 |access-date=23 April 2020 |archive-date=24 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724110351/https://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/influenza-1919-2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Fourth wave of 1920====
[[File:Illustrated Current News-1918-Thompson, Paul.png|thumb|Public health recommendations from the ''Illustrated Current News''|upright=1.2]]
In the Northern Hemisphere, fears of a "recurrence" of the flu grew as fall approached. Experts cited past flu epidemics, such as that of 1889–1890, to predict that such a recurrence a year later was not unlikely,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = | title = Public Health Weekly Reports for AUGUST 15, 1919 | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 34 | issue = 33 | pages = 1823–1926 | date = August 1919 | pmid = 19314682 | pmc = 1996932 | doi = 10.2307/4575271 | jstor = 4575271 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=15 August 1919 |title=WARNS OF INFLUENZA. |page=6 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/08/15/archives/warns-of-influenza-health-commissioner-expects-visitation-this.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031216/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/08/15/archives/warns-of-influenza-health-commissioner-expects-visitation-this.html |url-status=live }}</ref> though not all agreed.<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 August 1919 |title=AT ISSUE WITH COPELAND. |page=9 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/08/27/archives/at-issue-with-copeland-cincinnati-health-officer-expects-no.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031215/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/08/27/archives/at-issue-with-copeland-cincinnati-health-officer-expects-no.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In September 1919, [[U.S. Surgeon General]] [[Rupert Blue]] said a return of the flu later in the year would "probably, but by no means certainly," occur.<ref>{{Cite news |date=14 September 1919 |title=INFLUENZA RETURN EXPECTED BY BLUE |pages=4 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/09/14/archives/influenza-return-expected-by-blue-pandemic-in-mild-form-likely-this.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031220/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/09/14/archives/influenza-return-expected-by-blue-pandemic-in-mild-form-likely-this.html |url-status=live }}</ref> France had readied a public information campaign before the end of the summer,<ref>{{Cite news |date=19 August 1919 |title=PARIS FEARS RETURN OF "FLU" EPIDEMIC |pages=4 |work=The Sun |url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83030431/1919-08-20/ed-1/seq-4/ |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413025708/https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83030431/1919-08-20/ed-1/seq-4/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and Britain began preparations in the autumn with the manufacture of vaccine.<ref>{{Cite news |date=30 October 1919 |title=British Prepare for Influenza. |pages=17 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/10/30/archives/british-prepare-for-influenza.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031213/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/10/30/archives/british-prepare-for-influenza.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In Japan, the flu broke out again in December and spread rapidly throughout the country, a fact attributed at the time to cold weather.<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 December 1919 |title=GRIP IS EPIDEMIC IN JAPAN. |pages=6 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/12/28/archives/grip-is-epidemic-in-japan-measures-to-check-it-taken-by-tokio.html |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=17 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317035353/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/12/28/archives/grip-is-epidemic-in-japan-measures-to-check-it-taken-by-tokio.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="The Honolulu Advertiser-1920">{{Cite news |date=10 January 1920 |title=Influenza Gradually Spreading In Japan |pages=3 |work=The Honolulu Advertiser |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/268433358/ |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=17 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317035351/https://www.newspapers.com/image/268433358/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Pandemic-related measures were renewed to check the outbreak, and health authorities recommended the use of masks.<ref name="The Honolulu Advertiser-1920"/> The epidemic intensified in the latter part of December before swiftly peaking in January.<ref name="The Sydney Morning Herald-1920">{{Cite news |date=28 January 1920 |title=INFLUENZA IN JAPAN. |pages=10 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/97220933/ |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=21 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321222346/https://www.newspapers.com/image/97220933/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Between October 1919 and 23 January 1920, 780,000 cases were reported across the country, with at least 20,000 deaths recorded by that date. This apparently reflected "a condition of severity three times greater than for the corresponding period of" 1918–1919.<ref name="The Sydney Morning Herald-1920" /> Nonetheless, the disease was regarded as being milder than it had been the year before, albeit more infectious.<ref>{{Cite news |date=26 January 1920 |title=INFLUENZA. |pages=5 |work=The Age |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/126640866/ |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=21 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321222335/https://www.newspapers.com/image/126640866/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Despite its rapid peak at the beginning of the year, the outbreak persisted throughout the winter, before subsiding in the spring.<ref name="World Health Organization-2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Richard SA, Sugaya N, Simonsen L, Miller MA, Viboud C | title = A comparative study of the 1918–1920 influenza pandemic in Japan, USA and UK: mortality impact and implications for pandemic planning | journal = Epidemiology and Infection | volume = 137 | issue = 8 | pages = 1062–1072 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19215637 | pmc = 2704924 | doi = 10.1017/S0950268809002088 }}</ref>

In the United States, there were "almost continuously isolated or solitary cases" of flu throughout the spring and summer of 1919.<ref name="EpidemologicStudy">{{cite web |date=July 1921 |title=Influenza: An Epidemologic Study |url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/f/flu/0980flu.0016.890/108/--influenza-an-epidemiologic-study?page=root;size=100;view=image;q1=1920 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201006063708/https://quod.lib.umich.edu/f/flu/0980flu.0016.890/108/--influenza-an-epidemiologic-study?page=root;size=100;view=image;q1=1920 |archive-date=6 October 2020 |access-date=13 August 2020 |publisher=The American Journal of Hygiene |page=91 |vauthors=Vaughan WT}}</ref> An increase in scattered cases became apparent as early as September,<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 September 1919 |title=300 "FLU" CASES REPORTED |pages=5 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/09/28/archives/300-flu-cases-reported-31-in-this-stateall-said-to-be-of-mild-type.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031223/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/09/28/archives/300-flu-cases-reported-31-in-this-stateall-said-to-be-of-mild-type.html |url-status=live }}</ref> but Chicago experienced one of the first major outbreaks of the flu beginning in the middle of January.<ref>{{Cite news |date=15 January 1920 |title=Influenza Spreads in Chicago |pages=1 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/15/archives/influenza-spreads-in-chicago-106-new-cases-and-one-death.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322035543/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/15/archives/influenza-spreads-in-chicago-106-new-cases-and-one-death.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The Public Health Service announced it would take steps to "localize the epidemic",<ref>{{Cite news |date=17 January 1920 |title=525 NEW CASES IN CHICAGO. |pages=11 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/17/archives/525-new-cases-in-chicago-influenza-spreading-rapidly-there-health.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031212/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/17/archives/525-new-cases-in-chicago-influenza-spreading-rapidly-there-health.html |url-status=live }}</ref> but the disease was already causing a simultaneous outbreak in Kansas City and quickly spread outward from the center of the country.<ref name="EpidemologicStudy" /> A few days after its first announcement, PHS issued another assuring that the disease was under the control of state health authorities and that an outbreak of epidemic proportions was not expected.<ref>{{Cite news |date=21 January 1920 |title=Health Service Reports Influenza Under Control in All Parts of the Country |pages=A2 |work=The Evening Star |url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83045462/1920-01-21/ed-1/seq-2/ |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413030008/https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83045462/1920-01-21/ed-1/seq-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

It became apparent within days of the start of Chicago's explosive growth in cases that the flu was spreading in the city at an even faster rate than in winter 1919, though fewer were dying.<ref>{{Cite news |date=18 January 1920 |title=CHICAGO INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC SPREADS |pages=14 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/18/archives/chicago-influenza-epidemic-spreads-two-thousand-new-cases-are.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031214/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/18/archives/chicago-influenza-epidemic-spreads-two-thousand-new-cases-are.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Within a week, new cases in the city had surpassed its peak during the 1919 wave.<ref>{{Cite news |date=21 January 1920 |title=INFLUENZA CASES INCREASE IN CHICAGO |pages=32 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/21/archives/influenza-cases-increase-in-chicago-disease-now-regarded-as.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031217/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/21/archives/influenza-cases-increase-in-chicago-disease-now-regarded-as.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Around the same time, New York City began to see its own sudden increase in cases,<ref>{{Cite news |date=21 January 1920 |title=INFLUENZA SHOWS A LARGE INCREASE |pages=32 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/21/archives/influenza-shows-a-large-increase-health-department-reports-140-new.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322035538/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/21/archives/influenza-shows-a-large-increase-health-department-reports-140-new.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and other cities around the country were soon to follow.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 January 1920 |title=SPREADS IN OTHER CITIES. |pages=2 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/23/archives/spreads-in-other-cities-more-influenza-cases-reported-in.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413025709/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/23/archives/spreads-in-other-cities-more-influenza-cases-reported-in.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Certain pandemic restrictions, such as the closing of schools and theaters and the staggering of business hours to avoid congestion, were reimposed in cities like Chicago,<ref>{{Cite news |date=22 January 1920 |title=TOPICS OF THE TIMES. |pages=16 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/22/archives/topics-of-the-times-the-return-of-the-influenza-menace.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031220/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/22/archives/topics-of-the-times-the-return-of-the-influenza-menace.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Memphis,<ref name="The New York Times-1920">{{Cite news |date=25 January 1920 |title=INFLUENZA CASES GROW THROUGHOUT COUNTRY |pages=2 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/25/archives/influenza-cases-grow-throughout-country-chicago-sees-evidence-of.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031215/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/25/archives/influenza-cases-grow-throughout-country-chicago-sees-evidence-of.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and New York City.<ref name="The New York Times-1920-2">{{Cite news |date=27 January 1920 |title=COPELAND EXPECTS RISE IN INFLUENZA |pages=1 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/27/archives/copeland-expects-rise-in-influenza-monday-reports-show-only-1712.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322035549/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/01/27/archives/copeland-expects-rise-in-influenza-monday-reports-show-only-1712.html |url-status=live }}</ref> As they had during the epidemic in fall 1918, schools in New York City remained open,<ref name="The New York Times-1920-2" /> while those in Memphis were shuttered as part of restrictions on public gatherings.<ref name="The New York Times-1920"/>

[[File:1918 flu in Oakland.jpg|thumb|[[American Red Cross]] nurses tend to flu patients in temporary wards set up inside the [[Oakland]] Municipal Auditorium]]
The fourth wave in the United States subsided as swiftly as it had appeared, reaching a peak in early February.<ref>{{Cite news |date=8 February 1920 |title=Influenza Checked in 25 States. |pages=15 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1920/02/08/archives/influenza-checked-in-25-states.html |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413031213/https://www.nytimes.com/1920/02/08/archives/influenza-checked-in-25-states.html |url-status=live }}</ref> "An epidemic of considerable proportions marked the early months of 1920", the U.S. Mortality Statistics would later note; according to data at this time, the epidemic resulted in one third as many deaths as the 1918–1919 experience.<ref>{{Cite report |work=US Bureau of the Census |title=Mortality statistics, 1920. Twenty-First Annual Report. |date=1922 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/vsushistorical/mortstatsh_1920.pdf |via=CDC |archive-date=16 March 2023 |access-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230316205252/https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/vsushistorical/mortstatsh_1920.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> New York City alone reported 6,374 deaths between December 1919 and April 1920, almost twice the number of the first wave in spring 1918.<ref name="NIH-NYC"/> Detroit, Milwaukee, Kansas City, Minneapolis, and St. Louis were hit particularly hard, with death rates higher than all of 1918.<ref name="Vaughan1921" /> [[Territory of Hawaii|Hawaii]] experienced its peak of the pandemic in early 1920, recording 1,489 deaths from flu-related causes, compared with 615 in 1918 and 796 in 1919.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Schmitt RC, Nordyke EC |date=1999 |title=Influenza Deaths in Hawai'i, 1918—1920 |url=https://evols.library.manoa.hawaii.edu/handle/10524/538 |journal=Hawaiian Journal of History |volume=33 |pages=101–117 |via=eVols |archive-date=5 July 2022 |access-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705000357/https://evols.library.manoa.hawaii.edu/handle/10524/538 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Poland experienced a devastating outbreak during the winter months, with its capital [[Warsaw]] reaching a peak of 158 deaths in a single week, compared to the peak of 92 in December 1918; however, the 1920 epidemic passed in a matter of weeks, while the 1918–1919 wave had developed over the entire second half of 1918.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Grabowski ML, Kosińska B, Knap JP, Brydak LB | title = The Lethal Spanish Influenza Pandemic in Poland | journal = Medical Science Monitor | volume = 23 | pages = 4880–4884 | date = October 2017 | pmid = 29021518 | pmc = 5649514 | doi = 10.12659/MSM.906280 }}</ref> By contrast, the outbreak in western Europe was considered "benign", with the age distribution of deaths beginning to take on that of [[seasonal flu]].<ref name="NIHInfluenza2010"/> Spain, Denmark, Finland, Germany and Switzerland recorded a late peak between January–April 1920.<ref name="IORV2009"/>

Mexico experienced a fourth wave between February and March. In South America, [[Peru]] experienced "asynchronous recrudescent waves" throughout the year. A severe third wave hit [[Lima]], the capital city, between January and March, resulting in an all-cause excess mortality rate approximately four times greater than that of the 1918–1919 wave. [[Ica, Peru|Ica]] similarly experienced another severe pandemic wave in 1920, between July and October.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chowell G, Viboud C, Simonsen L, Miller MA, Hurtado J, Soto G, Vargas R, Guzman MA, Ulloa M, Munayco CV | title = The 1918–1920 influenza pandemic in Peru | journal = Vaccine | volume = 29 Suppl 2 | issue = Suppl 2 | pages = B21–B26 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 21757099 | pmc = 3144394 | doi = 10.1016/j.vaccine.2011.02.048 }}</ref> A fourth wave also occurred in Brazil, in February.<ref name="Chandra-2020"/>

[[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]] and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]] experienced pronounced outbreaks in late 1919 and early 1920.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Kim T |date=2017 |title=The 1918 Influenza Pandemic and Japanese Government-General of Korea's Preventive Measures against Epidemics |url=http://journal.kci.go.kr/snu-ioh/archive/articleView?artiId=ART002202446 |journal=Journal of Humanities, Seoul National University |language=Korean |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=203–207 |via=Korea Journal Central |archive-date=17 March 2023 |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317035414/http://journal.kci.go.kr/snu-ioh/archive/articleView?artiId=ART002202446 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hsieh YH | title = Excess deaths and immunoprotection during 1918–1920 influenza pandemic, Taiwan | journal = Emerging Infectious Diseases | volume = 15 | issue = 10 | pages = 1617–1619 | date = October 2009 | pmid = 19861055 | pmc = 2866376 | doi = 10.3201/eid1510.080811 }}</ref>

====Post-pandemic====
By mid-1920, the pandemic was largely considered to be "over" by the public as well as governments.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Nichols CM, Ewing ET, Gaston KH, Marinari M, Lessoff A, Huyssen D |date=April 2022 |title=What Came Next?: Reflections on the Aftermath(s) of the 1918–19 Flu Pandemic in the Age of COVID |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-gilded-age-and-progressive-era/article/abs/what-came-next-reflections-on-the-aftermaths-of-the-191819-flu-pandemic-in-the-age-of-covid/C34A023067C72795D6CFAB2A365AF66A |journal=The Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=126 |via=Cambridge Core |archive-date=27 February 2023 |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230227183514/https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-gilded-age-and-progressive-era/article/abs/what-came-next-reflections-on-the-aftermaths-of-the-191819-flu-pandemic-in-the-age-of-covid/C34A023067C72795D6CFAB2A365AF66A |url-status=live }}</ref> Though parts of Chile experienced a third, milder wave between November 1920 and March 1921,<ref name="Chowell-2014" /> the flu seemed to be mostly absent through the winter of 1920–1921.{{r|Jordan1927|p=167}} In the United States, for example, deaths from pneumonia and influenza were "very much lower than for many years".{{r|Jordan1927|p=167}}

Seasonal influenza began to be reported again from many places in 1921.{{r|Jordan1927|p=168}} Influenza continued to be felt in Chile, where a post-pandemic fourth wave affected 7 of its 24 provinces between June and December 1921.<ref name="Chowell-2014"/> The winter of 1921–1922 was the first major reappearance of seasonal influenza in the Northern Hemisphere, in many parts its most significant occurrence since the main pandemic in late 1918. Northwestern Europe was particularly affected. All-cause mortality in the [[Netherlands]] approximately doubled in January 1922 alone.{{r|Jordan1927|p=168}} In [[Helsinki]], a major epidemic (the fifth since 1918) prevailed between November and December 1921.<ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Linnanmäki E |title=Espanjantauti Suomessa — Influenssapandemia 1918–1920 |publisher=Suomalaisen Kirjallisuuden Seura |year=2005 |isbn=9789517467162 |location=Helsinki |pages=69 |language=fi}}</ref> The flu was also widespread in the United States, its prevalence in California reportedly greater in early March 1922 than at any point since the pandemic ended in 1920.{{r|Jordan1927|p=172}}

In the years after 1920, the disease came to represent the "seasonal flu". The virus, H1N1, remained endemic, occasionally causing more severe or [[Flu season#Notable occurrences|otherwise notable outbreaks]].<ref name="Taubenberger-2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Taubenberger JK, Morens DM | title = Influenza: the once and future pandemic | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 125 Suppl 3 | issue = Suppl 3 | pages = 16–26 | date = April 2010 | pmid = 20568566 | pmc = 2862331 | doi = 10.1177/00333549101250S305 }}</ref> The period since its initial appearance in 1918 has been termed a "pandemic era", in which all flu pandemics have been caused by its own descendants.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Morens DM, Taubenberger JK, Fauci AS | title = The persistent legacy of the 1918 influenza virus | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 361 | issue = 3 | pages = 225–229 | date = July 2009 | pmid = 19564629 | pmc = 2749954 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMp0904819 }}</ref> Following the [[1957–1958 influenza pandemic|first of these post-1918 pandemics]], in 1957, the virus was totally displaced by the novel [[H2N2]], the [[reassortant]] product of the human H1N1 and an [[avian influenza]] virus, which thereafter became the active influenza A virus in humans.<ref name="Taubenberger-2010"/>

In 1977, an influenza virus bearing a very close resemblance to the seasonal H1N1, which had not been seen since the 1950s, appeared in the USSR and subsequently initiated a "technical" [[1977 Russian flu|pandemic]] that principally affected those 26 and under.<ref name="Taubenberger-2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Taubenberger JK, Morens DM | title = Pandemic influenza – including a risk assessment of H5N1 | journal = Revue Scientifique et Technique | volume = 28 | issue = 1 | pages = 187–202 | date = April 2009 | pmid = 19618626 | pmc = 2720801 | doi = 10.20506/rst.28.1.1879 }}</ref><ref name="Rozo-2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rozo M, Gronvall GK | title = The Reemergent 1977 H1N1 Strain and the Gain-of-Function Debate | journal = mBio | volume = 6 | issue = 4 | date = August 2015 | article-number = e01013-15 | pmid = 26286690 | pmc = 4542197 | doi = 10.1128/mBio.01013-15 | doi-access = free}}</ref> While some natural explanations, such as the virus remaining in some frozen state for 20 years,<ref name="Rozo-2015"/> have been proposed to explain this unprecedented<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kung HC, Jen KF, Yuan WC, Tien SF, Chu CM | title = Influenza in China in 1977: recurrence of influenzavirus A subtype H1N1 | journal = Bulletin of the World Health Organization | volume = 56 | issue = 6 | pages = 913–918 | date = 1978 | pmid = 310732 | pmc = 2395678 | hdl = 10665/261795 }}</ref> phenomenon, the nature of influenza itself has been cited in favor of human involvement of some kind, such as an accidental leak from a lab where the old virus had been preserved for research purposes.<ref name="Rozo-2015"/> Following this miniature pandemic, the reemerged H1N1 became endemic again but did not displace the other active influenza A virus, [[H3N2]] (which itself had displaced H2N2 through a [[Hong Kong flu|pandemic in 1968]]).<ref name="Taubenberger-2009"/><ref name="Taubenberger-2010"/> For the first time, two influenza A viruses were observed in cocirculation.<ref name="Saunders-Hastings_2016"/> This state has persisted even after 2009, when a [[Pandemic H1N1/09 virus|novel H1N1 virus]] emerged, sparked a [[2009 swine flu pandemic|pandemic]], and thereafter took the place of the seasonal H1N1 to circulate alongside H3N2.<ref name="Saunders-Hastings_2016"/>

==Epidemiology and pathology==
===Transmission and mutation===
[[File:U.S. Army Field Hospital No. 29, Hollerich, Luxembourg Interior view- Influenza ward.jpg|thumb|U.S. Army flu patients at Field Hospital No. 29 near Hollerich, Luxembourg 1918. As U.S. troops deployed en masse for the [[United States in World War I|war effort in Europe]], they carried the Spanish flu with them.]]
The [[basic reproduction number]] of the virus was between 2 and 3.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mills CE, Robins JM, Lipsitch M | title = Transmissibility of 1918 pandemic influenza | journal = Nature | volume = 432 | issue = 7019 | pages = 904–906 | date = December 2004 | pmid = 15602562 | pmc = 7095078 | doi = 10.1038/nature03063 | bibcode = 2004Natur.432..904M }}</ref> The close quarters and massive troop movements of [[World War I]] hastened the pandemic, and probably both increased transmission and augmented mutation. The war may also have reduced people's resistance to the virus. Some speculate the soldiers' immune systems were weakened by malnourishment and the stresses of combat and chemical attacks, increasing their susceptibility.{{sfn|Qureshi|2016|p=42}}{{sfn|Ewald|1994}} Modern transportation systems and increased travel was a significant factor in the worldwide occurrence.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918|url=https://www.thehistorypress.co.uk/articles/the-spanish-flu-pandemic-of-1918/|url-status=live|access-date=20 February 2021|website=The History Press|archive-date=13 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210113105135/https://www.thehistorypress.co.uk/articles/the-spanish-flu-pandemic-of-1918/}}</ref> Another was lies and denial by governments, leaving the population ill-prepared to handle the outbreaks.<ref name="Illing">{{cite web | vauthors = Illing S |title=The most important lesson of the 1918 influenza pandemic: Tell the damn truth |url=https://www.vox.com/coronavirus-covid19/2020/3/20/21184887/coronavirus-covid-19-spanish-flu-pandemic-john-barry |website=Vox |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200325172129/https://www.vox.com/coronavirus-covid19/2020/3/20/21184887/coronavirus-covid-19-spanish-flu-pandemic-john-barry |archive-date=25 March 2020|date=20 March 2020 |quote=John M. Barry : The government lied. They lied about everything. We were at war and they lied because they didn't want to upend the war effort. You had public health leaders telling people this was just the ordinary flu by another name. They simply didn't tell the people the truth about what was happening. |url-status=live}}</ref>

The severity of the second wave has been attributed to the First World War.{{sfn|Gladwell|1997|p=55}} In civilian life, [[natural selection]] favors a mild strain. Those who get very ill stay home, and those mildly ill continue with their lives, preferentially spreading the mild strain. In the trenches, natural selection was reversed. Soldiers with a mild strain stayed where they were, while the severely ill were sent on crowded trains to crowded field hospitals, spreading the deadlier virus. The second wave began, and the flu quickly spread around the world again. (During modern pandemics, health officials look for deadlier strains of a virus when it reaches places with social upheaval.{{sfn|Gladwell|1997|p=63}}) The fact that most of those who recovered from first-wave infections had become [[immune]] showed that it must have been the same strain of flu. This was most dramatically illustrated in [[Copenhagen]], which escaped with a combined mortality rate of 0.29% (0.02% in the first wave and 0.27% in the second wave) because of exposure to the less-lethal first wave.<ref>{{cite web|author=Fogarty International Center|title=Summer Flu Outbreak of 1918 May Have Provided Partial Protection Against Lethal Fall Pandemic|url=https://www.fic.nih.gov/News/GlobalHealthMatters/Pages/Flu-1918.aspx|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727122221/http://www.fic.nih.gov/News/GlobalHealthMatters/Pages/Flu-1918.aspx|archive-date=27 July 2011|access-date=19 May 2012|publisher=Fic.nih.gov}}</ref>

After the lethal second wave, new cases dropped abruptly. In Philadelphia, for example, 4,597 people died in the week ending 16 October, but by 11 November, influenza had almost disappeared from the city. One explanation for the rapid decline in lethality is that doctors became more effective in the prevention and treatment of pneumonia that developed after the victims had contracted the virus. However, John Barry stated in his 2004 book ''[[The Great Influenza: The Epic Story of the Deadliest Plague In History]]'' that researchers have found no evidence to support this position.{{sfn|Barry|2004b}} Another theory holds that the 1918 virus mutated extremely rapidly to a less lethal strain. Such [[evolution of influenza]] is a common occurrence: there is a tendency for pathogenic viruses to become less lethal with time, as the hosts of more dangerous strains tend to die out.{{sfn|Barry|2004b}} Fatal cases did continue into 1919, however. One notable example was that of [[ice hockey]] player [[Joe Hall (ice hockey)|Joe Hall]], who died of the flu in April after an outbreak that resulted in the cancellation of the [[1919 Stanley Cup Final]].<ref>{{Cite web | vauthors = Joyce G |date=March 2020 |title=The 1919 Stanley Cup Final and modern-history's deadliest pandemic |url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1919-stanley-cup-spanish-flu-pandemic/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200331024901/https://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1919-stanley-cup-spanish-flu-pandemic/ |archive-date=31 March 2020 |access-date=23 March 2023 |website=Sportsnet}}</ref>

===Signs and symptoms===
[[File:3548786222 7a3d3208d3 bInfluenzaGrippe.jpg|thumb|US Army symptomology of the flu]]
The majority of the infected experienced only the typical flu symptoms of sore throat, headache, and fever, especially during the first wave.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=45–47}} However, during the second wave, the disease was much more serious, often complicated by [[bacterial pneumonia]], which was often the cause of death.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=45–47}} This more serious type would cause ''heliotrope cyanosis'' to develop, whereby the skin would first develop two mahogany spots over the cheekbones which would then over a few hours color the entire face blue, followed by black coloration first in the extremities and then the limbs and the torso.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=45–47}} Death would follow within hours or days due to the lungs being filled with fluids.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=45–47}} Other signs and symptoms reported included spontaneous mouth and nosebleeds, miscarriages for pregnant women, a peculiar smell, teeth and hair falling out, [[delirium]], dizziness, insomnia, loss of hearing or smell, and impaired vision.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=45–47}} One observer wrote, "One of the most striking of the complications was [[hemorrhage]] from [[mucous membrane]]s, especially from the nose, stomach, and intestine. Bleeding from the ears and [[petechia|petechial hemorrhages]] in the skin also occurred".{{sfn|Knobler|2005}}

The majority of deaths were from [[bacterial pneumonia]],<ref name="MorrisCleary2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Morris DE, Cleary DW, Clarke SC | title = Secondary Bacterial Infections Associated with Influenza Pandemics | journal = Frontiers in Microbiology | volume = 8 | article-number = 1041 | year = 2017 | pmid = 28690590 | pmc = 5481322 | doi = 10.3389/fmicb.2017.01041 | bibcode = 2017FrMic...801041M | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bacterial Pneumonia Caused Most Deaths in 1918 Influenza Pandemic |url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/bacterial-pneumonia-caused-most-deaths-1918-influenza-pandemic |date=23 September 2015 |access-date=17 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422191021/https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/bacterial-pneumonia-caused-most-deaths-1918-influenza-pandemic |archive-date=22 April 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>{{sfn|Taubenberger|Reid|Janczewski|Fanning|2001|pp=1829–39}} a common [[secondary infection]] associated with influenza. This pneumonia was itself caused by common upper respiratory-tract bacteria, which were able to get into the lungs via the damaged [[bronchial tubes]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Morens DM, Taubenberger JK, Fauci AS | title = Predominant role of bacterial pneumonia as a cause of death in pandemic influenza: implications for pandemic influenza preparedness | journal = The Journal of Infectious Diseases | volume = 198 | issue = 7 | pages = 962–970 | date = October 2008 | pmid = 18710327 | pmc = 2599911 | doi = 10.1086/591708 }}</ref> The virus also killed people directly by causing massive hemorrhages and [[edema]] in the lungs.{{sfn|Taubenberger|Reid|Janczewski|Fanning|2001|pp=1829–39}} Modern analysis has shown the virus to be particularly deadly because in animal trials it triggers an overreaction of the body's immune system ([[cytokine storm]]).{{sfn|Barry|2004b}} The strong immune reactions of young adults were postulated to have ravaged the body, whereas the weaker immune reactions of children and middle-aged adults resulted in fewer deaths.{{sfn|Barry|2004}}

===Misdiagnosis===
Because the virus that caused the disease was too small to be seen under a microscope at the time, there were problems with correctly diagnosing it.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=61}} The bacterium ''[[Haemophilus influenzae]]'' was instead mistakenly thought to be the cause, as it was big enough to be seen and was present in many, though not all, patients.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=61}} For this reason, a vaccine that was used against that bacillus did not make infection rarer but did decrease the death rate.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Washington State Board of Health pessimistic about influenza pandemic in a report to the governor on January 1, 1919. |url=https://www.historylink.org/File/20313 |access-date=21 July 2020 |website=historylink.org |archive-date=21 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200721231319/https://www.historylink.org/File/20313 |url-status=live }}</ref>

During the deadly second wave there were also fears that it was in fact [[Plague (disease)|plague]], [[dengue fever]], or [[cholera]].{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=62}} Another misdiagnosis was [[typhus]], which was common in circumstances of social upheaval, and was therefore also affecting Russia in the aftermath of the [[October Revolution]].{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=62}} In [[Chile]], the view of the country's elite was that the nation was in severe decline, and therefore doctors assumed that the disease was typhus caused by poor hygiene, causing a mismanaged response which did not ban mass gatherings.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=62}}

===Role of climate conditions===
[[File:CoughsAndSneezesSpreadDiseases.jpg|thumb|US poster with the slogan "[[Coughs and sneezes spread diseases]]" ]]
Studies have shown that the immune system of Spanish flu victims could have been weakened by unseasonably cold and wet weather for extended periods during the pandemic. This affected especially troops exposed to incessant rains and lower-than-average temperatures during World War I, and especially during the second wave of the pandemic. Climate data and mortality records analyzed at [[Harvard University]] and the Climate Change Institute at the [[University of Maine]] identified a severe climate anomaly that impacted Europe from 1914 to 1919, with several environmental indicators directly influencing the severity and spread of the pandemic.<ref name="The Impact of a Six‐Year Climate An"/> Specifically, a significant increase in precipitation affected all of Europe during the second wave of the pandemic, from September to December 1918. Mortality figures follow closely the concurrent increase in precipitation and decrease in temperatures. Several explanations have been proposed for this, including that lower temperatures and increased precipitation provided ideal conditions for virus replication and transmission, while also negatively affecting peoples' immune systems, a factor proven to increase likelihood of infection by both viruses and pneumococcal co-morbid infections documented to have affected a large percentage of pandemic victims (one fifth of them, with a 36% mortality rate).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Foxman EF, Storer JA, Fitzgerald ME, Wasik BR, Hou L, Zhao H, Turner PE, Pyle AM, Iwasaki A | title = Temperature-dependent innate defense against the common cold virus limits viral replication at warm temperature in mouse airway cells | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 112 | issue = 3 | pages = 827–832 | date = January 2015 | pmid = 25561542 | pmc = 4311828 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1411030112 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2015PNAS..112..827F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lowen AC, Steel J | title = Roles of humidity and temperature in shaping influenza seasonality | journal = Journal of Virology | volume = 88 | issue = 14 | pages = 7692–7695 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24789791 | pmc = 4097773 | doi = 10.1128/JVI.03544-13 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brown JD, Goekjian G, Poulson R, Valeika S, Stallknecht DE | title = Avian influenza virus in water: infectivity is dependent on pH, salinity and temperature | journal = Veterinary Microbiology | volume = 136 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 20–26 | date = April 2009 | pmid = 19081209 | doi = 10.1016/j.vetmic.2008.10.027 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Foxman EF, Storer JA, Vanaja K, Levchenko A, Iwasaki A | title = Two interferon-independent double-stranded RNA-induced host defense strategies suppress the common cold virus at warm temperature | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 113 | issue = 30 | pages = 8496–8501 | date = July 2016 | pmid = 27402752 | pmc = 4968739 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1601942113 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2016PNAS..113.8496F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Klugman KP, Chien YW, Madhi SA | title = Pneumococcal pneumonia and influenza: a deadly combination | journal = Vaccine | volume = 27 Suppl 3 | issue = s3 | pages = C9–C14 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19683658 | doi = 10.1016/j.vaccine.2009.06.007 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The climate anomaly likely influenced the migration of H1N1 avian vectors which contaminate bodies of water with their droppings, reaching 60% infection rates in autumn.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bengtsson D, Safi K, Avril A, Fiedler W, Wikelski M, Gunnarsson G, Elmberg J, Tolf C, Olsen B, Waldenström J | title = Does influenza A virus infection affect movement behaviour during stopover in its wild reservoir host? | journal = Royal Society Open Science | volume = 3 | issue = 2 | article-number = 150633 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26998334 | pmc = 4785985 | doi = 10.1098/rsos.150633 | bibcode = 2016RSOS....350633B | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tolf C, Bengtsson D, Rodrigues D, Latorre-Margalef N, Wille M, Figueiredo ME, Jankowska-Hjortaas M, Germundsson A, Duby PY, Lebarbenchon C, Gauthier-Clerc M, Olsen B, Waldenström J | title = Birds and viruses at a crossroad – surveillance of influenza A virus in Portuguese waterfowl | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 7 | issue = 11 | article-number = e49002 | year = 2012 | pmid = 23145046 | pmc = 3492218 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0049002 | bibcode = 2012PLoSO...749002T | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tucker MA, Böhning-Gaese K, Fagan WF, Fryxell JM, Van Moorter B, Alberts SC, Ali AH, Allen AM, Attias N, Avgar T, Bartlam-Brooks H, Bayarbaatar B, Belant JL, Bertassoni A, Beyer D, Bidner L, van Beest FM, Blake S, Blaum N,
