==Responses==
===Public health management===
{{multiple image
| align       = right
| direction   = horizontal
| total_width = 350
| image1      = Coromandel_Hospital_Board.jpg
| width1      = 
| caption1    = Coromandel Hospital Board ([[Dominion of New Zealand|New Zealand]]) advice to influenza sufferers (1918)
| image2      = 19180927 Gauze Mask to Halt Spread of Plague (Spanish flu) - The Washington Times.jpg
| width2      = 
| caption2    = In September 1918, the Red Cross recommended two-layer gauze masks to halt the spread of "plague".<ref name=WashTimes_19180927>{{cite news |title=Gauze Mask to Halt Spread of Plague |url=https://newspaperarchive.com/washington-times-sep-27-1918-p-3/ |work=The Washington Times |date=27 September 1918 |page=3 |access-date=5 October 2020 |archive-date=8 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008051659/https://newspaperarchive.com/washington-times-sep-27-1918-p-3/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
| image3      = 1918 Headlines from Chicago newspapers - Spanish flu - 1918 influenza pandemic.jpg
| caption3    = 1918 Chicago newspaper headlines reflect mitigation strategies such as increased ventilation, arrests for not wearing face masks, sequenced [[inoculation]]s, limitations on crowd size, selective closing of businesses, curfews, and lockdowns.<ref name=USAtoday_20201122/> After October's strict containment measures showed some success, Armistice Day celebrations in November and relaxed attitudes by Thanksgiving caused a resurgence.<ref name=USAtoday_20201122>{{cite news | vauthors = Hauck G, Gellis K |title=We're celebrating Thanksgiving amid a pandemic. Here's how we did it in 1918 – and what happened next |url=https://www.usatoday.com/in-depth/news/nation/2020/11/21/covid-and-thanksgiving-how-we-celebrated-during-1918-flu-pandemic/6264231002/ |work=USA Today |date=22 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201121183814/https://eu.usatoday.com/in-depth/news/nation/2020/11/21/covid-and-thanksgiving-how-we-celebrated-during-1918-flu-pandemic/6264231002/ |archive-date=21 November 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>
| perrow      = 2 / 1
}}

While systems for alerting public health authorities of infectious spread did exist in 1918, they did not generally include influenza, leading to a delayed response.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=83–84}} Nevertheless, actions were taken. Maritime quarantines were declared on islands such as Iceland, Australia, and American Samoa, saving many lives.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=83–84}} [[Social distancing]] measures were introduced, for example closing schools, theatres, and places of worship, limiting public transportation, and banning mass gatherings.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=87–88}} Wearing [[Surgical mask|face masks]] became common in some places, such as Japan, though there were debates over their efficacy.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=87–88}}<ref>{{cite book |last1=Segrave |first1=Kerry |title=Masking America, 1918–1919: Efforts to Control the Great Influenza Pandemic |date=2024 |publisher=McFarland and Co. |location=Jefferson, NC |isbn=978-1-4766-9449-8 |url=https://mcfarlandbooks.com/product/masking-america-1918-1919 |access-date=1 September 2024 |archive-date=1 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240901234543/https://mcfarlandbooks.com/product/masking-america-1918-1919/ |url-status=live }}</ref> There was also some resistance to their use, as exemplified by the [[Anti-Mask League of San Francisco]]. Vaccines were developed, but as these were based on bacteria and not the actual virus, they could only help with secondary infections.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=87–88}} The enforcement of restrictions varied.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=91}} To a large extent, the New York City health commissioner ordered businesses to open and close on staggered shifts to avoid overcrowding on the subways.<ref>{{Cite web|date=20 September 2021|title=How NYC beat deadly 1918 flu without vaccines, lockdowns, mask mandates or school closures|url=https://www.silive.com/news/2021/09/how-nyc-beat-deadly-1918-flu-without-vaccines-lockdowns-mask-mandates-or-school-closures.html|access-date=23 September 2021|website=silive|language=en|archive-date=21 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921151432/https://www.silive.com/news/2021/09/how-nyc-beat-deadly-1918-flu-without-vaccines-lockdowns-mask-mandates-or-school-closures.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
A later study found that measures such as banning mass gatherings and requiring the wearing of face masks could cut the death rate up to 50 percent, but this was dependent on their being imposed early in the outbreak and not being lifted prematurely.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bootsma MC, Ferguson NM | title = The effect of public health measures on the 1918 influenza pandemic in U.S. cities | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 104 | issue = 18 | pages = 7588–7593 | date = May 2007 | pmid = 17416677 | pmc = 1849868 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0611071104 | s2cid = 11280273 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2007PNAS..104.7588B }}</ref>

===Medical treatment===
As there were no [[antiviral drug]]s to treat the virus, and no [[antibiotic]]s to treat the secondary bacterial infections, doctors would rely on an assortment of medicines with varying degrees of effectiveness, such as [[aspirin]], [[quinine]], [[arsenic]]s, [[digitalis]], [[strychnine]], [[Magnesium sulfate|epsom salts]], [[castor oil]], and [[iodine]].{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=109–10}} [[traditional medicine|Traditional treatments]], such as [[bloodletting]], [[ayurveda]], and [[kampo]], were also applied.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=111–12}}

===Information dissemination===
Due to [[World War I]], many countries engaged in wartime censorship, and suppressed reporting of the pandemic.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Flecknoe D, Charles Wakefield B, Simmons A | title = Plagues & wars: the 'Spanish Flu' pandemic as a lesson from history | journal = Medicine, Conflict and Survival | volume = 34 | issue = 2 | pages = 61–68 | date = June 2018 | pmid = 29764189 | doi = 10.1080/13623699.2018.1472892 | s2cid = 21694687 }}</ref> For example, the Italian newspaper ''[[Corriere della Sera]]'' was prohibited from reporting daily death tolls.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=92}} The newspapers of the time were also generally [[paternalistic]] and worried about mass panic.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=92}} [[Misinformation]] also spread along with the disease. In Ireland there was a belief that [[Miasma theory|noxious gases]] were rising from the mass graves of [[Flanders Fields]] and being "blown all over the world by winds".{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=69}} There were also rumors that the Germans were behind it, for example by poisoning the [[aspirin]] manufactured by [[Bayer]], or by [[Chemical weapons in World War I|releasing poison gas]] from [[U-boat]]s.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=70}}

==Mortality==
{{see also|List of Spanish flu cases}}
[[File:W curve.png|thumb|Difference between the flu mortality age-distributions of the 1918 pandemic and normal epidemics – deaths per 100,000 persons in each age group, United States, for the interpandemic years 1911–1917 (dashed line) and the pandemic year 1918 (solid line){{sfn|Taubenberger|Morens|2006|p=19}}]]
[[File:1918 spanish flu waves.gif|thumb|upright=1|Three pandemic waves: weekly combined flu and pneumonia mortality, United Kingdom, 1918–1919{{sfn|Taubenberger|Morens|2006|p=17}}]]
The Spanish flu infected around 500 million people, about one-third of the world's population.{{sfn|Taubenberger|Morens|2006}} Estimates on deaths vary greatly, but it is considered to be one of the [[List of pandemics|deadliest pandemics]] in history.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Ten things you need to know about pandemic influenza (update of 14 October 2005) | journal = Relevé Épidémiologique Hebdomadaire | volume = 80 | issue = 49–50 | pages = 428–431 | date = December 2005 | pmid = 16372665 | url = https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/232955/WER8049_50_428-431.PDF | access-date = 11 March 2020 | url-status = live | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210727045636/https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/232955/WER8049_50_428-431.PDF | archive-date = 27 July 2021 | vauthors = World Health O }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Jilani TN, Jamil RT, Siddiqui AH | chapter-url = https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513241/ | chapter = H1N1 Influenza (Swine Flu) |date= 14 December 2019 |pmid=30020613 | title = StatPearls | place = Treasure Island, FL | publisher = StatPearls | via = [[NCBI]] |access-date=11 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200312134634/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513241/ |archive-date=12 March 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> An early estimate from 1927 put global mortality at 21.6 million.<ref name="pmid30202996"/> An estimate from 1991 states that the virus killed between 25 and 39 million people.{{sfn|Patterson|Pyle|1991}} A 2005 estimate put the death toll at 50 million, and possibly as high as 100 million.{{sfn|Knobler|2005}}{{sfn|Johnson|Mueller|2002}} However, a 2018 reassessment in the ''[[American Journal of Epidemiology]]'' estimated the total to be about 17 million,<ref name="pmid30202996">{{cite journal | vauthors = Spreeuwenberg P, Kroneman M, Paget J | title = Reassessing the Global Mortality Burden of the 1918 Influenza Pandemic | journal = American Journal of Epidemiology | volume = 187 | issue = 12 | pages = 2561–2567 | date = December 2018 | pmid = 30202996 | pmc = 7314216 | doi = 10.1093/aje/kwy191 | publisher = [[Oxford University Press]] }}</ref> though this has been contested.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chandra S, Christensen J | title = Re: "Reassessing the Global Mortality Burden of the 1918 Influenza Pandemic" | journal = American Journal of Epidemiology | volume = 188 | issue = 7 | pages = 1404–1406 | date = July 2019 | pmid = 30824934 | doi = 10.1093/aje/kwz044 }} and response {{cite journal | vauthors = Spreeuwenberg P, Kroneman M, Paget J | title = The Authors Reply | journal = American Journal of Epidemiology | volume = 188 | issue = 7 | pages = 1405–1406 | date = July 2019 | pmid = 30824908 | doi = 10.1093/aje/kwz041 | url = https://postprint.nivel.nl/PPpp7146.pdf | access-date = 12 March 2020 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200312204122/https://postprint.nivel.nl/PPpp7146.pdf | archive-date = 12 March 2020 }}</ref> Estimates done in 2021 by [[John M. Barry]] have the total death toll alone at well above 100 million.<ref name=":1" /> With a world population of 1.8 to 1.9 billion,<ref>{{cite web |title=Historical Estimates of World Population |url=https://www.census.gov/population/international/data/worldpop/table_history.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120709092946/https://www.census.gov/population/international/data/worldpop/table_history.php |url-status=dead |archive-date=9 July 2012 |access-date=29 March 2013}}</ref> these estimates correspond to between 1 and 6 percent of the population.

A 2009 study in ''[[Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses]]'' based on data from fourteen European countries estimated a total of 2.64 million excess deaths in Europe attributable to the Spanish flu during the 1918–1919 phase of the pandemic. This represents a mortality rate of about 1.1% of the European population ({{circa}} 250 million in 1918), considerably higher than the mortality rate in the U.S., which the authors hypothesize is likely due to the severe effects of the war in Europe.<ref name="IORV2009"/> The excess mortality rate in the U.K. has been estimated at 0.28%–0.4%, far below this European average.<ref name="pmid30202996"/>

Some 12–17 million people died in [[1918 flu pandemic in India|India]], about 5% of the population.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mayor S | title = Flu experts warn of need for pandemic plans | journal = BMJ | volume = 321 | issue = 7265 | pages = 852 | date = October 2000 | pmid = 11021855 | pmc = 1118673 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.321.7265.852 }}</ref> The death toll in [[British Raj|India's British-ruled districts]] was 13.88 million.{{sfn|Chandra|Kuljanin|Wray|2012}} Another estimate gives at least 12 million dead.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Arnold D | title = Death and the Modern Empire: The 1918–19 Influenza Epidemic in India. | journal = Transactions of the Royal Historical Society | date = December 2019 | volume = 29 | pages = 181–200 | doi = 10.1017/S0080440119000082 }}</ref> The decade between 1911 and 1921 was the only census period in which India's population fell, mostly due to devastation of the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.livemint.com/news/world/why-1918-matters-in-india-s-corona-war-11584033795146.html|title=Why 1918 matters in India's corona war | vauthors = Sreevatsan A |date=12 March 2020|website=mint|access-date=7 June 2020|archive-date=18 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200418110954/https://www.livemint.com/news/world/why-1918-matters-in-india-s-corona-war-11584033795146.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/analysis/what-the-history-of-pandemics-tells-us-about-coronavirus/story-Fb3XDfXe0lyk0JukqtdG1L.html|title=What the history of pandemics tells us about coronavirus|date=15 April 2020|website=Hindustan Times|access-date=7 June 2020|archive-date=21 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200421154324/https://www.hindustantimes.com/analysis/what-the-history-of-pandemics-tells-us-about-coronavirus/story-Fb3XDfXe0lyk0JukqtdG1L.html|url-status=live}}</ref> While India is generally described as the country most severely affected by the Spanish flu, at least one study argues that other factors may partially account for the very high excess mortality rates observed in 1918, citing unusually high 1917 mortality and wide regional variation (ranging from 0.47% to 6.66%).<ref name="pmid30202996"/> A 2006 study in ''[[The Lancet]]'' also noted that Indian provinces had excess mortality rates ranging from 2.1% to 7.8%, stating: "Commentators at the time attributed this huge variation to differences in nutritional status and diurnal fluctuations in temperature."<ref name="Lancet 2006 Murray, Lopez, Chin, Feehan">{{cite journal | vauthors = Murray CJ, Lopez AD, Chin B, Feehan D, Hill KH | title = Estimation of potential global pandemic influenza mortality on the basis of vital registry data from the 1918-20 pandemic: a quantitative analysis | journal = Lancet | volume = 368 | issue = 9554 | pages = 2211–2218 | date = December 2006 | pmid = 17189032 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(06)69895-4 | url = https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(06)69895-4/fulltext | access-date = 30 September 2020 | publisher = [[Elsevier]] | url-status = live | s2cid = 22787011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200927235224/https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(06)69895-4/fulltext | archive-date = 27 September 2020 | url-access = subscription }}</ref>

In Finland, 20,000 died out of 210,000 infected.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Historiallisia Papereita 1|issn=1456-8055|url=http://historiallinenyhdistys.fi/muinaiset_sivut/julk/taudit99/|access-date=24 June 2020|website=historiallinenyhdistys.fi|archive-date=6 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200206132858/http://historiallinenyhdistys.fi/muinaiset_sivut/julk/taudit99/|url-status=live}}</ref> In Sweden, 34,000 died.<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Åman M |title=Spanska sjukan: den svenska epidemin 1918–1920 och dess internationella bakgrund|date=1990|publisher=Ubsaliensis Academiae; Distributor, Almqvist & Wiksell International|isbn=978-91-554-2587-6|place=Uppsala; Stockholm|language=sv|oclc=22451542}}</ref>

In Japan, the flu killed nearly 500,000 people over two waves between 1918 and 1920, with nearly 300,000 excess deaths between October 1918 and May 1919 and 182,000 between December 1919 and May 1920.<ref name="World Health Organization-2013"/>

In the [[Dutch East Indies]] (now [[Indonesia]]), 1.5 million were assumed to have died among 30 million inhabitants.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Fitri E | title = Looking Through Indonesia's History For Answers to Swine Flu | url = http://thejakartaglobe.com/home/looking-through-indonesias-history-for-answers-to-swine-flu/337976 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091102151942/http://thejakartaglobe.com/home/looking-through-indonesias-history-for-answers-to-swine-flu/337976 | archive-date = 2 November 2009 | work = The Jakarta Globe | date = 28 October 2009 | access-date = 28 March 2017 | url-status = dead }}</ref> In [[Tahiti]], 13% of the population died in one month. Similarly, in [[Western Samoa Trust Territory|Western Samoa]] 22% of the population of 38,000 died within two months.{{sfn|Kohn|2007}}

In [[Istanbul]], capital of the Ottoman Empire, 6,403<ref name="İSPANYOL GRİBİNİN DÜNYA VE OSMANLI DEVLETİ ÜZERİNDEKİ ETKİLERİ">{{Cite web|title=İSPANYOL GRİBİNİN DÜNYA VE OSMANLI DEVLETİ ÜZERİNDEKİ ETKİLERİ|url=http://www.cihanharbi.com/ispanyol-gribinin-dunya-ve-osmanli-devleti-uzerindeki-etkileri-the-impact-of-spanish-influenza-on-the-world-and-the-ottoman-empire/|access-date=2 November 2020|language=tr-TR|archive-date=8 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108054237/http://www.cihanharbi.com/ispanyol-gribinin-dunya-ve-osmanli-devleti-uzerindeki-etkileri-the-impact-of-spanish-influenza-on-the-world-and-the-ottoman-empire/|url-status=live}}</ref> to 10,000<ref name="www.sozcu.com.tr"/> died, giving the city a mortality rate of at least 0.56%.<ref name="İSPANYOL GRİBİNİN DÜNYA VE OSMANLI DEVLETİ ÜZERİNDEKİ ETKİLERİ"/>

In New Zealand, the flu killed an estimated 6,400 {{lang|mi|[[Pākehā]]}} (or "New Zealanders primarily of European descent") and 2,500 [[Māori people|Māori]] in six weeks, with Māori dying at eight times the rate of {{lang|mi|Pākehā}}.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.noted.co.nz/health/1918-flu-centenary-how-to-survive-a-pandemic/ |title=1918 flu centenary: How to survive a pandemic|access-date=19 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190709072615/https://www.noted.co.nz/health/1918-flu-centenary-how-to-survive-a-pandemic/ |archive-date=9 July 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Black November: the 1918 influenza pandemic in New Zealand | vauthors = Rice G, Bryder L |isbn=978-1-927145-91-3 |edition=Second, revised and enlarged |place=Christchurch, NZ |oclc=960210402}}</ref>

In Australia, the flu killed around 12,000<ref name="VojnosanitetskiPregled">{{cite journal | vauthors = Radusin M | title = The Spanish flu – part II: the second and third wave | journal = Vojnosanitetski Pregled | volume = 69 | issue = 10 | pages = 917–927 | date = October 2012 | pmid = 23155616 | url = https://www.rastko.rs/cms/files/books/5218e8f259be8 | url-status = live | access-date = 23 April 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200709205413/https://www.rastko.rs/cms/files/books/5218e8f259be8 | archive-date = 9 July 2020 }}</ref> to 20,000 people.<ref name="vicparl">{{cite web |date=23 April 2020 |title=Epidemics and pandemics in Victoria: Historical perspectives |url=https://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/publications/research-papers/download/36-research-papers/13957-epidemics-and-pandemics-in-victoria-historical-perspectives |access-date=14 September 2022 |website=[[Parliament of Victoria]] |archive-date=14 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220914060458/https://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/publications/research-papers/download/36-research-papers/13957-epidemics-and-pandemics-in-victoria-historical-perspectives |url-status=dead }}</ref> The country's death rate, 2.7 per 1,000 people, was one of the lowest recorded; however, as much as 40 percent of the population were infected, and a mortality rate of 50 percent was recorded by some [[Aboriginal Australian|Aboriginal]] communities.<ref name="nma">{{cite web |title=Influenza pandemic |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/influenza-pandemic |access-date=14 September 2022 |website=[[National Museum of Australia]] |archive-date=14 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220914060440/https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/influenza-pandemic |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="vicparl"/> New South Wales and Victoria saw the greatest relative mortality, with 3.19 and 2.40 deaths per 1,000 people respectively, while Western Australia, Queensland, Southern Australia, and Tasmania experienced rates of 1.70, 1.14, 1.13, and 1.09 per 1,000 respectively. In Queensland, at least one-third of deaths recorded were in the Aboriginal population.<ref name="Shanks"/>

In the U.S., about 20 million out of a population of 105 million became infected in the 1918–1919 season, and an estimated 500,000 to 850,000 died (0.5 to 0.8 percent of the U.S. population).<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.usdeadlyevents.com/1918-1920-influenza-and-pneumonia-pandemic-nationwide-820000-850000/ | title=1918–1920 – Influenza and Pneumonia Pandemic – Nationwide ~820,000–850,000 – Deadliest American Disasters and Large-Loss-of-Life Events | date=January 1918 | access-date=22 May 2020 | archive-date=30 May 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200530205216/https://www.usdeadlyevents.com/1918-1920-influenza-and-pneumonia-pandemic-nationwide-820000-850000/ | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160923152823/http://www.flu.gov/pandemic/history/1918/ The Great Pandemic:  The United States in 1918–1919], U.S. Department of Health & Human Services.</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/catalog/nlm:nlmuid-8800017A-vid | title=The silent invader – Digital Collections – National Library of Medicine | access-date=15 April 2020 | archive-date=24 July 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724112317/https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/catalog/nlm:nlmuid-8800017A-vid | url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Native Americans]] tribes were particularly affected. In the [[Four Corners]] area, there were 3,293 registered deaths among Native Americans.<ref>{{cite web |title=Flu Epidemic Hit Utah Hard in 1918, 1919 |website = [[Deseret News]]|url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/412123/FLU-EPIDEMIC-HIT-UTAH-HARD-IN-1918-1919.html?pg=all |date=28 March 1995 |access-date=7 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121130180503/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/412123/FLU-EPIDEMIC-HIT-UTAH-HARD-IN-1918-1919.html?pg=all |archive-date=30 November 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Entire [[Inuit]] and [[Alaskan Native]] village communities died in [[Territory of Alaska|Alaska]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Great Pandemic of 1918: State by State |url=http://www.pandemicflu.gov/general/greatpandemic.html#alaska |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090506220116/http://www.pandemicflu.gov/general/greatpandemic.html |archive-date=6 May 2009 |url-status=dead |access-date=4 May 2009|date=5 March 2018 }}</ref> In Canada, 50,000 died.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090809000857/http://history.cbc.ca/history/?MIval=EpisContent.html&series_id=1&episode_id=12&chapter_id=2&page_id=6&lang=E "A deadly virus rages throughout Canada at the end of the First World War"]. CBC History.</ref>

In Brazil, 300,000 died, including president [[Rodrigues Alves]].<ref>{{cite web |title=A gripe espanhola no Brasil&nbsp;– Elísio Augusto de Medeiros e Silva, empresário, escritor e membro da AEILIJ |url=http://jornaldehoje.com.br/a-gripe-espanhola-no-brasil-elisio-augusto-de-medeiros-e-silva-empresario-escritor-e-membro-da-aeilij-elisiomercomix-com-br/ |publisher=Jornal de Hoje |access-date=22 January 2014 |language=pt |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202164917/http://jornaldehoje.com.br/a-gripe-espanhola-no-brasil-elisio-augusto-de-medeiros-e-silva-empresario-escritor-e-membro-da-aeilij-elisiomercomix-com-br/ |archive-date=2 February 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the UK, as many as 250,000 died; in France, more than 400,000.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/4350050.stm |title=The "bird flu" that killed 40&nbsp;million |work=BBC News |date=19 October 2005 |access-date=26 April 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107104411/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/4350050.stm |archive-date=7 November 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In [[Gold Coast (British colony)|Ghana]], the influenza epidemic killed at least 100,000 people.{{sfn|Hays|1998}} [[Tafari Makonnen]] (the future [[Emperor of Ethiopia]]) was one of the first Ethiopians who contracted influenza but survived.<ref name="Marcus">{{cite book | vauthors = Marcus H |title=Haile Sellassie I: The formative years, 1892–1936 |place=Trenton, NJ |publisher=Red Sea Press |year=1996 |pages=36ff}}</ref>{{sfn|Pankhurst|1991|pp=48f}} Estimates for fatalities in the capital city, [[Addis Ababa]], range from 5,000 to 10,000, or higher.{{sfn|Pankhurst|1991|p=63}}

The death toll in [[Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|Russia]] has been estimated at 450,000, though the epidemiologists who suggested this number called it a "shot in the dark".{{sfn|Patterson|Pyle|1991}} If it is correct, Russia lost roughly 0.4% of its population, meaning it suffered the lowest influenza-related mortality in Europe. Another study considers this number unlikely, given that the country was in the grip of a [[civil war]], and the infrastructure of daily life had broken down; the study suggests that Russia's death toll was closer to 2%, or 2.7 million people.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=167–69}}

=== Devastated communities ===
[[File:Spanish flu death chart.png|thumb|upright=1|Deaths from all causes for New York, London, Paris, and Berlin with peaks in October and November 1918]]
Even in areas where mortality was low, so many adults were incapacitated that daily life was hampered. Some communities closed all stores or required customers to leave orders outside. There were reports that healthcare workers could not tend the sick nor the gravediggers bury the dead because they too were ill. Mass graves were dug by [[steam shovel]] and bodies buried without coffins in many places.<ref>{{cite news|date=1 November 2004|title=Viruses of mass destruction|publisher=CNN|url=https://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/2004/11/01/8189572/index.htm|url-status=dead|access-date=30 April 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090506053835/http://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/2004/11/01/8189572/index.htm|archive-date=6 May 2009|series=Fortune}}</ref>

[[Bristol Bay]], a region of Alaska populated by [[Alaska Natives|Indigenous people]], suffered a death rate of 40 percent, with some villages entirely disappearing.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=134}} [[Nenana, Alaska]], avoided the extent of the pandemic between 1918 and 1919, but the flu at last reached the town in spring 1920. Reports suggested that during the first two weeks of May, the majority of the town's population became infected; 10% of the population were estimated to have died, most of whom were Alaska Natives.<ref>{{Cite web |date=27 October 2021 |title=The Flu Pandemic hit Nenana 100 Years Ago |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/dena-history-pandemic.htm |access-date=12 April 2022 |website=nps.gov |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413025708/https://www.nps.gov/articles/dena-history-pandemic.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

Several [[Pacific island]] territories were hit particularly hard. The pandemic reached them from New Zealand, which was too slow to implement measures to prevent ships carrying the flu from leaving its ports. From New Zealand, the flu reached [[Tonga]] (killing 8% of the population), [[Nauru]] (16%), and [[Colony of Fiji|Fiji]] (5%, 9,000&nbsp;people).{{sfn|Denoon|2004}} Worst affected was Western Samoa, which had been [[Occupation of German Samoa|occupied by New Zealand]] in 1914. 90% of the population was infected; 30% of adult men, 22% of adult women, and 10% of children died.{{sfn|Denoon|2004}} The disease spread fastest through the higher social classes among the Indigenous peoples, because of the custom of gathering [[oral tradition]] from chiefs on their deathbeds; many community elders were infected through this process.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Wishart S |date=July–August 2018|title=How the 1918 flu spread|url=https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/how-the-1918-flu-spread/|url-status=live|journal=New Zealand Geographic|issue=152|page=23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180803074604/https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/how-the-1918-flu-spread/|archive-date=3 August 2018|access-date=3 August 2018}}</ref>

In [[Qajar Iran|Iran]], the mortality was estimated at between 902,400 and 2,431,000, or 8% to 22% of the total population.{{Sfnm|1a1=Afkhami|1y=2003|2a1=Afkhami|2y=2012}} The country was going through the [[Persian famine of 1917–1919]] concurrently.

In [[History of Ireland (1801–1923)|Ireland]], during the worst 12 months, the Spanish flu accounted for one-third of all deaths.<ref>{{Cite news|vauthors=FitzGerald J|title=Coronavirus: forgotten lessons of the Spanish flu pandemic|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/coronavirus-forgotten-lessons-of-the-spanish-flu-pandemic-1.4234270|access-date=14 June 2020|newspaper=The Irish Times|quote=Yet the "Spanish" flu epidemic of 1918–19 resulted in about 25,000 extra deaths in Ireland, many of them young adults. This was almost as many deaths as occurred among the Irish fighting in the First World War.|archive-date=5 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200505231059/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/coronavirus-forgotten-lessons-of-the-spanish-flu-pandemic-1.4234270|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Official Ireland Statistics Office|url=https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-1916/1916irl/bmd/deaths/|access-date=14 June 2020|website=Central Statistics Office Ireland|quote=Total deaths in Ireland 1916: 50,627|archive-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200614193849/https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-1916/1916irl/bmd/deaths/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In South Africa it is estimated that about 300,000 people amounting to 6% of the population died within six weeks. Government actions in the early stages of the virus' arrival in the country in September 1918 are believed to have unintentionally accelerated its spread.<ref>{{Cite web|vauthors=Phillips H|title=South Africa bungled the Spanish flu in 1918. History mustn't repeat itself for COVID-19|url=http://theconversation.com/south-africa-bungled-the-spanish-flu-in-1918-history-mustnt-repeat-itself-for-covid-19-133281|access-date=26 May 2020|website=The Conversation|date=10 March 2020 |archive-date=13 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613084500/https://theconversation.com/south-africa-bungled-the-spanish-flu-in-1918-history-mustnt-repeat-itself-for-covid-19-133281|url-status=live}}</ref> Almost a quarter of the working population of [[Kimberley, Northern Cape|Kimberley]], consisting of workers in the diamond mines, died.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|p=72}} In [[British Somaliland]], one official estimated that 7% of the native population died.{{sfn|Pankhurst|1991|pp=51ff}} This huge death toll resulted from an extremely high [[infection rate]] of up to 50% and the extreme severity of the symptoms.{{sfn|Patterson|Pyle|1991}}

=== Other areas ===
In the Pacific, American Samoa<ref name="usnavyreport">{{cite web|title=Influenza of 1918 (Spanish Flu) and the US Navy|url=http://www.history.navy.mil/library/online/influenza_main.htm|url-status=dead|archive-url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20150111194407/http://www.history.navy.mil/library/online/influenza_main.htm|archive-date=11 January 2015|access-date=14 May 2009|website=history.navy.mil}}</ref> and the French colony of [[New Caledonia]]<ref name="whoreport">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bell D, Nicoll A, Fukuda K, Horby P, Monto A, Hayden F, Wylks C, Sanders L, Van Tam J | title = Non-pharmaceutical interventions for pandemic influenza, international measures | journal = Emerging Infectious Diseases | volume = 12 | issue = 1 | pages = 81–87 | date = January 2006 | pmid = 16494722 | pmc = 3291414 | doi = 10.3201/eid1201.051370 | bibcode = 2006EIDis..12...81. }}</ref> succeeded in preventing even a single death from influenza through effective [[quarantine]]s. However, the outbreak was delayed into 1926 for American Samoa and 1921 for New Caledonia as the quarantine period ended.<ref name="Shanks-2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shanks GD, Brundage JF | title = Pacific islands which escaped the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic and their subsequent mortality experiences | journal = Epidemiology and Infection | volume = 141 | issue = 2 | pages = 353–356 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 22564320 | pmc = 9152047 | doi = 10.1017/S0950268812000866 | s2cid = 23794327 }}</ref> On American Samoa, at least 25% of the island residents were clinically attacked and 0.1% died, and on New Caledonia, there was widespread illness and 0.1% population died.<ref name="Shanks-2013" /> Australia also managed to avoid the first two waves with a quarantine.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=83–84}} Iceland protected a third of its population from exposure by blocking the main road of the island.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=83–84}} By the end of the pandemic, the isolated island of [[Marajó]], in Brazil's Amazon River Delta had not reported an outbreak.<ref>{{cite book |title=Pandemic Influenza: Emergency planning and community preparedness |publisher=CRC Press |year=2009 | veditors = Ryan J |place=Boca Raton, FL |page=24}}</ref> [[Saint Helena]] also reported no deaths.<ref>"Colonial Annual Report", 1919</ref>

[[File:1920FluMasksTokyo.png|thumb|Japanese women in Tokyo during the Spanish flu pandemic, 1920]]
Estimates for the death toll in China have varied widely,<ref name="ijima">{{cite book|title=The Spanish Flu Pandemic of 1918: New Perspectives|vauthors=Iijima W|publisher=Routledge|year=2003|veditors=Phillips H, Killingray D|place=London and New York|pages=101–09|article=Spanish influenza in China, 1918–1920: a preliminary probe}}</ref>{{sfn|Patterson|Pyle|1991}} reflecting the lack of centralized collection of health data at the time due to the [[Warlord period]]. China may have experienced a relatively mild flu season in 1918 compared to other areas of the world.<ref name="Cheng_2007"/><ref name="Saunders-Hastings_2016"/><ref>{{Cite book |vauthors=Killingray D, Phillips H |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37 |title=The Spanish Influenza Pandemic of 1918–1919: New Perspectives |year=2003 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-56640-2 |access-date=9 November 2020 |archive-date=27 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210727045645/https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37 |url-status=live }}</ref> However, some reports from its interior suggest that mortality rates from influenza were perhaps higher in at least a few locations in 1918.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=167–69}} At the very least, there is little evidence that China as a whole was seriously affected by the flu compared to other countries.<ref>{{Cite book |vauthors=Killingray D, Phillips H |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37 |title=The Spanish Influenza Pandemic of 1918–1919: New Perspectives |publisher=Routledge |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-134-56640-2 |access-date=9 November 2020 |archive-date=27 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210727045657/https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The first estimate of the Chinese death toll was made in 1991 by Patterson and Pyle, which estimated a toll of between 5 and 9 million. However, this study was criticized by later studies due to flawed methodology, and newer studies have published estimates of a far lower mortality rate in China.<ref name="Killingray-2003"/><ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Iijima W | title = The Spanish influenza in China, 1918–1920 | date = 1998 | oclc = 46987588 }}</ref> For instance, Iijima in 1998 estimates the death toll in China to be between 1 and 1.28 million based on data available from Chinese port cities.<ref>{{Cite conference |vauthors=Iijima W |date=1998 |title=The Spanish influenza in China, 1918–1920 |url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/5409238 |conference=Spanish 'Flu 1918–1998: Reflections on the Influenza Pandemic of 1918 after 80 Years |place=Cape Town, South Africa |access-date=11 April 2020 |archive-date=11 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200411171040/https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/5409238 |url-status=live }}</ref> The lower estimates of the Chinese death toll are based on the low mortality rates that were found in Chinese port cities and on the assumption that poor communications prevented the flu from penetrating the interior of China.<ref name="ijima"/> However, some contemporary newspaper and post office reports, as well as reports from missionary doctors, suggest that the flu did penetrate the Chinese interior and that influenza was severe in at least some locations in the countryside of China.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=167–69}}

Although medical records from China's interior are lacking, extensive medical data were recorded in Chinese port cities, such as then [[British Empire|British]]-controlled Hong Kong, [[Guangzhou|Canton]], [[Peking]], [[Harbin]] and [[Shanghai]]. These data were collected by the [[Chinese Maritime Customs Service]], which was largely staffed by non-Chinese foreigners.<ref name="Killingray_2003">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37|title=The Spanish Influenza Pandemic of 1918–1919: New Perspectives|vauthors=Killingray D, Phillips H|publisher=Routledge|year=2003|isbn=978-1-134-56640-2|pages=105|access-date=9 November 2020|archive-date=27 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210727045638/https://books.google.com/books?id=k79_8QX8n44C&q=spanish+flu+china+ports+18+million+india&pg=PT37|url-status=live}}</ref> As a whole, data from China's port cities show low mortality rates compared to other cities in Asia.<ref name="Killingray_2003"/> For example, the British authorities at Hong Kong and Canton reported a mortality rate from influenza at a rate of 0.25% and 0.32%, much lower than the reported mortality rate of other cities in Asia, such as [[Calcutta]] or Bombay, where influenza was much more devastating.<ref name="Killingray_2003"/> Similarly, in the city of [[Shanghai]] – which had a population of over 2 million – there were only 266 recorded deaths from [[influenza]] among the Chinese population in 1918.<ref name="Killingray_2003"/> If extrapolated from the extensive data recorded from Chinese cities, the suggested mortality rate from influenza in China as a whole in 1918 was likely lower than 1% – much lower than the world average (which was around 3–5%).<ref name="Killingray_2003"/> In contrast, Japan and Taiwan had reported a mortality rate from influenza around 0.45% and 0.69% respectively, higher than the mortality rate collected from data in Chinese port cities, such as Hong Kong (0.25%), Canton (0.32%), and Shanghai.<ref name="Killingray_2003"/>

However, the influenza mortality rate in Hong Kong and Canton are under-recorded, because only the deaths that occurred in colony hospitals were counted.<ref name="Killingray_2003" /> Similarly, in Shanghai, these statistics are limited to that area of the city under the control of the health section of the Shanghai International Settlement; the actual death toll in Shanghai was much higher.<ref name="Killingray_2003" /> The medical records from China's interior indicate that, compared to cities, rural communities have substantially higher mortality rate.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Alita XP, Ling T, Bin ZH, Xiao-ting LI | title = Epidemic analysisi of 1918 Spanish influenza in China based on literatures. | journal = Journal of Medical Informatics | date = 2010 | volume = 31 | issue = 1 | pages = 47–50 | url = https://en.cnki.com.cn/Article_en/CJFDTotal-YXQB201001015.htm | access-date = 29 July 2021 | archive-date = 29 July 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210729164632/https://en.cnki.com.cn/Article_en/CJFDTotal-YXQB201001015.htm | url-status = dead }}</ref> A published influenza survey in Houlu County, Hebei Province, found that the case fatality rate was 9.77% and 0.79% of county population died from influenza in October and November 1918.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Hong NH |date=2015|title=Epidemic Analysis of 1918 Influenza in China – Research on Huolu County in Zhili Province|journal=Historical Research in Auhui | url = }}</ref>

===Patterns of fatality===
[[File:1918 at Spanish Flu Ward Walter Reed (cropped).jpg|thumb|A nurse wears a cloth face mask while treating a flu patient in Washington, DC, c. 1919]]
The pandemic mostly killed young adults. In 1918–1919, 99% of pandemic influenza deaths in the U.S. occurred in people under 65, and nearly half of deaths were in young adults 20 to 40 years old. In 1920, the mortality rate among people under 65 had decreased sixfold to half the mortality rate of people over 65, but 92% of deaths still occurred in people under 65.{{sfn|Simonsen|Clarke|Schonberger|Arden|1998}} This is unusual since influenza is typically most deadly to weak individuals, such as [[infant]]s under age two, adults over age 70, and the [[immunocompromise]]d. In 1918, older adults may have had partial protection caused by exposure to the 1889–1890 flu pandemic.<ref name=hansen>{{cite book | vauthors = Hanssen O | title = Undersøkelser over influenzaens optræden specielt i Bergen 1918–1922 | trans-title = Investigations into the appearance of influenza, especially in Bergen 1918–1922) | language = Norwegian | publisher = Grieg | date = 1923 | series = Skrifter utgit av Klaus Hansens fond, nr. III. Bergen: Haukeland Sykehus, 1923 (Writings published by the Klaus Hansen Foundation, No. III, Haukeland Hospital Bergen | page = 66 }}</ref> According to historian John M. Barry, the most vulnerable of all were pregnant women. He reported that in thirteen studies of hospitalized women in the pandemic, the death rate ranged from 23% to 71%.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Knobler SL, Mack A, Mahmoud A, Lemon SM |title=Institute of Medicine (US) Forum on Microbial Threats |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK22148/ |publisher=NCBI |access-date=17 August 2021 |archive-date=23 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201223130139/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK22148/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Of the pregnant women who survived childbirth, over one-quarter (26%) lost the child.{{sfn|Barry|2004|p=239}} Another oddity was that the outbreak was widespread in the summer and autumn (in the Northern Hemisphere); influenza is usually worse in winter.<ref>{{cite web |title=Key Facts about Swine Influenza | work = U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/swineflu/keyfacts_pigs.htm |access-date=30 April 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505011201/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/key_facts.htm |url-status=live |archive-date=5 May 2009}}</ref>

There were also geographic patterns to the disease's fatality. Some parts of Asia had 30 times higher death rates than some parts of Europe, and generally, Africa and Asia had higher rates, while Europe and North America had lower ones.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}} There was also great variation within continents, with three times higher mortality in Hungary and Spain compared to Denmark, two to three times higher chance of death in Sub-Saharan Africa compared to North Africa, and possibly up to ten times higher rates between the extremes of Asia.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}} Cities were affected worse than rural areas.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}} There were also differences between cities, which might have reflected exposure to the milder first wave giving immunity, as well as the introduction of social distancing measures.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=183–84}}

Another major pattern was the differences between social classes. In [[Oslo]], death rates were inversely correlated with apartment size, as the poorer people living in smaller apartments died at a higher rate.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mamelund SE | title = A socially neutral disease? Individual social class, household wealth and mortality from Spanish influenza in two socially contrasting parishes in Kristiania 1918–19 | journal = Social Science & Medicine | volume = 62 | issue = 4 | pages = 923–940 | date = February 2006 | pmid = 16084634 | doi = 10.1016/j.socscimed.2005.06.051 }}</ref> Social status was also reflected in the higher mortality among immigrant communities, with [[Italian Americans]], a recently arrived group at the time, nearly twice as likely to die compared to the average Americans.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}} These disparities reflected worse diets, crowded living conditions, and problems accessing healthcare.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}} Paradoxically, however, [[African Americans]] were relatively spared.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=180–82}}

More men than women were killed by the flu, as they were more likely to go out and be exposed, while women tended to [[Housewife|stay at home]].{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=183–84}} For the same reason men also were more likely to have pre-existing [[tuberculosis]], which severely worsened the chances of recovery.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=183–84}} However, in India the opposite was true, potentially because Indian women were neglected with poorer nutrition, and were expected to care for the sick.{{sfn|Spinney|2018|pp=183–84}}

A study conducted by He ''et al''. (2011) examined the factors that underlie variability in temporal patterns and their correlation to patterns of mortality and morbidity. Their analysis suggests that temporal variations in transmission rate provide the best explanation, and the variation in transmission required to generate these three waves is within biologically plausible values.{{sfn|He|Dushoff|Day|Ma|2011}} Another study by He ''et al''. (2013) used a simple [[epidemic model]] incorporating three factors to infer the cause of the three waves of the 1918 influenza pandemic. These factors were school opening and closing, temperature changes throughout the outbreak, and human behavioral changes in response to the outbreak. Their modeling results showed that all three factors are important, but human behavioral responses showed the most significant effects.{{sfn|He|Dushoff|Day|Ma|2013}}

==Effects==
===World War I===
Academic Andrew Price-Smith has argued that the virus helped tip the balance of power in the latter days of the war towards the Allied cause. He provides data that the viral waves hit the [[Central Powers]] before the Allied powers and that [[morbidity]] and mortality in Germany and Austria were considerably higher than in Britain and France.{{sfn|Price-Smith|2008}} A 2006 ''Lancet'' study corroborates higher excess mortality rates in Germany (0.76%) and Austria (1.61%) compared to Britain (0.34%) and France (0.75%).<ref name="Lancet 2006 Murray, Lopez, Chin, Feehan"/>

Kenneth Kahn at [[Oxford University Computing Services]] writes that "Many researchers have suggested that the conditions of the war significantly aided the spread of the disease. And others have argued that the course of the war (and subsequent peace treaty) was influenced by the pandemic." Kahn has developed a model that can be used to test these theories.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 'Spanish' Influenza pandemic and its relation to World War I |url=http://ww1centenary.oucs.ox.ac.uk/body-and-mind/the-spanish-influenza-pandemic-and-its-relation-to-the-first-world-war/ |website=World War I Centenary |publisher=University of Oxford JISC |access-date=11 August 2020 |archive-date=5 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805020700/http://ww1centenary.oucs.ox.ac.uk/body-and-mind/the-spanish-influenza-pandemic-and-its-relation-to-the-first-world-war/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Economic===
[[File:SpanishFluPosterAlberta.png|thumb|upright|Provincial Board of Health poster from [[Alberta, Canada]]]]
Many businesses in the entertainment and service industries suffered losses in revenue, while the healthcare industry reported profit gains.{{sfn|Garret|2007}} Historian Nancy Bristow has argued that the pandemic, when combined with the increasing number of women attending college, contributed to the success of women in nursing. This was due in part to the failure of medical doctors, who were predominantly men, to contain the illness. Nursing staff, who were mainly women, celebrated the success of their patient care and did not associate the spread of the disease with their work.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Lindley R |title=The Forgotten American Pandemic: Historian Dr. Nancy K. Bristow on the Influenza Epidemic of 1918 |url= http://hnn.us/article/146655 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140808052318/http://hnn.us/article/146655 |archive-date=8 August 2014 |access-date=4 August 2014 |website=hnn.us |date=6 June 2012 }}</ref>

A 2020 study found that U.S. cities that implemented early and extensive non-medical measures (quarantine, etc.) suffered no additional adverse economic effects due to implementing those measures.<ref>{{cite web|date=2 April 2020|title=What can the Spanish Flu teach us about the COVID-19 pandemic?|url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2020/04/pandemic-economy-lessons-1918-flu|website=[[World Economic Forum]]|access-date=8 April 2020|archive-date=9 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409101044/https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2020/04/pandemic-economy-lessons-1918-flu/|url-status=live}}
</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Correia S, Luck S, Verner E|s2cid=216202133|date=2020|title=Pandemics Depress the Economy, Public Health Interventions Do Not: Evidence from the 1918 Flu|url=https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=3561560|journal=SSRN Working Paper Series|doi=10.2139/ssrn.3561560|arxiv=2207.11636 |issn=1556-5068|access-date=14 April 2020|archive-date=27 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210727045639/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3561560|url-status=live}}
</ref> However, the validity of this study has been questioned because of the coincidence of WWI and other problems with data reliability.<ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Kemp J |title=RPT-COLUMN-Coronavirus lockdowns: can we learn from the 1918 influenza pandemic? Kemp |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/global-economy-kemp-idUSL8N2BV512 |access-date=17 August 2021 |publisher=Reuters |date=7 April 2020 |archive-date=17 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817174043/https://www.reuters.com/article/global-economy-kemp-idUSL8N2BV512 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Long-term effects===
A 2006 study in the ''Journal of Political Economy'' found that "cohorts ''in utero'' during the pandemic displayed reduced educational attainment, increased rates of physical disability, lower income, lower socioeconomic status, and higher [[transfer payments]] received compared with other birth cohorts."<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Almond D |s2cid=20055129 |date=1 August 2006 |title=Is the 1918 Influenza Pandemic Over? Long-Term Effects of In Utero Influenza Exposure in the Post-1940 U.S. Population |journal=Journal of Political Economy |volume=114 |issue=4 |pages=672–712 |doi=10.1086/507154 |bibcode=2006JPoEc.114..672A |issn=0022-3808}}</ref> A 2018 study found that the pandemic reduced educational attainment in populations.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Beach B, Ferrie JP, Saavedra MH |date=2018 |title=Fetal shock or selection? The 1918 influenza pandemic and human capital development |url= http://www.nber.org/papers/w24725|url-status=live|doi=10.3386/w24725 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180618131115/http://www.nber.org/papers/w24725 |archive-date=18 June 2018 |access-date=18 June 2018 |doi-access=free |website=nber.org|series=Working Paper Series }}</ref> The flu has also been linked to the outbreak of [[encephalitis lethargica]] in the 1920s.{{sfn|Vilensky|Foley|Gilman|2007}}

Survivors faced an elevated mortality risk. Some survivors did not fully recover from physiological conditions resulting from infection.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Fottrell Q | date = 25 August 2020 | title = Another warning from the 1918 flu for COVID-19: 'Survival does not mean that individuals fully recovered' | url = https://www.marketwatch.com/story/another-warning-from-1918-spanish-flu-for-covid-19-survival-does-not-mean-that-individuals-fully-recovered-2020-08-18 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200824075950/https://www.marketwatch.com/story/another-warning-from-1918-spanish-flu-for-covid-19-survival-does-not-mean-that-individuals-fully-recovered-2020-08-18 | archive-date = 24 August 2020 | work = MarketWatch }}</ref>

==Legacy==
[[File:1918 Influenza epidemic burial site.jpg|thumb|Mass burial site of flu victims from 1918 in [[Waikumete Cemetery]], Auckland, New Zealand]]
The Spanish flu began to fade from public awareness over the decades until the [[bird flu]] and other pandemics in the 1990s and 2000s.{{sfn|Honigsbaum|2008}}<ref name = "Beiner_2021">{{cite book |vauthors=Beiner G |veditors=Beiner G |title=Pandemic Re-Awakenings: The Forgotten and Unforgotten 'Spanish' Flu of 1918–1919 |date=2021 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780192843739 |pages=346–376 |url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/pandemic-re-awakenings-9780192843739 |chapter=Rediscovering the Great Flu between Pre-Forgetting and Post-Forgetting |archive-date=13 May 2024 |access-date=23 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240513132556/https://global.oup.com/academic/product/pandemic-re-awakenings-9780192843739 |url-status=live }}</ref> This has led some historians to label the Spanish flu a "forgotten pandemic".{{sfn|Crosby|2003}} However, this label has been challenged by the historian [[Guy Beiner]], who demonstrated how the pandemic was overshadowed by the commemoration of the First World War and mostly neglected in mainstream historiography, yet was remembered in private and local traditions across the globe.<ref name = "Beiner_2021" />

There are various theories of why the Spanish flu was "forgotten". The rapid pace of the pandemic, which killed most of its victims in the United States within less than nine months, resulted in limited media coverage. The general population was familiar with patterns of pandemic disease in the late 19th and early 20th centuries: typhoid, [[yellow fever]], [[diphtheria]], and cholera all occurred near the same time. These outbreaks probably lessened the significance of the influenza pandemic for the public.{{sfn|Morrisey|1986}} In some areas, the flu was not reported on, the only mention being that of advertisements for medicines claiming to cure it.{{sfn|Benedict|Braithwaite|2000|p=38}}

Additionally, the outbreak coincided with the deaths and media focus on the First World War.{{sfn|Crosby|2003|pp=320–322}} The majority of fatalities, from both the war and the epidemic, were among young adults. The high number of war-related deaths of young adults may have overshadowed the deaths caused by flu.{{sfn|Simonsen|Clarke|Schonberger|Arden|1998}} Particularly in Europe, where the war's toll was high, the flu may not have had a tremendous psychological impact or may have seemed an extension of the war's tragedies.{{sfn|Simonsen|Clarke|Schonberger|Arden|1998}}

The last known person to have survived the Spanish flu, José Ameal Peña, was alive as of 2020.<ref name="p516">{{cite web | last=Kassam | first=Ashifa | title='Be careful': Spain's last 1918 flu survivor offers warning on coronavirus | website=The Guardian | date=2020-03-22 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/mar/22/be-careful-spains-last-1918-flu-survivor-offers-warning-on-coronavirus | access-date=2026-04-09}}</ref>

===In literature and other media===
[[File:"Stuffy Cars Breed Disease" - Better Ventilation.png|thumb|US comic published in 1922]]
Despite the toll of the pandemic, it was never a large theme in American literature.<ref name=":0" /> Alfred Crosby suspects it was overshadowed by World War I.{{sfn|Crosby|2003|p=315}} [[Katherine Anne Porter]]'s 1939 novella ''[[Pale Horse, Pale Rider]]'' is one of the most well-known fictional accounts of the pandemic.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Why Did So Few Novels Tackle the 1918 Pandemic? |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/flu-novels-great-pandemic-180965205/ |access-date=2023-06-06 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en |archive-date=6 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230606064620/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/flu-novels-great-pandemic-180965205/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The 2006 novel ''[[The Last Town on Earth]]'' focuses on a town which attempts to limit the spread of the flu by preventing people from entering or leaving.<ref>{{Cite web |vauthors=Hansen L |date=24 September 2006 |title=Mullen's View from 'The Last Town on Earth' |url=https://www.npr.org/2006/09/24/6133594/mullens-view-from-the-last-town-on-earth |access-date=11 June 2023 |website=[[NPR]] |archive-date=11 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230611201702/https://www.npr.org/2006/09/24/6133594/mullens-view-from-the-last-town-on-earth |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[The Pull of the Stars]]'' is a 2020 novel by [[Emma Donoghue]] set in Dublin during the Spanish flu. Publishers fast-tracked publication because of the then ongoing [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{Cite web |vauthors=Corrigan M |date=20 July 2020 |title=1918 Flu Inspired Donoghue's 'Pull Of The Stars' — A Disquieting Pandemic Novel |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/07/20/892279658/1918-flu-inspired-donoghues-pull-of-the-stars-a-disquieting-pandemic-novel |access-date=6 June 2023 |website=[[NPR]] |archive-date=6 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230606064627/https://www.npr.org/2020/07/20/892279658/1918-flu-inspired-donoghues-pull-of-the-stars-a-disquieting-pandemic-novel |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Comparison with other pandemics===

==Research==
{{Main|Spanish flu research}}
[[File:Reconstructed Spanish Flu Virus.jpg|thumb|An electron micrograph showing recreated 1918 influenza virions]]
Similarities between a reconstruction of the virus and avian viruses, combined with the human pandemic preceding the first reports of influenza in swine, led researchers to conclude the influenza virus jumped directly from birds to humans, and swine caught the disease from humans.<ref name=influenzareport>{{cite book |quote=Sometimes a virus contains both avian-adapted genes and human-adapted genes. Both the [[H2N2]] and [[H3N2]] pandemic strains contained avian flu virus [[RNA]] segments. "While the pandemic human influenza viruses of 1957 (H2N2) and 1968 (H3N2) arose through reassortment between human and avian viruses, the influenza virus causing the 'Spanish flu' in 1918 appears to be entirely derived from an avian source (Belshe 2005). |chapter-url=http://www.influenzareport.com/ir/ai.htm |chapter=Chapter Two: Avian Influenza |vauthors=Harder TC, Ortrud W |title=Influenza Report 2006 |publisher=published online |access-date=26 October 2007 |archive-date=9 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170809185926/http://www.influenzareport.com/ir/ai.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|Taubenberger|Reid|Lourens|Wang|2005}} More recent research has suggested the strain may have originated in a nonhuman, mammalian species,{{sfn|Vana|Westover|2008}} in 1882–1913.{{sfn|dos Reis|Hay|Goldstein|2009}} This ancestor virus diverged about 1913–1915 into the classical swine and human H1N1 influenza lineages. The last common ancestor of human strains dates between February 1917 and April 1918. Because pigs are more readily infected with avian influenza viruses than are humans, they were suggested as the original recipients of the virus, passing the virus to humans sometime between 1913 and 1918.{{sfn|dos Reis|Hay|Goldstein|2009}}

[[File:Influenza virus research.jpg|thumb|upright|Dr Terrence Tumpey examines a reconstructed version of the Spanish flu virus at the [[CDC]]]]
An effort to recreate the Spanish flu strain (a [[Strain (biology)|strain]] of influenza A subtype H1N1) was a collaboration among the [[Armed Forces Institute of Pathology]], the [[USDA ARS]] Southeast Poultry Research Laboratory, and [[Mount Sinai School of Medicine]] in New York City. The effort resulted in the announcement in 2005 that the group had successfully determined the virus' [[genetic sequence]], using historic tissue samples recovered by pathologist [[Johan Hultin]] from an Inuit female flu victim buried in the Alaskan [[permafrost]] and samples preserved from American soldiers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/media/pressrel/r051005.htm |publisher=Center for Disease Control |title=Researchers reconstruct 1918 pandemic influenza virus; effort designed to advance preparedness |access-date=2 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111019045108/http://www.cdc.gov/media/pressrel/r051005.htm |archive-date=19 October 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Closing In On a Killer: Scientists Unlock Clues to the Spanish Influenz Virus |url=https://www.medicalmuseum.mil/index.cfm?p=exhibits.virtual.1918killerflu.page_01 |website=National Museum of Health and Medicine |access-date=23 March 2020 |archive-date=2 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200502042213/https://www.medicalmuseum.mil/index.cfm?p=exhibits.virtual.1918killerflu.page_01 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Kolata G |title=Scientists Uncover Clues To Flu Epidemic of 1918 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/02/16/us/scientists-uncover-clues-to-flu-epidemic-of-1918.html |access-date=23 March 2020 |work=The New York Times |date=16 February 1999 |archive-date=22 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200322015429/https://www.nytimes.com/1999/02/16/us/scientists-uncover-clues-to-flu-epidemic-of-1918.html |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|Taubenberger|Reid|Lourens|Wang|2005}} This enabled researchers at the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) and the [[Mount Sinai School of Medicine]], led by Dr Terrence Tumpey, to synthesize RNA segments from the H1N1 virus and reconstruct infective virus particles.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |vauthors=Jordan D, Tumpey T, Jester B |title=The Deadliest Flu: The Complete Story of the Discovery and Reconstruction of the 1918 Pandemic Virus |url=https://archive.cdc.gov/#/details?url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/pandemic-resources/reconstruction-1918-virus.html |access-date=2024-06-22 |website=archive.cdc.gov |archive-date=15 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200715061619/https://www.cdc.gov/media/releases/2019/s0424-highest-measles-cases-since-elimination.html#/details?url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/pandemic-resources/reconstruction-1918-virus.html |url-status=live }}</ref> These were subsequently used to experimentally infect mice, ferrets, and macaques, providing information about how to prevent and control future pandemics.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Taubenberger JK, Baltimore D, Doherty PC, Markel H, Morens DM, Webster RG, Wilson IA | title = Reconstruction of the 1918 influenza virus: unexpected rewards from the past | journal = mBio | volume = 3 | issue = 5 | date = November 2012 | article-number = e00201-12 | pmid = 22967978 | pmc = 3448162 | doi = 10.1128/mBio.00201-12 | doi-access = free}}</ref>

In 2007, Kobasa et al. reported that monkeys (''[[Macaca fascicularis]]'') infected with the recreated flu strain exhibited classic symptoms of the 1918 pandemic, and died from an overreaction of the immune system.{{sfn|Kobasa|et al.|2007}} This may explain why the Spanish flu had its surprising effect on younger, healthier people, as a person with a stronger immune system would potentially have a stronger overreaction.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.usatoday.com/tech/science/discoveries/flu-research.htm?POE=NEWISVA |newspaper=USA Today |title=Research on monkeys finds resurrected 1918 flu killed by turning the body against itself |access-date=14 August 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090305113915/http://www.usatoday.com/tech/science/discoveries/flu-research.htm?POE=NEWISVA |archive-date=5 March 2009 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In December 2008, research by [[Yoshihiro Kawaoka]] of the [[University of Wisconsin]] linked three specific genes (termed PA, PB1, and PB2) and a [[nucleoprotein]] derived from Spanish flu samples to the ability of the 1918 flu virus to invade the lungs and cause pneumonia. These genes were inserted into a modern H1N1 strain and triggered similar symptoms in animal testing.{{sfn|Fox|2008}}

In 2008 an investigation used the virus sequence to obtain the [[Hemagglutinin (influenza)|Hemagglutinin (HA)]] antigen and observe the adaptive immunity in 32 survivors of the 1918 pandemic; all of them presented seroreactivity and 7 of 8 further tested presented [[memory B cell]]s able to produce antibodies that bound to the HA antigen, highlighting the ability of [[immunological memory]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Yu X, Tsibane T, McGraw PA, House FS, Keefer CJ, Hicar MD, Tumpey TM, Pappas C, Perrone LA, Martinez O, Stevens J, Wilson IA, Aguilar PV, Altschuler EL, Basler CF, Crowe JE |date=September 2008 |title=Neutralizing antibodies derived from the B cells of 1918 influenza pandemic survivors |journal=Nature |volume=455 |issue=7212 |pages=532–536 |bibcode=2008Natur.455..532Y |doi=10.1038/nature07231 |pmc=2848880 |pmid=18716625}}</ref>{{sfn|Taubenberger|Reid|Lourens|Wang|2005}}

In June 2010, a team at the Mount Sinai School of Medicine reported the [[2009 flu pandemic vaccine]] provided some cross-protection against the Spanish flu pandemic strain.{{sfn|Fox|2010}}

In 2013, the AIR Worldwide Research and Modeling Group "estimated the effects of a similar pandemic occurring today using the AIR Pandemic Flu Model". In the model, "a modern-day 'Spanish flu' event would result in additional life insurance losses of between US$15.3–27.8&nbsp;billion in the United States alone", with 188,000–337,000&nbsp;deaths in the United States.{{sfn|Madhav|2013}}

In 2018, Michael Worobey, a professor at the [[University of Arizona]] who is examining the history of the 1918 pandemic, revealed that he obtained tissue slides created by William Rolland, a physician who reported on a respiratory illness likely to be the virus while a pathologist in the British military during World War One.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Branswell H |url=https://www.statnews.com/2018/12/05/1918-spanish-flu-unraveling-mystery |title=A shot-in-the-dark e-mail leads to a century-old family treasure&nbsp;– and hope of cracking a deadly flu's secret |magazine=Stat |date=5 December 2018 |access-date=5 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181205172533/https://www.statnews.com/2018/12/05/1918-spanish-flu-unraveling-mystery/ |archive-date=5 December 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hammond JA, Rolland W, Shore TH |title=Purulent bronchitis: A study of cases occurring amongst the British troops at a base in France |journal=The Lancet |date=14 July 1917 |volume=190 |issue=4898 |pages=41–45 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(01)56229-7 | url = https://www.statnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Hammond.1917.purulent.bronchitis.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190826134026/https://www.statnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Hammond.1917.purulent.bronchitis.pdf | archive-date=26 August 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://ww1centenary.oucs.ox.ac.uk/body-and-mind/the-influenza-pandemic-of-1918/ |title=The Influenza Pandemic of 1918 |website=World War 1 Centenary |publisher=University of Oxford |place=Oxford, England |access-date=8 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209125259/http://ww1centenary.oucs.ox.ac.uk/body-and-mind/the-influenza-pandemic-of-1918/ |archive-date=9 December 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref> Worobey extracted tissue from the slides to potentially reveal more about the origin of the pathogen.<ref name=Cox>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cox J, Gill D, Cox F, Worobey M | title = Purulent bronchitis in 1917 and pandemic influenza in 1918 | journal = The Lancet. Infectious Diseases | volume = 19 | issue = 4 | pages = 360–361 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30938298 | doi = 10.1016/s1473-3099(19)30114-8 | s2cid = 91189842 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
