The '''University of Virginia School of Medicine''' ('''UVA SOM''' or more commonly known as '''Virginia Medicine''') is the graduate [[medical school]] of the [[University of Virginia]]. The school's facilities are on the [[University of Virginia]] grounds adjacent to [[The Lawn|Academical Village]] in [[Charlottesville, Virginia]] as well as a second campus located in [[Falls Church, Virginia]]. 

Founded in 1819 by [[Thomas Jefferson]], UVA SOM is the tenth oldest medical school in the United States. The School of Medicine confers [[Doctor of Medicine]] (M.D.) and Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degrees, and is closely associated with both the [[University of Virginia Health System]] and [[Inova Health System]]. Notable distinguished alumni include [[Walter Reed]], [[Vivian Pinn]], and many other leaders in medicine. The School is widely considered to be one of the most prestigious medical schools in the United States with many medical discoveries made on Grounds.
 
== History ==
[[File:Robley Dunglison 1848 Portrait EC Bruce.jpg|thumb| Dr. [[Robley Dunglison]], the "Father of American Physiology" was the first professor of medicine at the University of Virginia]]

The UVA Health System's history can be traced to the original conception of the [[University of Virginia]] on August 1, 1818, whereupon [[Thomas Jefferson]], [[James Madison]], and twenty-one other men first compiled a report for the [[Virginia State Legislature]] to determine a site, building plans, and courses for study for the University of Virginia. Acknowledging that clinical lectures and medical training were not available in [[Charlottesville]] at that time, Jefferson and his colleagues determined that the university should offer education in "the elements of medical science...with a history and explanation of all its successive theories from [[Hippocrates]] to the present day," as a way to train both prospective physicians, as well as those students with a more dilettante interest in medicine.<ref name="auto">Thomas Jefferson to Joseph C. Cabell, January 11, 1825.</ref>

[[File:Webview-of-UVa-crop-300x278.jpg|thumb|Detail of the Anatomical Theatre from View of the University. A cupola was not part of Jefferson's design; it was probably added after the 1837 resolution to raise the roof. This image clearly shows the cupola was present in 1856. Hand colored.]]
At the first meeting of the university's Board of Visitors in 1819, a School of Medicine was authorized. The [[School of Medicine]] – the 10th medical school in the U.S. – officially opened in March 1825 with a single professor, Dr. [[Robley Dunglison]]. Dunglison had been actively recruited by Thomas Jefferson, and had traveled from London to take up his new position.<ref name="dung">{{cite web |url=http://www.medicine.virginia.edu/administration/office-of-the-dean/about/factbook/chapter-1-history |title=History-School of Medicine at the University of Virginia |work=School of Medicine Official Website |access-date=11 July 2011 |archive-date=October 15, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151015130333/http://www.medicine.virginia.edu/administration/office-of-the-dean/about/factbook/chapter-1-history |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Just weeks before Dunglison and his wife arrived in the United States, Jefferson had written to Joseph C. Cabell that an anatomical theater would be "indispensable to the school of anatomy," and that "there cannot be a single dissection until a proper theater is prepared giving an advantageous view of the operation to those within, and effectually excluding observation from without."<ref name="auto"/> This structure, which was eventually demolished in 1938, was one of the first of its kind in the entire United States, conceived and blueprinted by Jefferson himself, who pushed fervently for its construction up until the time of his death in 1825.

The University of Virginia School of Medicine graduated its first four students in 1828, and in 1832, became the first medical school in the United States to standardize the criteria for admission.

More than 75 years later, UVA opened its first hospital in March 1901 with 25 beds and three operating rooms. Just as medical education has been a part of UVA since its founding, so too has medical literature – the 8,000 books purchased by Jefferson to create the University Library included 710 books on the medical sciences. UVA's medical literature moved to the UVA Medical School building in 1929. Its current home was dedicated in April 1976.

In 2016, UVA announced a partnership with [[Inova Fairfax Hospital|Inova Fairfax]] to establish a satellite campus at the flagship Inova hospital in Northern Virginia. This agreement also included the establishment of a personal genomics center and a collaboration between the cancer centers of the two entities.
=== Historical Timeline ===
* 1826 – Anatomical Hall designed and built by Jefferson.
* 1828 – First University degrees awarded to four medical graduates.
* 1892 – Medical course lengthened to two years.
* 1895 – Medical course extended to three years.
* 1898 – Medical course lengthened to four years.
* 1901 – Opening of the University of Virginia Hospital (25 beds). Dr. Paul Barringer named superintendent.
* 1905 – Richard Henry Whitehead, M.D., LL.D., dean of the University of North Carolina School of Medicine named first dean of the University of Virginia School of Medicine. Whitehead reorganized the hospital to a primarily teaching facility. He emphasized scholarship and basic science well in advance of the [[Flexner Report]].
* 1924 – First Woman Graduate (and only in that year), Lila Morse Bonner (later married name Lila Bonner Miller, MD). 
* 1929 – New medical school building opened (cost $1.4&nbsp;million).
* 1960 – West Complex expanded into new hospital, completed at a cost of $6.5&nbsp;million.
* 1989 – University of Virginia Replacement Hospital (556 beds) was dedicated, at a cost of $230&nbsp;million.
* 2014 – Medical school curriculum updated to system-based instruction, and classroom program shortened to 1.5 years. Claude Moore Medical Education building opened.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Marshall |first=Amy-Sarah |date=2011-01-07 |title=School of Medicine welcomes class of 2014, opens Claude Moore Medical Education Building |url=https://newsroom.uvahealth.com/2011/01/07/school-of-medicine-welcomes-class-of-2014-opens-claude-moore-medical-education-building/ |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=UVA Health Newsroom |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Facilities ==
[[File:UVA SchoolofMedicine.jpg|thumb|upright=1.56|right|Exterior of the old building of The University of Virginia School of Medicine, located near "The Corner" of Grounds]]

The School of Medicine is affiliated with the [[University of Virginia Health System]].

The [[University of Virginia Medical Center|UVA Hospital]] is a large tertiary care hospital with more than 500 beds, not including a 45-bed [[neonatal intensive care unit]] and 20-bed [[Nursery (room)|nursery]]. The Children's Hospital is served by the Newborn Emergency Transport System (NETS), which transports critically ill newborns and pediatrics from all over the surrounding area and states back to UVA. The hospital is a [[Trauma center#Level I|Level I trauma center]] and is accessible by ambulance as well as Pegasus, UVA Health System's air and ground transport service for critically ill and injured patients. As an academic medical center, patients at UVA are treated by physicians who are also faculty members at the UVA School of Medicine.<ref name="hs-facts">{{cite web |url=http://uvahealth.com/about/about-us/facts-at-a-glance |title=Facts at a Glance |work=UVA Health System Official Website |access-date=26 October 2007 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

The Claude Moore Health Sciences Library opened in 2014 and serves the School of Medicine and the Health System. The library is located within the Medical Center.<ref name=":0" />

From years 2016–2019, UVA Hospital was named the number 1 hospital in Virginia.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.news.virginia.edu/content/us-news-ranks-uva-no-1-hospital-virginia-honors-8-specialties/ |title=U.S. News Ranks UVA No. 1 Hospital in Virginia, Honors 8 Specialties &#124; UVA Today |website=www.news.virginia.edu |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160804191804/https://www.news.virginia.edu/content/us-news-ranks-uva-no-1-hospital-virginia-honors-8-specialties |archive-date=4 August 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Clinical education and learning societies ==
UVA utilizes a unique "Next Generation" integrated curriculum that allows medical students to spend more time in the clinic by condensing the first 2 years of classes into 1.5 years. Uniquely, students enter Clerkship and take [[Step 1]] and [[Step 2]] together in their fourth year. UVA features accredited programs (via the [[Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education]]) of resident and fellowship education in general, specialty, and subspecialty fields.

Upon matriculation, students are divided into one of four learning communities. Reed College, Hunter College, Dunglinson College, and Pinn College are each named after influential UVA SOM alumni. 

== Research ==
UVA has many highly regarded departments with over 300 labs; laboratories are mainly housed in Medical Center in Pinn Hall, MR-4, MR-5, MR-6, and the West Complex (Hospital West).
 
In 1889, philanthropist [[Oliver Hazard Payne]] bequeathed a $100,000 grant to the medical school, to help establish laboratories of experimental medicine.<ref name="marist">{{cite web|title=Col. Oliver Hazard Payne and His Mansion on the Hudson|url=https://www.marist.edu/-/news-col-oliver-hazard-payne-and-his-mansion-on-the-hudson|publisher=[[Marist College]]|access-date=8 January 2019}}</ref>

Founded in 1967, the Department of Perceptual Studies is unusual in that it is one of the few academic research groups in the field of "supernatural phenomena" with board-certified physicians and scientists at a respected university.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/02/there-is-a-paranormal-activity-lab-at-the-university-of-virginia/283584/|title=There Is a Paranormal Activity Lab at the University of Virginia|first=Jake|last=Flanagin|date=February 10, 2014|website=The Atlantic|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref>

=== Notable discoveries ===
* 1928 – 1952 – Sidney William Britton, Ph.D., professor of physiology and Herbert Silvette, Ph.D., professor of pharmacology, demonstrated that the adrenal cortex contained a hormone, not epinephrine, which influenced carbohydrate storage and metabolism.
* 1935 – 1967 – Alfred Chanutin, Ph.D., professor and chair of biochemistry, discovered the role of red blood cell 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) in oxygen transfer from hemoglobin. This finding had enormous impact on the preservation of blood for transfusion therapy.
* 1939 – Dupont Guerry III, M.D. intern, and William Wirt Waddell Jr., a pediatrician, discovered the role of vitamin K in the etiology, treatment, and prevention of hypoprothrombinemia and hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
* 1966 – 1988 – Robert M. Berne, M.D., professor and chair of physiology, pioneered adenosine in cardiovascular function and introduced adenosine as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of [[supraventricular tachycardia]].
* 1971 – 1981 – Alfred G. Gilman, M.D., Ph.D., professor of pharmacology discovered G-proteins, cellular mediators of hormone action, for which he received the 1989 Albert Lasker Award and the 1994 [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]].
* 1970 – 1983 – Ferid Murad, M.D., PhD, professor of medicine, discovered that endothelium-derived relaxing factor is nitric oxide, which acts as a vasodilator by stimulating guanylyl cyclase. Murad received the Albert Lasker Award in 1996 and the Nobel Prize in Medicine or Physiology in 1998 for this discovery.
* 1976 – [[Michael O. Thorner]], M.B.B.S., D.Sc., professor of medicine, discovered a new hypothalamic hormone, growth hormone releasing hormone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Thorner |first=Michael O. |date=June 2008 |title=The discovery of growth hormone-releasing hormone: an update |journal=Journal of Neuroendocrinology |volume=20 |issue=6 |pages=653–654 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2826.2008.01740.x |issn=1365-2826 |pmid=18601685 }}</ref> Thorner received the 1995 NIH General Clinical Research Centers Award for his work in clinical neuroendocrinology.
* 1995 – Barry Marshall, M.B.B.S., Associate Professor of Internal Medicine, received the Albert Lasker Award Medicine for his discovery that the bacterium Helicobacter pylori is the cause of peptic ulcer disease and also is associated with gastric carcinoma.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Couturier |first=Marc Roger |date=2013-02-01 |title=The Evolving Challenges of Helicobacter pylori Disease, Diagnostics, and Treatment, Part I |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0196439913000020 |journal=Clinical Microbiology Newsletter |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=19–24 |doi=10.1016/j.clinmicnews.2013.01.001 |issn=0196-4399|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Research Centers and Core facilities ==

===Research Centers===
* The '''[[UVA Cancer Center]]''' is headed by [[Thomas P. Loughran Jr.]] and was ranked in 2016 by [[U.S. News & World Report]] as one of the top 2–3% of cancer specialty centers nationwide.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uvahealth.com/services/cancer|title=UVA Cancer Center - UVA Health System|website=Uvahealth.com|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref>
* The '''Carter Immunology Center''' is one of the largest research centers in the School of Medicine with over 50 faculty members. 
* '''Cardiovascular Research Center'''
* The '''Center for Brain Immunology & Glia''' is a group of labs in the Department of Neuroscience. In recent years, BIG has been one of UVA's most productive collaborative research centers, with research being nominated for Science's Breakthrough of the Year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://med.virginia.edu/big/2015/12/06/big-scientists-are-finalists-for-breakthrough-of-the-year/|title=BIG Scientists are Finalists for Breakthrough of the Year|date=December 6, 2015|website=Med.virginia.edu|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref> Notable discoveries as of late include discovering a link between the brain and the immune system,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://med.virginia.edu/big/2015/07/26/textbook-altering-link-between-brain-immune-system/|title=Textbook-Altering Link Between Brain, Immune System|date=July 26, 2015|website=Med.virginia.edu|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref> identifying major genetic causes of [[schizophrenia]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://med.virginia.edu/big/2015/09/06/big-identifies-major-genetic-causes-of-schizophrenia/|title=BIG Identifies Major Genetic Causes of Schizophrenia|date=September 6, 2015|website=Med.virginia.edu|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref> and a link between the immune system and social behavior.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://med.virginia.edu/neuroscience/2016/07/13/tony-filiano-publishes-amazing-breakthrough-in-nature/|title=Tony Filiano publishes breakthrough in Nature|first=Dayna Krueger|last=says|date=July 13, 2016|website=Med.virginia.edu|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref>
* The '''Center for Diabetes Technology''' has been the subject of publicity for its role in the development of the [[artificial pancreas]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.news.virginia.edu/content/power-artificial-pancreas/|title=Power of the Artificial Pancreas|date=October 10, 2016|website=UVA Today|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref> a major breakthrough in the treatment of [[type 1 diabetes]].
* '''Thaler Center for AIDS and HIV Research'''

=== Leadership allegations ===
In September of 2024, a letter of no confidence, signed by 128 faculty members and physicians, was raised against dean [[Melina Kibbe]] and CEO of UVA Health [[Craig Kent]], demanding their ousting and replacement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.Va. Health faculty demand removal of health system CEO, School of Medicine dean |url=https://www.cavalierdaily.com/article/2024/09/uva-health-faculty-demand-removal-of-health-system-ceo-school-of-medicine-dean |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=U.Va. Health faculty demand removal of health system CEO, School of Medicine dean - The Cavalier Daily - University of Virginia's Student Newspaper |language=en-US}}</ref> The letter accused Kibbe and Kent of allowing "egregious acts" such as harassment of resident physicians, overcharging patients in favor of profit, and lavish spending on C-suite executives. The letter also asserts that Kibbe and Kent have been pressuring healthcare workers to not report concerns of patient safety, and more generally, that they have ushered in "a culture of fear and retaliation" within the school and health network.

In response to the letter, university president [[James Edward Ryan|Jim Ryan]] wrote that "through some of their [the authors'] allegations, they have unfairly — and I trust unwittingly — cast a shadow over the great work of the entire health system and medical school.” The university brought in the law firm, [[Williams & Connolly]], to conduct an investigation into the allegations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Progress |first=EMILY HEMPHILL The Daily |date=2024-09-18 |title=UVa hires international law firm to investigate hospital complaints |url=https://dailyprogress.com/news/local/business/health-care/uva-hires-international-law-firm-to-investigate-hospital-complaints/article_8794f98c-7529-11ef-91a4-27c84e12ddbc.html |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=The Daily Progress |language=en}}</ref>

The results of the investigation were not released, however, Kent resigned shortly after the conclusion of the investigation in March 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Progress |first=EMILY HEMPHILL The Daily |date=2025-03-10 |title=UVa hospital official resigns in protest over 'irrational' treatment of former health system CEO |url=https://dailyprogress.com/news/local/education/higher-education/uva/article_ddeea63e-fb6b-11ef-93e6-4f3de291e17d.html |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=The Daily Progress |language=en}}</ref> Kibbe resigned in July 2025 after being named as the new president at The University of Texas Health Science Center.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Progress |first=CAROLINE KING The Daily |date=2025-07-16 |title=Embattled UVa Medical School dean stepping down |url=https://dailyprogress.com/news/local/education/higher-education/uva/article_c5c5c705-bab3-476d-8d2a-1253a59ed81c.html |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=The Daily Progress |language=en}}</ref>
==Medical Scientist Training Program==
The University of Virginia School of Medicine is one of only 43 [[NIH]] funded [[Medical Scientist Training Program|MD/PhD]] programs in the country.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nigms.nih.gov/Training/InstPredoc/Pages/PredocOverview-MSTP.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140104221855/http://www.nigms.nih.gov/Training/InstPredoc/Pages/PredocOverview-MSTP.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 4, 2014|title=Medical Scientist Training Program|website=Nigms.nih.gov|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref> The program director is Dr. [[Dean H. Kedes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mstp.med.virginia.edu/|title=Medical Scientist Training Program - University of Virginia School of Medicine|website=Mstp.med.virginia.edu|access-date=May 20, 2019}}</ref>

===History===
According to the handbook provided to all entering students: {{Blockquote|text=The University of Virginia undertook significant expansion of research and training programs in the basic biomedical sciences during the late 1960s and early 1970s. All chairmen of the basic science departments of the School of Medicine were newly appointed during this time, a major new research building was constructed, and individual departments grew several-fold in size and quality. Similar but less dramatic growth followed in the clinical departments. Interest in the training of medical scientists flourished rapidly in this environment, in part because many of the new faculty either had experience with MSTPs or were recent graduates of such programs. Accordingly, an MSTP committee was appointed in 1971 under the leadership of Dr. Robert C. Haynes Jr., and funds were provided by the University to initiate such training. An application for training funds was submitted to the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS) in 1972, just prior to the time when the appropriation for such training programs was withdrawn. The application was resubmitted in 1975, and NIH support was first received in 1977 under the future Nobel Laureate, Dr. Alfred G. Gilman. |title=History |source=MSTP Handbook, University of Virginia }} As such the program claims two founding dates: 1971 when the MSTP committee was first formed and 1977 when the first students matriculated.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Variants of SARS-CoV-2

{{Short description|none}}
{{Redirect|New coronavirus variant|recent species of coronavirus|Novel coronavirus|and|Coronavirus}}
{{pp-semi-indef|small=yes}}
{{Use British English|date=May 2025}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2025}}
{{cs1 config |name-list-style=vanc |display-authors=6}}
{{COVID-19 pandemic sidebar|expanded=variants}}
[[File:Biology of SARS-CoV-2 – Evolution and Mutations.webm|thumb|Positive, negative, and neutral mutations during the evolution of coronaviruses like SARS-CoV-2.]]

'''Variants of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2''' ([[SARS-CoV-2]]) are viruses that, while similar to the original, have genetic changes that are of enough significance to lead virologists to label them separately. SARS-CoV-2 is the virus that causes [[COVID-19|coronavirus disease 2019]] (COVID-19). Some have been stated to be of particular importance, due to their potential for increased transmissibility,<ref name="SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern">{{cite journal |author4-link=Gary Kobinger |vauthors=Shahhosseini N, Babuadze GG, Wong G, Kobinger GP |date=April 2021 |title=Mutation Signatures and In Silico Docking of Novel SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern |journal=Microorganisms |volume=9 |issue=5 |page=926 |doi=10.3390/microorganisms9050926 |pmc=8146828 |pmid=33925854 |doi-access=free}}</ref> increased virulence, or reduced effectiveness of vaccines against them.<ref>{{cite news |date=6 January 2021 |title=Coronavirus variants and mutations: The science explained |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-55404988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193151/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-55404988 |archive-date=22 February 2021 |access-date=2 February 2021 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{cite journal |last1=Kupferschmidt |first1=Kai |date=15 January 2021 |title=New coronavirus variants could cause more reinfections, require updated vaccines |journal=Science |doi=10.1126/science.abg6028}}</ref> These variants contribute to the continued circulation of SARS-CoV-2.<!-- second paragraph will be excerpted in SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant -->

{{As of|2025|6|25}}, the variants of interest as specified by the [[World Health Organization]] are JN.1, and the variants under monitoring are KP.3, KP.3.1.1, JN.1.18, LP.8.1, NB.1.8.1, XEC and XFG.<ref name="current_variants">{{cite web |title=WHO Coronavirus Network (CoViNet) |url=https://data.who.int/dashboards/covid19/variants |access-date=2024-09-01}}</ref>

{{Toclimit}}

== Overview ==
The origin of SARS-CoV-2 has not been identified.<ref>{{cite web |date=16 March 2022 |title=Origins of Coronaviruses |url=https://www.niaid.nih.gov/diseases-conditions/origins-coronaviruses |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230121161451/https://www.niaid.nih.gov/diseases-conditions/origins-coronaviruses |archive-date=21 January 2023 |access-date=3 February 2023 |website=NIH.gov |publisher=National Institutes of Health in the United States |quote="To date, the origin of SARS-CoV-2 which caused the COVID-19 pandemic has not been identified."}}</ref> However, the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 may have resulted from [[Genetic recombination|recombination events]] between a [[bat]] SARS-like coronavirus and a [[pangolin]] coronavirus through cross-species transmission.<ref name="SARS-CoV-2 emergence due to recombination event">{{cite journal |vauthors=Shahhosseini N, Wong G, Kobinger GP, Chinikar S |date=June 2021 |title=SARS-CoV-2 spillover transmission due to recombination event |journal=Gene Reports |volume=23 |article-number=101045 |doi=10.1016/j.genrep.2021.101045 |pmc=7884226 |pmid=33615041}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2022-08-01 |title=The rise and fall of the lab leak hypothesis for the origin of SARS-CoV-2 {{!}} Science-Based Medicine |url=https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-lab-leak-hypothesis-for-the-origin-of-sars-cov-2/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=sciencebasedmedicine.org |language=en-US |archive-date=23 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230223155852/https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-lab-leak-hypothesis-for-the-origin-of-sars-cov-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The earliest available SARS-CoV-2 viral genomes were collected from patients in December 2019, and Chinese researchers compared these early genomes with bat and pangolin coronavirus strains to estimate the ancestral human coronavirus type; the identified ancestral genome type was labeled "S", and its dominant derived type was labeled "L" to reflect the mutant amino acid changes. Independently, Western researchers carried out similar analyses but labeled the ancestral type "A" and the derived type "B". The B-type mutated into further types including B.1, which is the ancestor of the major global variants of concern, labeled in 2021 by the WHO as [[SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant|alpha]], [[SARS-CoV-2 Beta variant|beta]], [[SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant|gamma]], [[SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant|delta]] and [[SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant|omicron]] variants.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Xiaolu |last2=Wu |first2=Changcheng |last3=Li |first3=Xiang |last4=Song |first4=Yuhe |date=3 March 2020 |title=On the origin and continuing evolution of SARS-CoV-2 |journal=National Science Review |language=en |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=1012–1023 |doi=10.1093/nsr/nwaa036 |pmc=7107875 |pmid=34676127 |doi-access=free}}{{Erratum|doi=10.1093/nsr/nwaa036|http://retractionwatch.com/2020/05/11/aggressive-covid-19-strains-what-it-takes-to-correct-a-flawed-paper/#more-119425 ''Retraction Watch''|http://retractionwatch.com/retracted-coronavirus-covid-19-papers/ ''Retraction Watch''|checked=yes}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Forster |first1=Peter |last2=Forster |first2=Lucy |last3=Renfrew |first3=Colin |last4=Forster |first4=Michael |date=28 April 2020 |title=Phylogenetic network analysis of SARS-CoV-2 genomes |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=117 |issue=17 |pages=9241–9243 |bibcode=2020PNAS..117.9241F |doi=10.1073/pnas.2004999117 |pmc=7196762 |pmid=32269081 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rambaut |first1=Andrew |last2=Holmes |first2=Edward C. |last3=O'Toole |first3=Áine |last4=Hill |first4=Verity |last5=McCrone |first5=John T. |last6=Ruis |first6=Christopher |last7=du Plessis |first7=Louis |last8=Pybus |first8=Oliver G. |date=15 July 2020 |title=A dynamic nomenclature proposal for SARS-CoV-2 lineages to assist genomic epidemiology |journal=Nature Microbiology |volume=5 |issue=11 |pages=1403–1407 |bibcode=2020NatMb...5.1403R |doi=10.1038/s41564-020-0770-5 |pmc=7610519 |pmid=32669681 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Early in the pandemic, the relatively low number of infections (compared with later stages of the pandemic) resulted in fewer opportunities for mutation of the viral genome and, therefore, fewer opportunities for the occurrence of differentiated variants.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tregoning |first1=John S. |last2=Flight |first2=Katie E. |last3=Higham |first3=Sophie L. |last4=Wang |first4=Ziyin |last5=Pierce |first5=Benjamin F. |date=9 August 2021 |title=Progress of the COVID-19 vaccine effort: viruses, vaccines and variants versus efficacy, effectiveness and escape |journal=Nature Reviews Immunology |volume=21 |issue=10 |pages=626–636 |bibcode=2021NatRI..21..626T |doi=10.1038/s41577-021-00592-1 |pmc=8351583 |pmid=34373623}}</ref> Since the occurrence of variants was rarer, the observation of S-protein mutations in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) region interacting with ACE2 was also not frequent.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Piplani |first1=Sakshi |last2=Singh |first2=Puneet Kumar |last3=Winkler |first3=David A. |last4=Petrovsky |first4=Nikolai |date=December 2021 |title=In silico comparison of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein-ACE2 binding affinities across species and implications for virus origin |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=13063 |bibcode=2021NatSR..1113063P |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-92388-5  |doi-access=free|pmc=8225877 |pmid=34168168}}</ref>

As time went on, the evolution of SARS-CoV-2's genome (by means of random mutations) led to mutant specimens of the virus (i.e., genetic variants), observed to be more transmissible, to be naturally selected. Notably, both the Alpha and the Delta variants were observed to be more transmissible than previously identified viral strains.<ref>{{cite web |date=12 June 2021 |title=Covid: Is there a limit to how much worse variants can get? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-57431420 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210615170043/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-57431420 |archive-date=15 June 2021 |access-date=12 June 2021 |work=[[BBC]] |vauthors=Gallagher J}}</ref>

Some SARS-CoV-2 variants are considered to be of concern as they maintain (or even increase) their replication fitness in the face of rising population immunity,<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Tao |first1=Kaiming |last2=Tzou |first2=Philip L. |last3=Nouhin |first3=Janin |last4=Gupta |first4=Ravindra K. |last5=de Oliveira |first5=Tulio |last6=Kosakovsky Pond |first6=Sergei L. |last7=Fera |first7=Daniela |last8=Shafer |first8=Robert W. |date=17 September 2021 |title=The biological and clinical significance of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants |journal=Nature Reviews Genetics |volume=22 |issue=12 |pages=757–773 |doi=10.1038/s41576-021-00408-x |pmc=8447121 |pmid=34535792}}</ref> either by infection recovery or via vaccination. Some of the variants of concern show mutations in the RBD of the S-protein.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hendy |first1=Mohamed |last2=Kaufman |first2=Samuel |last3=Ponga |first3=Mauricio |date=December 2021 |title=Molecular strategies for antibody binding and escape of SARS-CoV-2 and its mutations |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=21735 |bibcode=2021NatSR..1121735H |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-01081-0  |doi-access=free|pmc=8571385 |pmid=34741079}}</ref>

== Definitions ==
The term '''variant of concern''' ('''VOC''') for [[SARS-CoV-2]], which causes [[COVID-19]], is a category used for variants of the virus where mutations in their [[coronavirus spike protein|spike protein]] receptor binding domain (RBD) substantially increase binding affinity (e.g., N501Y) in RBD-hACE2 complex (genetic data), while also being linked to rapid spread in human populations (epidemiological data).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shahhosseini |first1=Nariman |last2=Babuadze |first2=George (Giorgi) |last3=Wong |first3=Gary |last4=Kobinger |first4=Gary P. |author4-link=Gary Kobinger |date=May 2021 |title=Mutation Signatures and In Silico Docking of Novel SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern |journal=Microorganisms |language=en |volume=9 |issue=5 |page=926 |doi=10.3390/microorganisms9050926 |pmc=8146828 |pmid=33925854 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Before being allocated to this category, an emerging variant may have been labeled a '''variant of interest''' ('''VOI'''),<ref name="WHO_tracking">{{Cite web |title=Tracking SARS-CoV-2 variants |url=https://www.who.int/activities/tracking-SARS-CoV-2-variants |access-date=2021-11-28 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=9 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609115218/https://www.who.int/en/activities/tracking-SARS-CoV-2-variants/ |url-status=live }}</ref> or in some countries a '''variant under investigation''' ('''VUI''').<ref name="VDoCD">{{cite web |date=28 January 2021 |title=Variants: distribution of cases data |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/covid-19-variants-genomically-confirmed-case-numbers/variants-distribution-of-cases-data#variant1 |access-date=19 February 2021 |website=GOV.UK |at=At "Differences between a Variant of Concern and Variant Under Investigation" |quote=SARS-CoV-2 variants, if considered to have concerning epidemiological, immunological, or pathogenic properties, are raised for formal investigation. At this point they are designated Variant Under Investigation (VUI) with a year, month, and number. Following a risk assessment with the relevant expert committee, they may be designated Variant of Concern (VOC) |archive-date=7 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210607111658/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/covid-19-variants-genomically-confirmed-case-numbers/variants-distribution-of-cases-data#variant1 |url-status=live }}</ref> During or after fuller assessment as a variant of concern the variant is typically assigned to a lineage in the [[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|Pango]] nomenclature system<ref name="RambautETAL." /> and to clades in the [[Nextstrain]]<ref name="nextstrain-amendation" /> and [[GISAID]]<ref name="GCTree" /> systems.

Historically, the WHO regularly listed updates on variants of concern (VOC), which are variants with an increased rate of transmission, virulence, or resistance against mitigations, like vaccines. The variant submissions from member states are then submitted to [[GISAID]], followed by field investigations of the variant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Historical working definitions and primary actions for SARS-CoV-2 variants |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/annex2_previous_vocs_and_definitions.pdf |access-date=9 September 2024 |website=World Health Organization |archive-date=7 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250307170623/https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/annex2_previous_vocs_and_definitions.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Updated definitions, published on 4 October 2023, add variants of interest (VOI) and '''variants under monitoring''' ('''VUM''') to the World Health Organization's working definitions for SARS-CoV-2 variants. The updated definition of VUMs includes having a suspected epidemiological growth advantage or community transmission in at least two countries over a 2–4 week period; while the definition of VOIs requires known genetic changes related to greater epidemiological risk and a known growth advantage in at least two WHO regions and increasing prevalence, or other epidemiological evidence "suggest[ing] an emerging risk to global public health". A VOC, under the October 2023 definition, must satisfy the definition of VOIs and satisfy other criteria defining a risk to global health. Greek letter names for the variants are restricted to VOCs since March 2023.<ref name="WHO_variant_definitions_20231004">{{Cite web |title=Updated working definitions and primary actions for SARSCoV2 variants |url=https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/updated-working-definitions-and-primary-actions-for--sars-cov-2-variants |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613190805/https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/annex1_updated_working_definitions_17-08-2023.pdf |archive-date=2025-06-13 |access-date=2024-09-09 |website=www.who.int |language=en}}</ref><ref name="who-variants" />

Other organisations such as the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] in the United States typically define their variants of concern slightly differently; for example, the CDC de-escalated the Delta variant on 14 April 2022,<ref name="cdc-variants" /> while the WHO did so on 7 June 2022.[[File:Novel Coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (50960620707) (cropped).jpg|thumb|False-colour [[Transmission electron microscopy|transmission electron micrograph]] of a B.1.1.7 variant coronavirus. The variant's increased transmissibility is believed to be due to changes in structure of the spike proteins, shown here in green.]]

{{As of|2023|3|15}},<ref name=":10">{{cite web |title=Statement on the update of WHO's working definitions and tracking system for SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants of interest |url=https://www.who.int/news/item/16-03-2023-statement-on-the-update-of-who-s-working-definitions-and-tracking-system-for-sars-cov-2-variants-of-concern-and-variants-of-interest |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=8 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230608191442/https://www.who.int/news/item/16-03-2023-statement-on-the-update-of-who-s-working-definitions-and-tracking-system-for-sars-cov-2-variants-of-concern-and-variants-of-interest |url-status=live }}</ref> the WHO defines a VOI as a variant "with genetic changes that are predicted or known to affect virus characteristics such as transmissibility, virulence, antibody evasion, susceptibility to therapeutics and detectability" and that is circulating more than other variants in over one WHO region to such an extent that a global public health risk can be suggested.<ref name=":11">{{cite web |title=Updated working definitions and primary actions for SARSCoV2 variants |url=https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/updated-working-definitions-and-primary-actions-for--sars-cov-2-variants |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=13 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613190805/https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/annex1_updated_working_definitions_17-08-2023.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Furthermore, the update stated that "VOIs will be referred to using established scientific nomenclature systems such as those used by Nextstrain and Pango".<ref name=":11" />

== Notability criteria ==
Viruses generally acquire mutations over time, giving rise to new variants. When a new variant appears to be growing in a population, it can be labelled as an "emerging variant". In the case of SARS-CoV-2, new lineages often differ from one another by just a few nucleotides.<ref name="auto" />

Some of the potential consequences of emerging variants are the following:<ref name=":33" /><ref>IDSA Contributor {{cite web |date=2 February 2021 |title=COVID "Mega-variant" and eight criteria for a template to assess all variants |url=https://sciencespeaksblog.org/2021/02/02/covid-mega-variant-and-eight-criteria-for-a-template-to-assess-all-variants/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421035437/https://sciencespeaksblog.org/2021/02/02/covid-mega-variant-and-eight-criteria-for-a-template-to-assess-all-variants/ |archive-date=21 April 2021 |access-date=20 February 2021 |website=Science Speaks: Global ID News |language=en-US}}</ref>
* Increased transmissibility
* Increased [[Disease#Morbidity|morbidity]]
* Increased [[Mortality rate|mortality]]
* Ability to evade detection by diagnostic tests
* Decreased susceptibility to [[Antiviral drug|antiviral]] drugs (if and when such drugs are available)
* Decreased susceptibility to neutralising antibodies, either therapeutic (e.g., convalescent plasma or monoclonal antibodies) or in laboratory experiments
* Ability to evade natural immunity (e.g., causing reinfections)
* Ability to infect vaccinated individuals
* Increased risk of particular conditions such as multisystem inflammatory syndrome or [[long COVID]].
* Increased affinity for particular demographic or clinical groups, such as children or immunocompromised individuals.

Variants that appear to meet one or more of these criteria may be labelled '''"variants under investigation"''' or '''"variants of interest"''' pending verification and validation of these properties. The primary characteristic of a variant of interest is that it shows evidence that demonstrates it is the cause of an increased proportion of cases or unique outbreak clusters; however, it must also have limited prevalence or expansion at national levels, or the classification would be elevated to a "[[SARS-CoV-2 variant of concern|variant of concern]]".<ref name="phe-voc" /><ref name="CanSum">{{cite report |url=https://nccid.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2021/02/CanCOGeN-Interim-Recommendations-for-Naming-Identifying-and-Reporting-SARS-CoV-2-Variants.pdf |title=CanCOGeN Interim Recommendations for Naming, Identifying, and Reporting SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern |date=15 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417134703/https://nccid.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2021/02/CanCOGeN-Interim-Recommendations-for-Naming-Identifying-and-Reporting-SARS-CoV-2-Variants.pdf |archive-date=17 April 2021 |url-status=live |version=1.0 |website=CanCOGeN (nccid.ca) |vauthors=Griffiths E, Tanner J, Knox N, Hsiao W, Van Domselaar G}}</ref> If there is clear evidence that the effectiveness of prevention or intervention measures for a particular variant is substantially reduced, that variant is termed a "variant of high consequence".<ref name="cdc-variants" />

=== Lineages and clades ===
While there are many thousands of variants of SARS-CoV-2,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Koyama T, Platt D, Parida L |date=July 2020 |title=Variant analysis of SARS-CoV-2 genomes |journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization |volume=98 |issue=7 |pages=495–504 |doi=10.2471/BLT.20.253591 |pmc=7375210 |pmid=32742035 |quote=We detected in total 65776 variants with 5775 distinct variants. |doi-access=free}}</ref> subtypes of the virus can be put into larger groupings such as lineages or [[clade]]s.{{efn|According to the WHO, "Lineages or clades can be defined based on viruses that share a phylogenetically determined common ancestor".<ref name="3.6">{{cite book |author=WHO Headquarters |url=https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-2019-nCoV-genomic_sequencing-2021.1 |title=SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequencing for public health goals: Interim guidance, 8 January 2021 |date=8 January 2021 |publisher=World Health Organization |page=6 |chapter=3.6 Considerations for virus naming and nomenclature |access-date=2 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210123001849/https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-2019-nCoV-genomic_sequencing-2021.1 |archive-date=23 January 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>}} Three main, generally used nomenclatures<ref name="3.6" /> have been proposed:
* {{as of|2021|01}}, [[GISAID]]—referring to SARS-CoV-2 as hCoV-19<ref name="AlmETAL.">{{cite journal |vauthors=Alm E, Broberg EK, Connor T, Hodcroft EB, Komissarov AB, Maurer-Stroh S, Melidou A, Neher RA, O'Toole Á, Pereyaslov D |date=August 2020 |title=Geographical and temporal distribution of SARS-CoV-2 clades in the WHO European Region, January to June 2020 |journal=Euro Surveillance |volume=25 |issue=32 |doi=10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2020.25.32.2001410 |pmc=7427299 |pmid=32794443 |ref={{sfnref|Alm et al.}} |collaboration=The WHO European Region sequencing laboratories and GISAID EpiCoV group}}</ref>—had identified eight global clades (S, O, L, V, G, GH, GR, and GV).<ref>{{cite web |date=18 January 2021 |title=Global phylogeny, updated by Nextstrain |url=https://www.gisaid.org/phylodynamics/global/nextstrain/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120112916/https://www.gisaid.org/phylodynamics/global/nextstrain/ |archive-date=20 January 2021 |access-date=19 January 2021 |publisher=GISAID}}</ref>
* In 2017, Hadfield et al. announced [[Nextstrain]], intended "for real-time tracking of pathogen evolution".<ref name="nextstrain-about">{{cite journal |vauthors=Hadfield J, Megill C, Bell SM, Huddleston J, Potter B, Callender C, Sagulenko P, Bedford T, Neher RA |date=December 2018 |title=Nextstrain: real-time tracking of pathogen evolution |journal=Bioinformatics |volume=34 |issue=23 |pages=4121–4123 |doi=10.1093/bioinformatics/bty407 |pmc=6247931 |pmid=29790939 |veditors=Kelso J}}</ref> Nextstrain has later been used for tracking SARS-CoV-2, identifying 13 major clades{{efn|name=Nextstrain_criteria}} (19A–B, 20A–20J and 21A) {{as of|2021|06|lc=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nextstrain COVID-19 |url=https://nextstrain.org/ncov/global |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121104048/https://nextstrain.org/ncov/global |archive-date=21 January 2021 |access-date=1 June 2021 |website=[[Nextstrain]]}}</ref>
* In 2020, Rambaut et al. of the [[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages]] (PANGOLIN)<ref>{{cite web |title=cov-lineages/pangolin: Software package for assigning SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences to global lineages |url=https://github.com/cov-lineages/pangolin |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215054819/https://github.com/cov-lineages/pangolin |archive-date=15 February 2021 |access-date=2 January 2021 |publisher=Github}}</ref> software team proposed in an article<ref name="RambautETAL.">{{cite journal |vauthors=Rambaut A, Holmes EC, O'Toole Á, Hill V, McCrone JT, Ruis C, du Plessis L, Pybus OG |date=November 2020 |title=A dynamic nomenclature proposal for SARS-CoV-2 lineages to assist genomic epidemiology |journal=Nature Microbiology |volume=5 |issue=11 |pages=1403–1407 |bibcode=2020NatMb...5.1403R |doi=10.1038/s41564-020-0770-5 |pmc=7610519 |pmid=32669681 |doi-access=free}} Cited in {{harvp|Alm et al.}}</ref> "a dynamic nomenclature for SARS-CoV-2 lineages that focuses on actively circulating virus lineages and those that spread to new locations";<ref name="3.6" /> {{as of|2021|08|lc=on}}, 1340 lineages had been designated.<ref name="pango-lineages" /><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rambaut A, Holmes EC, O'Toole Á, Hill V, McCrone JT, Ruis C, du Plessis L, Pybus OG |date=March 2021 |title=Addendum: A dynamic nomenclature proposal for SARS-CoV-2 lineages to assist genomic epidemiology |journal=Nature Microbiology |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=415 |doi=10.1038/s41564-021-00872-5 |pmc=7845574 |pmid=33514928}}</ref>

[[National public health institutes]] may also create their own nomenclature system for the purposes of tracking specific variants.  For example, [[Public Health England]] designated each tracked variant by year, month and number in the format [YYYY] [MM]/[NN] (where YYYY is the year, MM is the month and NN is a sequential number within the month), prefixing 'VUI' or 'VOC' for variant under investigation or [[variant of concern]] respectively.<ref name="phe-voc" /> This system has been modified and now uses the format [YY] [MMM]-[NN], where the month is written out using a three-letter code.<ref name="phe-voc" />

== Reference sequence ==
As it is currently not known when the [[index case]] or "patient zero" occurred, the choice of reference sequence for a given study is relatively arbitrary, with different notable research studies' choices varying as follows:
* The earliest sequence, ''Wuhan-1'', was collected on 24 December 2019.<ref name="progenitor_SARS-CoV-2" />
* One group (Sudhir Kumar et al.)<ref name="progenitor_SARS-CoV-2" /> refers extensively to an [[NCBI]] [[reference genome]] (GenBankID:NC_045512; GISAID ID: EPI_ISL_402125),<ref name="pmid32015508">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wu F, Zhao S, Yu B, Chen YM, Wang W, Song ZG, Hu Y, Tao ZW, Tian JH, Pei YY, Yuan ML, Zhang YL, Dai FH, Liu Y, Wang QM, Zheng JJ, Xu L, Holmes EC, Zhang YZ |date=March 2020 |title=A new coronavirus associated with human respiratory disease in China |journal=Nature |volume=579 |issue=7798 |pages=265–269 |bibcode=2020Natur.579..265W |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2008-3 |pmc=7094943 |pmid=32015508}}</ref> this sample was collected on 26 December 2019,<ref name="pmid33605421">{{cite journal |vauthors=Chiara M, Horner DS, Gissi C, Pesole G |date=May 2021 |title=Comparative Genomics Reveals Early Emergence and Biased Spatiotemporal Distribution of SARS-CoV-2 |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=2547–2565 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msab049 |pmc=7928790 |pmid=33605421}}</ref> although they also used the ''WIV04'' GISAID reference genome (ID: EPI_ISL_402124),<ref name="zhengli03-2020">{{cite journal |author1-link=Shi Zhengli |vauthors=Zhou P, Yang XL, Wang XG, Hu B, Zhang L, Zhang W, Si HR, Zhu Y, Li B, Huang CL, Chen HD, Chen J, Luo Y, Guo H, Jiang RD, Liu MQ, Chen Y, Shen XR, Wang X, Zheng XS, Zhao K, Chen QJ, Deng F, Liu LL, Yan B, Zhan FX, Wang YY, Xiao GF, Shi ZL |date=March 2020 |title=A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin |journal=Nature |volume=579 |issue=7798 |pages=270–273 |bibcode=2020Natur.579..270Z |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2012-7 |pmc=7095418 |pmid=32015507}}</ref> in their analyses.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Okada P, Buathong R, Phuygun S, Thanadachakul T, Parnmen S, Wongboot W, Waicharoen S, Wacharapluesadee S, Uttayamakul S, Vachiraphan A, Chittaganpitch M, Mekha N, Janejai N, Iamsirithaworn S, Lee RT, Maurer-Stroh S |date=February 2020 |title=Early transmission patterns of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in travellers from Wuhan to Thailand, January 2020 |journal=Euro Surveillance |volume=25 |issue=8 |doi=10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2020.25.8.2000097 |pmc=7055038 |pmid=32127124}}</ref>
* According to another source (Zhukova et al.), the sequence ''WIV04/2019'', belonging to the [[GISAID]] S&nbsp;clade&nbsp;/ [[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|PANGO]] A&nbsp;lineage&nbsp;/ [[Nextstrain]] 19B&nbsp;clade, is thought to most closely reflect the sequence of the original virus infecting humans—known as "sequence zero".<ref name=Zhukova /> ''WIV04/2019'' was sampled from a symptomatic patient on 30 December 2019 and is widely used (especially by those collaborating with GISAID)<ref>{{cite web |title=Official hCoV-19 Reference Sequence |url=https://www.gisaid.org/epiflu-applications/hcov-19-reference-sequence/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506170302/https://www.gisaid.org/epiflu-applications/hcov-19-reference-sequence/ |archive-date=6 May 2021 |access-date=14 May 2021 |work=www.gisaid.org}}</ref> as a [[reference sequence]].<ref name=Zhukova />

The variant first sampled and identified in Wuhan, China is considered by researchers to differ from the progenitor genome by three mutations.<ref name="progenitor_SARS-CoV-2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kumar S, Tao Q, Weaver S, Sanderford M, Caraballo-Ortiz MA, Sharma S, Pond SL, Miura S |date=May 2021 |title=An evolutionary portrait of the progenitor SARS-CoV-2 and its dominant offshoots in COVID-19 pandemic |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=38 |issue=8 |pages=3046–3059 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msab118 |pmc=8135569 |pmid=33942847}}</ref><ref name="SARS-CoV-2_ancestor">{{cite web |title=The ancestor of SARS-CoV-2's Wuhan strain was circulating in late October 2019 |url=https://www.news-medical.net/news/20210507/The-ancestor-of-SARS-CoV-2e28099s-Wuhan-strain-was-circulating-in-late-October-2019.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210724173715/https://www.news-medical.net/news/20210507/The-ancestor-of-SARS-CoV-2e28099s-Wuhan-strain-was-circulating-in-late-October-2019.aspx |archive-date=24 July 2021 |access-date=10 May 2020 |website=News Medical |quote=Journal reference: Kumar, S. et al. (2021). An evolutionary portrait...}}</ref> Subsequently, many distinct lineages of SARS-CoV-2 have evolved.<ref name="pango-lineages">{{cite web |title=Lineage descriptions |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineages.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210604174159/https://cov-lineages.org/lineages.html |archive-date=4 June 2021 |access-date=24 December 2020 |website=cov-lineages.org |publisher=[[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|Pango]] team}}</ref>

== Previously circulating and formerly monitored variants (WHO) ==
The WHO defines a previously circulating variant as a variant that "has demonstrated to no longer pose a major added risk to global public health compared to other circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants", but should still be monitored.<ref name="WHO21Nov" />

On 15 March 2023, the WHO released an update on the tracking system of VOCs, announcing that only VOCs will be assigned Greek letters.<ref name=":10" />

=== Previously circulating variants of concern (VOC) ===
The variants listed below had previously been designated as variants of concern, but were displaced by other variants. {{as of|2022|05}}, the WHO lists the following under "previously circulating variants of concern":<ref name="WHO21Nov" />

===== B.1.1.7 with E484K =====
Variant of Concern 21FEB-02 (previously written as <abbr>VOC</abbr>-202102/02), described by [[Public Health England]] (PHE) as "B.1.1.7 with E484K"<ref name="phe-voc" /> is of the same lineage in the Pango nomenclature system, but has an additional [[#E484K|E484K]] mutation. As of 17 March 2021, there were 39 confirmed cases of <abbr>VOC</abbr>-21FEB-02 in the UK.<ref name="phe-voc" /> On 4 March 2021, scientists reported [[SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant|B.1.1.7]] with [[#E484K|E484K]] mutations in the state of [[Oregon]]. A, Neide B, Everett J, Reddy S, Rabut E, Deseignora J, Feldman MD, Rodino KG, Bushman F, Harris RM, Mell JC, Planet PJ |date=2021 |title=Comparative Analysis of Emerging B.1.1.7+E484K SARS-CoV-2 Isolates |journal=Open Forum Infectious Diseases |volume=8 |issue=7 |article-number=ofab300 |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.04.21.440801 |doi=10.1093/ofid/ofab300  |doi-access=free|pmc=8244812 |pmid=34254040}}</ref> and B.1.1.7 Lineage with S:E484K.<ref>{{cite web |title=B.1.1.7 Lineage with S:E484K Report |url=https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?pango=B.1.1.7&muts=S%3AE484K |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210703045440/https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?pango=B.1.1.7&muts=S%3AE484K |archive-date=3 July 2021 |access-date=28 May 2021 |work=outbreak.info}}</ref>

==== Beta (lineage B.1.351) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Beta variant}}

On 18 December 2020, the [[501.V2 variant]], also known as 501.V2, 20H (V2),<ref name="who-update-22june" /> 20H/501Y.V2<ref name="who-update-8june" /> (formerly 20C/501Y.V2), 501Y.V2,<ref name="ECDC1">{{cite tech report |url=https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/covid-19-risk-assessment-spread-new-variants-concern-eueea-first-update |title=Risk related to the spread of new SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern in the EU/EEA – first update |date=2 February 2021 |access-date=22 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210325174702/https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/covid-19-risk-assessment-spread-new-variants-concern-eueea-first-update |url-status=live |archive-date=25 March 2021 |type=Risk assessment |institution=European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control}}</ref> VOC-20DEC-02 (formerly <abbr>VOC</abbr>-202012/02), or lineage B.1.351,<ref name=":33" /> was first detected in [[South Africa]] and reported by the country's [[Department of Health (South Africa)|health department]].<ref name="nytimes">{{cite web |date=18 December 2020 |title=South Africa announces a new coronavirus variant |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/19/world/south-africa-announces-a-new-coronavirus-variant.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221073359/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/19/world/south-africa-announces-a-new-coronavirus-variant.html |archive-date=21 December 2020 |access-date=20 December 2020 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> It has been labelled as Beta variant by WHO. Researchers and officials reported that the prevalence of the variant was higher among young people with no underlying health conditions, and by comparison with other variants it is more frequently resulting in serious illness in those cases.<ref name="post">{{cite news |date=18 December 2020 |title=South Africa coronavirus: Second wave fueled by new strain, teen 'rage festivals' |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/africa/south-africa-coronavirus-second-wave/2020/12/18/d4a51aec-3ff7-11eb-b58b-1623f6267960_story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201227073826/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/africa/south-africa-coronavirus-second-wave/2020/12/18/d4a51aec-3ff7-11eb-b58b-1623f6267960_story.html |archive-date=27 December 2020 |access-date=20 December 2020 |newspaper=The Washington Post |vauthors=Wroughton L, Bearak M}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |title=Update on Covid-19 (18th December 2020) |date=18 December 2020 |location=South Africa |url=https://sacoronavirus.co.za/2020/12/18/update-on-covid-19-18th-december-2020/ |quote=Our clinicians have also warned us that things have changed and that younger, previously healthy people are now becoming very sick. |access-date=23 December 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504151326/https://sacoronavirus.co.za/2020/12/18/update-on-covid-19-18th-december-2020/ |archive-date=4 May 2021 |vauthors=Mkhize Z |agency=COVID-19 South African Online Portal}}</ref> The South African health department also indicated that the variant may be driving the second wave of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa|COVID-19 epidemic in the country]] due to the variant spreading at a more rapid pace than other earlier variants of the virus.<ref name="nytimes" /><ref name="post" />

Scientists noted that the variant contains several mutations that allow it to attach more easily to human cells because of the following three mutations in the [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2#Structural biology|receptor-binding domain]] (RBD) in the [[coronavirus spike protein|spike glycoprotein]] of the virus: [[#N501Y|N501Y]],<ref name="nytimes" /><ref>{{cite web |author=Abdool Karim |first=Salim S. |date=19 December 2020 |title=The 2nd Covid-19 wave in South Africa:Transmissibility & a 501.V2 variant, 11th slide |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/488618010/Full-Presentation-by-SSAK-18-Dec |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210106143155/https://www.scribd.com/document/488618010/Full-Presentation-by-SSAK-18-Dec |archive-date=6 January 2021 |access-date=23 December 2020 |publisher=www.scribd.com}}</ref> K417N, and [[#E484K|E484K]].<ref name="Lowe">{{cite web |date=22 December 2020 |title=The New Mutations |url=https://www.science.org/content/blog-post/new-mutations |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210129073128/https://blogs.sciencemag.org/pipeline/archives/2020/12/22/the-new-mutations |archive-date=29 January 2021 |access-date=23 December 2020 |website=In the Pipeline |publisher=[[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] |quote=I should note here that there's another strain in South Africa that is bringing on similar concerns. This one has eight mutations in the Spike protein, with three of them (K417N, E484K and N501Y) that may have some functional role. |vauthors=Lowe D}}</ref><ref name="WhoCOMVariants">{{cite web |date=22 December 2020 |title=Statement of the WHO Working Group on COVID-19 Animal Models (WHO-COM) about the UK and South African SARS-CoV-2 new variants |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/blue-print/who-com-statement_new-variant_rev1.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504151202/https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/blue-print/who-com-statement_new-variant_rev1.pdf |archive-date=4 May 2021 |access-date=23 December 2020 |publisher=World Health Organization}}</ref> The N501Y mutation has also been detected in the United Kingdom.<ref name="nytimes" /><ref>{{cite press release |title=Novel mutation combination in spike receptor binding site |date=21 December 2020 |publisher=[[GISAID]] |url=https://www.gisaid.org/references/gisaid-in-the-news/novel-mutation-combination-in-spike-receptor-binding-site/ |access-date=23 December 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222193121/https://www.gisaid.org/references/gisaid-in-the-news/novel-variant-combination-in-spike-receptor-binding-site/ |archive-date=22 February 2021 |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->}}</ref>

On 16 March 2022, the WHO has de-escalated the Beta variant and its subvariants to "previously circulating variants of concern".<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":9" />

==== Gamma (lineage P.1) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant}}

The Gamma variant or lineage P.1, termed Variant of Concern 21JAN-02<ref name="phe-voc" /> (formerly VOC-202101/02) by Public Health England,<ref name="phe-voc" /> 20J (V3)<ref name="who-update-22june" /> or 20J/501Y.V3<ref name="who-update-8june" /> by [[Nextstrain]], or just 501Y.V3,<ref name="b117e484k" /> was detected in Tokyo on 6 January 2021 by the National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID). It has been labelled as Gamma variant by WHO. The new variant was first identified in four people who arrived in Tokyo having travelled from the Brazilian [[Amazonas (Brazilian state)|Amazonas state]] on 2 January 2021.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=11 January 2021 |title=Japan finds new coronavirus variant in travelers from Brazil |url=https://japantoday.com/category/national/corrected-update-3-japan-finds-new-coronavirus-variant-in-travellers-from-brazil |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111105845/https://japantoday.com/category/national/corrected-update-3-japan-finds-new-coronavirus-variant-in-travellers-from-brazil |archive-date=11 January 2021 |access-date=14 January 2021 |work=[[Japan Today]] |location=Japan}}</ref> On 12 January 2021, the [https://www.caddecentre.org/ Brazil-UK CADDE Centre] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200722142850/https://www.caddecentre.org/ |date=22 July 2020 }} confirmed 13 local cases of the new Gamma variant in the Amazon rainforest.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |date=12 January 2021 |title=Genomic characterisation of an emergent SARS-CoV-2 lineage in Manaus: preliminary findings |url=https://virological.org/t/genomic-characterisation-of-an-emergent-sars-cov-2-lineage-in-manaus-preliminary-findings/586 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210520082806/https://virological.org/t/genomic-characterisation-of-an-emergent-sars-cov-2-lineage-in-manaus-preliminary-findings/586 |archive-date=20 May 2021 |access-date=23 January 2021 |website=virological.org |vauthors=Faria NR, Claro IM, Candido D, Moyses Franco LA, Andrade PS, Coletti TM, Silva CA, Sales FC, Manuli ER, Aguiar RS, Gaburo |department=CADDE Genomic Network}}</ref> This variant of SARS-CoV-2 has been named lineage P.1 (although it is a descendant of B.1.1.28, the name B.1.1.28.1<ref name="aci-variants" /><ref name="GR-P1">{{cite web |date=1 July 2021 |title=P.1 |url=https://cov-lineages.org/global_report_P.1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609174826/https://cov-lineages.org/global_report_P.1.html |archive-date=9 June 2021 |access-date=7 March 2021 |website=cov-lineages.org |publisher=[[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|Pango]] team}}</ref> is not permitted and thus the resultant name is P.1), and has 17 unique amino acid changes, 10 of which in its spike protein, including the three concerning mutations: [[#N501Y|N501Y]], [[#E484K|E484K]] and K417T.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="GR-P1" /><ref name="C1b">{{cite web |date=15 January 2021 |title=COG-UK Report on SARS-CoV-2 Spike mutations of interest in the UK |url=https://www.cogconsortium.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Report-2_COG-UK_SARS-CoV-2-Mutations.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416040009/https://www.cogconsortium.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Report-2_COG-UK_SARS-CoV-2-Mutations.pdf |archive-date=16 April 2021 |access-date=25 January 2021 |website=www.cogconsortium.uk |publisher=Covid-19 Genomics UK Consortium}}</ref><ref name="Voloch_2020">{{cite journal |vauthors=Voloch CM, da Silva Francisco R, de Almeida LG, Cardoso CC, Brustolini OJ, Gerber AL, Guimarães AP, Mariani D, da Costa RM, Ferreira OC, Frauches TS, de Mello CM, Leitão IC, Galliez RM, Faffe DS, Castiñeiras TM, Tanuri A, de Vasconcelos AT |date=March 2021 |title=Genomic characterization of a novel SARS-CoV-2 lineage from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil |journal=Journal of Virology |volume=95 |issue=10 |article-number=e00119-21 |doi=10.1128/jvi.00119-21 |pmc=8139668 |pmid=33649194 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|Figure 5}}

The N501Y and E484K mutations favour the formation of a stable RBD-hACE2 complex, thus, enhancing the binding affinity of RBD to hACE2. However, the K417T mutation disfavours complex formation between RBD and hACE2, which has been demonstrated to reduce the binding affinity.<ref name="SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern" />

The new variant was absent in samples collected from March to November 2020 in [[Manaus]], Amazonas state, but it was detected for the same city in 42% of the samples from 15 to 23 December 2020, followed by 52.2% during 15–31 December and 85.4% during 1–9 January 2021.<ref name=":1" /> A study found that infections by Gamma can produce nearly ten times more viral load compared to persons infected by one of the other lineages identified in Brazil (B.1.1.28 or B.1.195). Gamma also showed 2.2 times higher transmissibility with the same ability to infect both adults and older persons, suggesting P.1 and P.1-like lineages are more successful at infecting younger humans irrespective of sex.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naveca |first1=Felipe Gomes |last2=Nascimento |first2=Valdinete |last3=De Souza |first3=Victor Costa |last4=Corado |first4=André de Lima |last5=Nascimento |first5=Fernanda |last6=Silva |first6=George |last7=Costa |first7=Ágatha |last8=Duarte |first8=Débora |last9=Pessoa |first9=Karina |last10=Mejía |first10=Matilde |last11=Brandão |first11=Maria Júlia |last12=Jesus |first12=Michele |last13=Gonçalves |first13=Luciana |last14=Da Costa |first14=Cristiano Fernandes |last15=Sampaio |first15=Vanderson |date=2021 |title=COVID-19 in Amazonas, Brazil, was driven by the persistence of endemic lineages and P.1 emergence |url=https://www.arca.fiocruz.br/handle/icict/47834 |journal=Nature Medicine |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=1230–1238 |doi=10.1038/s41591-021-01378-7 |pmid=34035535 |id={{doi-inline|10.21203/rs.3.rs-275494|Preprint}} |last16=Barros |first16=Daniel |last17=Silva |first17=Marineide |last18=Mattos |first18=Tirza |last19=Pontes |first19=Gemilson |last20=Abdalla |first20=Ligia |last21=Santos |first21=João Hugo |last22=Arantes |first22=Ighor |last23=Dezordi |first23=Filipe Zimmer |last24=Siqueira |first24=Marilda Mendonça |last25=Wallau |first25=Gabriel Luz |last26=Resende |first26=Paola Cristina |last27=Delatorre |first27=Edson |last28=Gräf |first28=Tiago |last29=Bello |first29=Gonzalo}}</ref>

A study of samples collected in Manaus between November 2020 and January 2021, indicated that the Gamma variant is 1.4–2.2 times more transmissible and was shown to be capable of evading 25–61% of inherited immunity from previous coronavirus diseases, leading to the possibility of [[Coronavirus disease 2019#Immunity|reinfection]] after recovery from an earlier COVID-19 infection. As for the fatality ratio, infections by Gamma were also found to be 10–80% more lethal.<ref name="cadde-p1">{{cite journal |last1=Faria |first1=Nuno R. |last2=Mellan |first2=Thomas A. |last3=Whittaker |first3=Charles |last4=Claro |first4=Ingra M. |last5=Candido |first5=Darlan da S. |last6=Mishra |first6=Swapnil |last7=Crispim |first7=Myuki A. A study found that people fully vaccinated with [[Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine|Pfizer]] or [[Moderna COVID-19 vaccine|Moderna]] have significantly decreased [[neutralizing antibody|neutralisation]] effect against Gamma, although the actual impact on the course of the disease is uncertain.

==== Delta (lineage B.1.617.2) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant}}

The Delta variant, also known as B.1.617.2, G/452R.V3, 21A<ref name="who-update-22june" /> or 21A/S:478K,<ref name="who-update-8june" /> was a globally dominant variant that spread to at least 185 countries.<ref>{{cite web |date=22 September 2021 |title=Delta Globally Dominant Covid Strain, Now Spread To 185 Countries: WHO |url=https://www.india.com/news/world/delta-globally-dominant-covid-strain-now-spread-to-185-countries-who-4974794/ |access-date=23 September 2021 |archive-date=22 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211222014039/https://www.india.com/news/world/delta-globally-dominant-covid-strain-now-spread-to-185-countries-who-4974794/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It was first discovered in [[India]]. Descendant of lineage B.1.617, which also includes the Kappa variant under investigation, it was first discovered in October 2020 and has since spread internationally.<ref>{{cite web |title=PANGO lineages |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.617.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603085048/https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.617.html |archive-date=3 June 2021 |access-date=18 April 2021 |website=cov-lineages.org}}</ref><ref name="Koshy">{{cite news |date=8 April 2021 |title=Coronavirus {{!}} Indian 'double mutant' strain named E484Q.

On 3 June 2021, Public Health England reported that twelve of the 42 deaths from the Delta variant in England were among the fully vaccinated, and that it was spreading almost twice as fast as the Alpha variant.<ref>{{cite tech report |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/991343/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_14.pdf |title=SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants under investigation in England, technical briefing 14 |date=3 June 2021 |access-date=26 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210704205416/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/991343/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_14.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=4 July 2021 |format=PDF |type=Briefing |id=GOV-8530 |institution=Public Health England}}</ref> Also on 11 June, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary, Canada reported that half of their 22 cases of the Delta variant occurred among the fully vaccinated.<ref>{{cite news |date=11 June 2021 |title=AHS breaks down vaccination data of COVID-19 Delta variant outbreak at Calgary hospital |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/7943610/calgary-foothills-hospital-covid-19-delta-outbreak-vaccinations/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210612051503/https://globalnews.ca/news/7943610/calgary-foothills-hospital-covid-19-delta-outbreak-vaccinations/ |archive-date=12 June 2021 |access-date=12 June 2021 |work=Global News |vauthors=Pearson H, Pullen L, Dao C}}</ref>

In June 2021, reports began to appear of a variant of Delta with the K417N mutation.<ref>{{cite news |date=4 June 2021 |title='Nepal variant': What's the mutation stopping green list trips to Portugal? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-57356109 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210619162008/https://www.bbc.com/news/health-57356109 |archive-date=19 June 2021 |access-date=18 June 2021 |work=BBC News |vauthors=Schraer R}}</ref> The mutation, also present in the Beta and Gamma variants, raised concerns about the possibility of reduced effectiveness of vaccines and antibody treatments and increased risk of reinfection.<ref>{{cite news |date=23 June 2021 |title=Explainer: What is the Delta variant of coronavirus with K417N mutation? |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/what-is-delta-variant-coronavirus-with-k417n-mutation-2021-06-23/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623101838/https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/what-is-delta-variant-coronavirus-with-k417n-mutation-2021-06-23/ |archive-date=23 June 2021 |access-date=23 June 2021 |work=Reuters |vauthors=Acharya B, Jamkhandikar S}}</ref> The variant, called "Delta with K417N" by Public Health England, includes two clades corresponding to the Pango lineages AY.1 and AY.2.<ref name="briefing17">{{cite tech report |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/996740/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_17.pdf |title=SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants under investigation in England, technical briefing 17 |date=25 June 2021 |access-date=26 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625212314/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/996740/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_17.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=25 June 2021 |format=PDF |type=Briefing |id=GOV-8576 |institution=Public Health England}}</ref> It has been nicknamed "Delta plus"<ref>{{cite web |date=14 June 2021 |title=New 'Delta Plus' variant of SARS-CoV-2 identified; here's what we know so far |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/coronavirus-outbreak/story/delta-plus-variant-covid-corona-coronavirus-sarscov2-1814768-2021-06-14 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210617134931/https://www.indiatoday.in/coronavirus-outbreak/story/delta-plus-variant-covid-corona-coronavirus-sarscov2-1814768-2021-06-14 |archive-date=17 June 2021 |access-date=16 June 2021 |website=India Today |language=en |vauthors=Sharma M}}</ref> from "Delta plus K417N".<ref>{{cite news |date=18 June 2021 |title='Nepal variant': what we've learned so far |url=https://theconversation.com/nepal-variant-what-weve-learned-so-far-162227 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210618153113/https://theconversation.com/nepal-variant-what-weve-learned-so-far-162227 |archive-date=18 June 2021 |access-date=18 June 2021 |work=The Conversation |vauthors=Cutler S}}</ref> The name of the mutation, K417N, refers to an exchange whereby [[lysine]] (K) is replaced by [[asparagine]] (N) at position 417.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Julian W. |last2=Oliver |first2=T.R. |date=2021 |title=Introduction of the South African SARS-CoV-2 variant 501Y.V2 into the UK |journal=The Journal of Infection |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=e8–e10 |doi=10.1016/j.jinf.2021.01.007 |pmc=7813514 |pmid=33472093}}</ref> On 22 June, India's [[Ministry of Health and Family Welfare]] declared the "Delta plus" variant of COVID-19 a variant of concern, after 22 cases of the variant were reported in India.<ref>{{cite news |date=22 June 2021 |title=India says new COVID variant is a concern |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-reports-42640-new-covid-19-cases-1167-deaths-2021-06-22/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623002010/https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-reports-42640-new-covid-19-cases-1167-deaths-2021-06-22/ |archive-date=23 June 2021 |access-date=23 June 2021 |work=Reuters |location=Bengaluru}}</ref> After the announcement, leading virologists said there was insufficient data to support labelling the variant as a distinct variant of concern, pointing to the small number of patients studied.<ref>{{cite news |date=23 June 2021 |title=Delta plus: Scientists say too early to tell risk of Covid-19 variant |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-57564560 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623050608/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-57564560 |archive-date=23 June 2021 |access-date=23 June 2021 |work=BBC News |vauthors=Biswas S}}</ref> In the UK in July 2021, AY.4.2 was identified. Alongside those previously mentioned it also gained the nickname 'Delta Plus', on the strength of its extra mutations, Y145H and A222V. These are not unique to it, but distinguish it from the original Delta variant.<ref>{{cite web |last=Roberts |first=Michelle |date=19 October 2021 |title=Covid-19: New mutation of Delta variant under close watch in UK |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-58965650 |access-date=19 October 2021 |work=www.bbc.co.uk |archive-date=20 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211220180015/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-58965650 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 7 June 2022, the WHO has de-escalated the Delta variant and its subvariants to "previously circulating variants of concern".<ref name=":9" /><ref>{{cite web |date=2022-06-07 |title=Tracking SARS-CoV-2 variants |url=https://www.who.int/activities/tracking-SARS-CoV-2-variants |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220622021003/https://www.who.int/en/activities/tracking-SARS-CoV-2-variants/ |archive-date=2022-06-22 |access-date=2022-06-23 |website=www.who.int |language=en}}</ref>
