==== <span class="anchor" id="B.1.429"></span><span class="anchor" id="CAL.20C"></span><span class="anchor" id="Epsilon"></span>Epsilon (lineages B.1.429, B.1.427, CAL.20C) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Epsilon variant}}

The Epsilon variant or lineage B.1.429, also known as CAL.20C<ref name="B.1.429 other names">{{cite news |date=11 February 2021 |title=Southern California COVID-19 Strain Rapidly Expands Global Reach |url=https://www.cedars-sinai.org/newsroom/southern-california-covid-19-strain-rapidly-expands-global-reach/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416012748/https://www.cedars-sinai.org/newsroom/southern-california-covid-19-strain-rapidly-expands-global-reach/ |archive-date=16 April 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021 |work=[[Cedars-Sinai Medical Center|Cedars-Sinai]] Newsroom |location=[[Los Angeles]]}}</ref> or CA{{nbsp}}VUI1,<ref>{{cite web |title=B.1.429 Lineage Report |url=https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?pango=B.1.429&loc=USA&loc=USA_US-CA&selected=USA_US-CA |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210703013524/https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?pango=B.1.429&loc=USA&loc=USA_US-CA&selected=USA_US-CA |archive-date=3 July 2021 |access-date=28 May 2021 |work=outbreak.info |vauthors=Latif AA, Mullen JL, Alkuzweny M, Tsueng G, Cano M, Haag E, Zhou J, Zeller M, Matteson N, Wu C, Andersen KG, Su AI, Gangavarapu K, Hughes LD |collaboration=The Center for Viral Systems Biology}}</ref> 21C<ref name="who-update-22june" /> or 20C/S:452R,<ref name="who-update-8june" /> is defined by five distinct mutations (I4205V and D1183Y in the [[ORF1ab]] gene, and S13I, W152C, L452R in the spike protein's S-gene), of which the L452R (previously also detected in other unrelated lineages) was of particular concern.<ref name="SoCalLetter" /><ref name="New York Times CAL.20C">{{cite news |date=19 January 2021 |title=New California Variant May Be Driving Virus Surge There, Study Suggests |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/01/19/health/coronavirus-variant-california.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609201341/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/01/19/health/coronavirus-variant-california.html |archive-date=9 June 2021 |access-date=20 January 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> From 17 March to 29 June 2021, the CDC listed B.1.429 and the related B.1.427 as "variants of concern".<ref name="20A_617" /><ref>{{cite news |date=17 March 2021 |title=Coronavirus strains first detected in California are officially 'variants of concern,' CDC says |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2021/03/17/health/california-variants-of-concern-cdc/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210606142729/https://edition.cnn.com/2021/03/17/health/california-variants-of-concern-cdc/index.html |archive-date=6 June 2021 |access-date=6 June 2021 |work=CNN |vauthors=Azad A}}</ref><ref name="pmid33826819">{{cite journal |vauthors=Shen X, Tang H, Pajon R, Smith G, Glenn GM, Shi W, Korber B, Montefiori DC |date=June 2021 |title=Neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 Variants B.1.429 and B.1.351 |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=384 |issue=24 |pages=2352–2354 |doi=10.1056/NEJMc2103740 |pmc=8063884 |pmid=33826819 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="cdc-variants-23June2021">{{cite web |date=23 June 2021 |title=SARS-CoV-2 Variant Classifications and Definitions: Updated June 23, 2021 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/variants/variant-info.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210629194456/https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/variants/variant-info.html |archive-date=29 June 2021 |website=CDC.gov |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}}</ref> As of July 2021, Epsilon is no longer considered a variant of interest by the WHO,<ref name="who-variants" /> as it was overtaken by Alpha.<ref name="NYTimes 17 May">{{cite news |date=14 May 2021 |title=How the United States Beat the Variants, for Now |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/14/health/coronavirus-variants-united-states-of-america.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210516211623/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/14/health/coronavirus-variants-united-states-of-america.html |archive-date=16 May 2021 |access-date=17 May 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |vauthors=Zimmer C, Mandavilli A}}</ref>

From September 2020 to January 2021, it was 19% to 24% more transmissible than earlier variants in California. Neutralisation against it by antibodies from natural infections and vaccinations was moderately reduced,<ref name="CaliNews">{{cite news |date=23 February 2021 |title=California coronavirus strain may be more infectious – and lethal |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/coronavirus-strain-first-identified-california-may-be-more-infectious-and-cause-more |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501092349/https://www.sciencemag.org/news/2021/02/coronavirus-strain-first-identified-california-may-be-more-infectious-and-cause-more |archive-date=1 May 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021 |work=[[Science (journal)|Science]] News |doi=10.1126/science.abh2101 |vauthors=Wadman M}}</ref> but it remained detectable in most diagnostic tests.<ref>{{cite news |date=28 February 2021 |title=Do coronavirus tests work on variants? |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/health/article/Do-coronavirus-tests-work-on-variants-15980646.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624212500/https://www.sfchronicle.com/health/article/Do-coronavirus-tests-work-on-variants-15980646.php |archive-date=24 June 2021 |access-date=24 June 2021 |work=San Francisco Chronicle |vauthors=Ho C}}</ref>

Epsilon (CAL.20C) was first observed in July 2020 by researchers at the [[Cedars-Sinai Medical Center]], [[California]], in one of 1,230 virus samples collected in [[Los Angeles County]] since the start of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in California|COVID-19 epidemic]].<ref name=":28">{{cite press release |title=Local COVID-19 Strain Found in Over One-Third of Los Angeles Patients |date=19 January 2021 |publisher=Cedars Sinai Medical Center |location=California |url=https://www.newswise.com/coronavirus/local-covid-19-strain-found-in-over-one-third-of-los-angeles-patients2 |access-date=3 March 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613110049/https://www.newswise.com/coronavirus/local-covid-19-strain-found-in-over-one-third-of-los-angeles-patients2 |archive-date=13 June 2021 |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |website=news wise}}</ref> It was not detected again until September when it reappeared among samples in California, but numbers remained very low until November.<ref name="Pango B.1.429">{{cite web |date=15 February 2021 |title=B.1.429 |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.429.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428155149/https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.429.html |archive-date=28 April 2021 |access-date=16 February 2021 |work=Rambaut Group, University of Edinburgh |publisher=PANGO Lineages}}</ref><ref name="OB B.1.429">{{cite web |date=15 February 2021 |title=B.1.429 Lineage Report |url=https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?country=United%20States%20of%20America&division=California&pango=B.1.429&selected=California&selectedType=division |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609094343/https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?country=United%20States%20of%20America&division=California&pango=B.1.429&selected=California&selectedType=division |archive-date=9 June 2021 |access-date=16 February 2021 |work=[[Scripps Research]] |publisher=outbreak.info}}</ref> In November 2020, the Epsilon variant accounted for 36 per cent of samples collected at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and by January 2021, the Epsilon variant accounted for 50 per cent of samples.<ref name="New York Times CAL.20C" /> In a joint press release by [[University of California, San Francisco]], [[California Department of Public Health]], and [[Santa Clara County Public Health Department]],<ref>{{cite web |title=COVID-19 Variant First Found in Other Countries and States Now Seen More Frequently in California |url=https://www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/OPA/Pages/NR21-020.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210616204152/https://www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/OPA/Pages/NR21-020.aspx |archive-date=16 June 2021 |access-date=30 January 2021 |website=California Department of Public Health}}</ref> the variant was also detected in multiple counties in Northern California. From November to December 2020, the frequency of the variant in sequenced cases from Northern California rose from 3% to 25%.<ref>{{cite web |title=New strains of COVID swiftly moving through the US need careful watch, scientists say |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2021/01/22/covid-new-virus-mutations-but-vaccines-fight-outbreak/4216815001/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304154958/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2021/01/22/covid-new-virus-mutations-but-vaccines-fight-outbreak/4216815001/ |archive-date=4 March 2021 |access-date=30 January 2021 |website=USA Today |language=en-US |vauthors=Weise E, Weintraub K}}</ref> In a preprint, CAL.20C is described as belonging to clade 20C and contributing approximately 36% of samples, while an emerging variant from the 20G clade accounts for some 24% of the samples in a study focused on Southern California. Note, however, that in the US as a whole, the 20G&nbsp;clade predominates, as of January 2021.<ref name="SoCalLetter" /> Following the increasing numbers of Epsilon in California, the variant has been detected at varying frequencies in most US states. Small numbers have been detected in other countries in North America, and in Europe, Asia and Australia.<ref name="Pango B.1.429" /><ref name="OB B.1.429" /> After an initial increase, its frequency rapidly dropped from February 2021 as it was being outcompeted by the more transmissible [[SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant|Alpha]]. In April, Epsilon remained relatively frequent in parts of northern California, but it had virtually disappeared from the south of the state and had never been able to establish a foothold elsewhere; only 3.2% of all cases in the United States were Epsilon, whereas more than two-thirds were Alpha.<ref name="NYTimes 17 May" />

==== <span class="anchor" id="P.2"></span><span class="anchor" id="Zeta"></span>Zeta (lineage P.2) ====
{{excerpt|SARS-CoV-2 Zeta variant|only=paragraphs|paragraph=2}}

==== <span class="anchor" id="B.1.525"></span><span class="anchor" id="Eta"></span>Eta (lineage B.1.525) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Eta variant}}

The Eta variant or lineage B.1.525, also called <abbr>VUI</abbr>-21FEB-03<ref name="phe-voc" /> (previously VUI-202102/03) by Public Health England (PHE) and formerly known as UK1188,<ref name="phe-voc" /> 21D<ref name="who-update-22june" /> or 20A/S:484K,<ref name="who-update-8june" /> does not carry the same N501Y mutation found in [[SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant|Alpha]], [[SARS-CoV-2 Beta variant|Beta]] and [[SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant|Gamma]], but carries the same E484K-mutation as found in the Gamma, Zeta, and Beta variants, and also carries the same ΔH69/ΔV70 deletion (a deletion of the amino acids [[histidine]] and [[valine]] in positions 69 and 70) as found in Alpha, N439K variant (B.1.141 and B.1.258) and Y453F variant ([[Cluster 5]]).<ref name="DeltaPCR">{{cite web |date=25 February 2021 |title=Delta-PCR-testen |trans-title=The Delta PCR Test |url=https://covid19.ssi.dk/diagnostik/delta-pcr-testen |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210207104212/https://covid19.ssi.dk/diagnostik/delta-pcr-testen |archive-date=7 February 2021 |access-date=27 February 2021 |publisher=Statens Serum Institut |language=Danish}}</ref> Eta differs from all other variants by having both the E484K-mutation and a new F888L mutation (a substitution of [[phenylalanine]] (F) with [[leucine]] (L) in the S2 domain of the spike protein). As of 5 March 2021, it had been detected in 23 countries.<ref name="GISAID">{{cite web |title=GISAID hCOV19 Variants (see menu option 'G/484K.V3 (B.1.525)') |url=https://www.gisaid.org/hcov19-variants/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623103745/https://www.gisaid.org/hcov19-variants/ |archive-date=23 June 2021 |access-date=4 March 2021 |website=GISAID}}</ref><ref name="DEN">{{cite web |date=27 February 2021 |title=Status for udvikling af SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern (VOC) i Danmark |trans-title=Status of development of SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern (VOC) in Denmark |url=https://files.ssi.dk/covid19/virusvarianter/status/status-virusvarianter-27022021-l9k7 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827180250/https://files.ssi.dk/covid19/virusvarianter/status/status-virusvarianter-27022021-l9k7 |archive-date=27 August 2021 |access-date=27 February 2021 |publisher=Statens Serum Institut |language=Danish}}</ref><ref name="Pango B.1.525">{{cite web |date=19 May 2021 |title=B.1.525 international lineage report |url=https://cov-lineages.org/global_report_B.1.525.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609174829/https://cov-lineages.org/global_report_B.1.525.html |archive-date=9 June 2021 |access-date=16 February 2021 |website=cov-lineages.org |publisher=[[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|Pango]] team}}</ref> It has also been reported in [[Mayotte]], the [[Overseas department and region|overseas department/region]] of France.<ref name="GISAID" /> The first cases were detected in December 2020 in the UK and Nigeria, and as of 15 February 2021, it had occurred in the highest frequency among samples in the latter country.<ref name="Pango B.1.525" /> As of 24 February 56 cases were found in the UK.<ref name="phe-voc" /> Denmark, which sequences all its COVID-19 cases, found 113 cases of this variant from 14 January to 21 February 2021, of which seven were directly related to foreign travel to Nigeria.<ref name="DEN" />

As of July 2021, UK experts are studying it to ascertain how much of a risk it could be. It was then regarded as a "variant under investigation", but pending further study, it was anticipated to possibly become a "[[variant of concern]]". [[Ravindra Gupta|Ravi Gupta]], from the [[University of Cambridge]] said in a [[BBC News|BBC]] interview that lineage B.1.525 appeared to have "significant mutations" already seen in some of the other newer variants, which means their likely effect is to some extent more predictable.<ref name="UK">{{cite news |date=16 February 2021 |title=Another new coronavirus variant seen in the UK |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-56082573 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210620152732/https://www.bbc.com/news/health-56082573 |archive-date=20 June 2021 |access-date=16 February 2021 |work=BBC News |vauthors=Roberts M}}</ref>

==== Theta (lineage P.3) ====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 Theta variant}}

On 18 February 2021, the [[Department of Health (Philippines)|Department of Health]] of the Philippines confirmed the detection of two mutations of COVID-19 in [[Central Visayas]] after samples from patients were sent to undergo genome sequencing. The mutations were later named as E484K and N501Y, which were detected in 37 out of 50 samples, with both mutations co-occurrent in 29 out of these.<ref>{{cite web |date=18 February 2021 |title=DOH confirms detection of 2 SARS-CoV-2 mutations in Region 7 |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/02/18/21/doh-to-investigate-2-mutations-of-concern-found-in-cebu |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503224212/https://news.abs-cbn.com/news/02/18/21/doh-to-investigate-2-mutations-of-concern-found-in-cebu |archive-date=3 May 2021 |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=ABS-CBN News |language=en}}</ref>

On 13 March, the Department of Health confirmed the mutations constitutes a variant which was designated as lineage P.3.<ref>{{cite news |date=13 March 2021 |title=DOH reports COVID-19 variant 'unique' to PH, first case of Brazil variant |url=https://cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/Philippines-new-COVID-19-variant-Brazil-UK-South-Africa.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210316224353/https://cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/Philippines-new-COVID-19-variant-Brazil-UK-South-Africa.html |archive-date=16 March 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021 |work=CNN Philippines |vauthors=Santos E}}</ref> On the same day, it also confirmed the first COVID-19 case caused by the [[SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant|Gamma variant]] in the country. The Philippines had 98 cases of the Theta variant on 13 March.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |date=13 March 2021 |title=DOH confirms new COVID-19 variant first detected in PH, first case of Brazil variant |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/03/13/21/doh-confirms-new-covid-19-variant-first-detected-in-ph-first-case-of-brazil-variant |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502100947/https://news.abs-cbn.com/news/03/13/21/doh-confirms-new-covid-19-variant-first-detected-in-ph-first-case-of-brazil-variant |archive-date=2 May 2021 |access-date=13 March 2021 |website=ABS-CBN News |language=en}}</ref> On 12 March it was announced that Theta had also been detected in Japan.<ref>{{cite news |date=13 March 2021 |title=PH discovered new COVID-19 variant earlier than Japan, expert clarifies |url=https://cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/PH-COVID-19-variant-Japan.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210317013626/https://www.cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/PH-COVID-19-variant-Japan.html |archive-date=17 March 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021 |work=CNN Philippines}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=13 March 2021 |title=Japan detects new coronavirus variant from traveler coming from PH |url=https://cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/Japan-detects-new-coronavirus-variant-from-traveler-coming-from-PH.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210316215007/https://cnnphilippines.com/news/2021/3/13/Japan-detects-new-coronavirus-variant-from-traveler-coming-from-PH.html |archive-date=16 March 2021 |access-date=21 March 2021 |work=CNN Philippines}}</ref> On 17 March, the United Kingdom confirmed its first two cases,<ref>{{cite news |date=17 March 2021 |title=UK reports 2 cases of COVID-19 variant first detected in Philippines |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/overseas/03/17/21/uk-reports-2-cases-of-covid-19-variant-first-detected-in-philippines |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210318044336/https://news.abs-cbn.com/overseas/03/17/21/uk-reports-2-cases-of-covid-19-variant-first-detected-in-philippines |archive-date=18 March 2021 |access-date=21 March 2021 |work=ABS-CBN}}</ref> where PHE termed it VUI-21MAR-02.<ref name="phe-voc" />
On 30 April 2021, Malaysia detected 8 cases of the Theta variant in Sarawak.<ref>{{cite web |date=30 April 2021 |title=Covid-19: Sarawak detects variant reported in the Philippines |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2021/04/30/covid-19-sarawak-detects-variant-reported-in-the-philippines |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501095348/https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2021/04/30/covid-19-sarawak-detects-variant-reported-in-the-philippines |archive-date=1 May 2021 |access-date=30 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

As of July 2021, Theta is no longer considered a variant of interest by the WHO.<ref name="who-variants" />

==Omicron==
{{further information|SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant}}<!-- Heavy excerpting in this article, be careful -->

=== Lineage B.1.1.529 ===
The Omicron variant, known as lineage B.1.1.529, was declared a variant of concern by the World Health Organization on 26 November 2021.<ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=Classification of Omicron (B.1.1.529): SARS-CoV-2 Variant of Concern |url=https://www.who.int/news/item/26-11-2021-classification-of-omicron-(b.1.1.529)-sars-cov-2-variant-of-concern |access-date=2021-11-26 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=26 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211126181619/https://www.who.int/news/item/26-11-2021-classification-of-omicron-(b.1.1.529)-sars-cov-2-variant-of-concern |url-status=live }}</ref>

The variant has a large number of [[mutation]]s, of which some are concerning. Some evidence shows that this variant has an increased risk of [[COVID-19 reinfection|reinfection]]. Studies are underway to evaluate the exact impact on transmissibility, mortality, and other factors.<ref name="nature-2021-11-25">{{cite journal |last1=Callaway |first1=Ewen |date=2 December 2021 |title=Heavily mutated Omicron variant puts scientists on alert |journal=Nature |volume=600 |issue=7887 |pages=21 |bibcode=2021Natur.600...21C |doi=10.1038/d41586-021-03552-w |pmid=34824381 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Named [[SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant|Omicron]] by the WHO,<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Fernando |first1=Michael James and Christine |title=World experts hold special meeting on worrying new COVID-19 variant in South Africa: Latest updates |url=https://eu.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2021/11/26/fast-spreading-and-mutating-covid-variant-south-africa-worrying-who-experts/8759122002/ |url-status=live }}</ref> it was identified in November 2021 in [[Botswana]] and [[South Africa]];<ref>{{cite web |title=outbreak.info |url=https://outbreak.info/situation-reports?pango&muts=s%3AS371L&loc=ZAF&loc=BWA&overlay=false |access-date=2021-11-26 |website=outbreak.info |language=en |archive-date=28 November 2021 === BA sublineages ===
According to the WHO, BA.1, BA.1.1, and BA.2 were the most common sublineages of Omicron globally {{as of|2022|02|lc=yes}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Statement on Omicron sublineage BA.2 |url=https://www.who.int/news/item/22-02-2022-statement-on-omicron-sublineage-ba.2 |access-date=2022-04-04 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=13 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313005023/https://www.who.int/news/item/22-02-2022-statement-on-omicron-sublineage-ba.2 |url-status=live }}</ref> BA.2 contains 28 unique genetic changes, including four in its spike protein, compared to BA.1, which had already acquired 60 mutations since the ancestral Wuhan strain, including 32 in the spike protein.<ref name=":7">{{cite web |last=Schmidt |first=Charles |title=What We Know About Omicron's BA.2 Variant So Far |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-we-know-about-omicrons-ba-2-variant-so-far1/ |access-date=2022-04-04 |website=Scientific American |language=en |archive-date=4 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220404155138/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-we-know-about-omicrons-ba-2-variant-so-far1/ |url-status=live }}</ref> BA.2 is more transmissible than BA.1.<ref name="ba2">{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=11 March 2022 |title=Covid infections rising again across UK - ONS |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-60709712 |work=BBC News |archive-date=13 March 2022 |access-date=11 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313191916/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-60709712 |url-status=live }}</ref> It was causing most cases in England by mid-March 2022, and by the end of March, BA.2 became dominant in the US.<ref name="usba2">{{cite news |author=Jessica Rendall |date=29 March 2022 |title=BA.2 is Now the Dominant COVID Variant in US, CDC Data Shows |url=https://www.cnet.com/health/medical/ba-2-is-now-the-dominant-covid-variant-in-us-cdc-data-shows/ |archive-date=30 March 2022 |access-date=31 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220330180302/https://www.cnet.com/health/medical/ba-2-is-now-the-dominant-covid-variant-in-us-cdc-data-shows/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":7" /> {{As of|2022|05}}, the sublineages BA.1 to BA.5 including all their descendants are classified as variants of concern by the WHO,<ref name="WHO21Nov" /> the CDC,<ref name="cdc-variants" /> and the [[European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control|ECDC]]<ref>{{cite web |last=ECDC |date=2022-05-12 |title=Changes to list of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern, variants of interest, and variants under monitoring |url=https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/Variants%20page%20changelog%20220513.pdf |access-date=25 May 2022 |archive-date=18 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220618025929/https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/Variants%20page%20changelog%20220513.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> (with the latter excluding BA.3).

=== XBB sublineages{{anchor|EG.5}} ===
During 2022, a number of further new strains emerged in different localities, including XBB.1.5, which evolved from a recombination of BJ.1 and BM.1.1.1, both descended from Omicron. The first case involving XBB in England was detected from a specimen sample taken on 10 September 2022 and further cases have since been identified in most English regions. By the end of the year, XBB.1.5 accounted for 40.5% of new cases across the US, and was the dominant strain; variant of concern BQ.1 was running at 18.3% and BQ.1.1 represented 26.9% of new cases, while the BA.5 strain was in decline, at 3.7%. At this stage, it was uncommon in many other countries, for example in the UK it was represented about 7% of new cases, according to UKHSA sequencing data.<ref name="MS">{{cite web |author=Peter Russell |date=6 January 2023 |title=Omicron XBB.1.5: What Do We Know So Far? |url=https://www.medscape.co.uk/viewarticle/omicron-xbb-1-5-what-do-we-know-so-far-2023a10000ak?uac=358469BK&faf=1&sso=true&impID=5065732&src=WNL_ukmdpls_230107_mscpedit_gen |access-date=8 January 2023 |work=Medscape |archive-date=14 April 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref> BQ.1 and BQ1.1 became known informally as "cerberus".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sanjuan |first1=Laura Martin |date=7 November 2022 |title=The reason why the new variant of covid-19 is called the Hound of Hades |url=https://en.as.com/latest_news/the-reason-why-the-new-variant-of-covid-19-is-called-the-hound-of-hades-n/ |access-date=11 January 2025 |website=AS USA |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scarpa |first1=Fabio |last2=Sanna |first2=Daria |last3=Benvenuto |first3=Domenico |last4=Borsetti |first4=Alessandra |last5=Azzena |first5=Ilenia |last6=Casu |first6=Marco |last7=Fiori |first7=Pier Luigi |last8=Giovanetti |first8=Marta |last9=Maruotti |first9=Antonello |last10=Ceccarelli |first10=Giancarlo |last11=Caruso |first11=Arnaldo |last12=Caccuri |first12=Francesca |last13=Cauda |first13=Roberto |last14=Cassone |first14=Antonio |last15=Pascarella |first15=Stefano |date=3 December 2022 |title=Genetic and Structural Data on the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BQ.1 Variant Reveal Its Low Potential for Epidemiological Expansion |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |volume=23 |issue=23 |article-number=15264 |doi=10.3390/ijms232315264 |pmc=9739521 |pmid=36499592 |doi-access=free |last16=Ciccozzi |first16=Massimo}}</ref>

On 22 December 2022, the European Centre for Disease Control wrote in a summary that XBB strains accounted for circa 6.5% of new cases in five EU countries with sufficient volume of sequencing or genotyping to provide estimates.<ref name="MS"/>

EG.5, a subvariant of XBB.1.9.2, (nicknamed "Eris" by some media<ref>{{cite web |last=Johnson |first=Arianna |title=What We Know About 'Eris' Covid Variant EG.5: The Dominant Strain Driving An Uptick In Cases |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/ariannajohnson/2023/08/10/what-we-know-about-eris-covid-variant-eg5-the-dominant-stain-driving-an-uptick-in-cases/ |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=Forbes |language=en |archive-date=23 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230823032627/https://www.forbes.com/sites/ariannajohnson/2023/08/10/what-we-know-about-eris-covid-variant-eg5-the-dominant-stain-driving-an-uptick-in-cases/ |url-status=live }}</ref>) emerged in February 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=cov-lineages.org |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineage_list.html |access-date=11 August 2023 |archive-date=27 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327093523/https://cov-lineages.org/lineage_list.html |url-status=live }}</ref> On 6{{nbsp}}August 2023, the UK Health Security Agency reported the EG.5 strain was responsible for one in seven new cases in the UK during the third week of July.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mundasad |first=Smitha |date=10 August 2023 |title=What we know about the Covid variant EG.5 dubbed 'Eris' |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-66461727 |access-date=10 August 2023 |work=BBC News |publisher=BBC |archive-date=18 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230918130247/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-66461727 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Lineage BA.2.86 ===
{{Main|BA.2.86}}
During 2023, SARS-CoV-2 continued to circulate in the global population and to evolve, with a number of new subvariants. Testing, sequencing and reporting rates reduced.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 December 2023 |title=SARS-CoV-2 genome sequence prevalence and growth rate update: 8 November 2023 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sars-cov-2-genome-sequence-prevalence-and-growth-rate/sars-cov-2-genome-sequence-prevalence-and-growth-rate-update-8-november-2023 |access-date=21 December 2023 |website=GOV.UK |language=en |archive-date=21 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231221105824/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sars-cov-2-genome-sequence-prevalence-and-growth-rate/sars-cov-2-genome-sequence-prevalence-and-growth-rate-update-8-november-2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[BA.2.86]] was first detected in a sample from 24{{nbsp}}July 2023, and was designated as a variant under monitoring by the World Health Organization on 17 August 2023.<ref>{{cite web |date=17 August 2023 |title=COVID-19 Weekly Epidemiological Update (Edition 156 published 17 August 2023) |url=https://reliefweb.int/attachments/7488fa08-d0aa-428b-9f60-0451dd102f3b/20230817_weekly_epi_update_156.pdf |access-date=30 August 2023 |publisher=World Health Organization |archive-date=16 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230916010451/https://reliefweb.int/attachments/7488fa08-d0aa-428b-9f60-0451dd102f3b/20230817_weekly_epi_update_156.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

JN.1 (sometimes referred to as "Pirola"), a subvariant of BA.2.86, emerged during August 2023 in Luxembourg. By December 2023, it had been detected in 12 countries, including the UK and US.<ref>{{cite web |date=8 December 2023 |title=Covid: Everything we know about the new Omicron descendant as winter flu surges |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/health/new-covid-variant-omicron-symptoms-b2460924.html |access-date=16 December 2023 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bartel |first1=Alexander |last2=Grau |first2=José Horacio |last3=Bitzegeio |first3=Julia |last4=Werber |first4=Dirk |last5=Linzner |first5=Nico |last6=Schumacher |first6=Vera |last7=Garske |first7=Sonja |last8=Liere |first8=Karsten |last9=Hackenbeck |first9=Thomas |last10=Rupp |first10=Sofia Isabell |last11=Sagebiel |first11=Daniel |last12=Böckelmann |first12=Uta |last13=Meixner |first13=Martin |date=10 January 2024 |title=Timely Monitoring of SARS-CoV-2 RNA Fragments in Wastewater Shows the Emergence of JN.1 (BA.2.86.1.1, Clade 23I) in Berlin, Germany |journal=Viruses |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=102 |doi=10.3390/v16010102 |pmc=10818819 |pmid=38257802 |doi-access=free}}</ref> On 19 December, JN.1 was declared by the WHO to be a variant of interest independently of its parent strain BA.2.86, but overall risk for public health was determined as low.<ref name="who-jn1">{{cite news |date=19 December 2023 |title=Initial Risk Evaluation of JN.1, 19 December 2023 |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/18122023_jn.1_ire_clean.pdf |access-date=11 January 2024 |publisher=World Health Organization}}</ref> With JN.1 accounting for some 60% of cases in Singapore, in December 2023, Singapore and Indonesia recommended wearing masks at airports.<ref>{{cite web |date=14 December 2023 |title=Return of the mask? Singapore, Indonesia bring back limits as Covid cases jump |url=https://www.livemint.com/news/world/singapore-government-implements-preventive-norms-for-travellers-amid-covid-scare-11702518104782.html |access-date=16 December 2023 |website=mint |language=en |archive-date=16 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231216075249/https://www.livemint.com/news/world/singapore-government-implements-preventive-norms-for-travellers-amid-covid-scare-11702518104782.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] estimated that the variant accounted for 44% of cases in the US on 22 December 2023 and 62% of cases on 5 January 2024.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 January 2024 |title=COVID-19 Activity Increases as Prevalence of JN.1 Variant Continues to Rise |url=https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/whats-new/JN.1-update-2023-12-22.html |access-date=11 January 2024 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |archive-date=11 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240111045709/https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/whats-new/JN.1-update-2023-12-22.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{As of|2024|02|09}}, JN.1 was estimated by the WHO to be the most prevalent variant of SARS-CoV-2 (70–90% prevalence in four out of six global regions; insufficient data in the East Mediterranean and African regions). The general level of population immunity and immunity from [[#XBB and XBB.1|XBB.1.5]] booster versions of the [[COVID-19 vaccine]] was expected to provide some protection (cross-reactivity) to JN.1.<ref name="WHO_updated_risk_evaluation_JN.1_20240209">{{cite Q |Q124477897 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Sublineages by year ===
<!-- Please add a Level-4 heading for new sub variants by year, to keep all excerpted articles updated! -->

==== 2024 ====
Late in April 2024, CDC data showed KP.2 to be the most common U.S. variant, with a quarter of all cases, just ahead of JN.1. KP1.1 represented 7 percent of U.S. cases.<ref>{{cite news |last=Leventis Lourgos |first=Angie |date=9 May 2024 |title=New COVID 'FLiRT' variants are spreading nationwide. Chicago health experts urge up to date vaccination |url=https://uk.news.yahoo.com/covid-flirt-variants-spreading-nationwide-171200824.html |access-date=14 May 2024 |work=[[Yahoo News]] |via=[[Chicago Tribune]]}}</ref>  These two are sometimes referred to as the 'FLiRT' variants because they are characterized by a [[phenylalanine]] (F) to [[leucine]] (L) mutation and an [[arginine]] (R) to [[threonine]] (T) mutation in the virus's spike protein.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kee |first=Caroline |date=2024-05-20 |title=The new COVID variants spreading in the US are called 'FLiRT.' But why? |url=https://www.today.com/health/coronavirus/new-covid-variant-flirt-name-meaning-rcna152650 |access-date=2024-05-29 |website=TODAY.com |archive-date=29 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529173032/https://www.today.com/health/coronavirus/new-covid-variant-flirt-name-meaning-rcna152650 |url-status=live }}</ref> By July 2024, a descendant of KP.2 with an extra amino acid change in the spike protein, Q493E, was given the names KP.3 and, informally, 'FLuQE,' and became a major variant in [[New South Wales]] during the Australian winter. Initial research suggested that the Q493E change could help KP.3 be more effective at binding to human cells than KP.2.<ref name="Conversation_FLiRT2FLuQE">{{cite Q |Q127329080 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Early in August 2024, XEC was discovered in Germany.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaku |first1=Yu |last2=Okumura |first2=Kaho |last3=Kawakubo |first3=Shusuke |last4=Uriu |first4=Keiya |last5=Chen |first5=Luo |last6=Kosugi |first6=Yusuke |last7=Uwamino |first7=Yoshifumi |last8=Begum |first8=MST Monira |last9=Leong |first9=Sharee |last10=Ikeda |first10=Terumasa |last11=Sadamasu |first11=Kenji |last12=Asakura |first12=Hiroyuki |last13=Nagashima |first13=Mami |last14=Yoshimura |first14=Kazuhisa |last15=Ito |first15=Jumpei |date=December 2024 |title=Virological characteristics of the SARS-CoV-2 XEC variant |journal=The Lancet Infectious Diseases |volume=24 |issue=12 |pages=e736 |doi=10.1016/S1473-3099(24)00731-X |pmid=39521009 |last16=Sato |first16=Kei}}</ref> XEC is a recombination of two subvariants: KS.1.1 and KP.3.3. In early December 2024, CDC data showed XEC to be the most common U.S. variant, with 45% of all cases, ahead of KP3.1.1, which accounted for 24% of all cases.<ref>{{cite web |title=3 Things to Know About XEC, the Dominant COVID Strain |url=https://www.yalemedicine.org/news/3-things-to-know-about-xec-the-latest-covid-strain |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=Yale Medicine |language=en |archive-date=24 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250724172603/https://www.yalemedicine.org/news/3-things-to-know-about-xec-the-latest-covid-strain |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== 2025 ====
Late in January 2025, XFG (sometimes referred to as "Stratus")<ref>{{cite news |date=12 August 2025 |title=What is new 'Stratus' Covid strain? Symptoms to look out for as UK cases grow |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/covid-symptoms-2025-stratus-new-variant-strain-xfg-b2805973.html |access-date=24 September 2025 |work=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> was discovered in Canada.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Caiwan |last2=Yu |first2=Yuanling |last3=Liu |first3=Jingyi |last4=Jian |first4=Fanchong |last5=Yang |first5=Sijie |last6=Song |first6=Weiliang |last7=Yu |first7=Lingling |last8=Shao |first8=Fei |last9=Cao |first9=Yunlong |date=July 2025 |title=Antigenic and virological characteristics of SARS-CoV-2 variants BA.3.2, XFG, and NB.1.8.1 |journal=The Lancet Infectious Diseases |volume=25 |issue=7 |pages=e374–e377 |doi=10.1016/S1473-3099(25)00308-1 |pmid=40484018}}</ref> XFG is a recombination of two subvariants: LF.7 and LP.8.1.2. In late May 2025, WHO reported that XFG was the 2nd most common variant globally, making up 22.7% of all global cases, behind NB.1.8.1 (named "Nimbus", often with extremely sore throat)<ref>{{cite news |date=19 June 2025 |title=What is new 'Nimbus' Covid variant? Symptoms as cases grow in UK |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/covid-new-variant-nimbus-nb-1-8-1-symptoms-cases-b2773272.html |access-date=24 September 2025 |work=The Independent |language=en |archive-date=17 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251017160843/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/covid-new-variant-nimbus-nb-1-8-1-symptoms-cases-b2773272.html |url-status=live }}</ref> with 24.9% of global cases, and closely followed by LP.8.1 accounting for 22.6% of global cases.<ref>{{cite web |title=WHO TAG-VE Risk Evaluation for SARS-CoV-2 Variant Under Monitoring: XFG |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/25062025_xfg_ire.pdf?sfvrsn=fab54cd7_1 |access-date=25 July 2025 |website=[[World Health Organization]]}}</ref> In late June 2025, CDC estimate data shows XFG to be the 3rd most common U.S. variant, with 14% of all cases, behind NB.1.8.1 and LP.8.1, which account for 43% and 31% of all cases respectively.{{citation needed|date=September 2025}}

On 14 September 2025, WHO listed JN.1 as a {{abbreviation|VOI|variant of interest}}; and KP.3.1.1, LP.8.1, NB.1.8.1, XEC, and XFG as {{abbreviation|VUM|variant under monitoring}}s. The estimated prevalence for the week ending 7 September 2025 was 68% for XFG (an increase compared to 61% for the week ending 10 August), 20% for NB.1.8.1 (a decrease compared to 24% for the week ending 10 August), and 4% or lower for the other four variants.<ref name="WHODashboard_20250914">{{cite Q |Q136406665}}</ref> In late September, the [[European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control|ECDC]] listed no {{abbreviation|VOC|variant of concern}}s, and listed BA.2.86 as a VOI, and NB.1.8.1 and XFG as VUMs.<ref name="ECDC_variants_concern_20250926">{{cite Q |Q136406441}}</ref>

==== 2026 ====
In late April, the ECDC again listed no VOCs, BA.2.86 as a VOI, and NB.1.8.1 and XFG as VUMs; and added BA.3.2, which had first been detected in South Africa in November 2024, as another VUM.<ref name="ECDC_variants_concern_20260426">{{cite Q|Q139683767}}</ref> In late August, the ECDC classification was unchanged from April, with no VOCs, BA.2.86 as a VOI, and NB.1.8.1, XFG, and BA.3.2 as VUMs.<ref name="ECDC_variants_concern_20260828">{{cite Q|Q141549442}}</ref> XFG was the dominant variant in the European area in both April<ref name="ECDC_variants_concern_20260426" /> and August.<ref name="ECDC_variants_concern_20260828" />

== Omicron variants under monitoring (WHO, 2022/2023) ==
On 25 May 2022, the World Health Organization introduced a new category for potentially concerning sublineages of widespread variants of concern, initially called VOC lineages under monitoring (VOC-LUMs). This decision was made to reflect that in February 2022, over 98% of all GISAID sequenced samples belonged to the Omicron family, within which much of the variants' evolution took place.<ref name="WHO_tracking_variants_20220529">{{cite Q |Q127329189}}</ref> By 9 February 2023, the category had been renamed as "Omicron variants under monitoring."<ref name="WHO_tracking_variants_20230211">{{cite Q |Q127329489}}</ref>

== Other notable variants ==
{{anchor|B.1.1.207}}Lineage B.1.1.207 was first sequenced in August 2020 in Nigeria;<ref name=":0">{{cite web |date=23 December 2020 |title=Detection of SARS-CoV-2 P681H Spike Protein Variant in Nigeria |url=https://virological.org/t/detection-of-sars-cov-2-p681h-spike-protein-variant-in-nigeria/567 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613184057/https://virological.org/t/detection-of-sars-cov-2-p681h-spike-protein-variant-in-nigeria/567 |archive-date=13 June 2021 |access-date=1 January 2021 |website=Virological |language=en-US}}</ref> the implications for [[transmission (medicine)|transmission]] and [[virulence]] are unclear but it has been listed as an emerging variant by the US [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control]].<ref name=":33" /> Sequenced by the African Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases in Nigeria, this variant has a P681H mutation, shared in common with the [[SARS-CoV-2 Alpha variant|Alpha variant]]. It shares no other mutations with the Alpha variant and as of late December 2020 this variant accounts for around 1% of viral genomes sequenced in Nigeria, though this may rise.<ref name=":0" /> As of May 2021, lineage B.1.1.207 has been detected in 10 countries.<ref name="pango-b-1-1-207">{{cite web |title=Lineage B.1.1.207 |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.1.207.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127172920/https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.1.207.html |archive-date=27 January 2021 |access-date=11 March 2021 |website=cov-lineages.org |publisher=[[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|Pango]] team}}</ref>

Lineage B.1.1.317, while not considered a [[variant of concern]], is noteworthy in that [[Queensland Health]] forced 2 people undertaking hotel quarantine in [[Brisbane]], Australia to undergo an additional 5 days' quarantine on top of the mandatory 14 days after it was confirmed they were infected with this variant.<ref>{{cite news |date=3 March 2021 |title=Queensland travellers have hotel quarantine extended after Russian variant of coronavirus detected |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-03-03/coronavirus-queensland-russian-variant-quarantine-qantas-flight/13191524 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210303020815/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-03-03/coronavirus-queensland-russian-variant-quarantine-qantas-flight/13191524 |archive-date=3 March 2021 |access-date=3 March 2021 |work=www.abc.net.au |language=en-AU}}</ref>

Lineage B.1.616, being identified in [[Brittany]], Western France in early January 2021<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Chaqroun A, Hartard C, Schvoerer E |date=18 June 2021 |title=Anti-SARS-CoV-2 Vaccines and Monoclonal Antibodies Facing Viral Variants |journal=Viruses |volume=13 |issue=6 |page=1171 |doi=10.3390/v13061171 |pmc=8234553 |pmid=34207378 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and designated by WHO as "Variant under investigation" in March 2021, was reported to be difficult to detect from [[nasopharyngeal swab]] sampling method of coronavirus detection, and detection of the virus needs to rely on samples from lower respiratory tract.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fillâtre P, Dufour MJ, Behillil S, Vatan R, Reusse P, Gabellec A, Velmans N, Montagne C, Geffroy Du Coudret S, Droumaguet E, Merour V, Enouf V, Buzelé R, Valence M, Guillotel E, Gagnière B, Baidaliuk A, Zhukova A, Tourdjman M, Thibault V, Grolhier C, Pronier C, Lescure FX, Simon-Loriere E, Costagliola D, Van Der Werf S, Tattevin P, Massart N |date=February 2022 |title=A new SARS-CoV-2 variant with high lethality poorly detected by RT-PCR on nasopharyngeal samples: an observational study |journal=Clin Microbiol Infect |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=298.e9–298.e15 |doi=10.1016/j.cmi.2021.09.035 |pmc=8496927 |pmid=34627988}}</ref>

{{anchor|B.1.618}}Lineage B.1.618 was first isolated in October 2020. It has the E484K mutation in common with several other variants, and showed significant spread in April 2021 in [[West Bengal]], India.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Koshy |first1=Jacob |date=21 April 2021 |title=New coronavirus variant found in West Bengal |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/health/new-coronavirus-variant-found-in-west-bengal/article34373083.ece |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526091411/https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/health/new-coronavirus-variant-found-in-west-bengal/article34373083.ece |archive-date=26 May 2021 |access-date=23 April 2021 |work=www.thehindu.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=22 April 2021 |title=What is the new 'triple mutant variant' of Covid-19 virus found in Bengal? How bad is it? |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/science/story/what-is-triple-mutant-variant-of-covid19-virus-bengal-strain-details-1793991-2021-04-22 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428055736/https://www.indiatoday.in/amp/science/story/what-is-triple-mutant-variant-of-covid19-virus-bengal-strain-details-1793991-2021-04-22 |archive-date=28 April 2021 |access-date=23 April 2021 |work=www.indiatoday.in}}</ref> As of 23 April 2021, the PANGOLIN database showed 135 sequences detected in India, with single-figure numbers in each of eight other countries worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |title=PANGO lineages Lineage B.1.618 |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.618.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514093826/https://cov-lineages.org/lineages/lineage_B.1.618.html |archive-date=14 May 2021 |access-date=23 April 2021 |work=cov-lineages.org}}</ref>

In July 2021,<!--https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.07.26.21261142v1.article-info--> scientists reported in a [[preprint]] which was published in a journal in February 2022, the detection of anomalous unnamed unknown-host SARS-CoV-2 lineages via [[wastewater surveillance]] in New York City. They hypothesized that "these lineages are derived from unsampled human COVID-19 infections or that they indicate the presence of a non-human [[COVID-19 pandemic and animals|animal reservoir]]".<ref>{{cite news |title=Detecting novel SARS-CoV-2 variants in New York City wastewater |url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2022-02-sars-cov-variants-york-city-wastewater.html |access-date=10 March 2022 |work=[[University of Missouri]] |language=en |archive-date=10 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220310165537/https://medicalxpress.com/news/2022-02-sars-cov-variants-york-city-wastewater.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="10.1038/s41467-022-28246-3">{{cite journal |last1=Smyth |first1=Davida S. |last2=Trujillo |first2=Monica |last3=Gregory |first3=Devon A. |last4=Cheung |first4=Kristen |last5=Gao |first5=Anna |last6=Graham |first6=Maddie |last7=Guan |first7=Yue |last8=Guldenpfennig |first8=Caitlyn |last9=Hoxie |first9=Irene |last10=Kannoly |first10=Sherin |last11=Kubota |first11=Nanami |last12=Lyddon |first12=Terri D. |last13=Markman |first13=Michelle |last14=Rushford |first14=Clayton |last15=San |first15=Kaung Myat |date=3 February 2022 |title=Tracking cryptic SARS-CoV-2 lineages detected in NYC wastewater |journal=Nature Communications |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=635 |bibcode=2022NatCo..13..635S |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-28246-3  |doi-access=free|pmc=8813986 |pmid=35115523 |last16=Sompanya |first16=Geena |last17=Spagnolo |first17=Fabrizio |last18=Suarez |first18=Reinier |last19=Teixeiro |first19=Emma |last20=Daniels |first20=Mark |last21=Johnson |first21=Marc C. |last22=Dennehy |first22=John J.}}</ref>

In March 2022, researchers reported SARS-CoV-2 variant [[recombinant virus]]es that contain elements of [[Delta variant|Delta]] and [[Omicron variant|Omicron]] – Deltacron (also called "Deltamicron").<ref>{{cite news |date=11 March 2022 |title=What is the Deltacron variant of Covid and where has it been found? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/mar/11/what-is-deltacron-covid-variant-uk |access-date=18 April 2022 |work=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426094252/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/mar/11/what-is-deltacron-covid-variant-uk |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lapid |first1=Nancy |date=9 March 2022 |title=Variant that combines Delta and Omicron identified; dogs sniff out virus with high accuracy |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/variant-that-combines-delta-omicron-identified-dogs-sniff-out-virus-with-high-2022-03-09/ |access-date=18 April 2022 |work=Reuters |language=en |archive-date=25 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220425135556/https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/variant-that-combines-delta-omicron-identified-dogs-sniff-out-virus-with-high-2022-03-09/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=COVID-19, Ukraine & Other Global Health Emergencies Virtual Press conference transcript - 16 March 2022 |url=https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/covid-19-ukraine-other-global-health-emergencies-virtual-press-conference-transcript---16-march-2022 |access-date=24 April 2022 |website=www.who.int |language=en |archive-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424203304/https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/covid-19-ukraine-other-global-health-emergencies-virtual-press-conference-transcript---16-march-2022 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Snider |first1=Mike |title=There may be a new COVID variant, Deltacron. In July 2023, Lawrence Young, a virologist at [[University of Warwick|Warwick University]] announced a super mutated [[SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant|Delta variant]] from a swab of an Indonesian case with 113 unique mutations, with 37 affecting the spike protein.<ref>{{cite web |last=Sundaravelu |first=Anugraha |date=28 July 2023 |title=Scientists find 'most mutated' and 'most extreme' Covid variant ever in patient |url=https://metro.co.uk/2023/07/28/most-mutated-covid-virus-spotted-by-scientists-in-indonesia-19210241/?ito=push-notification&ci=dWtYdXLH3j&cri=ozr-O749rG&si=mH5e9WE_MZib&xi=492afe45-44cc-4454-96ad-32dd10ceced3&ai=19210241 |access-date=28 July 2023 |publisher=[[Metro News]] |archive-date=28 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230728151110/https://metro.co.uk/2023/07/28/most-mutated-covid-virus-spotted-by-scientists-in-indonesia-19210241/?ito=push-notification&ci=dWtYdXLH3j&cri=ozr-O749rG&si=mH5e9WE_MZib&xi=492afe45-44cc-4454-96ad-32dd10ceced3&ai=19210241 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Between November 2023 and July 2024, an extremely mutated cryptic variant was identified in [[New Jersey]]. This variant had the strongest [[Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2|ACE2]] binding affinity out of any SARS-CoV-2 variant observed by far, had the most divergent spike protein profile observed to date, and it was also highly-resistant to every single antibody that researchers tested against it. The New Jersey cryptic variant had a sequence identity of just 80.6% compared to the ancestral Wuhan wildtype virus, the lowest observed in any COVID variant so far. The cryptic variant most likely originated from a B.1 lineage that predated the Omicron Variant, with the ancestral lineage circulating in 2021 or earlier, and it was unrelated to the B.1.1 lineage. This cryptic variant had 39 mutations in its spike protein's [[binding domain|Receptor Binding Domain]] (RBD) compared to the Wuhan wildtype virus; only four of the spike mutations (R403K, S477N, V483del, and Y505H) were present in other COVID VOCs and VOIs. Notably, 13 of the remaining RBD mutations had been observed in other cryptic COVID variants, as identified by wastewater sequencing. Three of the novel RBD mutations, S477N, Q493L, and G496N, were identified as likely contributing to the cryptic variant's high ACE2 binding affinity, which was 11.4 times stronger than the ancestral Wuhan RBD. Despite the variant's advantages, it had not circulated since mid-2024, and was presumed to be extinct.<ref name="NJ cryptic variant">{{cite medRxiv|title=A highly divergent cryptic SARS-CoV-2 lineage exhibits strong receptor binding and immune evasion|pages=|author1=Ziqi Feng|author2=Qi Wen Teo|author3=Barikisu A. Ibrahim|author4=Wenkan Liu|author5=Ding Zhang|author6=Kevin J. Mao|author7=Evan K. Shao|author8=Devon A. Gregory|author9=Ian A. Wilson|author10=Marc C. Johnson|author11=Meng Yuan|author12=Nicholas C. Wu|date=20 November 2025|medrxiv=10.1101/2025.11.18.25340485}}</ref>

== Recombinant variants ==
In 2022, the British government reported a number of recombinant variants of SARS-CoV-2.<ref name="Tech-Briefing-39-25March2022">{{cite web |date=25 March 2022 |title=SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants under investigation in England : Technical briefing 39 |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1063424/Tech-Briefing-39-25March2022_FINAL.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220404075240/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1063424/Tech-Briefing-39-25March2022_FINAL.pdf |archive-date=2022-04-04 |access-date=2022-04-06 |website=gov.uk |publisher=UK Health Security Agency}}</ref> These recombinant lineages have been given the Pango lineage identifiers XD, XE, and XF.<ref>{{cite web |date=2 March 2022 |title=COVID-19 Weekly Epidemiological Update : Edition 84, published 22 March 2022 |url=https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20220322_weekly_epi_update_84.pdf?sfvrsn=9ec904fc_8&download=true |access-date=2022-04-06 |website=who.int |publisher=World Health Organization |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325195103/https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20220322_weekly_epi_update_84.pdf?sfvrsn=9ec904fc_8&download=true |url-status=live }}</ref>

XE is a recombinant lineage of Pango lineages BA.1 and BA.2.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cov-Lineages |url=https://cov-lineages.org/lineage_list.html |access-date=2022-04-06 |website=cov-lineages.org |archive-date=27 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327093523/https://cov-lineages.org/lineage_list.html |url-status=live }}</ref> {{As of|2022|03}} XE was believed to have a growth rate 9.8% greater than BA.2.<ref name=Tech-Briefing-39-25March2022/>

== Incubation theory for multiple mutated variants ==
{{See also|Antigenic escape|Escape mutation}}
Researchers have suggested that multiple mutations can arise in the course of the persistent infection of an [[immunocompromised]] patient, particularly when the virus develops [[Antigenic escape|escape mutations]] under the [[selection pressure]] of antibody or [[convalescent plasma]] treatment,<ref>{{cite journal |date=29 March 2021 |title=U.K. variant puts spotlight on immunocompromised patients' role in the COVID-19 pandemic |journal=Science |doi=10.1126/science.abg2911}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=23 February 2021 |title=COVID Variants May Arise in People with Compromised Immune Systems |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/covid-variants-may-arise-in-people-with-compromised-immune-systems/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210606220535/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/covid-variants-may-arise-in-people-with-compromised-immune-systems/ |archive-date=6 June 2021 |access-date=25 February 2021 |work=Scientific American |vauthors=Sutherland S}}</ref> with the same deletions in surface antigens repeatedly recurring in different patients.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=McCarthy KR, Rennick LJ, Nambulli S, Robinson-McCarthy LR, Bain WG, Haidar G, Duprex WP |date=March 2021 |title=Recurrent deletions in the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein drive antibody escape |journal=Science |volume=371 |issue=6534 |pages=1139–1142 |bibcode=2021Sci...371.1139M |doi=10.1126/science.abf6950 |pmc=7971772 |pmid=33536258 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Notable missense mutations ==
There have been a number of [[missense mutation]]s observed of SARS-CoV-2.

=== del 69-70 ===
The name of the mutation, del 69-70, or 69-70 del, or other similar notations, refers to the deletion of amino acid at position 69 to 70. The mutation is found in the Alpha variant, and could lead to "spike gene target failure" and result in false negative result in PCR virus test.<ref>{{cite web |title=新型コロナウイルス変異株とは {{pipe}} 日本医学臨床検査研究所 |trans-title=What is the novel coronavirus mutation {{pipe}} Japan Medical Laboratory Laboratory |url=https://www.jcl.co.jp/covheni |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903040942/https://www.jcl.co.jp/covheni |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021}}</ref>

=== RSYLTPGD246-253N ===
Otherwise referred to as del 246-252, or other various similar expression, refer to the deletion of amino acid from the position of 246 to 252, in the N-terminal domain of spike protein, accompanied with a replacement of the [[aspartic acid]] (D) at the position 253 for [[asparagine]] (N).<ref>{{cite web |title=Variant: 21G (Lambda) |url=https://covariants.org/variants/21G.Lambda |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210721095150/https://covariants.org/variants/21G.Lambda |archive-date=21 July 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=CoVariants}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Frank Diamond |date=7 August 2021 |title=More Data Point to Lambda Variant's Potential Lethality |url=https://www.infectioncontroltoday.com/view/more-data-point-to-lambda-variant-s-potential-lethality |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903142009/https://www.infectioncontroltoday.com/view/more-data-point-to-lambda-variant-s-potential-lethality |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=Infection Control Today}}</ref>

The 7 amino acid deletion mutation is currently (September 2021) described as unique in the Lambda variant, and have been attributed to as one of the cause of the strain's increased capability to escape from neutralizing antibodies according to preprint paper.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=Izumi |last2=Kosugi |first2=Yusuke |last3=Wu |first3=Jiaqi |last4=Zahradnik |first4=Jiri |last5=Yamasoba |first5=Daichi |last6=Butlertanaka |first6=Erika P. |last7=Tanaka |first7=Yuri L. |last8=Uriu |first8=Keiya |last9=Liu |first9=Yafei |last10=Morizako |first10=Nanami |last11=Shirakawa |first11=Kotaro |last12=Kazuma |first12=Yasuhiro |last13=Nomura |first13=Ryosuke |last14=Horisawa |first14=Yoshihito |last15=Tokunaga |first15=Kenzo |date=January 2022 |title=The SARS-CoV-2 Lambda variant exhibits enhanced infectivity and immune resistance |journal=Cell Reports |volume=38 |issue=2 |article-number=110218 |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.07.28.454085 |doi=10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110218 |hdl=2433/267436 |pmc=8683271 |pmid=34968415 |last16=Ueno |first16=Takamasa |last17=Takaori-Kondo |first17=Akifumi |last18=Schreiber |first18=Gideon |last19=Arase |first19=Hisashi |last20=Motozono |first20=Chihiro |last21=Saito |first21=Akatsuki |last22=Nakagawa |first22=So |last23=Sato |first23=Kei}}</ref>

=== R346T ===
The name of the mutation, R346T, refers to an exchange where the [[arginine]] (R) is replaced by [[threonine]] (T) at position 346.<ref name="recurrent" />

This mutation has been observed to increase ACE2 binding affinity and increase antibody resistance. In cell culture assays, R346T appeared to enhance more efficient engagement with the ACE2 receptor by ~1.5-fold, which modestly increased viral infectivity. This mutation has showed up in an increasing number of Omicron and [[BA.2.86|JN.1]] sublineages, demonstrating an example of convergent evolution.<ref name="recurrent">{{cite journal |author1=Qian Wang |author2=Ian A Mellis |author3=Jerren Ho |author4=Anthony Bowen |author5=Theresa Kowalski-Dobson |author6=Riccardo Valdez |author7=Phinikoula S Katsamba |author8=Madeline Wu |author9=Caitlin Lee |author10=Lawrence Shapiro |author11=Aubree Gordon |author12=Yicheng Guo |author13=David D Ho |author14=Lihong Liu |date=16 September 2024 |title=Recurrent SARS-CoV-2 spike mutations confer growth advantages to select JN.1 sublineages |journal=Emerging Microbes & Infections |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis|Taylor & Francis Online]] |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=2402880 |doi=10.1080/22221751.2024.2402880 |pmc=11407393 |pmid=39259045 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== N440K ===
The name of the mutation, N440K, refers to an exchange whereby the [[asparagine]] (N) is replaced by [[lysine]] (K) at position 440.<ref name=vgreenwood />

This mutation has been observed in cell cultures to be 10 times more infective compared to the previously widespread A2a strain (A97V substitution in RdRP sequence) and 1000 times more in the lesser widespread A3i strain (D614G substitution in Spike and a and P323L substitution in RdRP).<ref>{{cite bioRxiv |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.04.30.441434 |title=N440K variant of SARS-CoV-2 has Higher Infectious Fitness |date=30 April 2021 |language=en |vauthors=Tandel D, Gupta D, Sah V, Harshan KH}}</ref> It was involved in rapid surges of COVID-19 cases in India in May 2021.<ref>{{cite news |date=3 May 2021 |title=COVID-19 {{!}} A.P. strain at least 15 times more virulent |url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/andhra-pradesh/ap-strain-at-least-15-times-more-virulent/article34474035.ece |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210510130106/https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/andhra-pradesh/ap-strain-at-least-15-times-more-virulent/article34474035.ece |archive-date=10 May 2021 |access-date=4 May 2021 |work=The Hindu |language=en-IN |vauthors=Bhattacharjee S}}</ref> India has the largest proportion of N440K mutated variants followed by the US and Germany.<ref>{{cite news |date=2 May 2021 |title=N440k Covid Variant: Mutant N440K 10 times more infectious than parent strain {{pipe}} Hyderabad News |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/hyderabad/mutant-n440k-10-times-more-infectious-than-parent-strain/articleshow/82348011.cms |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210830122055/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/hyderabad/mutant-n440k-10-times-more-infectious-than-parent-strain/articleshow/82348011.cms |archive-date=30 August 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=The Times of India}}</ref>

=== G446V ===
The name of the mutation, G446V, refers to an exchange whereby the [[glycine]] (G) is replaced by [[valine]] (V) at position 446.<ref name=vgreenwood />

The mutation, identified in Japan among inbound travelers starting from May, and among 33 samples from individuals related to [[2020 Tokyo Olympic Games]] and [[2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games]], are said to be possible to impact affinity of multiple [[monoclonal antibody]], although its clinical impact against the use of antibody medicine is still yet to be known.<ref>{{cite web |title=感染・伝播性の増加や抗原性の変化が懸念される 新型コロナウイルス(SARS-CoV-2)の新規変異株について (第13報) |trans-title=New Mutant Strains of the Novel Coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) Concerned About Increased Infectivity and Transmissibility and Changes in Antigenicity (13th Report) |url=https://www.niid.go.jp/niid/ja/2019-ncov/2484-idsc/10623-covid19-57.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903035806/https://www.niid.go.jp/niid/ja/2019-ncov/2484-idsc/10623-covid19-57.html |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021}}</ref>

=== <span class="anchor" id="L452R"></span>L452R ===
The name of the mutation, L452R, refers to an exchange whereby the [[leucine]] (L) is replaced by [[arginine]] (R) at position 452.<ref name=vgreenwood />

L452R is found in both the Delta and Kappa variants which first circulated in India, but have since spread around the world. L452R is a relevant mutation in this strain that enhances ACE2 receptor binding ability and can reduce vaccine-stimulated antibodies from attaching to this altered spike protein.

L452R, some studies show, could even make the coronavirus resistant to [[T cell]]s, that are necessary to target and destroy virus-infected cells. They are different from antibodies that are useful in blocking coronavirus particles and preventing it from proliferating.<ref name=Koshy />

=== Y453F ===
The name of the mutation, Y453F, refers to an exchange whereby the [[tyrosine]] (Y) is replaced by [[phenylalanine]] (F) at position 453. The mutation have been found potentially linked to the spread of SARS-CoV-2 among minks in the Netherlands in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mutations in spike putatively linked to outbreak at Danish mink farms |url=https://www.gisaid.org/references/gisaid-in-the-news/mutations-in-spike-putatively-linked-to-outbreak-in-danish-mink-farms/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903145541/https://www.gisaid.org/references/gisaid-in-the-news/mutations-in-spike-putatively-linked-to-outbreak-in-danish-mink-farms/ |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=GISAID}}</ref>

=== S477G/N ===
A highly flexible region in the receptor binding domain (RBD) of SARS-CoV-2, starting from residue 475 and continuing up to residue 485, was identified using bioinformatics and statistical methods in several studies. The University of Graz<ref>{{cite web |title=University of Graz |url=https://www.uni-graz.at/en/university/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506213944/https://www.uni-graz.at/en/university/ |archive-date=6 May 2021 |access-date=22 February 2021 |website=www.uni-graz.at}}</ref> and the Biotech Company Innophore<ref>{{cite web |date=23 January 2020 |title=Coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (formerly known as Wuhan coronavirus and 2019-nCoV) – what we can find out on a structural bioinformatics level |url=https://innophore.com/2019-ncov/ |access-date=22 February 2021 |website=Innophore |language=en-US |archive-date=13 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211213224025/https://innophore.com/2019-ncov/ |url-status=live }}</ref> have shown in a recent publication that structurally, the position S477 shows the highest flexibility among them.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Singh A, Steinkellner G, Köchl K, Gruber K, Gruber CC |date=February 2021 |title=Serine 477 plays a crucial role in the interaction of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein with the human receptor ACE2 |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=11 |issue=1 |article-number=4320 |bibcode=2021NatSR..11.4320S |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-83761-5 |pmc=7900180 |pmid=33619331 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

At the same time, S477 is hitherto the most frequently exchanged amino acid residue in the RBDs of SARS-CoV-2 mutants. By using molecular dynamics simulations of RBD during the binding process to hACE2, it has been shown that both S477G and S477N strengthen the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike with the hACE2 receptor. The vaccine developer BioNTech<ref>{{cite web |title=BioNTech: We aspire to individualize cancer medicine |url=https://www.biontech.de/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210618140029/https://biontech.de/ |archive-date=18 June 2021 |access-date=22 February 2021 |website=BioNTech |language=en}}</ref> referenced this amino acid exchange as relevant regarding future vaccine design in a paper published in September 2021.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Schroers B, Gudimella R, Bukur T, Roesler T, Loewer M, Sahin U |date=2021 |title=Large-scale analysis of SARS-CoV-2 spike-glycoprotein mutants demonstrates the need for continuous screening of virus isolates |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=16 |issue=9 |article-number=e0249254 |bibcode=2021PLoSO..1649254S |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.02.04.429765 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0249254 |pmc=8475993 |pmid=34570776 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== E484Q ===
The name of the mutation, E484Q, refers to an exchange whereby the [[glutamic acid]] (E) is replaced by [[glutamine]] (Q) at position 484.<ref name=vgreenwood />

The [[SARS-CoV-2 Kappa variant|Kappa]] variant circulating in India has E484Q. These variants were initially (but misleadingly) referred to as a "double mutant".<ref>{{cite news |title=People Are Talking About A 'Double Mutant' Variant In India. What Does That Mean? |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2021/04/24/988744811/people-are-talking-about-a-double-mutant-variant-in-india-what-does-that-mean |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427002806/https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2021/04/24/988744811/people-are-talking-about-a-double-mutant-variant-in-india-what-does-that-mean |archive-date=27 April 2021 |access-date=27 April 2021 |work=NPR |language=en |quote=...scientifically, the term "double mutant" makes no sense, Andersen says. "SARS-CoV-2 mutates all the time. So there are many double mutants all over the place. The variant in India really shouldn't be called that."}}</ref> E484Q may enhance ACE2 receptor binding ability, and may reduce vaccine-stimulated antibodies' ability to attach to this altered spike protein.<ref name=Koshy />

=== E484K ===
The name of the mutation, E484K, refers to an exchange whereby the [[glutamic acid]] (E) is replaced by [[lysine]] (K) at position 484.<ref name="vgreenwood">{{cite web |date=15 January 2021 |title=What Mutations of SARS-CoV-2 are Causing Concern? |url=https://www.news-medical.net/health/What-Mutations-of-SARS-CoV-2-are-Causing-Concern.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116155515/https://www.news-medical.net/health/What-Mutations-of-SARS-CoV-2-are-Causing-Concern.aspx |archive-date=16 January 2021 |access-date=16 January 2021 |website=News Medical Lifesciences |vauthors=Greenwood M}}</ref> It is nicknamed "Eeek".<ref name="nyt-mandavilli-mueller">{{cite news |date=2 March 2021 |title=Why Virus Variants Have Such Weird Names |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/02/health/virus-variant-names.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210620205741/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/02/health/virus-variant-names.html |archive-date=20 June 2021 |access-date=2 March 2021 |newspaper=The New York Times |id={{ProQuest|2494898089}} |vauthors=Mandavilli A, Mueller B}}</ref>

E484K has been reported to be an [[escape mutation]] (i.e., a mutation that improves a virus's ability to evade the host's [[immune system]]<ref>{{cite web |date=11 October 2012 |title=escape mutation |url=https://i-base.info/escape-mutation/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210509061951/https://i-base.info/escape-mutation/ |archive-date=9 May 2021 |access-date=19
