=== F490S ===
F490S denotes a change from [[phenylalanine]] (F) to [[serine]] (S) in [[amino-acid]] position 490.<ref>{{cite web |title=東京五輪で"最凶"の「ラムダ株」が上陸 ワクチン効果は5分の1? |trans-title="Lambda strain" landed at the Tokyo Olympics, and the vaccine effect is one-fifth? |url=https://news.goo.ne.jp/article/dot/nation/dot-2021070600072.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903142009/https://news.goo.ne.jp/article/dot/nation/dot-2021070600072.html |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=gooニュース}}</ref>

It is one of the mutation found in Lambda, and have been associated with reduced susceptibility to antibody generated by those who were infected with other strains, meaning antibody treatment against people infected with strains carrying such mutation would be less effective.<ref>{{cite web |date=21 July 2021 |title=The Lambda variant: is it more infectious, and can it escape vaccines? A virologist explains |url=https://theconversation.com/the-lambda-variant-is-it-more-infectious-and-can-it-escape-vaccines-a-virologist-explains-164156 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903163715/https://theconversation.com/the-lambda-variant-is-it-more-infectious-and-can-it-escape-vaccines-a-virologist-explains-164156 |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=The Conversation}}</ref>

=== N501Y ===
N501Y denotes a change from [[asparagine]] (N) to [[tyrosine]] (Y) in [[amino-acid]] position 501.<ref name=":5">{{cite report |url=https://www.cogconsortium.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Report-1_COG-UK_20-December-2020_SARS-CoV-2-Mutations_final_updated2.pdf |title=COG-UK update on SARS-CoV-2 Spike mutations of special interest: Report 1 |date=20 December 2020 |publisher=COVID-19 Genomics UK Consortium (COG-UK) |page=7 |access-date=31 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201225050316/https://www.cogconsortium.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Report-1_COG-UK_20-December-2020_SARS-CoV-2-Mutations_final_updated2.pdf |archive-date=25 December 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref> N501Y has been nicknamed "Nelly".<ref name="nyt-mandavilli-mueller" />

This change is believed by PHE to increase [[binding affinity]] because of its position inside the [[coronavirus spike protein|spike glycoprotein]]'s [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2#Structural biology|receptor-binding domain]], which binds [[Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2|ACE2]] in human cells; data also support the hypothesis of increased binding affinity from this change.{{sfnp|Chand ''et al.''|2020|p=6|loc=Potential impact of spike variant N501Y}} Molecular interaction modelling and the free energy of binding calculations has demonstrated that the mutation N501Y has the highest binding affinity in variants of concern RBD to hACE2.<ref name="SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern" /> Variants with N501Y include Gamma,<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" /> Alpha (VOC 20DEC-01), Beta, and COH.20G/501Y (identified in [[Columbus, Ohio|Columbus]], Ohio).<ref name="SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern" /> This last became the dominant form of the virus in Columbus in late December 2020 and January and appears to have evolved independently of other variants.<ref>{{cite web |date=13 January 2021 |title=Researchers Discover New Variant of COVID-19 Virus in Columbus, Ohio |url=https://wexnermedical.osu.edu/mediaroom/pressreleaselisting/new-sars-cov2-variant |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115204337/https://wexnermedical.osu.edu/mediaroom/pressreleaselisting/new-sars-cov2-variant |archive-date=15 January 2021 |access-date=16 January 2021 |website=wexnermedical.osu.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite bioRxiv |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.01.12.426407 |title=Distinct Patterns of Emergence of SARS-CoV-2 Spike Variants including N501Y in Clinical Samples in Columbus Ohio |date=26 January 2021 |language=en |vauthors=Tu H, Avenarius MR, Kubatko L, Hunt M, Pan X, Ru P, Garee J, Thomas K, Mohler P, Pancholi P, Jones D}}</ref>

=== N501S ===
N501S denotes a change from [[asparagine]] (N) to [[serine]] (S) in [[amino-acid]] position 501.<ref>{{cite web |date=31 August 2021 |title=新たな変異ある「デルタ株」検出 感染力への影響分からず |trans-title=Detection of a new mutant "Delta strain" The effect on infectivity is unknown |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20210831/k10013233451000.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901171436/https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20210831/k10013233451000.html |archive-date=1 September 2021 |access-date=2 September 2021 |website=NHKニュース}}</ref>

As of September 2021, there are 8 cases of patients around the world infected with Delta variant which feature this N501S mutation. As it is considered a mutation similar to N501Y, it is suspected to have similar characteristics as N501Y mutation, which is believed to increase the infectivity of the virus, however the exact effect is unknown yet.<ref>{{cite web |title=「N501S 変異を有する新たなデルタ株(B.1.617.2 系統)の市中感染事例(国内第1例目)を確認」 〜医科歯科大 新型コロナウイルス全ゲノム解析プロジェクト 第8報〜 |trans-title="Confirmed a case of community-acquired infection (first case in Japan) of a new delta strain (B.1.617.2 strain) with N501S mutation" -Medical and Dental University New Coronavirus Whole Genome Analysis Project 8th Report- |url=https://www.tmd.ac.jp/files/topics/55788_ext_04_2.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210830063820/https://www.tmd.ac.jp/files/topics/55788_ext_04_2.pdf |archive-date=30 August 2021 |access-date=2 September 2021}}</ref>

=== <span class="anchor" id="D614G"></span>D614G ===
[[File:Graph of the prevalence of mutation D614G across all reported GISAID strains during the course of 2020.jpg|thumb|Prevalence of mutation D614G across all reported GISAID strains during the course of 2020. Convergence with unity closely matches the upper limb of the [[logistics curve]].<ref name="10.1101/2021.01.06.425497" />]]
D614G is a missense mutation that affects the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. From early appearances in Eastern China early in 2020, the frequency of this mutation in the global viral population increased early on during the pandemic.<ref name="nytimes-coronavirus-variant-tracker">{{cite news |last1=Corum |first1=Jonathan |last2=Zimmer |first2=Carl |date=9 February 2021 |title=Coronavirus Variant Tracker |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/health/coronavirus-variant-tracker.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130040553/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/health/coronavirus-variant-tracker.html |archive-date=30 November 2021 |access-date=1 December 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |quote=Constantly Updated}}</ref> G ([[glycine]]) quickly replaced D ([[aspartic acid]]) at position 614 in Europe, though more slowly in China and the rest of East Asia, supporting the hypothesis that G increased the transmission rate, which is consistent with higher viral titres and infectivity in vitro.<ref name=Zhukova /> Researchers with the [[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|PANGOLIN]] tool nicknamed this mutation "Doug".<ref name="nyt-mandavilli-mueller" />

In July 2020, it was reported that the more infectious D614G SARS-CoV-2 variant had become the dominant form in the pandemic.<ref>{{cite news |date=18 July 2020 |title=Coronavirus: Are mutations making it more infectious? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-53325771 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201230185809/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-53325771 |archive-date=30 December 2020 |access-date=3 January 2021 |work=BBC News |vauthors=Schraer R}}</ref><ref name="Medicalxpress.com">{{cite news |title=New, more infectious strain of COVID-19 now dominates global cases of virus: study |url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-07-infectious-strain-covid-dominates-global.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201117010819/https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-07-infectious-strain-covid-dominates-global.html |archive-date=17 November 2020 |access-date=16 August 2020 |work=medicalxpress.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Korber et al. 2020">{{cite journal |vauthors=Korber B, Fischer WM, Gnanakaran S, Yoon H, Theiler J, Abfalterer W, Hengartner N, Giorgi EE, Bhattacharya T, Foley B, Hastie KM, Parker MD, Partridge DG, Evans CM, Freeman TM, de Silva TI, McDanal C, Perez LG, Tang H, Moon-Walker A, Whelan SP, LaBranche CC, Saphire EO, Montefiori DC |date=August 2020 |title=Tracking Changes in SARS-CoV-2 Spike: Evidence that D614G Increases Infectivity of the COVID-19 Virus |journal=Cell |volume=182 |issue=4 |pages=812–827.e19 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2020.06.043 |pmc=7332439 |pmid=32697968 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hou YJ, Chiba S, Halfmann P, Ehre C, Kuroda M, Dinnon KH, Leist SR, Schäfer A, Nakajima N, Takahashi K, Lee RE, Mascenik TM, Graham R, Edwards CE, Tse LV, Okuda K, Markmann AJ, Bartelt L, de Silva A, Margolis DM, Boucher RC, Randell SH, Suzuki T, Gralinski LE, Kawaoka Y, Baric RS |date=December 2020 |title=SARS-CoV-2 D614G variant exhibits efficient replication ex vivo and transmission in vivo |journal=Science |volume=370 |issue=6523 |pages=1464–1468 |bibcode=2020Sci...370.1464H |doi=10.1126/science.abe8499 |pmc=7775736 |pmid=33184236 |quote=an emergent Asp614→Gly (D614G) substitution in the spike glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 strains that is now the most prevalent form globally}}</ref> PHE confirmed that the D614G mutation had a "moderate effect on transmissibility" and was being tracked internationally.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Volz EM, Hill V, McCrone JT, Price A, Jorgensen D, O'Toole A, Southgate J, Johnson R, Jackson B, Nascimento FB, Rey SM |date=4 August 2020 |title=Evaluating the effects of SARS-CoV-2 Spike mutation D614G on transmissibility and pathogenicity |journal=Cell |language=en |volume=184 |issue=1 |pages=64–75.e11 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.020 |hdl=10044/1/84079 |pmc=7674007 |pmid=33275900 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

The global prevalence of D614G correlates with the prevalence of loss of smell ([[anosmia]]) as a symptom of COVID-19, possibly mediated by higher binding of the RBD to the ACE2 receptor or higher protein stability and hence higher infectivity of the [[olfactory epithelium]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Butowt R, Bilinska K, Von Bartheld CS |date=October 2020 |title=Chemosensory Dysfunction in COVID-19: Integration of Genetic and Epidemiological Data Points to D614G Spike Protein Variant as a Contributing Factor |journal=ACS Chemical Neuroscience |volume=11 |issue=20 |pages=3180–3184 |doi=10.1021/acschemneuro.0c00596 |pmc=7581292 |pmid=32997488 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Variants containing the D614G mutation are found in the G&nbsp;clade by GISAID<ref name="Zhukova">{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhukova A, Blassel L, Lemoine F, Morel M, Voznica J, Gascuel O |date=November 2020 |title=Origin, evolution and global spread of SARS-CoV-2 |journal=Comptes Rendus Biologies |volume=344 |pages=57–75 |doi=10.5802/crbiol.29 |pmid=33274614 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and the B.1&nbsp;clade by the [[Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages|PANGOLIN]] tool.<ref name=Zhukova />

=== Q677P/H ===
The name of the mutation, Q677P/H, refers to an exchange whereby the [[glutamine]] (Q) is replaced by [[proline]] (P) or [[histidine]] (H) at position 677.<ref name=vgreenwood /> There are several sub-lineages containing the Q677P mutation; six of these, which also contain various different combinations of other mutations, are referred to by names of birds. One of the earlier ones noticed for example is known as "Pelican," while the most common of these as of early 2021 was provisionally named "Robin 1."<ref name="677PH">{{cite medRxiv |last1=Hodcroft |first1=Emma B. |last2=Domman |first2=Daryl B. |last3=Snyder |first3=Daniel J. |last4=Oguntuyo |first4=Kasopefoluwa Y. |last5=Van Diest |first5=Maarten |last6=Densmore |first6=Kenneth H. |last7=Schwalm |first7=Kurt C. |last8=Femling |first8=Jon |last9=Carroll |first9=Jennifer L. |last10=Scott |first10=Rona S. |last11=Whyte |first11=Martha M. |last12=Edwards |first12=Michael W. |last13=Hull |first13=Noah C. |last14=Kevil |first14=Christopher G. |last15=Vanchiere |first15=John A. |last16=Lee |first16=Benhur |last17=Dinwiddie |first17=Darrell L. |last18=Cooper |first18=Vaughn S. |last19=Kamil |first19=Jeremy P. |title=Emergence in late 2020 of multiple lineages of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein variants affecting amino acid position 677 |date=21 February 2021 |medrxiv=10.1101/2021.02.12.21251658}}</ref>

The mutation has been reported in multiple lineages circulating inside the United States as of late 2020 and also some lineages outside the country. 'Pelican' was first detected in Oregon, and as of early 2021 'Robin 1' was found often in the [[Midwestern United States]], while another Q667H sub-lineage, 'Robin 2', was found mostly in the southeastern United States.<ref name=677PH /> The frequency of such mutation being recorded has increased from late 2020 to early 2021.<ref>{{cite web |date=15 February 2021 |title=Study finds 7 newly-identified COVID-19 variants circulating in the United States |url=https://abc11.com/10342025/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210903124612/https://abc11.com/10342025/ |archive-date=3 September 2021 |access-date=3 September 2021 |website=ABC11 Raleigh-Durham}}</ref>

=== P681H ===
[[File:Prevalence of P681H.png|thumb|250px|Logarithmic prevalence of P681H in 2020 according to sequences in the GISAID database<ref name="10.1101/2021.01.06.425497" />]]<!--[[File:The Distribution and Frequency of P681H and D614G Mutations Among All SARS-CoV-2 Sequences by Month Reported in the GISAID Database in Year 2020.png|thumb]]-->
The name of the mutation, P681H, refers to an exchange whereby the [[proline]] (P) is replaced by [[histidine]] (H) at position 681.<ref name="10.1101/2021.01.06.425497" />

In January 2021, scientists reported in a [[preprint]] that the mutation P681H, a characteristic feature of the Alpha variant and lineage B.1.1.207 (identified in Nigeria), is showing a significant exponential increase in worldwide frequency, thus following a trend to be expected in the lower limb of the logistics curve. This may be compared with the trend of the now globally prevalent D614G.<ref name="10.1101/2021.01.06.425497">{{cite bioRxiv |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.01.06.425497 |title=Genetic Characteristics and Phylogeny of 969-bp S Gene Sequence of SARS-CoV-2 from Hawaii Reveals the Worldwide Emerging P681H Mutation |date=January 2021 |vauthors=Maison DP, Ching LL, Shikuma CM, Nerurkar VR}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Available under [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ CC BY 4.0] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=16 October 2017 }}.</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=10 January 2021 |title=Study shows P681H mutation is becoming globally prevalent among SARS-CoV-2 sequences |url=https://www.news-medical.net/news/20210110/Study-shows-P681H-mutation-is-becoming-globally-prevalent-among-SARS-CoV-2-sequences.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214132128/https://www.news-medical.net/news/20210110/Study-shows-P681H-mutation-is-becoming-globally-prevalent-among-SARS-CoV-2-sequences.aspx |archive-date=14 February 2021 |access-date=11 February 2021 |work=News-Medical.net |language=en}}</ref>

=== P681R ===
The name of the mutation, P681R, refers to an exchange whereby the [[proline]] (P) is replaced by [[arginine]] (R) at position 681.<ref name=vgreenwood />

Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium ([[INSACOG]]) found that other than the two mutations E484Q and L452R, there is also a third significant mutation, P681R in lineage B.1.617. All three concerning mutations are on the spike protein, the operative part of the coronavirus that binds to receptor cells of the body.<ref name=Koshy />

=== A701V ===
According to initial media reports, the [[Malaysia]]n [[Ministry of Health (Malaysia)|Ministry of Health]] announced on 23 December 2020 that it had discovered a mutation in the SARS-CoV-2 genome which they designated as A701B(sic), among 60 samples collected from the Benteng Lahad Datu cluster in [[Sabah]]. The mutation was characterised as being similar to the one found recently at that time in South Africa, Australia, and the Netherlands, although it was uncertain if the strain with the mutation was more infectious than usual.<ref>{{cite news |date=23 December 2020 |title=Malaysia identifies new Covid-19 strain, similar to one found in 3 other countries |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/se-asia/malaysia-has-identified-new-covid-19-strain-similar-to-one-found-in-3-other-nations |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201223152941/https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/se-asia/malaysia-has-identified-new-covid-19-strain-similar-to-one-found-in-3-other-nations |archive-date=23 December 2020 |access-date=10 January 2021 |work=The Straits Times |language=en |quote=Tan Sri Dr Noor Hisham Abdullah, said it is still unknown whether the strain – dubbed the "A701B" mutation – is more infectious than usual}}</ref> The provincial government of [[Sulu]] in neighbouring [[Philippines]] temporarily suspended travel to Sabah in response to the discovery of 'A701B' due to uncertainty over the nature of the mutation.<ref>{{cite news |date=27 December 2020 |title=Duterte says Sulu seeking help after new COVID-19 variant detected in nearby Sabah, Malaysia |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/news/nation/769466/duterte-says-sulu-seeking-help-after-new-covid-19-strain-detected-in-nearby-sabah-malaysia/story/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103070045/https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/news/nation/769466/duterte-says-sulu-seeking-help-after-new-covid-19-strain-detected-in-nearby-sabah-malaysia/story/ |archive-date=3 January 2021 |access-date=10 January 2021 |work=GMA News |language=en}}</ref>

On 25 December 2020, the Malaysian Ministry of Health described a mutation A701V as circulating and present in 85% of cases (D614G was present in 100% of cases) in Malaysia.<ref name=kkm /><ref name="FocusM">{{cite web |date=25 December 2020 |title=COVID-19 A701V mutation spreads to third wave clusters |url=https://focusmalaysia.my/mainstream/covid-19-a701v-mutation-spreads-to-third-wave-clusters/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514041003/https://focusmalaysia.my/mainstream/covid-19-a701v-mutation-spreads-to-third-wave-clusters/ |archive-date=14 May 2021 |access-date=13 May 2021 |work=focusmalaysia.my}}</ref> These reports also referred to samples collected from the Benteng Lahad Datu cluster.<ref name=kkm /><ref name=FocusM /> The text of the announcement was mirrored verbatim on the Facebook page of [[Noor Hisham Abdullah]], Malay Director-General of Health, who was quoted in some of the news articles.<ref name=FocusM />

The A701V mutation has the amino acid [[alanine]] (A) substituted by [[valine]] (V) at position 701 in the spike protein. Globally, South Africa, Australia, Netherlands and England also reported A701V at about the same time as Malaysia.<ref name=kkm /> In GISAID, the prevalence of this mutation is found to be about 0.18%. of cases.<ref name="kkm">{{cite news |date=25 December 2020 |title=The current situation and Information on the Spike protein mutation of Covid-19 in Malaysia |url=https://covid-19.moh.gov.my/semasa-kkm/122020/current-situation-and-information-on-the-spike-protein-mutation-of-covid-19-in-malaysia |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210702224231/https://covid-19.moh.gov.my/semasa-kkm/122020/current-situation-and-information-on-the-spike-protein-mutation-of-covid-19-in-malaysia |archive-date=2 July 2021 |access-date=15 January 2021 |website=Kementerian Kesihatan Malaysia – Covid-19 Malaysia}}</ref>

On 14 April 2021, the Malaysian Ministry of Health reported that the third wave, which had started in Sabah, has involved the introduction of variants with D614G and A701V mutations.<ref>{{cite web |date=14 April 2021 |title=Variants of Concerns (VOC), B.1.524, B.1.525, South African B.1.351, STRAIN D614G, A701V, B1.1.7 |url=https://covid-19.moh.gov.my/semasa-kkm/2021/04/perkembangan-mutasi-covid-19-di-malaysia-14042021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210702203225/https://covid-19.moh.gov.my/semasa-kkm/2021/04/perkembangan-mutasi-covid-19-di-malaysia-14042021 |archive-date=2 July 2021 |access-date=15 May 2021 |work=covid-19.moh.gov.my}}</ref>

== Data and methods ==
[[DNA sequencing#History|Modern DNA sequencing]], where available, may permit rapid detection (sometimes known as 'real-time detection') of genetic variants that appear in pathogens during disease outbreaks.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Yurkovetskiy L, Wang X, Pascal KE, Tomkins-Tinch C, Nyalile TP, Wang Y, Baum A, Diehl WE, Dauphin A, Carbone C, Veinotte K, Egri SB, Schaffner SF, Lemieux JE, Munro JB, Rafique A, Barve A, Sabeti PC, Kyratsous CA, Dudkina NV, Shen K, Luban J |date=October 2020 |title=Structural and Functional Analysis of the D614G SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein Variant |journal=Cell |volume=183 |issue=3 |pages=739–751.e8 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2020.09.032 |pmc=7492024 |pmid=32991842}}</ref> Through use of [[List of phylogenetic tree visualization software|phylogenetic tree visualisation software]], records of genome sequences can be clustered into groups of identical genomes all containing the same set of mutations. Each group represents a 'variant', 'clade', or 'lineage', and comparison of the sequences allows the evolutionary path of a virus to be deduced. For SARS-CoV-2, until  March 2021, over 330,000 viral genomic sequences had been generated by molecular epidemiology studies across the world.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Thomson EC, Rosen LE, Shepherd JG, Spreafico R, da Silva Filipe A, Wojcechowskyj JA, Davis C, Piccoli L, Pascall DJ, Dillen J, Lytras S, Czudnochowski N, Shah R, Meury M, Jesudason N, De Marco A, Li K, Bassi J, O'Toole A, Pinto D, Colquhoun RM, Culap K, Jackson B, Zatta F, Rambaut A, Jaconi S, Sreenu VB, Nix J, Zhang I, Jarrett RF, Glass WG, Beltramello M, Nomikou K, Pizzuto M, Tong L, Cameroni E, Croll TI, Johnson N, Di Iulio J, Wickenhagen A, Ceschi A, Harbison AM, Mair D, Ferrari P, Smollett K, Sallusto F, Carmichael S, Garzoni C, Nichols J, Galli M, Hughes J, Riva A, Ho A, Schiuma M, Semple MG, Openshaw PJ, Fadda E, Baillie JK, Chodera JD, Rihn SJ, Lycett SJ, Virgin HW, Telenti A, Corti D, Robertson DL, Snell G |date=March 2021 |title=Circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike N439K variants maintain fitness while evading antibody-mediated immunity |journal=Cell |volume=184 |issue=5 |pages=1171–1187.e20 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2021.01.037 |pmc=7843029 |pmid=33621484}}</ref>

=== New variant detection and assessment ===
On 26 January 2021, the British government said it would share its [[Genomics|genomic]] sequencing capabilities with other countries in order to increase the [[DNA sequencing|genomic sequencing]] rate and trace new variants, and announced a "New Variant Assessment Platform".<ref>{{cite web |date=26 January 2021 |title=Britain to help other countries track down coronavirus variants |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-health-coronavirus-britain-genome-idUSKBN29V00B |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210126084735/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-health-coronavirus-britain-genome-idUSKBN29V00B |archive-date=26 January 2021 |access-date=27 January 2021 |website=Reuters |vauthors=Smout A}}</ref> {{As of|2021|01}}, more than half of all genomic sequencing of COVID-19 was carried out in the UK.<ref>{{cite news |date=26 January 2021 |title=UK to help sequence mutations of Covid around world to find dangerous new variants |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/01/26/uk-help-sequence-mutations-covid-around-world-find-dangerous/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127230601/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/01/26/uk-help-sequence-mutations-covid-around-world-find-dangerous/ |archive-date=27 January 2021 |access-date=28 January 2021 |newspaper=The Telegraph |vauthors=Donnelly L}}</ref>

[[Wastewater surveillance]] was demonstrated to be one technique to detect SARS-CoV-2 variants<ref name="10.1038/s41467-022-28246-3"/> and to track their rise for studying related ongoing infection dynamics.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Galani |first1=Aikaterini |last2=Aalizadeh |first2=Reza |last3=Kostakis |first3=Marios |last4=Markou |first4=Athina |last5=Alygizakis |first5=Nikiforos |last6=Lytras |first6=Theodore |last7=Adamopoulos |first7=Panagiotis G. |last8=Peccia |first8=Jordan |last9=Thompson |first9=David C. |last10=Kontou |first10=Aikaterini |last11=Karagiannidis |first11=Apostolos |last12=Lianidou |first12=Evi S. |last13=Avgeris |first13=Margaritis |last14=Paraskevis |first14=Dimitrios |last15=Tsiodras |first15=Sotirios |date=January 2022 |title=SARS-CoV-2 wastewater surveillance data can predict hospitalizations and ICU admissions |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=804 |article-number=150151 |bibcode=2022ScTEn.80450151G |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.150151 |pmc=8421077 |pmid=34623953 |last16=Scorilas |first16=Andreas |last17=Vasiliou |first17=Vasilis |last18=Dimopoulos |first18=Meletios-Athanasios |last19=Thomaidis |first19=Nikolaos S.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baaijens |first1=Jasmijn A. |last2=Zulli |first2=Alessandro |last3=Ott |first3=Isabel M. |last4=Petrone |first4=Mary E. |last5=Alpert |first5=Tara |last6=Fauver |first6=Joseph R. |last7=Kalinich |first7=Chaney C. |last8=Vogels |first8=Chantal B. F. |last9=Breban |first9=Mallery I. |last10=Duvallet |first10=Claire |last11=McElroy |first11=Kyle |last12=Ghaeli |first12=Newsha |last13=Imakaev |first13=Maxim |last14=Mckenzie-Bennett |first14=Malaika |last15=Robison |first15=Keith |date=2022 |title=Lineage abundance estimation for SARS-CoV-2 in wastewater using transcriptome quantification techniques |journal=Genome Biology |volume=23 |issue=1 |article-number=236 |doi=10.1186/s13059-022-02805-9 |pmc=9643916 |pmid=36348471 |doi-access=free |last16=Plocik |first16=Alex |last17=Schilling |first17=Rebecca |last18=Pierson |first18=Martha |last19=Littlefield |first19=Rebecca |last20=Spencer |first20=Michelle |last21=Simen |first21=Birgitte B. |last22=Hanage |first22=William P. |last23=Grubaugh |first23=Nathan D. |last24=Peccia |first24=Jordan |last25=Baym |first25=Michael |medrxiv=10.1101/2021.08.31.21262938}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heijnen |first1=Leo |last2=Elsinga |first2=Goffe |last3=Graaf |first3=Miranda de |last4=Molenkamp |first4=Richard |last5=Koopmans |first5=Marion P. G. |last6=Medema |first6=Gertjan |date=2021 |title=Droplet digital RT-PCR to detect SARS-CoV-2 signature mutations of variants of concern in wastewater |journal=Science of the Total Environment |language=en |volume=799 |article-number=149456 |bibcode=2021ScTEn.79949456H |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149456 |pmc=8332926 |pmid=34371414 |medrxiv=10.1101/2021.03.25.21254324v1}}</ref>

=== Testing ===
Whether one or more mutations visible in RT-PCR tests can be used reliably to identify a variant depends on the prevalence of other variants concurrently circulating in the same population.<ref name="ecdc-variant-identification">{{cite tech report |url=https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/methods-detection-and-identification-sars-cov-2-variants |title=Methods for the detection and identification of SARS-CoV-2 variants |date=3 March 2021 |at=Diagnostic screening assays of known VOCs |institution=European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control |work=European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, World Health Organization |location=Stockholm}}</ref><ref name="briefing15">{{cite tech report |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/993879/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_15.pdf |title=SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants under investigation in England, technical briefing 15 |date=11 June 2021 |access-date=15 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210704221717/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/993879/Variants_of_Concern_VOC_Technical_Briefing_15.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=4 July 2021 |format=PDF |type=Briefing |id=GOV-8576 |institution=Public Health England}}</ref>

== Cross-species transmission ==
{{Further|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on animals|List of animals that can get SARS-CoV-2}}

There is a risk that COVID-19 could transfer from humans to other animal populations and could combine with other animal viruses to create yet more variants that are dangerous to humans.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Green ST, Cladi L |date=26 January 2021 |title=Covid-19 and evolutionary pressure – can we predict which genetic dangers lurk beyond the horizon? |url=https://www.bmj.com/content/372/bmj.n230/rr |url-status=live |journal=BMJ |article-number=n230 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608083850/https://www.bmj.com/content/372/bmj.n230/rr |archive-date=8 June 2021 |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> [[Reverse zoonosis]] spillovers may cause reservoirs for mutating variants that spill back to humans – another possible source for variants of concern, in addition to immunocompromised people.<ref name="nyt-deer">{{cite news |last1=Jacobs |first1=Andrew |date=2 November 2021 |title=Widespread Coronavirus Infection Found in Iowa Deer, New Study Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/science/deer-covid-infection.html |url-access=limited |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20211228/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/science/deer-covid-infection.html |archive-date=2021-12-28 |access-date=12 December 2021 |work=The New York Times |quote=Researchers and outside experts characterized the study's findings as a troubling development in the course of the pandemic. Widespread infection among North America's most ubiquitous game species could make eradicating the pathogen even more difficult, especially if they became a reservoir for mutations that eventually spilled back over to humans. [...] they are alerting deer hunters and others who handle deer to take precautions to avoid transmission. [...] If the virus were to become endemic in wild animals like deer, it could evolve over time to become more virulent and then infect people with a new strain capable of evading the current crop of vaccines.}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

=== Cluster 5 ===
{{Main|Cluster 5}}
In early November 2020, [[Cluster 5]], also referred to as ΔFVI-spike by the Danish [[Statens Serum Institut|State Serum Institute]] (SSI),<ref name="SSI short report">{{cite tech report |url=https://files.ssi.dk/Mink-cluster-5-short-report_AFO2 |title=SARS-CoV-2 spike mutations arising in Danish mink, their spread to humans and neutralization data |date=10 November 2020 |access-date=11 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201110135434/https://files.ssi.dk/Mink-cluster-5-short-report_AFO2 |url-status=live |archive-date=10 November 2020 |type=[[Preprint]] |institution=[[Statens Serum Institut]] |vauthors=Lassaunière R, Fonager J, Rasmussen M, Frische A, Strandh C, Rasmussen T, Bøtner A, Fomsgaard A}}</ref> was discovered in [[Northern Jutland]], Denmark. It is believed to have been spread from [[mink]]s to humans via [[fur farming|mink farms]]. On 4 November 2020, it was announced that the [[mink industry in Denmark|mink population in Denmark]] would be [[2020 Danish mink cull|culled]] to prevent the possible spread of this mutation and reduce the risk of new mutations happening. A lockdown and travel restrictions were introduced in seven municipalities of Northern Jutland to prevent the mutation from spreading, which could compromise [[COVID-19 pandemic in Denmark|national]] or international responses to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. By 5 November 2020, some 214 mink-related human cases had been detected.<ref name="ECDC full">{{cite web |date=12 November 2020 |title=Detection of new SARS-CoV-2 variants related to mink |url=https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/RRA-SARS-CoV-2-in-mink-12-nov-2020.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108142429/https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/RRA-SARS-CoV-2-in-mink-12-nov-2020.pdf |archive-date=8 January 2021 |access-date=12 November 2020 |website=ECDC.eu |publisher=European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control}}</ref>

The WHO stated that cluster 5 had a "moderately decreased sensitivity to neutralising antibodies".<ref name="DenmarkWho">{{cite news |date=6 November 2020 |title=SARS-CoV-2 mink-associated variant strain – Denmark |url=https://www.who.int/csr/don/06-november-2020-mink-associated-sars-cov2-denmark/en/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112034824/https://www.who.int/csr/don/06-november-2020-mink-associated-sars-cov2-denmark/en/ |archive-date=12 November 2020 |access-date=19 March 2021 |work=[[World Health Organization|WHO]] Disease Outbreak News}}</ref> SSI warned that the mutation could reduce the effect of [[COVID-19 vaccine]]s under development, although it was unlikely to render them useless. Following the lockdown and mass-testing, SSI announced on 19 November 2020 that cluster 5 in all probability had become extinct.<ref name="guardian_9nov">{{cite web |date=19 November 2020 |title=Danish Covid mink variant 'very likely extinct', but controversial cull continues |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/nov/19/danish-covid-mink-variant-very-likely-extinct-but-controversial-cull-continues |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424001442/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/nov/19/danish-covid-mink-variant-very-likely-extinct-but-controversial-cull-continues |archive-date=24 April 2021 |access-date=19 April 2021 |work=The Guardian |vauthors=Kevany S, Carstensen T}}</ref>  By 1 February 2021, authors of a [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] paper, all of whom were from the SSI, assessed that cluster 5 was not in circulation in the human population.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Larsen HD, Fonager J, Lomholt FK, Dalby T, Benedetti G, Kristensen B, Urth TR, Rasmussen M, Lassaunière R, Rasmussen TB, Strandbygaard B, Lohse L, Chaine M, Møller KL, Berthelsen AN, Nørgaard SK, Sönksen UW, Boklund AE, Hammer AS, Belsham GJ, Krause TG, Mortensen S, Bøtner A, Fomsgaard A, Mølbak K |date=February 2021 |title=Preliminary report of an outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 in mink and mink farmers associated with community spread, Denmark, June to November 2020 |journal=Euro Surveillance |volume=26 |issue=5 |doi=10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2021.26.5.210009 |pmc=7863232 |pmid=33541485}}</ref>

== Vaccines ==
{{main|COVID-19 vaccine}}
During the COVID-19 pandemic, a variety of vaccines was developed. The vaccines were rolled out for administering to a broad range of recipients, typically beginning with the most vulnerable demographic groups.

=== Differential vaccine effectiveness ===
{{See also|Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine#Effectiveness|Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine#Effectiveness|Moderna COVID-19 vaccine#Effectiveness|Janssen COVID-19 vaccine#Efficacy|Novavax COVID-19 vaccine#Efficacy|Sinopharm BIBP COVID-19 vaccine#Effectiveness|Sputnik V COVID-19 vaccine#Effectiveness|CoronaVac#Effectiveness|Covaxin#Efficacy|ZF2001#Efficacy|Abdala (vaccine)#Efficacy|SCB-2019#Efficacy|COVID-19 vaccine clinical research#Variants}}

The interplay between the SARS-CoV-2 virus and its human hosts was initially natural but then started being altered by the rising availability of [[COVID-19 vaccine|vaccines]] seen in 2021.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Burioni R, Topol EJ |date=June 2021 |title=Has SARS-CoV-2 reached peak fitness? |journal=Nature Medicine |volume=27 |issue=8 |pages=1323–24 |doi=10.1038/s41591-021-01421-7 |pmid=34155413 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The potential emergence of a SARS-CoV-2 variant that is moderately or fully resistant to the antibody response elicited by the COVID-19 vaccines may necessitate modification of the vaccines.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |author=Office of the Commissioner |date=23 February 2021 |title=Coronavirus (COVID-19) Update: FDA Issues Policies to Guide Medical Product Developers Addressing Virus Variants |url=https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-issues-policies-guide-medical-product-developers-addressing-virus |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210222195516/https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-issues-policies-guide-medical-product-developers-addressing-virus |archive-date=22 February 2021 |access-date=7 March 2021 |website=U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA)}}</ref> The emergence of vaccine-resistant variants is more likely in a highly vaccinated population with uncontrolled transmission.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rella |first1=Simon A. |last2=Kulikova |first2=Yuliya A. |last3=Dermitzakis |first3=Emmanouil T. |last4=Kondrashov |first4=Fyodor A. |date=30 July 2021 |title=Rates of SARS-CoV-2 transmission and vaccination impact the fate of vaccine-resistant strains |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=11 |issue=1 |article-number=15729 |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-95025-3  |doi-access=free|pmc=8324827 |pmid=34330988}}</ref>

As of February 2021, the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] believed that all FDA authorized vaccines remained effective in protecting against circulating strains of SARS-CoV-2.<ref name=":02" />

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Vivian Lee

{{Use mdy dates|date=October 2022}}
{{short description|American radiologist}}
{{for|the Australian weightlifter|Vivian Lee (weightlifter)}}
{{Infobox scientist
| name = Vivian Lee
| image = Vivian S. Lee M.D.jpg
| birth_date = {{birth year and age|1966|9}}
| birth_place = [[Morristown, New Jersey]], U.S.

| awards = [[National Academy of Medicine]]
}}
'''Vivian S. Lee''' (born September 1966) is an American radiologist and health care/health technology executive. An Executive Fellow at [[Harvard Business School]] and senior lecturer at [[Harvard Medical School]] and [[Massachusetts General Hospital]], Lee is the author of the book, ''The Long Fix: Solving America's Health Care Crisis with Strategies That Work for Everyone'' (W.W. Norton, 2020). Lee is also a senior fellow at the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ihi.org/about/Pages/default.aspx|title=About IHI|website=Ihi.org|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> in Cambridge, Massachusetts. In 2019, she was named No. 11 in [[Modern Healthcare]]'s 100 Most Influential People in Healthcare<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 6, 2019|title=100 Most Influential People in Healthcare – 2019|url=https://www.modernhealthcare.com/awards/100-most-influential-people-healthcare-2019|access-date=2020-06-19|website=Modern Healthcare|language=en}}</ref> and is a frequent speaker at national and international meetings on the applications of [[big data]], AI, and technology in healthcare, leadership and managing change, [[health equity]], and on climate change and [[health system]] [[Business continuity planning#Resilience|resilience]].

Raised in Norman, Oklahoma, and trained in biomedical engineering and medicine, Lee established an [[NIH]]-funded research program in [[magnetic resonance imaging]] at [[NYU]]. She was elected Fellow of the [[International Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine]] (ISMRM)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ismrm.org/12/LeeBio.htm|title=Vivian Lee, M.D., Ph.D., M.B.A.|website=Ismrm.org|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> in 2006 and served as the president in 2008–2009. For her scientific discoveries, she was elected to the [[American Society of Clinical Investigation]]<ref>[https://www.the-asci.org/controllers/asci/AsciProfileController.php?pid=501310] {{dead link|date=July 2018}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Medicine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://healthcare.utah.edu/publicaffairs/news/2015/10/NAM_VSL_Capecchi_2015.php|title=High Honor for the U of U Medical School's Vivian S. Lee, Mario R. Capecchi: Election to the National Academy of Medicine – University of Utah Health|website=Healthcare.utah.edu|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref>

From 2018-2022, she was founding President of Health Platforms at [[Verily]] ([[Alphabet Inc.|Alphabet]]), launching and growing a number of successful health technology companies. Among her leadership roles in academic medicine, Lee served  as the CEO of [[University of Utah Health]], dean of the [[University of Utah School of Medicine]] and senior vice-president for health sciences of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City.<ref name="leebio">[http://healthcare.utah.edu/fad/mddetail.php?physicianID=u0777981 "Vivian S. Lee, MD, PhD, MBA"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121209061716/http://healthcare.utah.edu/fad/mddetail.php?physicianID=u0777981 |date=December 9, 2012 }}, ''University of Utah Health'', Salt Lake City, UT, Retrieved on March 14, 2017.</ref> And before that as the inaugural chief scientific officer and vice dean for science at [[NYU Langone Medical Center]]. She is also a member of the scientific advisory boards of the Massachusetts General Hospital,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.massgeneral.org/|title=Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts – Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA|website=Massgeneral.org|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> and previously served on the [[University of Pennsylvania]]'s Center for Health Incentives & Behavioral Economics (CHIBE) external advisory board,<ref>{{Cite web |title=External Advisory Board |url=https://chibe.upenn.edu/about/directory/external-advisory-board/ |access-date=2022-05-06 |website=Center for Health Incentives and Behavioral Economics |language=en-US |archive-date=May 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220508210241/https://chibe.upenn.edu/about/directory/external-advisory-board/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> and on the Defense Health Board of the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]]. She serves as editor-at-large for ''[[New England Journal of Medicine|The New England Journal of Medicine]] Catalyst''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Editors and Publishers {{!}} About NEJM Catalyst|url=https://catalyst.nejm.org/about/editors-and-publishers|access-date=2020-06-19|website=catalyst.nejm.org}}</ref>

Lee has studied the management and improvement of health care, with an emphasis on data measurement and feedback to create learning health systems and her work has demonstrated the virtuous cycle of improved [[patient-centeredness]], higher quality with better outcomes, and lower costs.

She is married to international legal scholar [[Benedict Kingsbury]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://its.law.nyu.edu/facultyprofiles/index.cfm?fuseaction=profile.overview&personid=20046|title=Benedict Kingsbury – Overview – NYU School of Law|website=its.law.nyu.edu|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> Lee also serves on the board of directors of the American Association of [[Rhodes Scholarship|Rhodes Scholars]] and the [[Commonwealth Fund]], and is also a director of [[Zions Bancorporation]].

==Education and training==
A U.S. Presidential Scholar and National Merit Scholar, Lee graduated from Norman High School, in Norman, Oklahoma, in 1983. In 1984 she was a Fleming Scholar in the Sir Alexander Fleming Scholarship Program for student researchers at the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation, Oklahoma City, OK.

Lee graduated from [[Radcliffe College]] of [[Harvard University]] ''magna cum laude'' in 1986 before receiving a Rhodes Scholarship to study at [[Balliol College, Oxford]] where she received a doctorate in medical engineering.<ref name="leeutahhealthmedical">Maffly, Brian. [https://archive.sltrib.com/story.php?ref=/sltrib/news/53163390-78/lee-utah-health-medical.html.csp "University of Utah's new health science chief has high hopes for flagship's future"], ''[[The Salt Lake Tribune]]'', Salt Lake City, UT, January 2, 2012. Retrieved on March 14, 2017.</ref> She then earned an M.D. with honors from [[Harvard Medical School]] and subsequently completed a residency in diagnostic [[radiology]] at [[Duke University]]<ref name="leeutahhealthmedical" /> and a fellowship in [[MRI]] at [[NYU Medical Center]].

In 2006, she completed a [[Master of Business Administration]] degree at NYU's [[Stern School of Business]], graduating as valedictorian. She later delivered the [[commencement speech]] for the class of 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stern.nyu.edu/experience-stern/tales-in-possible/celebrate-possible-emba-graduation-2017|title=Tales in Possible : Celebrate Possible 2017 Executive MBA Graduation Ceremony|website=Stern.nyu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-03-31}}</ref>

==Research in MRI==

dose gadolinium-contrast enhanced MRI.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lee | first1 = VS | last2 = Rusinek | first2 = H | last3 = Johnson | first3 = G | last4 = Rofsky | first4 = NM | last5 = Krinsky | renovascular disease,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Zhang | first1 = JL | last2 = Rusinek | first2 = H | last3 = Bokacheva | first3 = L | last4 = Lim | first4 = RP | last5 = Chen | first5 = Q | last6 = While a part of the NYU MRI research team, Lee contributed to multiple advances in clinical body MRI, including pioneering 3D (volumetric) liver imaging for routine clinical care and for improved detection of [[hepatocellular carcinoma]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Krinsky | first1 = GA | last2 = Lee | first2 = VS | last3 = Theise | first3 = ND | last4 = Weinreb | first4 = JC | last5 = Rofsky | first5 = NM | last6 = Diflo | first6 = T | last7 = Teperman | first7 = LW | year = 2001 | title = Hepatocellular carcinoma and dysplastic nodules in patients with cirrhosis: prospective diagnosis with MR imaging and transplant correlation | journal = Radiology | volume = 219 | issue = 2| pages = 445–454 | doi = 10.1148/radiology.219.2.r01ma40445 | pmid = 11323471 }}</ref> improved methods for assessing vascular disease with 3D gadolinium-enhanced MR angiography<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Pandharipande | first1 = PV | last2 = Lee | first2 = VS | last3 = Reuss | first3 = PM | last4 = Charles | first4 = HW | last5 = Rosen | first5 = RJ | last6 = Rofsky | first6 = NM | year = 2002 | title = Two-station bolus-chase MR angiography with a stationary table: A simple alternative to automated-table techniques | journal = American Journal of Roentgenology| volume = 179 | issue = 6| pages = 1583–1589 | doi = 10.2214/ajr.179.6.1791583 | pmid = 12438059 }}</ref> and venography,<ref>Shinde TS, Lee VS, Rofsky NM, Krinsky GA, Weinreb JC. Three-dimensional gadolinium-enhanced MR venographic evaluation of central veins in the thorax: Initial experience ''Radiology'' 1999; 213:555–560.</ref> and improved surgical planning for living related transplant donor planning in liver and kidney transplantation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lee | first1 = VS | last2 = Krinsky | first2 = GA | last3 = Nazzaro | first3 = CA | last4 = Chang | first4 = JS | last5 = Babb | first5 = JS | last6 = Lin | first6 = JC | last7 = Morgan | first7 = GR | last8 = Teperman | first8 = LW | year = 2004 | title = Defining intrahepatic biliary anatomy in living liver transplant donor candidates at mangafodipir trisodium-enhanced MR cholangiography versus conventional T2-weighted MR cholangiography | journal = Radiology | volume = 233 | issue = 3| pages = 659–666 | doi = 10.1148/radiol.2333031977 | pmid = 15516606 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Israel | first1 = GM | last2 = Lee | first2 = VS | last3 = Edye | first3 = M | last4 = Krinsky | first4 = GA | last5 = Lavelle | first5 = MT | last6 = Diflo | first6 = T | last7 = Weinreb | first7 = JC | year = 2002 | title = Comprehensive MR imaging evaluation of living donor candidates of laparoscopic nephrectomy: Initial experience | journal = Radiology | volume = 225 | issue = 2| pages = 427–432 | doi = 10.1148/radiol.2252011671 | pmid = 12409576 }}</ref>

As the director of Cardiothoracic MR imaging at NYU, Lee developed new MR methods for fast cardiac imaging<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lee | first1 = VS | last2 = Resnick | first2 = D | last3 = Bundy of myocardial infarcts.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lee | first1 = VS | last2 = Resnick | first2 = D | last3 = Tiu | first3 = SS | last4 = Sanger | first4 = JJ | last5 = Nazzaro | first5 = CA | last6 A popular lecturer who has received multiple teaching awards, Lee authored a textbook entitled ''Cardiovascular MRI: Physical Principles to Practical Protocols'' (Lippincott 2006).

==Administrative and leadership roles==
===NYU Langone Medical Center===
During her 5-year tenure as vice-chair for research in radiology, Lee helped build a research administrative infrastructure that enabled the department, previously unranked in NIH research funding, to reach the top 20.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://brimr.org/|title=Blue Ridge Institute for Medical Research|website=brimr.org|access-date=2018-03-31}}</ref> During that time, NYU Langone was also the first U.S. site to install a whole-body 7-tesla MRI scanner.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://med.nyu.edu/radiology/research/center-biomedical-imaging/facilities-and-equipment/siemens-7-tesla-whole-body-mri|title=Siemens 7-tesla Whole Body MRI : Radiology|website=Med.nyu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-03-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180401075654/https://med.nyu.edu/radiology/research/center-biomedical-imaging/facilities-and-equipment/siemens-7-tesla-whole-body-mri|archive-date=2018-04-01|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2007, Lee became the inaugural vice dean for science, chief scientific officer and senior vice-president, serving as a member of NYU's executive leadership team. Initiatives as chief scientific officer included establishing a new philanthropically-funded Neurosciences Institute<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nyulangone.org/press-releases/nyu-langone-medical-center-receives-100-million-gift-establish-neuroscience-institute|title=NYU Langone Medical Center Receives $100 Million Gift to Establish Neuroscience Institute|website=nyulangone.org|access-date=2018-03-31}}</ref> and a new NIH-funded Center for Translational Science Institute (CTSI),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bioprocessonline.com/doc/294m-grant-establishes-clinical-and-0001|title=$29.4M Grant Establishes Clinical And Translational Science Institute At NYU In Partnership With NYC Health And Hospitals|website=Bioprocessonline.com|language=en|access-date=2018-03-31}}</ref> upgrading core facilities, educational initiatives in grantsmanship, and establishment of a new Center for [[Health informatics|Health Informatics]] and Bioinformatics<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nyulangone.org/files/publication_issues/2008-NYU_Full_book_final_1_.pdf|title=Re:Search Report 2008|website=Nyulangone.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610070323/http://nyulangone.org/files/publication_issues/2008-NYU_Full_book_final_1_.pdf|archive-date=2016-06-10|url-status=dead|access-date=July 16, 2018}}</ref> and a new department of statistics and epidemiology. During her four-year tenure, NYU's ranking among NIH-funded schools of medicine increased from No. 36 to No. 26, and continued to rise thereafter.<ref name="auto"/>

===International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM)===
While at NYU, Lee held a number of leadership positions in the [[International Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine|ISMRM]], the preeminent professional organization of clinical and research MR scientists. She served on the board of trustees from 2002 to 2010, president 2008–2009, and as Scientific Program Chair for 2005 Annual ISMRM meeting. During her tenure, the ISMRM increased financial reserves, enhanced clinician membership and supported sustainability efforts through new "virtual" meetings.

===University of Utah===
From 2011 to 2017, Lee served as senior vice-president for health sciences, dean of the school of medicine, and the CEO of University of Utah Health. Lee was responsible for an academic health sciences complex that includes five major schools (School of Medicine, School of Dentistry, and Colleges of Nursing, Pharmacy and Health) and a health care system comprising four hospitals, dozens of clinical and research specialty centers, a network of 12 Salt Lake City-area health centers, a regional affiliate network of 19 partner facilities, a health plan, and over 1,400 board-certified physicians. Under her leadership, the University of Utah established a new School of Dentistry, the first new academic dental school in the nation in over 25 years, graduating its first class in 2017.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.deseretnews.com/article/865626029/Utahs-first-academic-dental-school-is-up-and-running.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150811213707/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865626029/Utahs-first-academic-dental-school-is-up-and-running.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 11, 2015|title=Utah's first academic dental school is up and running|last=Leonard|first=Wendy|date=April 8, 2015|work=DeseretNews.com|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en}}</ref>

Lee led University of Utah Health to recognition for its health care delivery system innovations<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://uofuhealth.utah.edu/innovation/|title=Home – Algorithms for Innovation|website=uofuhealth.utah.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-04-19}}</ref> that enable higher quality at lower costs<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Vivian S.|last2=Kawamoto|first2=Kensaku|last3=Hess|first3=Rachel|last4=Park|first4=Charlton|last5=Young|first5=Jeffrey|last6=Hunter|first6=Cheri|last7=Johnson|first7=Steven|last8=Gulbransen|first8=Sandi|last9=Pelt|first9=Christopher E.|date=September 13, 2016|title=Implementation of a Value-Driven Outcomes Program to Identify High Variability in Clinical Costs and Outcomes and Association With Reduced Cost and Improved Quality|journal=JAMA|language=en|volume=316|issue=10|pages=1061–72|doi=10.1001/jama.2016.12226|pmid=27623461|issn=0098-7484|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Porter|first1=Michael E.|last2=Lee|first2=Thomas H.|date=September 13, 2016|title=From Volume to Value in Health Care|journal=JAMA|language=en|volume=316|issue=10|pages=1047–8|doi=10.1001/jama.2016.11698|pmid=27623459|issn=0098-7484}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/08/health/what-are-a-hospitals-costs-utah-system-is-trying-to-learn.html|title=What Are a Hospital's Costs? Utah System Is Trying to Learn|last=Kolata|first=Gina|date=September 7, 2015|work=The New York Times|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and with higher patient satisfaction,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/18/health/doctors-strive-to-do-less-harm-by-inattentive-care.html|title=Doctors Strive to Do Less Harm by Inattentive Care|date=February 17, 2015|work=The New York Times|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://hbr.org/2014/06/online-reviews-could-help-fix-medicine|title=Online Reviews Could Help Fix Medicine|date=June 3, 2014|work=Harvard Business Review|access-date=2018-04-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://hbr.org/2014/06/engaging-doctors-in-the-health-care-revolution|title=Engaging Doctors in the Health Care Revolution|date=June 1, 2014|work=Harvard Business Review|access-date=2018-04-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lee|first=Vivian|date=January 19, 2017|title=Transparency and Trust — Online Patient Reviews of Physicians|journal=New England Journal of Medicine|volume=376|issue=3|pages=197–199|doi=10.1056/NEJMp1610136|issn=0028-4793|pmid=28099823}}</ref> as well as successful strategies of faculty development and mentorship.<ref>Byington C, Keenan H, Phillips JD, Childs R, Wachs E, Berzins MA, Clark K, Torres MK, Abramson J, Lee VS, Clark EB. A matrix mentoring model effectively supports clinical and translational scientists and increases inclusion in biomedical research. Acad Med. 2016; 91(4):497–502.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Byington | first1 = CL | last2 = Lee | first2 = VS | year = 2015 | title = Addressing disparities in academic medicine moving forward | journal = JAMA | volume = 314 | issue = 11| pages = 1139–1141 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2015.10664 | pmid = 26372582 }}</ref> In 2012, the University of Utah become the first health system in the country to post patient reviews online.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://hbr.org/2014/06/online-reviews-could-help-fix-medicine|title=Online Reviews Could Help Fix Medicine|date=June 3, 2014|journal=Harvard Business Review|access-date=July 16, 2018|last1=Lee|first1=Thomas H.}}</ref>

In 2016, University of Utah was ranked first among university hospitals in quality and safety,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://newsroom.vizientinc.com/press-release/vizient/vizient-inc-presents-bernard-birnbaum-md-quality-leadership-award-27-top-perfo|title=Vizient, Inc. Presents the Bernard A. Birnbaum, MD, Quality Leadership Award to 27 Top-performing Academic Medical Centers and Community Hospitals|website=newsroom.vizientinc.com|language=en|access-date=2018-04-19}}</ref> with NYU Langone and Mayo Clinic rounding out the top three. That year marked the 7th consecutive year that the University of Utah was ranked in the top 10 in quality in the nation. The university's health insurance plan acquired a commercial license, grew five-fold, and was successful in the individual exchange. Improved financial performance of the clinical enterprise enabled increased support and growth of education, research, and community service initiatives.

As dean, Lee led the significant expansion of the school of medicine class size from 82 to 125 students per year with increased ongoing state funding.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ksl.com/?sid=36226587&nid=148|title=First expanded class of medical students welcomed to U of U |website=KSL.com|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en}}</ref> A number of significant philanthropic commitments were made during her tenure, including the establishment of a new Rehabilitation Hospital,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.deseret.com/2017/11/2/20635716/u-health-officials-celebrate-new-rehabilitation-center/|title=U. health officials celebrate new rehabilitation center|last=Stilson|first=Ashley|date=November 1, 2017|work=DeseretNews.com|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en}}</ref> funding for a number of research initiatives including the Utah Genome Project,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2017/06/mormon-genetic-testing/530781/|title=What Mormon Family Trees Tell Us About Cancer|last=Zhang|first=Sarah|work=The Atlantic|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en-US}}</ref> the Center for Medical Innovation,<ref>{{Cite press release|url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/university-of-utah-center-for-medical-innovations-bench-to-bedside-program-completes-7th-year-with-presentation-of-39-new-medical-technologies-300452233.html|title=University of Utah Center for Medical Innovation's Bench to Bedside Program Completes 7th Year with Presentation of 39 New Medical Technologies|last=Innovation|first=University of Utah, Center for Medical|website=Prnewswire.com|language=en|access-date=2018-04-19}}</ref> and Driving Out Diabetes: A Larry H. Miller Family Foundation Wellness Initiative,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/health/2017/11/13/miller-family-donates-53m-to-uofu-hospital-to-fight-diabetes/|title=Miller Family donates $5.3M to UofU Hospital to fight diabetes|work=The Salt Lake Tribune|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en-US}}</ref> as well as both private and state funding for a new School of Medicine building.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.deseret.com/2017/1/22/20604552/2017-legislature-preview-new-u-med-school-funds-for-growth-top-higher-education-needs-officials-say/|title=2017 Legislature preview: New U. med school, funds for growth top higher education needs, officials say|last=Cortez|first=Marjorie|date=January 22, 2017|work=DeseretNews.com|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en}}</ref> During her tenure, the University of Utah's health sciences budget grew 50 percent to over $3.5&nbsp;billion.

====Huntsman Cancer Institute controversy====
	
Lee became embroiled in a public controversy when University leadership fired Huntsman Cancer Institute CEO, [[Mary Beckerle]], on April 17, 2017. Lee and university leadership were publicly criticized for the move by HCI's founder and prime benefactor, billionaire philanthropist [[Jon Huntsman, Sr.]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ksl.com/?sid=43916078&nid=148|title=Huntsman Sr. blasts the U. for firing of Cancer Institute director, says there is 'no excuse' for it |website=KSL.com|access-date=2017-04-19|language=en}}</ref> The decision prompted public protests by University of Utah faculty and staff,<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/top-researchers-departure-prompts-faculty-protest-at-u-of-utah-institute/117835|title=Top Researcher's Departure Prompts Faculty Protest at U. of Utah Institute|website=Chronicle.com|access-date=2017-04-20|language=en}}</ref> including an online petition calling for University leadership to reverse the decision and reinstate Beckerle.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.sciencemag.org/news/2017/04/power-struggle-erupts-utah-cancer-institute-over-director-s-firing|title= Power struggle erupts at Utah cancer institute over director's firing |website=Sciencemag.org|access-date=2017-04-20|language=en}}</ref> Jon Huntsman, Sr., publicly called for Lee and University President [[David W. Pershing]] to be fired from their leadership positions on April 21, 2017,<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://fox13now.com/2017/04/21/jon-huntsman-sr-weighs-in-as-protests-continue-over-firing-of-ceo-at-huntsman-cancer-institute/|title=Jon Huntsman Sr. weighs in as protests continue over firing of CEO at Huntsman Cancer Institute |website=Fox13now.com|access-date=2017-04-22|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sltrib.com/home/5203352-155/huntsman-calls-top-u-administrators-inept/|title=Huntsman calls for 'inept' U. administrators to be fired over cancer institute CEO's termination|website=Sltrib.com|access-date=2017-04-22|language=en}}</ref> questioning their ethics and predicting that the governor and state legislature would become involved to ensure their removal.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://cancerletter.com/articles/20170421_2/|title=Conversation with Cancer Letter|website=Cancerletter.com|access-date=2017-04-22|language=en}}{{subscription required}}</ref> On April 22, 2017, the Editorial Board of the ''Salt Lake Tribune'' (a newspaper owned by a member of the Huntsman family) called for Lee's removal as the "only remedy in this case."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sltrib.com/opinion/5195473-155/tribune-editorial-it-is-time-for/|title=Tribune Editorial: It is time for new leadership at the University of Utah and its Health Sciences colleges |website=Sltrib.com|access-date=2017-04-22|language=en}}</ref> The University Board of Trustees met with Pershing and Lee on April 25, 2017.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://kuer.org/post/university-shifts-course-reinstating-head-huntsman-cancer-institute#stream/0|title= University Shifts Course, Reinstating Head Of Huntsman Cancer Institute |website=Kuer.org|access-date=2017-04-25|language=en}}</ref> Within hours after the meeting, Pershing released a written statement announcing that Beckerle was immediately resuming her service as CEO and Director of Huntsman Cancer Institute and would report directly to the President of the University.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.sciencemag.org/news/2017/04/cancer-institute-reinstates-director-after-uproar-staff-and-funder|title= Cancer institute reinstates director after uproar from staff and funder |website=Sciencemag.org|access-date=2017-04-25|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/after-a-week-of-protest-u-of-utah-cancer-researcher-is-reinstated/117973|title= After a Week of Protest, U. of Utah Cancer Researcher Is Reinstated |website=Chronicle.com|access-date=2017-04-25|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.statnews.com/2017/04/25/protests-cancer-institute-director/|title= After protests, a fired cancer center director gets her job back |website=Statnews.com|access-date=2017-04-25|language=en}}</ref> Pershing's announcement signaled that Lee would no longer oversee the Huntsman Cancer Institute, raising questions about the future direction of the University Health system.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865678610/What-now-Rift-exposes-tensions-in-University-of-Utah-health-care-system.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426062815/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865678610/What-now-Rift-exposes-tensions-in-University-of-Utah-health-care-system.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2017|title= What now? Rift exposes tensions in University of Utah health care system |website=Deseretnews.com|access-date=2017-04-26|language=en}}</ref>
	
Huntsman stated that a planned donation of $250M dollars would have been withheld unless the university's decision was reversed and Beckerle reinstated. On 28 April, Lee announced via email that, effective the same day, she was stepping down as the university's senior vice president for health sciences, dean of the medical school, and CEO of the healthcare system.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/5231822-155/u-health-care-ceo-vivian-lee|title=U. Health Care CEO Vivian Lee resigns after cancer institute controversy|website=Sltrib.com|accessdate=16 July 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ksl.com/?sid=44043827&nid=148&title=dr-vivian-lee-resigns-post-at-u-health-care-|title=Dr. Vivian Lee resigns post at University of Utah - KSL.com|website=Ksl.com|accessdate=16 July 2018}}</ref>
	
After her resignation, local reporters at the ''Deseret News'' discovered more details about the dispute over finances with Huntsman Cancer Institute, including demands for substantial increases in financial transfers from the University to the Huntsman Cancer Institute. <ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865679041/The-inside-story-Power-and-money-at-center-of-U-controversy.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170502073448/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865679041/The-inside-story-Power-and-money-at-center-of-U-controversy.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 2, 2017|title=The inside story: Power and money at center of U. controversy |website=Deseretnews.com|access-date=2017-05-06|language=en}}</ref>

=== Verily Health Platforms ===
From 2018 to 2022, Lee served as President of Health Platforms at Verily, an Alphabet company. As the founding leader of health platforms, she helped to launch and grow several new successful businesses in areas of digital health, precision risk insurance, healthcare analytics, mental and behavioral health, and pandemic management, with substantial year-over-year growth during her tenure. She announced her departure at the end of 2022 to move to Harvard University to focus on the intersection of tech, climate change and health care, with the aim of building more resilient systems for the future.

==Awards and recognition==
In her academic career Lee was awarded a [[Rhodes Scholarship]] to study at [[Balliol College, Oxford]], and was recognized as one of Crain's "40 Under 40." In 2009, she received the Chang-Lin Tien Leadership award.<ref>{{cite web|last=Education Leadership Award|first=Chang-Lin Tien|title=Vivian Lee|url=http://asianpacificfund.org/award-recipient/2009-dr-vivian-s-lee/|access-date=2017-03-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626190157/http://asianpacificfund.org/award-recipient/2009-dr-vivian-s-lee/|archive-date=2015-06-26|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was elected to the American Society of Clinical Investigation in 2015 and to the [[National Academy of Medicine]] in October 2015.<ref>[https://nam.edu/nam-elects-80-new-members/ "NAM Elects 80 New Members"], ''[[National Academy of Medicine]]'', October 19, 2015. Retrieved on March 14, 2017.</ref> In 2019 she received the gold medal, the highest award from the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine. Modern Healthcare listed her among the 100 Most Influential People in Healthcare, ranking her at No. 11.

{{Main|2009 flu pandemic}}

[[File:H1N1 map by confirmed community outbreaks.svg|upright=1.35|thumb|Community outbreaks, June 2009]]
[[File:H1N1 June 3 2009 USA.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Confirmed cases by [[U.S. state]], June 3, 2009]]

This article covers the chronology of the 2009 novel influenza A ([[H1N1]]) pandemic.<ref name="cdc.gov">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/ |title=CDC 2009 H1N1 Flu |author=<!--not specified--> |date=11 August 2010 |website=cdc.gov |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] |access-date=20 June 2013 |archive-date=10 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090910132855/http://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  Flag icons denote the first announcements of confirmed cases by the respective nation-states, their first deaths (and other major events such as their first intergenerational cases, cases of [[zoonosis]], and the start of national vaccination campaigns), and relevant sessions and announcements of the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO), the [[European Union]] (and its agency the [[European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control]]),
and the U.S. [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control]] (CDC).

Unless otherwise noted, references to terms like S-OIV, H1N1 and such, all refer to this new A(H1N1) strain and not to sundry other strains of H1N1 which are endemic in humans, birds and pigs.

{{TOC limit|limit=3}}

==Timeline==
Take note that the date of the first confirmations of the disease or any event in a country may be before or after the date of the events in local time because of the [[International Dateline]].

[[File:CDC MMWR M8d0430a2f.png|upright=1.35|thumb|Probable and confirmed Mexican cases by date of illness onset, March 15 – April 26. —CDC]]

===March 2009===

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
In [[La Gloria, Veracruz]] 60% of the town's population is sickened by a [[Acute respiratory infection|respiratory illness]] of unknown provenance. The government of Mexico believes it to be caused by [[H3N2]] influenza, though at least one patient in La Gloria tested positive for A/H1N1. Two babies died in the outbreak but both were buried without testing.<ref name='Guardian Tuckman 04-27-09'>{{cite news|first=Jo|last=Tuckman|title=Four-year-old could hold key in search for source of swine flu outbreak|date=2009-04-27|work=[[The Guardian]]|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/apr/27/swine-flu-search-outbreak-source|location=London|access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->|archive-date=2009-04-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430094704/http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2009/apr/27/swine-flu-search-outbreak-source|url-status=live}}</ref>

====March 7====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' In the ninth week of its routine influenza surveillance, the CDC reports on FluView that thirty-five states have reported widespread influenza activity, and 14 states have reported regional activity, but that although the rate of activity was high, that the proportion of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza (P&I) was below the epidemic threshold.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly09.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 09, 2008-2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170706233133/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly09.htm |date=2017-07-06 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====March 14====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' The CDC reports on the 10th week of FluView that thirty states reported widespread influenza activity and 18 states reported regional activity.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly10.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 10, 2008-2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170618223004/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly10.htm |date=2017-06-18 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====March 17====
{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
Earliest known onset of a case that is later to be confirmed as Swine-Origin Influenza A (H1N1) Virus Infection.<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2">{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm58d0430a2.htm |title=Outbreak of Swine-Origin Influenza A (H1N1) Virus Infection --- Mexico, March--April 2009 |date=2009-04-30 |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |work=[[Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090909002833/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm58d0430a2.htm |archive-date=2009-09-09 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=ProjectDisaster ' Blog Archive ' Mexico & H1N1 |url=http://projectdisaster.com/?p=13947 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715120719/http://projectdisaster.com/?p=13947 |archive-date=2011-07-15 |url-status=dead |access-date=2009-06-18 }}</ref>

====March 21====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' CDC FluView, Week 11: Widespread influenza activity in twenty-four states; regional activity in 19. Influenza activity continues to decrease.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly11.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 11, 2008-2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170618223002/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly11.htm |date=2017-06-18 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====March 28====
