====March 30====

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
A sample is collected from a nine-year-old female patient which is later confirmed to contain the novel virus strain (genetically sequenced as A/California/05/2009(H1N1)).<ref name="NCBI-20090502-Flu">{{cite web|url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/FLU/SwineFlu.html |title=GenBank sequences from 2009 H1N1 influenza outbreak |date=2009-05-01 |work=Influenza Virus Resource |publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430165147/http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/FLU/SwineFlu.html |archive-date=2009-04-30 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/FJ966955 |title=Influenza A virus (A/California/05/2009(H1N1)) segment 1 polymerase PB2 (PB2) gene, complete cds |publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] |access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot--> |date=June 2009 |archive-date=30 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170930040852/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/FJ966955 |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
Onset of illness for a ten-year-old boy residing in [[San Diego County, California]]; his case is eventually the first to be confirmed as swine flu in the US.<ref name="MMWR5815a5" />

===April 2009===

====April 1====

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
A [[nasopharynx|nasopharyngeal]] swab is collected from a ten-year-old male patient in San Diego County, later confirmed as containing the novel virus and the first organism of that strain to be completely [[Full genome sequencing|sequenced]] (A/California/04/2009(H1N1)).<ref name="MMWR5815a5" /><ref name="NCBI-20090502-Flu" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/FJ966079 |title=Influenza A virus (A/California/04/2009(H1N1)) segment 1 polymerase PB2 (PB2) gene, complete cds |publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] |access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot--> |date=June 2009 |archive-date=27 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170327081105/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/FJ966079 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====April 2====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
In [[La Gloria, Veracruz]], a four-year-old boy falls ill at the end of the outbreak. Only his sample, which was eventually sent abroad, tested positive for A(H1N1). Veracruz officials state that there were no plans to exhume the bodies of two infants who died in the outbreak.<ref name="Guardian Tuckman 04-27-09" />

====April 4====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' CDC FluView, Week 13: Widespread influenza activity in four states, regional activity in 18.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly13.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 12, 2008–2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170618222957/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly13.htm |date=2017-06-18 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====April 5====
{{flagicon|EU}} '''European Union'''
The media monitoring website MedISys reports on a Mexican article about the epidemiological alert.<ref name="MED-20090405-Jrc">{{cite news |url=http://medusa.jrc.it/medisys/dynamic?language=all&page=1&edition=searchresults&option=&category=&articleType=all&foralert=Diarrhoea&forsource=&duplicates=false&querytype=simple&atLeast=Alerta+epidemiol%F3gica+en+Perote+por+brote+de+males+respiratorios |title=First article on novel influenza reported by MedISys |last=MedISys |first=EC |date=2008-04-05 |publisher=EC |access-date=2 August 2010 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. [https://www.webcitation.org/5jhQjJqow?url=https://webcitation.org/5jhQjJqow?url=http://medusa.jrc.it/medisys/dynamic?language=all&page=1&edition=searchresults&option=&category=&articleType=all&foralert=Diarrhoea&forsource=&duplicates=false&querytype=simple&atLeast=Alerta+epidemiol%F3gica+en+Perote+por+brote+de+males+respiratorios Archived] 2009-09-10.</ref><ref name="MED-20090405-Jor">{{cite news|url=http://www.jornada.unam.mx/2009/04/05/index.php?section=estados&article=025n1est&partner=rss|title=Alerta epidemiológica en Perote por brote de males respiratorios|last=Jornada|first=La|date=2008-04-05|publisher=LaJornada|access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->|archive-date=2017-08-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810092318/http://www.jornada.unam.mx/2009/04/05/index.php?section=estados&article=025n1est&partner=rss|url-status=live}}</ref>

====April 6====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
Public health authorities begin investigating unusual cases of [[pneumonia]].<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/29/AR2009042904911.html |title=Reporting Health Threats: System Set Up After SARS Epidemic Was Slow to Alert Global Authorities |last=Brown |first=David |date=2009-04-30 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090507163851/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/29/AR2009042904911.html |archive-date=2009-05-07 |url-status=live }}</ref> 400 people had reportedly sought treatment for pneumonia/[[influenza-like illness]] (ILI) in La Gloria the preceding week.<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" />

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
Biosurveillance firm [[Veratect Corporation|Veratect]] reports the unusual respiratory illness in Mexico.<ref name="McC-20090430-Blu">{{cite news|url=http://www.mcclatchydc.com/2009/04/30/67283/company-warned-officials-of-flu.html|title=Company warned officials of flu 18 days before alert was issued|last=Blumenthal|first=Les|date=2009-05-01|publisher=McClatchy Newspapers|access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140423085700/http://www.mcclatchydc.com/2009/04/30/67283/company-warned-officials-of-flu.html|archive-date=23 April 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://veratect.com/media/042609_release.pdf |title=Veratect the Company to First Sound Alarm on Swine Influenza Makes Data on the Spread of this Disease Public |date=2009-04-27 |work=Corporate press release |publisher=Veratect Inc |access-date=2 August 2010  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090521005845/http://veratect.com/media/042609_release.pdf |archive-date=21 May 2009 |url-status=usurped }}</ref> Veratect publishes the alert "La Gloria: 'Strange' Respiratory Affects 60% of Local Population; Three Pediatric Deaths May be Associated with the Outbreak."<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" /><ref name="McC-20090430-Blu" />

====April 11====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' CDC FluView, Week 14: Widespread influenza activity in one state; regional activity in 14.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly14.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 12, 2008-2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170618222955/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly14.htm |date=2017-06-18 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====April 12====
{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
The [[General Directorate of Epidemiology]] (DGE) reports the outbreak of an ILI in a small community in Veracruz to the '''[[Pan American Health Organization]]''' ('''PAHO'''), which is the Regional Office of the '''[[World Health Organization]]''' ('''WHO''').<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Outbreak of Swine-Origin Influenza A (H1N1) Virus Infection --- Mexico, March--April 2009 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm58d0430a2.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090909002833/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm58d0430a2.htm |archive-date=2009-09-09 |url-status=live }}</ref> Furthermore, a 39-year-old woman dies of severe [[viral pneumonia]] in the city of [[San Luis Potosí, San Luis Potosí|San Luis Potosí]]; this is later believed to be the earliest known fatality related to the outbreak.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/25/AR2009042501335.html |title=U.S. Slow to Learn of Mexico Flu: Canadian Officials Knew of Rare Strain Before Americans Did |last=Brown |first=David |date=2009-04-26 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |quote=The earliest case found in Mexico was a 39-year-old woman who died April 12 of severe viral pneumonia in San Luis Potosi, a city of about 700,000 in central Mexico. "That attracted the attention of the epidemiologist there," said Mauricio Hernández, deputy minister for disease prevention and health promotion in Mexico's Federal Department of Health |access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot--> |archive-date=2019-01-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190118101621/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/04/25/AR2009042501335.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

====April 13====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
First death in [[Oaxaca]] due to what would later be identified as swine flu.<ref>{{cite news|last=Orsi |first=Peter |url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5gfYcVCw5PiKbk5yaX7JaF9NqhPygD97R0QOO0 |title=Mexico says suspected swine flu deaths now at 149 |agency=Associated Press |work=Google News |date=2009-04-27 |archive-date=2009-04-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429184039/http://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5gfYcVCw5PiKbk5yaX7JaF9NqhPygD97R0QOO0 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
The U.S. [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control]] (CDC) is advised of a ten-year-old boy with a respiratory illness in San Diego County, California. Test results revealed an [[Influenza A virus]] but were negative for standard human strains. The San Diego County [[Health departments in the United States|Health Department]] is notified.<ref name="MMWR5815a5" />

====April 14====
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
The CDC receives its first sample from California (from the ten-year-old boy in San Diego County), and identifies the virus as a strain of swine influenza A(H1N1).<ref name="MMWR5815a5" />

====April 16====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
Authorities notify the '''PAHO''' of the [[atypical pneumonia]].<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" />

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
Veratect publishes the alert "Atypical Pneumonia Cases Reported at Hospital" regarding the Oaxaca cases.<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" /><ref name="McC-20090430-Blu" />

====April 17====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
A case of atypical pneumonia in Oaxaca prompts enhanced national surveillance. A field investigation is started.<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" />
Mexico contacts '''Canada''' to request more specialized testing.<ref name="PHAC-20090424-Adv">{{cite web |url=http://www.phac-aspc.gc.ca/alert-alerte/h1n1/sn_swine-eng.php?option=print |title=Human Swine Influenza Outbreak. Message from the Minister of Health and the Chief Public Health Officer on Human Swine Flu |date=2009-04-24 |work=Advisories |publisher=[[Public Health Agency of Canada]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429084559/http://www.phac-aspc.gc.ca/alert-alerte/h1n1/sn_swine-eng.php |archive-date=2009-04-29 |url-status=dead |access-date=2009-05-02 }}</ref>

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
The CDC receives a second sample from Southern California (taken from the nine-year-old girl in Imperial County), and again identifies the virus as a strain of swine influenza A(H1N1). The [[California Department of Public Health]] is notified.<ref name="MMWR5815a5" />

====April 18====
{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
Mexico sends 14 mucus samples to the CDC and dispatches health teams hospitals to look for patients showing severe influenza- or pneumonia-like symptoms.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://komonews.com/news/local/us-mexico-battle-deadly-flu-outbreak-11-21-2015 |title=U.S., Mexico battle deadly flu outbreak |last=Stevenson |first=Mark |agency=[[Associated Press|AP]] |date=2009-04-26 |work=KomoNews.com |publisher=Fisher Communications, Inc. |access-date=22 July 2016 <!--DASHBot--> |archive-date=2016-08-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817090345/http://komonews.com/news/local/us-mexico-battle-deadly-flu-outbreak-11-21-2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' CDC FluView, Week 15: "Nine states reported regional activity; 17 states reported local influenza activity; the District of Columbia and 22 states reported sporadic influenza activity; and two states reported no influenza activity. Seven human infections with swine influenza A (H1N1) virus have been confirmed." This is the first mention of A(H1N1) in FluView.<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly15.htm CDC - Influenza (Flu)|Weekly Report: Influenza Summary Update Week 15, 2008-2009 Season] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170618222954/https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2008-2009/weekly15.htm |date=2017-06-18 }}. Cdc.gov</ref>

====April 20====

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
Veratect advises the CDC of the Mexican events.<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" /><ref name="McC-20090430-Blu" />
The CDC is already investigating the California and [[Texas]] cases.<ref name="WP-20090430-Brown" /><ref name="McC-20090430-Blu" /><ref name="AP-20090430-Stobbe">{{cite news

====April 21====

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
The CDC alerts physicians to a similar novel strain of swine influenza A(H1N1) in two cases from Southern California in a [[Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report]] Early Release on its website.<ref name="autogenerated2">[https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5815a5.htm Swine Influenza A (H1N1) Infection in Two Children - Southern California, March-April 2009] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091001131355/http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5815a5.htm |date=2009-10-01 }}. Cdc.gov</ref> Local investigations, including investigations in Texas, are already underway, and overall surveillance is enhanced.<ref name="MMWR5815a5" /><ref>{{cite journal |author=((Novel Swine-Origin Influenza A (H1N1) Virus Investigation Team; Dawood FS, Jain S, Finelli L, Shaw MW, Lindstrom S, Garten RJ, Gubareva LV, Xu X, Bridges CB, Uyeki TM)) |title=Emergence of a novel swine-origin influenza A (H1N1) virus in humans |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=360 |issue=25 |pages=2605–15 |year=2009 |pmid=19423869 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa0903810|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Associated Press|The Associated Press]] covers the alert, the first mention of the A(H1N1) outbreak in English-language news media.<ref name="AP-20090430-Stobbe" /><ref>

====April 22====

{{flagicon|Canada}} '''Canada'''
Canada receives the samples from Mexico for testing.<ref name="PHAC-20090424-Adv" />

====April 23====

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
The [[Public Health Agency of Canada|Public Health Agency of '''Canada''']] confirms Mexico cases of swine-origin influenza A (H1N1) virus (S-OIV) infection.<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" />
Genetic sequence analysis reveals that the Mexican patients were infected with the same S-OIV strain detected in two California children.<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" />
The '''PAHO''' is informed that a cluster in Mexico of severe respiratory illnesses has been laboratory-confirmed as S-OIV infection.<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" />

====April 24====

{{flagicon|WHO}}The '''WHO''' issues its first Disease Outbreak Notice on the matter, confirming the infection of a number of people in Mexico and the United States by "Swine Influenza A/H1N1 viruses... not... previously detected in pigs or humans".<ref name="who_don_2009-04-24">{{cite web|url=https://www.who.int/csr/don/2009_04_24/en/index.html |title=(Update 1) Influenza-Like Illness in the United States and Mexico |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |date=2009-04-24 |access-date=2 August 2010  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628210557/http://www.who.int/csr/don/2009_04_24/en/index.html |archive-date=28 June 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

{{flagicon|Mexico}} '''Mexico'''
The [[Secretary of Health (Mexico)|Minister of Health]] confirms the Mexican cases of human infection by swine influenza and states that it believes that some of these cases had resulted in death.<ref name="CDC-20090424-Brief" />
Health authorities implement public health measures for all airport passengers and the vaccination of health care workers with [[Flu season|seasonal]] [[influenza vaccine]].<ref name="MMWR-58d0430a2" />

[[File:Barack Obama being briefed on swine flu oubreak 4-29.jpg|thumb|President Obama is briefed in the Situation Room about the H1N1 outbreak.]]
{{flagicon|US}} '''United States'''
The CDC tells a press conference that seven of the 14 Mexican samples contained the same virus strain as the known in California and Texas, and that indications suggested that containment in the USA was "not very likely".<ref name="CDC-20090424-Brief">{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/media/transcripts/2009/t090424.htm |title=CDC Briefing on Public Health Investigation of Human Cases of Swine Influenza (April 24, 2009) |date=2009-04-24 |work=Press Briefing Transcripts |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) |access-date=2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot--> |archive-date=2012-05-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120509225108/http://www.cdc.gov/media/transcripts/2009/t090424.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>
The novel strain had already been reported on the CDC's [[Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report]] website.<ref name="autogenerated2"/>

====April 25====

{{flagicon|WHO}} '''WHO''' Under the [[International Health Regulations]] (IHR), the Emergency Committee convenes for the first time since its establishment in 2007,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.insidejustice.com/intl/2009/04/30/swine_flu_who_pheic/|title=Inside Justice - Swine Flu: Legal Obligations and Consequences When the World Health Organization Declares a "Public Health Emergency of International Concern"|website=www.insidejustice.com|access-date=2014-05-06|archive-date=2017-09-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170901154600/http://www.insidejustice.com/intl/2009/04/30/swine_flu_who_pheic/|url-status=live}}</ref> resulting in the [[WHO Director-General|'''WHO''' Director-General]] declaring a formal "public health emergency of international concern,"<ref name="WHO-20090425-Chan">{{cite news|url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090425/en/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090428084007/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/statements/2009/h1n1_20090425/en/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 28, 2009 |title=Statement by WHO Director-General, Dr Margaret Chan (25 April 2009): Swine influenza |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |date=2009-04-25 | access-date= 2 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.who.int/csr/don/2009_04_26/en/index.html |title=WHO &#124; Swine flu illness in the United States and Mexico - update 2 |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |date=2009-04-26 |access-date=2 August 2010  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822215512/http://www.who.int/csr/don/2009_04_26/en/index.html |archive-date=22 August 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ([[PHEIC]]),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.who.int/ihr/procedures/pheic/en/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131008225947/http://www.who.int/ihr/procedures/pheic/en/|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 8, 2013|title=WHO - IHR Procedures concerning public health emergencies of international concern (PHEIC)|website=www.who.int}}</ref> the first ever.

Some countries, such as the United States, Brazil and France, have agreed to make 10 percent of their national vaccine stockpile available to developing countries. Manufacturers have also donated about 150 million doses of vaccine.<ref>[http://www.iol.co.za/index.php?set_id=1&click_id=31&art_id=nw20091004233828440C114736 News - Science: UN calls for sharing of flu vaccines] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430180521/http://www.iol.co.za/index.php?set_id=1 |date=2009-04-30 }}. ====November 30====
{{flagicon|USA}} '''United States''' The [[Centers for Disease Control|CDC]] states that H1N1 may have peaked as the number of states reporting widespread influenza dropped from 43 the previous week to 32 this week. Furthermore, influenza-like illness now account for 4.3% of doctor visits, down from 8% four weeks ago (on average, influenza accounts for 2.5% of doctor visits). The proportion of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza continues to be higher than expected for this time of year, however. This proportion has remained elevated for eight weeks now.<ref name="ReferenceC">[https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/update.htm CDC H1N1 Flu|Situation Update]. Cdc.gov</ref>

{{flagicon|US}} '''United States''' A sophisticated [[Bayesian analysis]] of public health data from April to the end of June from New York City and Milwaukee<ref>[http://www.plosmedicine.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1000207 The Severity of Pandemic H1N1 Influenza in the United States, from April to July 2009: A Bayesian Analysis]. {{flagicon|WHO}} '''WHO''' In Geneva Dr. [[Margaret Chan]], Director-General of the WHO, remarks in the context of the [[H5N1]] bird flu virus that "The fact that the long overdue influenza pandemic is so moderate in its impact is probably the best health news of the decade" but that "No, the world is not ready for a pandemic to be caused by H5N1." Given that H1N1 could still mutate, however, the WHO shall continue to monitor the pandemic for six months to a year. She also said that it would take at least two years before a true death total is established. Among children Georgia had the lowest vaccination rate, with 21%; the state currently has the highest level of H1N1 flu activity.<ref>[http://vaccinenewsdaily.com/news/212664-cdc-reports-states-h1n1-flu-inoculation-rates-vary-widely CDC reports states' H1N1 flu inoculation rates vary widely] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100421161350/http://vaccinenewsdaily.com/news/212664-cdc-reports-states-h1n1-flu-inoculation-rates-vary-widely |date=2010-04-21 }}. Vaccine News Daily (2010-03-31)</ref>

This has been the case with the A/ H1N1 influenza pandemic... The virus did not mutate to a more lethal form. Cases of resistance to oseltamivir remained few and isolated. The vaccine closely matched circulating viruses and showed an excellent safety record," Chan said. <!--WP:CREDENTIAL: Academic/professional titles (such as "Doctor" or "Professor") and postnominal degree abbreviations (such as "PhD") should not be used-->'''Claude Robert Cloninger''' (born April 4, 1944) is an American psychiatrist and [[geneticist]] noted for his research on the biological, psychological, social, and spiritual foundation of both mental health and mental illness.<ref name="Who 2009" /><ref name="Highly Cited Researchers 2008">''Highly Cited Researchers''. Claude Robert Cloninger. Version 1.5, ISI Highly Cited.com. Institute for Scientific Information, 2008.</ref><ref name="NYTimes">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/14/science/novelty-seeking-neophilia-can-be-a-predictor-of-well-being.html|title=What's New? Exuberance for Novelty Has Benefits|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|author=John Tierney|date=February 13, 2012|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref><ref name="ChicagoTribune">{{cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1990/02/28/legacy-of-addiction/|title=Legacy Of Addiction|newspaper=Chicago Tribune|author=Tom Siegfried|date=February 28, 1990|access-date=December 16, 2013}}</ref><ref name="STLMag">{{cite web|url=http://www.stlmag.com/St-Louis-Magazine/March-2007/The-Pursuit-of-Happiness/|title=The Pursuit of Happiness|work=[[St. Louis Magazine]]|author=Jeannette Batz Cooperman|date=March 2007|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref> He previously held the Wallace Renard Professorship of Psychiatry, and served as professor of psychology and genetics, as well as director of the Sansone Family Center for Well-Being at [[Washington University in St. Louis]].<ref name="dbbs.wustl.edu">Washington University, Division of Biology & Biomedical Sciences, http://dbbs.wustl.edu</ref><ref name="wuphysicians.wustl.edu">Washington University Physicians, Department of Psychiatry, http://wuphysicians.wustl.edu</ref><ref name="Gothenburg">{{cite web|url=http://psy.gu.se/english/current/news/newsdetail/professor-robert-cloninger---new-honorary-doctor-of-psychology-at-the-university-of-gothenburg..cid1079158|title=Professor Robert Cloninger - new honorary doctor of psychology at the University of Gothenburg|publisher=University of Gothenburg|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref><ref name="WholeLiving">{{cite web|url=http://www.wholeliving.com/185567/going-it|title=Going for It|author=Whitney Joiner|date=October 2012|work=[[Whole Living]]|accessdate=December 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817193724/http://www.wholeliving.com/185567/going-it|archive-date=August 17, 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> Cloninger is a member of the evolutionary, neuroscience, and [[statistical genetics]] programs of the Division of Biology and Biomedical Sciences at Washington University,<ref name="dbbs.wustl.edu" /> and is recognized as an expert clinician in the treatment of general [[psychopathology]], [[substance dependence]], and personality disorders.<ref name="wuphysicians.wustl.edu" /><ref>Hellinga G, van Luyn B, Dalwijk H-J (eds.). ''Personalities: Master Clinicians Confront the Treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder''. Robert Cloninger (biography and interview). Northvale NJ and London: Jason Aronson, 2001, pp. 99-120.</ref> Dr. Cloninger is currently professor emeritus [https://psychiatry.wustl.edu/people/c-robert-cloninger-md-phd/].

Cloninger is known for his research on the genetics, neurobiology, and development of personality and personality disorders.<ref>''Highly Cited Researchers''. Claude Robert Cloninger. Version 1.5, ISI Highly Cited.com. [[Institute for Scientific Information]], 2008.</ref><ref>5.	Hellinga G, van Luyn B, Dalwijk H-J (eds.). ''Personalities: Master clinicians confront the treatment of borderline personality disorder''&nbsp;– Robert Cloninger (biography and interview). Northvale NJ and London: Jason Aronson, 2001, pp. 99-120.</ref><ref name=Inc>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.inc.com/jeff-haden/9-qualities-of-remarkable-entrepreneurs.html|title=9 Qualities of Remarkable Entrepreneurs|magazine=[[Inc. (magazine)|Inc.]]|author=Jeff Haden|date=May 14, 2012|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref><ref name=NYMag>{{cite magazine|url=http://nymag.com/news/features/27840/index3.html|title=How Not to Talk to Your Kids|magazine=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref> He identified and described heritable [[personality traits]] predictive of vulnerability to alcoholism and other mental disorders in prospective studies of adoptees reared apart from their biological parents.<ref name="Cloninger">Cloninger CR, Bohman M, Sigvardsson S. Inheritance of alcohol abuse: cross-fostering analysis of adopted men. ''Archives of General Psychiatry'' 1981; 38:861-869.</ref><ref name="Cloninger_a">Cloninger CR, Bohman M, Sigvardsson S. Childhood personality predicts alcohol abuse in young adults. ''Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research'' 1988; 12:494-505.</ref><ref name="ReferenceA">Cloninger CR, von Knorring A-L, Sigvardsson S, Bohman M. Symptom patterns and causes of somatization in men. ''Genetic Epidemiology'' 1986; 3:171-185.</ref><ref name=Adoption>{{cite web|url=http://encyclopedia.adoption.com/entry/alcohol-abuse-and-adopted-persons/35/1.html|title=Alcohol Abuse And Adopted Persons|publisher=Adoption.com|accessdate=December 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228063443/http://encyclopedia.adoption.com/entry/alcohol-abuse-and-adopted-persons/35/1.html|archive-date=December 28, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Classification>{{cite web|url=http://quizlet.com/12587383/classification-of-alcoholics-typology-theories-flash-cards/|title=Classification of Alcoholics Typology Theories|publisher=Quizlet|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}</ref> Cloninger also carried out the first genome-wide association and linkage study of normal personality traits,<ref>Cloninger CR, van Eerdewegh P, Goate A, et al. Anxiety proneness linked to epistatic loci in genome scan of human personality traits. ''Am J Med Genet'' 1998; 81:313-317.</ref> and has developed two widely used tools for measuring personality: the [[Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire]] (TPQ) and the [[Temperament and Character Inventory]] (TCI).<ref name="ReferenceB">Cloninger CR. A systematic method for clinical description and classification of personality variants. ''Arch Gen Psychiatry'' 1987; 44:573-588.</ref><ref>11.	Cloninger CR, Svrakic DM, Przybeck TR. A psychobiological model of temperament and character. ''Arch Gen Psychiatry'' 1993; 50:975-990.</ref>

In 2004, he published ''Feeling Good: The Science of Well-Being''.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004">Cloninger CR. ''Feeling Good: The Science of Well-Being''. New York: Oxford University Press, 2004.</ref><ref name=Oxford>{{cite book|url=http://global.oup.com/academic/product/feeling-good-9780195051377;jsessionid=1D37A9347A7DD7374FADE210B029A61C?cc=us&lang=en&|title=Feeling Good|publisher=Oxford|accessdate=December 16, 2013|isbn=9780195051377|date=May 6, 2004}}</ref><ref name=BJPsych>{{cite journal|url=http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/186/2/171.1.full|title=Feeling Good: The Science of Well-Being|journal=[[British Journal of Psychiatry]] |volume=186|issue=2|pages=171–172|accessdate=December 16, 2013 |doi=10.1192/bjp.186.2.171|last1=Sims|first1=Andrew|date=February 2005 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Cloninger serves as director of the Anthropedia Institute, the research branch of the Anthropedia Foundation.<ref name=Psychobiology>{{cite web|url=http://psychobiology.wustl.edu/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=62&Itemid=66|title=Anthropedia Foundation|publisher=Washington University in St. Louis|accessdate=December 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228075405/http://psychobiology.wustl.edu/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=62&Itemid=66|archive-date=December 28, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> In collaboration with Anthropedia, he helped develop the ''Know Yourself'' DVD series.<ref name="anthropedia.org">http://anthropedia.org and http://psychobiology.wustl.edu {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604141728/https://anthropedia.org/ |date=June 4, 2023 }}</ref><ref name=Anthropedia>{{cite web|url=http://www.anthropediafoundation.org/site/PageServer?pagename=wwd_knowyourself|title=Know Yourself|publisher=Anthropedia Foundation|accessdate=December 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228030821/http://www.anthropediafoundation.org/site/PageServer?pagename=wwd_knowyourself|archive-date=December 28, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Cloninger has earned lifetime achievement awards from many academic and medical associations, and is a member of the [[Institute of Medicine]] of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Who 2009">''Who's Who in the World 2009''. Claude Robert Cloninger. 26th edition. New Providence, NJ. Marquis Who's Who, 2008.</ref> He has authored or co-authored nine books and more than four hundred and fifty articles, and is a highly cited psychiatrist and psychologist recognized by the [[Institute for Scientific Information]] (ISI).<ref name="Highly Cited Researchers 2008" /> He has served in an editorial capacity on many journals, including ''Behavior Genetics'', ''American Journal of Human Genetics'', ''Archives of General Psychiatry'', ''Comprehensive Psychiatry'',<ref name="Highly Cited Researchers 2008" /><ref name="Who 2009" /> and the [[Mens Sana Monographs]].<ref>[http://www.msmonographs.org/aboutus.asp Hon Int Adv Board Member, Mens Sana Monographs]</ref>

==Education and early research==

Cloninger was born in Beaumont, Texas in 1944.<ref name="Who 2009" /><ref name="Hellinga G 2001, pp. 99-120">Hellinga G, van Luyn B, Dalwijk H-J (eds.). ''Personalities: Master clinicians confront the treatment of borderline personality disorder''. Robert Cloninger (biography and interview). Northvale NJ and London: Jason Aronson, 2001, pp. 99-120.</ref><ref>Biographical report on Cloninger, in Bishop JE, Waldholz M, ''Genome''. New York: Simon & Schuster, 1990, pp. 249-266.</ref> His father Morris Cloninger was a former English teacher and businessman, and his mother Concetta was a former actress who directed the local community theater.<ref name="Who 2009" /><ref name="Hellinga G 2001, pp. 99-120" /> He attended the University of Texas in Austin from 1962 to 1966 in the Plan II Honors program.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Who 2009" /><ref>Hellinga G, van Luyn B, Dalwijk H-J (eds.). ''Personalities: Master clinicians confront the treatment of borderline personality disorder'' Robert Cloninger (biography and interview). Northvale NJ and London: Jason Aronson, 2001, pp. 99-120.</ref> In addition to pre-medical studies, he studied philosophy, cultural anthropology, and psychology for which he received honors.<ref name="Who 2009" />

Cloninger attended a research-intensive medical school at Washington University in St. Louis from 1966 to 1970, and has remained on the faculty there throughout his career.<ref name="Who 2009" /> In addition to regular medical training, he did a research fellowship in preventive medicine and public health. He began research in psychiatry in 1969 under the guidance of [[Samuel Guze]].<ref>Cloninger CR. In Memoriam&nbsp;– Samuel B. Guze: October 18, 1923 – July 19, 2000. ''Am J Med Genet'' 2001; 105:1-3.</ref> Cloninger wanted to understand why [[antisocial personality disorder]], substance dependence, and somatization disorder were so often found together in the same individual and in the same family. This question led to longitudinal studies of people with each of these disorders and then family and adoption studies.<ref name="ReferenceA" /><ref>Cloninger CR, Reich T, Guze SB. The Multifactorial Model of Disease Transmission: III. Familial Relationship between Sociopathy and Hysteria (Briquet's Syndrome). ''Br J Psychiatry'' 1975; 127:23-32.</ref>

In order to better quantify and test hypotheses about the inheritance of psychiatric disorders, he studied [[quantitative genetics]] with Theodore Reich in St. Louis and with Newton Morton and D.C. Rao of the [[Population genetics|Population Genetics]] Lab of the University of Hawaii.<ref>''CR Cloninger&nbsp;– 2003 Lifetime Achievement Award: announcement and biographical citation''. ''Am J Med Genet'' 2004; 126: 128.</ref> During the late 70s, Cloninger worked on modeling complex patterns of inheritance using path analysis to allow for both genetic and cultural inheritance.<ref>Cloninger CR, Rice J, Reich T. Multifactorial inheritance with cultural transmission and assortative mating. II. A general model of combined polygenic and cultural inheritance. ''[[American Journal of Human Genetics]]'' 1979; 31:176-198.</ref> He extended path analysis with the introduction of the "copath" to facilitate the analysis of assortative mating and cultural inheritance.<ref>Cloninger CR. Interpretation of intrinsic and extrinsic structural relations by path analysis: Theory and applications to assortative mating. ''Genetical Research'', Cambridge 1980; 36:122-145.</ref> He worked to develop methods for disentangling genetic, cultural, and other environmental influences on mental disorders until he concluded that such statistical modeling would never convince skeptics or provide precise estimates when biological parents also reared their own children.<ref>Cloninger CR, Rice J, Reich T. Multifactorial inheritance with cultural transmission and assortative mating. III. Family structure and the analysis of separation experiments. ''American Journal of Human Genetics'' 1979; 31:366-388.</ref> His clinical studies of psychiatric disorders also revealed much complexity in the clinical features of mental disorders: people often had multiple overlapping syndromes and changed over time in unpredictable ways.<ref>Maser JD & Cloninger CR (eds). ''Comorbidity of mood and anxiety disorders''. Washington, D.C.: American Psychiatric Press, 1990.</ref> As a result, he shifted his efforts after 1980 to more compelling experimental designs, such as adoption and linkage studies.

==Work==
===Stockholm adoption study===

The answer to the need for better data about separation experiments came in the form of a long-term collaboration between Cloninger and Michael Bohman, the head of child psychiatry at the University of Umea in Sweden.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://psychobiology.wustl.edu/ |title=Center for Well-Being |publisher=Psychobiology.wustl.edu |date= |accessdate=2012-04-18 |archive-date=June 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604141728/https://anthropedia.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Bohman had read some of Cloninger's papers on the analysis of separation experiments and asked for Cloninger's assistance in his own research. For several years, Bohman had been studying the behavior of a large birth cohort of children born in Stockholm. The children had been separated from their biological parents at birth and reared in adopted homes.<ref name=Adoption/><ref name=Classification/> Extensive data about alcohol abuse, criminality, and physical and mental complaints to physicians were available in Sweden as a result of the extensive health and social records for all people in the country.<ref name=Adoption/><ref name=Classification/> Cloninger developed methods for what he called a "cross-fostering" analysis. Information about the genetic background of adoptees was measured by data about their biological parents.<ref name=Adoption/><ref name=Classification/> Information about their rearing environment was measured by data about their adoptive parents and home environment.<ref name=Adoption/><ref name=Classification/> This permitted study of the independent contributions of the genetic and environmental backgrounds independently and in combination in a sample of thousands of adoptees.<ref name=Adoption/> Their first joint paper on a cross-fostering analysis of the inheritance of alcoholism in men<ref name="Cloninger" /> became an ISI Science Citation Classic that convinced most scientists that vulnerability to alcoholism was genetically heritable in part.<ref name="Highly Cited Researchers 2008" /><ref name=Classification/>

Cloninger, Bohman, and Soren Sigvardson distinguished two subtypes of alcoholism that differed in their clinical features and pattern of inheritance: type 1, associated with anxiety proneness and loss of control over alcohol intake after age 25; and type 2, associated with [[impulsivity]] and antisocial behavior before age 25.<ref name="Cloninger" /><ref>Cloninger CR. Neurogenetic adaptive mechanisms in alcoholism. ''Science'' 1987; 236:410-416.</ref> Cloninger proposed that the differences between these two groups of people were explained by personality traits that were observable in childhood, long before any exposure to alcohol.<ref name=Adoption/> He confirmed this by measuring the personality of boys when they were in the fourth grade, about 10 years of age, based on detailed interviews with their teachers and without any knowledge of their drinking status as adults.<ref name="Cloninger_a" /> The personality ratings of Cloninger were based on his tridimensional model of temperament.<ref name="ReferenceB" /> The personality model also helped the team to understand other findings they obtained about the inheritance of criminal behavior, somatization (i.e., many physical complaints), anxiety, and depressive disorders.<ref name="ReferenceA" /> The original findings were later confirmed by a replication study using the same methods conducted in Gothenburg, Sweden.<ref>Sigvardsson S, Bohman M, Cloninger CR. Replication of the Stockholm Adoption Study of alcoholism: Confirmatory cross-fostering analysis. ''Arch Gen Psychiatry'' 1996; 53:681-687.</ref> Overall, these adoption studies provided strong evidence for the contribution of both genetic and environmental influences on vulnerability to alcoholism, somatization, criminality, anxiety, and depressive disorders. Without this research the general public would have never known that both genetic and environmental factors play a role in these conditions.<ref name=Adoption/><ref name=Classification/>

===Temperament and character inventory===

Observations about personality provided Cloninger a practical way to predict vulnerability to mental disorders. In the mid-1980s, he developed a general model of temperament based on genetic, neurobiological, and neuropharmacological data, rather than using factor analysis of behavior or self-reports as has usually been done by personality psychologists.<ref name="ReferenceB" /><ref name="Cloninger_b">Cloninger CR. A unified biosocial theory of personality and its role in the development of anxiety states. ''Psychiatric Developments'' 1986; 4:167-226.</ref> He focused on the structure of learning abilities within the person, as has long been desired by social-cognitive psychologists.<ref name="Cervone">Cervone D. The architecture of personality. ''Psychological Reviews'' 2004; 111:183-204.</ref> To test the adequacy of his structural model, Cloninger compared his model of development within the individual (i.e., ontogeny) to the evolution of learning abilities in animal phylogeny.<ref>Cloninger CR, Gilligan SB: Neurogenetic mechanisms of learning: a phylogenetic perspective. ''[[Journal of Psychiatric Research]]''. 1987; 21: 457-472.</ref><ref>Cloninger CR. The genetic structure of personality and learning: a phylogenetic model. ''[[Clinical Genetics (journal)|Clinical Genetics]]'' 1994; 46 (1 Spec No): 124-137.</ref> Initially he described three dimensions of temperament that he suggested were independently inherited: [[harm avoidance]] (anxious, pessimistic vs. outgoing, optimistic), [[novelty seeking]] (impulsive, quick-tempered vs. rigid, slow-tempered) and [[reward dependence]] (warm, approval-seeking vs. cold, aloof).<ref name=NYTimes/> These dimensions are measured by using his [[Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire]] (TPQ).<ref name="ReferenceB" /><ref name="Cloninger_b" />

Studies quickly showed that Persistence (persevering, ambitious vs. easily discouraged, underachieving) was a fourth independently inherited temperament dimension with specific brain circuitry, rather than a facet of Reward Dependence.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> These temperament dimensions proved to be a powerful way to distinguish subtypes of personality disorders and vulnerability to a wide range of mental disorders.<ref name=NYTimes/><ref>Svrakic DM, Whitehead C, Przybeck TR, Cloninger CR. Differential diagnosis of personality disorders by the seven factor model of temperament and character. ''Arch Gen Psychiatry'' 1993; 50:991-999.</ref><ref>Cloninger CR (ed). ''Personality and psychopathology''. Washington, D.C.: American Psychiatric Press, 1999.</ref> Cloninger was initially criticized for reducing personality to emotional drives. For example, in his book ''Listening to Prozac'', Peter Kramer called the temperament model of personality "a humanist's nightmare".<ref name="Cloninger_c">Cloninger CR, Svrakic NM, Svrakic DM. Role of personality self-organization in development of mental order and disorder. ''Development and Psychopathology'' 1997; 9:881-906.</ref>

Likewise, Cloninger and his colleague Dragan Svrakic found that temperament alone did not capture the full range of personality. They found that, by itself, temperament could not reveal whether a person was mature or had a personality disorder.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> On average, there were differences in the probability of personality disorder in people with different temperament configurations, but every configuration could be found in people who were mentally healthy as well as in people who had personality disorders.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Cloninger_c" /> Consequently, Cloninger identified a second domain of personality variables, using character traits to measure a person's humanistic and transpersonal style: self-directedness (reliable, purposeful vs. blaming, aimless), cooperativeness (tolerant, helpful vs. prejudiced, revengeful) and self-transcendence (self-forgetful, spiritual vs. self-conscious, materialistic). These character dimensions measure the components of an individual's mental self-government and can strongly measure the presence and severity of personality disorder. Cloninger often cites Immanuel Kant, who defines character as "what people make of themselves intentionally".<ref>Cloninger CR. Temperament and personality. ''Current Opinion in Neurobiology'' 1994; 4:166-173.</ref> Character dimensions have strong relations with recently evolved regions of the brain—such as the frontal, temporal, and parietal neocortex—that regulate learning of facts and propositions.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Kaasinen">Kaasinen V, Maguire EA, Kurki T, et al. Mapping brain structure and personality in late adulthood. ''Neuroimage'' 2005; 24: 315-322.</ref><ref name="Borg J 1969">Borg J, Andree B, Soderstrom H, Farde L. The serotonin system and spiritual experiences. ''Am J Psychiatry'' 2003; 160: 1965-1969.</ref><ref name="Turner RM 1163">Turner RM, Hudson IL, Butler PH, Joyce PR. Brain function and personality in normal males. ''Neuroimage'' 2003; 19:1145-1163.</ref> By contrast, the temperament dimensions have strong relations with the older cortico-striatal and limbic systems that regulate habits and skills.<ref name="Turner RM 1163"/><ref name="Kaasinen V 1351">Kaasinen V, Aalto S, Nagren K, Rinne JO. Insular dopamine D2 receptors and novelty seeking personality in Parkinson's disease. ''Movement Disorders'' 2004; 19: 1348-1351.</ref><ref name="Tomer">Tomer R, Aharon-Peretz J. Novelty Seeking and Harm Avoidance in Parkinson's disease: effects of asymmetric dopamine deficiency. ''J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiat'' 2004; 75:972-975.</ref><ref name="Gusnard">Gusnard DA, Ollinger JM, Shulman GL, Cloninger CR, et al. Persistence and brain circuitry. ''Proc Natl Acad Sci USA'' 2003; 100: 3479-3484.</ref>

These three character dimensions have been found to be as heritable as the four temperament dimensions, each with about 50% heritability in twin studies.<ref name="Gillespie2003">Gillespie NA, Cloninger CR, Heath AC, Martin NG. The genetic and environmental relationship between Cloninger's dimensions of temperament and character. ''Personality and Individual Differences'' 2003; 35:1931-1946.</ref> All seven dimensions of temperament and character have been found to have unique genetic determinants<ref name="Gillespie2003"/> and to be regulated by different brain systems as measured by functional brain imaging.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Kaasinen" /><ref name="Borg J 1969" /><ref name="Turner RM 1163"/><ref name="Kaasinen V 1351"/><ref name="Tomer" /><ref name="Gusnard" /> Each dimension is influenced by complex interaction between many genetic and environmental variables, so personality develops as a complex adaptive system.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> Cloninger's temperament and character inventories have been extensively used in a wide variety of clinical and research purposes, and cited in thousands of peer-reviewed publications.<ref>PubMed listings available at http://psychobiology.wustl.edu {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604141728/https://anthropedia.org/ |date=June 4, 2023 }}</ref> The construction of the inventories on the basis of genetic and neurobiological considerations challenges the traditional statistical assumptions of factor analytically derived inventories,<ref>Cloninger CR. The psychobiological theory of temperament and character: comment on Farmer and Goldberg. ''Psychological Assessment'' 2008; 20:292-304.</ref> which have been targeted by social and cognitive psychologists for many years.<ref name="Cervone" /> Fortunately, in terms of overall statistical information, there is extensive overlap among the TCI and other multidimensional personality inventories, except that other inventories lack the dimension of Self-Transcendence.<ref>Zuckerman M, Cloninger CR. Relationships between Cloninger, Zuckerman, and Eysenck's dimensions of personality. ''Personality and Individual Differences'' 1996; 21: 283-285.</ref><ref>Grucza RA, Goldberg LR. The comparative validity of 11 modern personality inventories: predictions of behavioral acts, informant reports, and clinical indicators. ''J Pers Assess''. 2007; 89: 167-187.</ref>

=== Tobacco Testimony ===
Cloninger was an [[expert witness]] for several [[Tobacco industry|tobacco companies]] during the 1990s. He [[Testimony|testified]] that, by his definition, smoking was [[Tobacco industry playbook|not addictive]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trial testimony of CLAUDE ROBERT CLONINGER, M.D., April 19, 1999, ENGLE v. R.J. REYNOLDS TOBACCO CO. |url=https://www.industrydocuments.ucsf.edu/tobacco/docs/#id=zywg0021 |access-date=2023-01-01 |website=www.industrydocuments.ucsf.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tobacco Dream Team: Experts Who Insist Nicotine Isn't Addictive |url=https://apnews.com/article/5e11991ee5bf4faf852b22b1eeeace1f |access-date=2023-01-01 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}}</ref>

===Self-transcendence===

Self-transcendence refers to the interest people have in searching for something elevated, something beyond their individual existence.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> According to Cloninger's model, self-transcendence can manifest as an intuitive understanding of elevated aspects of humanity, like compassion, ethics, art, and culture.<ref name=STLMag/> Others who experience it may also describe an awareness of a divine presence.<ref name=STLMag/> People scoring high in TCI Self-Transcendence report frequent experiences of boundlessness and inseparability.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Hamer D. 2004">Hamer D. ''The God Gene: How faith is hardwired in our genes''. New York, Doubleday, 2004.</ref><ref name="The Quiz 2004">{{cite magazine |url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,995499,00.html |title=The Quiz: How spiritual are you? |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=October 25, 2004}}</ref> They lose awareness of their separateness when absorbed in what they love to do or when appreciating the wonders and mysteries of life. Cloninger observes that such experiences of self-forgetfulness and transpersonal identification correspond to what Freud called "oceanic feelings",<ref>Freud S. ''Civilization and Its Discontents''. New York, Jonathan Cape and Harrison Smith, 1929.</ref> which is different from intellectual adherence to particular religious dogmas or rituals.<ref name=NYTimes/><ref name=STLMag/> The TCI Self-Transcendence scale is often used as a measure of spirituality.<ref name="Borg J 1969" /><ref name="Hamer D. 2004"/><ref name="The Quiz 2004"/> Cloninger proposed that the psyche is the aspect of a human being that motivates the search for self-transcendence and underlies the human capacities for self-awareness, creativity, and freedom of will.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> As suggested by transpersonal psychologists and other psychiatrists like [[Carl Jung]] and [[Viktor Frankl]], Cloninger has emphasized that self-transcendence is an essential component in the processes of integration and maturation of personality.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> He found that when people who score high on all three character traits are compared to others, they have the highest level of well-being, as measured by presence of positive emotions, absence of negative emotions, satisfaction with life, or virtuous conduct.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> The capacity for love and work have long been recognized as important for well-being, but Cloninger also observed that people need to experience self-transcendence in order to cope well with suffering and to enjoy life's wonders and mysteries fully.<ref name=NYTimes/><ref name=STLMag/>

===''The Science of Well-Being''===
In his book ''Feeling Good: The Science of Well-Being'', Cloninger describes the impetus for his new work:

<blockquote>I think it is important that we bring a scientific basis to psychiatry and psychology at a level that goes beyond the level of description. In order for us to advance systematically, as for instance chemistry and physics have done, we need a specific theory of the person and our nature of being. As a result of that I have tried to work out such a systematic model, and have progressed by stages to more and more inclusive theoretical frameworks. The basic position I have now is that we have to see the whole person as more than a collection of disease states: a person is composed of multiple elements of body, mind, and spirit. Each of these has to be carefully defined and measurable, so that we can avoid fantasy and speculation and have testable models.&nbsp;... What has become increasingly clear to me is that man has a natural integrative tendency that leads to health, and that disease emerges whenever there is a block. Blocks can come from a genetic predisposition that interferes with natural development, from social learning, or from prior experiences that are unique to the individual.<ref>Hellinga G, van Luyn B, Dalwijk H-J (eds.). ''Personalities: Master clinicians confront the treatment of borderline personality disorder''&nbsp;– Robert Cloninger (biography and interview). Northvale NJ and London: Jason Aronson, 2001, pp. 99-120.</ref></blockquote>

Cloninger has also suggested that not only is there a natural integrative tendency, but that "all human beings have spontaneous needs for happiness, self-understanding and love."<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /> He describes practices that improve character development and satisfy these strong basic needs.<ref name=NYTimes/><ref name=STLMag/> Just as people can become stronger in the body through physical exercise, he has found they can become mentally and spiritually healthier with mental and spiritual exercises, including certain meditations that enhance mindfulness and spirituality. He describes examples of such exercises<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="anthropedia.org"/> in detail in a DVD series called ''Know Yourself'', which was developed with the Anthropedia Foundation.<ref name="anthropedia">{{cite web|url=http://anthropedia.org |title=Anthropedia Foundation |publisher=Anthropedia.org |date= |accessdate=2012-04-18}}</ref> The ''Know Yourself'' series is intended for use as well-being coaching or as an adjunct in psychotherapy.<ref name="anthropedia" /><ref name="Cloninger_d">Cloninger CR. The science of well-being: An integrated approach to mental health and its disorders: ''World Psychiatry'' 2006; 5: 71-76.</ref>

The mental exercises described by Cloninger are intended to stimulate character development and self-awareness, thereby fostering a healthy way of living with three sets of goals and values:

Working in the service of others, thereby increasing love and cooperativeness; letting go of fighting and worrying, thereby increasing hope and self-directedness; and growing in awareness, thereby increasing faith and Self-Transcendence.<ref name=NYTimes/> Cloninger's approach combines principles of cognitive-behavioral therapy, person-centered therapy, and [[positive psychology]] with personality assessment and meditative practices that enhance mindfulness and self-awareness of the cognitive schemas that organize and direct our attention and motivation in different situations.<ref name="Cloninger_d" /> His approach differs from other forms of psychotherapy by its emphasis on integration of a person's awareness of their body, thoughts, and psyche. He suggests that the separation of biomedical, psychosocial, and spiritual approaches interferes with the development of well-being, whereas their integration has been shown to reduce drop-out, relapse, and recurrence rates in randomized controlled trials of well-being therapy.<ref name="Cloninger CR. 2004" /><ref name="Cloninger_d" /> Cloninger's integrative approach is intended to synthesize work done in the mental health field, fostering what Juan Mezzich of the World Psychiatric Association has called "psychiatry for the person".<ref>Mezzich J. Psychiatry for the person: Articulating medicine's science and humanism. ''World Psychiatry'' 2007; 6:65-67.</ref> Several studies show that psychotherapy, alone or in combination with medications, can help people with mental disorders recover faster and stay well longer, but that a declining number of psychiatrists are providing psychotherapy to their patients.<ref>{{cite magazine |first=Arline |last=Kaplan |date=November 1, 2008 |url=http://www.psychiatrictimes.com/display/article/10168/1353217 |title=The Decline of Psychotherapy |magazine=[[Psychiatric Times]] |volume=25 |issue=13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081209061954/http://www.psychiatrictimes.com/display/article/10168/1353217 |archive-date=December 9, 2008}}</ref> Cloninger is working with the World Psychiatric Association and the International College of Person-centered Medicine to advance a more integrated approach to mental health and well-being.<ref name="anthropedia.org"/> The [[American Psychiatric Association]] has recognized Cloninger for his contributions to better understanding the biopsychosocial basis of mental health and illness with its 2009 Judd Marmor Award.<ref name=Missouri>{{cite web|url=http://missouri.psych.org/news/Documents/20093rdQuarterNewsletter.pdf|title=Dr. Paul Simon, Independence Center Recognized at Annual Meeting|publisher=Eastern Missouri Psychiatry|accessdate=December 16, 2013|archive-date=December 28, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228003203/http://missouri.psych.org/news/Documents/20093rdQuarterNewsletter.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Genome>{{cite web|url=http://eg.sib.uc.pt/bitstream/10316/8453/1/obra.pdf|title=Genome-Wide Scan in Portuguese Island Families Implicates Multiple Loci in Bipolar Disorder: Fine Mapping Adds Support on Chromosomes 6 and 11|work=[[American Journal of Medical Genetics Part B: Neuropsychiatric Genetics]]|accessdate=December 16, 2013}}{{Dead link|date=October 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

The '''COVID-19 pandemic in India''' is a part of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. [[COVID-19]] is caused by [[SARS-CoV-2]]. As of {{date}}, according to Indian government figures, India has the second-highest number of confirmed cases in the world (after the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|United States]]) with {{COVID-19 data/Text|IN|cases}} reported cases of COVID-19 infection and the third-highest number of COVID-19 deaths (after the United States and [[COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil|Brazil]]) at {{COVID-19 data/Text|IN|deaths}} deaths.<ref name="BBCNews-2021-1">{{#invoke:Cite|news|date=2 May 2021|title=India coronavirus: New record deaths as virus engulfs India|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-56961940|access-date=3 May 2021}}</ref><ref>Multiple sources:

* {{#invoke:Cite|news|last=Yeung|first=Jessie|date=28 April 2021|title=As Covid sweeps India, experts say cases and deaths are going unreported|publisher=CNN|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2021/04/27/india/india-covid-underreporting-intl-hnk-dst/index.html}}
* {{#invoke:Cite|news |last1=Gettleman |first1=Jeffrey |last2=Yasir |first2=Sameer |last3=Kumar |first3=Hari |last4=Raj |first4=Suhasini |last5=Loke |first5=Atul |title=As Covid-19 Devastates India, Deaths Go Undercounted |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/24/world/asia/india-coronavirus-deaths.html |date=24 April 2021 | url-access=limited |issn=0362-4331}}

excess deaths, both directly and indirectly related to COVID-19 to have taken place in India.<ref name="Biswas">{{#invoke:Cite|news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-india-60981318 |title=Why The first cases of COVID-19 in India were reported on 30 January 2020 in three towns of [[Kerala]], among three Indian medical students who had returned from [[Wuhan]], the epicenter of the pandemic.<ref name="Andrews-2020">{{#invoke:Cite|journal |last1= Andrews |first1= MA |last2= Areekal |first2= Binu |last3= Rajesh |first3= KR |last4= Krishnan |first4= Jijith |last5= Suryakala |first5= R |last6= Krishnan |first6= Biju |last7= Muraly |first7= CP |last8= Santhosh |first8= PV |date= May 2020 |title= First confirmed case of COVID-19 infection in India: A case report |url= https://www.ijmr.org.in/article.asp?issn=0971-5916;year=2020;volume=151;issue=5;spage=490;epage=492;aulast=Andrews |journal= Indian Journal of Medical Research |volume= 151 |issue= 5 |pages= 490–492 |doi= 10.4103/ijmr.IJMR_2131_20 |pmid= 32611918 |pmc= 7530459 |access-date= 1 June 2021 |doi-access= free }}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:Cite|news|last1=Narasimhan|first1=T. E.|title=India's first coronavirus case: Kerala student in Wuhan tested positive|url=https://www.business-standard.com/article/current-affairs/india-s-first-coronavirus-case-kerala-student-in-wuhan-tested-positive-120013001782_1.html|work=Business Standard India|date=30 January 2020|access-date=7 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200311040438/https://www.business-standard.com/article/current-affairs/india-s-first-coronavirus-case-kerala-student-in-wuhan-tested-positive-120013001782_1.html|archive-date=11 March 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|date=20 February 2020|title=India's first coronavirus patient discharged after being cured|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/india-s-first-coronavirus-patient-discharged-after-being-cured/story-mjVW4VnSwT9mgYU5V1F4jK.html|access-date=24 July 2021|website=Hindustan Times|language=en}}</ref> Lockdowns were announced in Kerala on 23 March, and in the rest of the country on 25 March. Infection rates started to drop in September.<ref name="Infectiondrop">{{#invoke:Cite|news|title=With very high COVID-19 testing, India's positivity rate fallen below 8%: MoHFW|url=https://m.economictimes.com/news/politics-and-nation/with-very-high-covid-19-testing-indias-positivity-rate-fallen-below-8-mohfw/articleshow/78727824.cms|newspaper=The Economic Times|date=18 October 2020|access-date=19 October 2020}}</ref> Daily cases peaked mid-September with over 90,000 cases reported per-day, dropping to below 15,000 in January 2021.<ref name="Safi-2021" /> A second wave beginning in March 2021 was much more devastating than the first, with shortages of vaccines, hospital beds, [[Gas cylinder|oxygen cylinders]] and other medical supplies in parts of the country.<ref name="Safi-2021">{{#invoke:Cite|news|author=Michael Safi|title=India's shocking surge in Covid cases follows baffling decline|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/apr/21/india-shocking-surge-in-covid-cases-follows-baffling-decline|work=The Guardian|date=21 April 2021|access-date=29 April 2021}}</ref> By late April, India led the world in new and active cases. On 30 April 2021, it became the first country to report over 400,000 new cases in a 24-hour period.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|news|date=30 April 2021|title=Coronavirus {{!}} India becomes first country in the world to report over 4 lakh new cases on 30 April 2021|work=The Hindu|url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/coronavirus-india-becomes-first-country-in-the-world-to-report-over-400000-new-cases-on-april-30-2021/article34453081.ece|access-date=2 May 2021|issn=0971-751X}}</ref><ref name="BBCNews-2021-1" /> Experts stated that the virus ''may'' reach an [[Endemic (epidemiology)|endemic]] stage in India rather than completely disappear;<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|last=Manral|first=Karan|date=9 July 2021|title=When will India be free of Covid-19? Virus will become endemic, says top ICMR official|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/when-will-india-be-free-of-covid-19-virus-may-become-endemic-says-top-icmr-official-101625833444281.html|url-status=live|access-date=25 August 2021|website=Hindustan Times|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709132019/https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/when-will-india-be-free-of-covid-19-virus-may-become-endemic-says-top-icmr-official-101625833444281.html |archive-date=9 July 2021 }}</ref> in late August 2021, [[Soumya Swaminathan]] said India may be in some stage of endemicity where the country learns to live with the virus.<ref name="Bhaduri-2021">{{#invoke:Cite|web|last=Bhaduri|first=Ayshee|date=25 August 2021|editor-last=Goswami|editor-first=Sohini|title=Learning to live with Covid? India may be entering endemic stage, says top doc|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/learning-to-live-with-covid-india-may-be-entering-endemic-stage-says-top-doc-101629875895940.html|url-status=live|access-date=25 August 2021|website=Hindustan Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210825094418/https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/learning-to-live-with-covid-india-may-be-entering-endemic-stage-says-top-doc-101629875895940.html |archive-date=25 August 2021 }}</ref>

India began its [[COVID-19 vaccination in India|vaccination programme]] on 16 January 2021 with [[Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine|AstraZeneca vaccine]] (Covishield) and the indigenous [[Covaxin]].<ref name="MyGov.in-2020">{{#invoke:Cite|web |title=#IndiaFightsCorona COVID-19 |url=https://www.mygov.in/covid-19 |website=MyGov.in |date=16 March 2020 |publisher=Govt of India |access-date=12 June 2021}}</ref><ref>[https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/daily-covid-19-vaccination-doses?tab=chart&country=~IND Daily COVID-19 vaccine doses administered – India], Our World in Data. Retrieved 13 May 2021.</ref> Later, [[Sputnik V vaccine|Sputnik V]] and the [[Moderna COVID-19 vaccine|Moderna vaccine]] was approved for emergency use too.<ref name="Livemint">{{#invoke:Cite|web|website=Livemint|date=29 June 2021|title=Cipla gets nod to import Moderna's vaccine for emergency use in India: Report|url=https://www.livemint.com/companies/news/cipla-gets-nod-to-import-moderna-s-covid-vaccine-for-emergency-use-in-india-11624959964096.html|access-date=29 June 2021|language=en}}</ref> On 30 January 2022, India announced that it administered about 1.7 billion doses of vaccines and more than 720 million people were fully vaccinated.<ref name="UNSDG">{{#invoke:Cite|web | title=United with India: Supporting India's COVID-19 vaccination drive | website=UNSDG | date=2022-05-02 | url=https://unsdg.un.org/latest/stories/united-india-supporting-indias-covid-19-vaccination-drive | access-date=2022-05-08|quote=On January 30, 2022, India announced that 75 percent of its adult population had received two doses of the COVID-19 vaccine, with some 1.7 billion doses of vaccines administered and over 720 million people fully vaccinated in just over a year.}}</ref>

=== 2020 ===
On 12 January 2020, the [[World Health Organization|WHO]] confirmed that a [[novel coronavirus]] was the cause of a respiratory illness in a cluster of people in [[Wuhan|Wuhan, Hubei, China]], which was reported to the WHO on 31 December 2019.<ref name="Reynolds4March2020">{{#invoke:Cite|news |last1=Reynolds |first1=Matt |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/china-coronavirus |title=What is coronavirus and how close is it to becoming a pandemic? |date=4 March 2020 |magazine=Wired UK|access-date=5 March 2020 |issn=1357-0978|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200305104806/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/china-coronavirus|archive-date=5 March 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 30 January 2020, India reported its first case of COVID-19 in [[Thrissur]], Kerala,<ref name="Andrews-2020" /> which rose to three cases by 3 February 2020; all were students returning from Wuhan.<ref name="Raza2020">{{#invoke:Cite|book|last=Kumar|first=K. Reji |editor=Khalid Raza|title=Computational Intelligence Methods in COVID-19: Surveillance, Prevention, Prediction and Diagnosis|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vmsDEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA166|year=2020|publisher=Springer |location=New Delhi|language=English|isbn=978-981-15-8533-3|page=166|chapter=A comparative study of the SIR prediction models and disease control strategies: A case study of the state of Kerala, India}}</ref> Apart from these, no significant rise in transmissions was observed in February. On 4 March 22 new cases were reported, including 14 infected members of an Italian tourist group.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|news|last1=Perappadan|first1=Bindu Shajan|date=4 March 2020|title=COVID-19 {{!}} 6 members of Delhi patient's family test positive for coronavirus|work=The Hindu|url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/Delhi/covid-19-6-members-of-delhi-patients-family-test-positive-for-coronavirus/article30980724.ece|access-date=2 May 2020|issn=0971-751X}}</ref> Transmissions increased over the month after several people with travel history to affected countries, and their contacts, tested positive.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|journal |last1=Laxminarayan |first1=Ramanan |last2=Wahl |first2=Brian |last3=Dudala |first3=Shankar Reddy |last4=Gopal |first4=K. |last5=Mohan B |first5=Chandra |last6=Neelima |first6=S. |last7=Jawahar Reddy |first7=K. S. |last8=Radhakrishnan |first8=J. |last9=Lewnard |first9=Joseph A. |date=2020-11-06 |title=Epidemiology and transmission dynamics of COVID-19 in two Indian states |journal=Science |language=en |volume=370 |issue=6517 |pages=691–697 |doi=10.1126/science.abd7672 |issn=0036-8075 |pmc=7857399 |pmid=33154136|bibcode=2020Sci...370..691L }}</ref> On 12 March, a 76-year-old man, with a travel history to Saudi Arabia, became the first COVID-19 fatality of India.<ref name="death1">{{#invoke:Cite|web |title=India's first coronavirus death is confirmed in Karnataka |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/india-s-first-coronavirus-death-in-karnataka-confirmed/story-2ZJ6IuxJ38EiGndBq5pfHO.html |website=Hindustan Times |date=12 March 2020|access-date=27 March 2020}}</ref>

In July 2020, it was estimated based on antibody tests that at least 57% of the inhabitants of Mumbai's slums may have been infected with COVID-19 at some point.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|author=Hollingsworth|first1=Julia|last2=Mitra|first2=Esha|date=29 July 2020|title=More than half of Mumbai slum residents may have been infected with Covid-19, study suggests|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/29/asia/india-mumbai-slum-coronavirus-intl-hnk/index.html|url-status=live|access-date=23 February 2021|publisher=CNN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729143836/https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/29/asia/india-mumbai-slum-coronavirus-intl-hnk/index.html |archive-date=29 July 2020 }}</ref>

A government panel on COVID-19 stated in October 2020 that the pandemic had peaked in India, and could come under control by February 2021.<ref name="Peak">{{#invoke:Cite|news|author=Preeti Biswas|date=18 October 2020|title=Covid-19 peak over; pandemic can be controlled by February 2021: Govt-appointed panel|newspaper=The Times of India|url=https://m.timesofindia.com/india/no-fresh-lockdowns-recommended-at-local-level-government-appointed-panel-on-covid-19/articleshow/78732643.cms|access-date=19 October 2020}}</ref> This prediction was based on a mathematical simulation referred to as the "Indian Supermodel", assuming that India reaches [[herd immunity]].<ref>Multiple sources:
* {{#invoke:Cite|citation|title=Modelling the spread of SARS-CoV-2 pandemic – Impact of lockdowns & interventions|date=October 2020|periodical=Indian Journal of Medical Research|language=German|doi=10.4103/ijmr.IJMR_4051_20|pmid=33146155|author1=Manindra Agrawal|author2=Madhuri Kanitkar|author3=M. === 2021: Second wave ===

[[File:India & Delhi daily cases wave comparison.png|thumb|478x478px|India's two waves versus Delhi's four waves in the same time period taking into account daily COVID-19 cases]]

cases had fallen to 9,000 per-day.<ref name="Yeung-2021">{{#invoke:Cite|web|last1=Yeung|first1=Jessie|last2=Sud|first2=Vedika|last3=Mitra|first3=Esha|date=5 April 2021|title=India reports new record material for vaccines and ventilators.<ref>Multiple sources:

The number of new cases had begun to steadily drop by late-May; on 25 May, the country reported 195,994 new cases—its lowest daily increase since 13 April. However, the mortality rate has remained high;<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|last=Bhattacharya|first=Amit|date=25 May 2021|title=Coronavirus cases in India: After 40 days, daily Covid cases fall below 2 lakh|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/after-40-days-daily-covid-cases-fall-below-2-lakh/articleshow/82927909.cms|url-status=live|access-date=26 May 2021|website=The Times of India|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210525012757/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/after-40-days-daily-covid-cases-fall-below-2-lakh/articleshow/82927909.cms |archive-date=25 May 2021 }}</ref> by 24 May, India recorded over 300,000 deaths attributed to COVID-19.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|last=Mackintosh|first=Eliza|date=24 May 2021|title=India's Covid deaths top 300,000|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/05/24/world/coronavirus-newsletter-intl-05-24-21/index.html|url-status=live|access-date=24 May 2021|publisher=CNN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210524130844/https://www.cnn.com/2021/05/24/world/coronavirus-newsletter-intl-05-24-21/index.html |archive-date=24 May 2021 }}</ref> Around 100,000 deaths had occurred in the last 26 days, and 50,000 in the last 12.<ref name="Bhattacharya-2021">{{#invoke:Cite|web|last=Bhattacharya|first=Amit|date=24 May 2021|title=India's Covid toll tops 3 lakh, 50,000 deaths in 12 days|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/indias-covid-toll-tops-3-lakh-50000-deaths-in-12-days/articleshow/82892432.cms|url-status=live|access-date=24 May 2021|website=The Times of India|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210523223339/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/indias-covid-toll-tops-3-lakh-50000-deaths-in-12-days/articleshow/82892432.cms |archive-date=23 May 2021 }}</ref> In May 2021, WHO declared that two variants first found in India will be referred to as 'Delta' and 'Kappa'.<ref>{{#invoke:Cite|web|date=31 May 2021|title=COVID Variants Found in India to Be Labelled 'Delta', 'Kappa': WHO|url=https://www.thequint.com/coronavirus/covid-variants-found-in-india-to-be-labelled-delta-and-kappa-who|url-status=live|access-date=6 June
